This game's for fans of turn-based strategy games, Ankama's ealier game Dofus and just for plain MMORPG fun! :)

This game has a pretty unique turn based, tactical gameplay which is actually kind of fun. What makes it tactical is the fact that you might block other players view, you have a limited amount of steps you can take per turn, and stuff like that.
It also has an interesting ecological system in which you can take part. To take part in it you can plant new trees, spawn new enemies, plant crops and of course harvest all this stuff, etc.
BUT if you are looking for something like a "classic" MMORPG with straight questlines you might want to try another game because this game is a pure grinder. Except for the starting zone there are like no quests. All you do is to go from one group of enemies to another. While doing so, do not expect to meet any other players.
All in all, I'd say that this game has a great potential because the tactial fighting system is a lot of fun but there are hardly other players except for the starter city but still there are like a 100 servers. What ruins the game for me is the lack of quests.

In short; DiRT 4 is a more accessible DiRT Rally.
The vehicles are easier to handle at the most difficult simulator settings. This is probably the biggest disappointment for many hardcore rally fans, but despite this, I found them very fun to drive.
Biggest improvements from Rally is the career mode. With the inclusion of sponsors and more in depth financial management, career is rather enjoyable, as opposed to Rally where some might find it a grind to feel any sort of progression.
Another nice addition is "Your stage". Whilst it doesn't make entirely new tracks, it does tweak the predictability of tracks to the point where you cannot rely on muscle memory and rather focus on the pacenotes.

Well, there you have it, a game so smack-bang in the middle of the golden era of videogames that it shows in every single aspect. BioWare knocked it out of the park with MDK 2 and there are so many things done right in this game I can just end this review here and say "go play it, no need to go into details".
...but that's not how I roll, so let's get this over with as quickly as possible so I can go finish this masterpiece. Again.
Graphics wise, yeah, OK, it's not really Crysis since it was made in 2000, but even today the art style and everything else in the visual department ooze style, detail and depth. My favourite part here is that it runs on modern resolutions with no patches, no .ini file tweaking, nothing, just pop into the options, select your poison and off you go, 16:9 aspect ratio and FOV corrected grace.
The sound in this game, OH MY GOD the sound. The music is intense, hardcore stuff and I think some people might be slightly familiar with a man called JESPER freakin' KYD, that went on to do (all the...?) Hitman games, Assassin's Creed, Splinter Cell Chaos Theory (another title well-renowned for its sound design), I think this title is what put him on the map. Stellar music, powerful and appropriate gunshot sounds, even the footsteps and pain noises sound amazing. The voice acting is beyond corny but if you take two looks at this game, I don't know what else the voicework would be but cornylicious.
The story this time around (as opposed to the original MDK) is a bit more fleshed out, nothing too fancy but it's just enough to keep you interested. Aliens invade Earth, Kurt and co. are there to kick their butts and save ours in the process.
Well, what else to touch upon than the gameplay? In MDK 2, you have a rotating lineup of amazing characters: Kurt Hectic returns with his signature sniper and hand-mounted chaingun, only this time around, the movement is butter-smooth, the camera is perfect and the item system is leaps and bounds more intuitive and user-friendly than MDK1. Max, the six-legged canine killing machine is now a playable character, who can wield any combination of 4 guns at a time (yes, it's as cool as it sounds), and so is Dr. Fluke Hawkins, whose playstyle includes a very basic but rewarding crafting-on-the-fly system (ATOMIC. TOAST. That's all I'm saying) and more puzzle oriented gameplay.
And this is by far the biggest strength of MDK 2, right behind the unbelievably smooth controls and wonderful daffy humour and style. It tries to do many things and it does them SO well. The platforming is challenging and precise, but never frustrating and unfair. The shooting is deep, intense, fastpaced and well-balanced. The puzzles are tricky, but not nervewrackingly so. Everything just... works.
If I had to yank some faults out of my backside for this one, I'd have two things to say: once again, sadly, the whole experience is over a bit too quickly, 6-7 hours is not bad, but still short and secondly, why is this game so expensive? I mean, sure, compared to MDK 1, which is easily completed in 3 hours, this game is a bit longer, but it's still a fairly old title and even though it's a classic, I still don't think it's worth 15€, 10€ MAYBE but once again, if it's not on sale, I'd have a hard time recommending it at full price. If it's on sale, then don't even think about it, just go for it, I promise you, no matter what kind of games you like (unless you play RTS games or point-and-click adventures exclusively or something), you will enjoy the living daylights out of this.

this game is a real nostalgia bomb for me - I bought it with my first console: the ps2, in 2001. it's not at all surprising that nobody knows this game because it wasn't a game that had huge publicity, and to top it off, it didn't set any records or new innovations. However, that never stopped it being fun as ♥♥♥♥. the level design in this game, firstly, is awesome. The atmosphere is always brilliant, and at times it gets pretty chilling (or it did when I played it as an eight year old). The character variety and diversity of strategies for such a game is also pretty nice - when you use three characters like this (a sniper, a shooter and a mad scientist) it's difficult to feel like you're doing the same thing over and over. In terms of the story, there isn't a huge amount of depth, but it's not intending to be as gripping as a novel...it's meant to be a simple story with simple characters, within a brilliantly designed, goofy yet serious action adventure game. they definitely don't make games like these any more, and if they tried, they'd be slammed for being too "out there" or experimental. for those interested in playing an old school run and gun arcade-esque game, definitely give this one a go: 8/10 - recommended af. <3

[Note: for those pissy beancounters looking up at my time spent with the game: 1)CONGRATS! You're likely CMANO's detail-oriented potential audience, and 2)I bought this game, full price, for Matrix Games back in the day and played it before I rolled it on to steam.  So roll 2d100 and add the number you get to the hours above.]
Before buying this game, you need to ask yourself: "What do I want from life?"
If your answer is "I want to spend my life on a deep simulation of modern naval combat," you may want to think again.
Do you really want to stare for hours on end at simplistic world maps and icons with no 3D graphics to be found?  Do you really want to babysit all of those icons and marshal them in like wandering cats?  Do you want to dive into nested menus to try to wring some order out of all of the finely-simulated weapons systems at your command?  Losing yourself in the endless minutae of ranges, delivery payloads, radar limitations, AWACS, ToTs, BARCAPs, ASuW vs ASW, CZs, SEAD, and FUBAR?
Really?
You really are a freak.
So, that being said, what you're looking at is the boardgame computer conversion of "Larry Bond's HARPOON"... after 30 years or so of OCD-level study and development by naval grogards the world over.  Seriously.  So there is complexity, lots of complexity.  And a learning curve.  And numbers.  Boy, are there lots of numbers. There was and is already an "official" conversion of HARPOON out there.  CMANO is what you get when that ancient and respected conversion still isn't enough.
But you know, like, this is the real deal.  Distilled modern naval warfare poured into your computer.  And there are many scenarios, from the simple (Israeli vs. Syrian fast attack boats during '73) to the massively mondo (multiple air and land group control scenarios, where I just chuckle and shake my head over).  Plus more community scenarios, like, all the time. CMANO is basically one of those Desert Island Games, if you're any kind of naval grog.
So, recommendation time.  If you're a naval grognard, or were the kind of kid to push cardboard around in Harpoon, Fifth Fleet, or whatever, well yeah, duh, A++++, finest modern naval sim/wargame evar, would buy again.
Otherwise: stay far away.  I'm not trying to sound like an elitist jerk here, but this is not a mainstream or even close to mainstream game.  If you have any doubts, CMANO is $80 not for you.  Track down FLEET COMMAND first and play it.  FC is old, but cheap, and is accessible in ways CMANO doesn't even want to be.  If you like FC and crave even more detail, well, you should know what to do by now.

CMANO is simply the best Modern Air and Naval operations simulator on the market. Its pricy because it literally has every single weapon and platform you can think of from 1945 to the near future. While it isn't easy to get into once you start learning and experiencing it nothing can compare.

Command: Modern Air / Naval Operations is a highly detailed simulator of air, surface and subsurface operations. The scope of gameplay is unrivaled; you can command a single ship or submarine for a few hours all the way through to an entire country or operational theatre for weeks on end.
While there is a bit of a learning curve, part of the fun is learning about modern (and historical) military platforms and operations. There is a very welcoming and helpful community, and in my experience the developers are exceptionally responsive and dedicated--the amount of improvements and additions from when I bought the game (1.02) to now (1.12) is staggering; Lua scripting, improved tanker ops, weapon release authorisation (WRA), doctrine settings, ports and docking operations, enhanced aerodynamic modelling, sonar masking... the list goes on. And these are the free additions that don't require DLC.
CMANO is more expensive than other games on Steam, but when you consider the open, sandbox nature of scenario editing as well as the constant additions to free community content (and developer updates), the price is not such a big deal. In my case I've racked up nearly 2,000 hours, so the price per hour is miniscule compared to other games I've paid less for but gotten bored with after a couple of days or weeks. If the price is a big hurdle, there are also frequent Steam sales.
If you have an interest in air or naval warfare, CMANO will give you hours and hours of entertainment, and you'll learn a lot along the way.

Command Modern Air/Naval Operations is the true definition of a simulation.
It is incredibly in depth and your imagination is the limit when creating scenarios. With Command's extensive database you get access to thousands to units and hundreds of thousands of loadouts for aircraft.
The map offers a clear and easy to customise view. The ability to toggle all aspects on and off help get the experience you want. Whether you want detailed satellite maps via imported files or just a simple wireframe style borders. Or anything inbetween including a great relief layer to help with planning over different terrain types.
The simulation accurately models so many aspects of air and naval combat it is far too long to list here. Suffice to say if you want accuracy at the highest level and a enjoyable, engaging experience; Command Modern Air/Naval Operations is definitely for you.
It offers tutorial scenarios to help anyone new, along with multiple official scenarios and lots of community made ones. The included scenario editor will ensure maximum replayability and help you create or edit the scenario of your choice. For those who want to take it to the next level in scenario design, Commands included Lua capability really unlocks the potential to create anything required.
The UI is clear and simple to use. With lots of context sensitive menus and all the options you need in easy to find locations. It's never been easier to plan and execute your operation. The mission editor allows you to set up automated missions for the AI to cut down on micromanagement if you prefer or you can take control of all aspects of every unit.
The developers are quick to fix any bugs and often release free updates that include fixes, optimisations and best of all free new features.
The community is exceedingly active and welcoming making your Command Modern Air/Naval Operations experience great from the moment you get it.
I would recommend purchasing at the first opportunity and invest in a fantastic product.

There are already a number of great reviews on here regarding this game, so I'll just throw this in there to bolster the game.
I went into this game a bit apprehensive, I had never heard of the team that made this game before and most recent Warhammer games (mainly 40k) in recent history have been very sub-par…
However, I kept in mind that back in the early 90s when I was a kid, the Skaven were my army of choice when playing Warhammer tabletop and after seeing a lot of glowing reviews (Total Biscuit etc) and finding the game at a decent price, I thought stuff it I’ll give it a punt. And I’m glad I did.
The game play really took me back to the days where me and 3 other mates would jump on Left 4 Dead and just have a blast. This game seems to have taken all the good aspects of that and improved on them by adding classes, loot and collectables to improve the chances of getting better loot.
However, that’s not to say that this game doesn’t have faults. I have experienced a number of graphical glitches where instead of heads being severed, the neck will extend with the head giving the character models a kind of crazy giraffe effect.  Clipping issues where I would for whatever reason get stuck in the ground or in a wall resulting in me either having to hope a special unit comes and kills me or I quickly reconnect (no good if I have a grimoire on me).
Speaking of the special units, the 5 that they have got (gutter runner, packmaster, poison wind globadier, ratling gunner, rat ogre)…. Let’s face it, they are direct copy and pastes of the Left 4 Dead specials. (in order, hunter, smoker, boomer…. Ok so the ratling gun is new but the rat ogre is the same as the tank). Vermintide even has its own version of the witch in the form of a patrol of Stormvermin (which should be avoided at all costs, especially on harder difficulties).

Well, I read alot of reviews saying that the game pretty much sucks.  It does not suck.  Despite the bad reviews I couldn't pass it up on sale for $0.49.  This game has some neat features in it.  The main issue is that there's really no need to use the neat features.  The game is very linear so there's never an opportunity to experiment using different abilities to clear an area.
What I liked: The use of fire, water, electricity, gravity was done pretty well.  The manipulation of world objects wasn't really as limited as most games.  If you see a box it can be moved, thrown, blown up, etc.  You can use bad guys and world objects equally to create havok.
The animations were pretty good.  The character struggled through hip deep water, sloshed through knee deep water, and gasped for air appropriately.  The character acts like it's running out of air when the breath meter gets to a certain point (swimming more erratically and paniced) Cover animations were decent and there were even fairly good proximity animations which alot of games tend to ignore. (Stand close to fire and the character shields her face.)
The story wasn't blockbuster but was fast paced. There were a lot of cutscenes too, which I'm a fan of.  I want to see things unfold, not just hit a button and proceed.  Makes it more cinematic.
What I didn't like: The boss fight was challenging but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.  Also slightly confusing.
The level design was pretty weak.  There isn't really any sense to the layout of this place.
Two achievements are for 1. getting all the objects and 2. getting all the medals.  There's no indication of how many you missed.  As far as I know there's no list of medals that can be obtained either. You just play and try to get them?  Not cool.
You couldn't use abilities creatively enough.  You get a chance to open doors with hazards behind them as a learning part of the story, but then really never get to do it again.  Using the handheld tool you can see if there's water or fire or nothing behind a door but if it's off the path it's either locked or malfunctioning which means it might as well just be another wall.  You can shoot out glass doors, which is great fun, but pointless since there's nothing to do but then just move on content with the knowledge that you just shot a door.
The bad guys weren't intelligently placed.  They just kind of showed up in places that made no sense here and there to make you shoot things.  The bad guy placement was so bad that the majority of boss fight baddies can be left to the boss to take out.
All in all it's another linear shooter.  If it's linear, and a shooter, 99% of the time it'll also be generic.  It'd be worth it at $9.99.

Warhammer in chess form. What else needs to be said?

Chess has never been so Brutal
Its sometimes easy to forget, that Chess is one of the earliest war strategy games. and what better way to remind people of this, than to put chess in one of the best universes for war and strategy? Warhammer 40,000
Even thought this game is early access at the time of this review, I have to say I am very curious and excited to see what they can add to this game, because its already pretty fun and challenging.
Oh and did I mention the brutal kills?
I'm also glad to see that Warhammer 40,000 has not forgotten its roots as a turn based, table-top game (Don't get me wrong, I love Dawn of War)
The Future is bright of Warhammer 40,000: Regicide
(Despite a few salty Warhammer 40,000 veterans, that will never admit it)

Based on the hour I've played so far, I can say that I'm very excited to see what this game will blossom into. For less than 15 bucks, you get a pretty neat rendition of chess, AND a re-imagined version of chess (Regicide), too.
While you can't go wrong with chess in the first place, this game supplements it with some pretty brutal kill scenes, hell, watching an ork get vaporized is rewarding enough for the price tag of $14.
On top of that, you have Regicide. Regicide follows by the same rules as chess, but with the twist of each piece having various attacks it can perform at different ranges across the board. So, not only can you get an instant kill by jumping on another piece on the board, but your piece can shoot up other pieces if it's within range and has a clear field of view. Again, kickarss kill scenes to be had.
A campaign mode is on the way, but for now, you can play online or with a bot. There's some progress to be made yet, but as it is right now, I'm extremely satisfied with where this game is at!
4/5 would praise the Emperor again.

Warhammer 40,000: Regicide provides something new for the lover of chess, strategy games, and Warhammer 40,000.
1. Traditional chess with a Warhammer 40,000 theme and the universe's violent deaths, in the vein of Battle Chess.
2. Regicide mode that contains the movement phases and patterns of chess with additional abilities and powers thrown into the mix.
- Ignore the reviews that say there is no chess mode. It is there. -
Yes, the game is in early access and it's missing its story line; however, single-player and multi-player skirmish modes are available as well as a tutorial. Is it enough to warrant a $14.99 purchase right now? Well, that depends.
If you like playing chess against AI or friends and want some violent animations to follow each kill, by all means buy this game. If you like Warhammer 40,000 and want something a bit different, then you should buy this game. If you want to play as your favorite chapter or 40k race, then hold off because those things haven't been implemented yet. If you want pulse-pounding 40k action like Dawn of War or Space Marine, then don't. You won't find the brutal action here. The chess-like aspect of the game slows it down tremendously. I enjoy it, but there's some slight disconnect between 40k and slow-paced action.
I preordered the game for its collector's edition, so I'm already invested and I'm very pleased so far. But you need to know what type of game you are getting and what type of gamer you are before buying. All that being said, I recommend it for what it is and what it promises to be.

Here's a bit of background on how I got into the game - I started the game a few days ago on a whim when my friend invited me to play - and I've had lots of fun! It's reintroduced me to some old friends I thought I'd lost contact with and introduced me to some new people and I've been having a blast with everyone playing the game, it's really helped take my mind off things and made me a quite a bit happier!
Let me first say that this game isn't gonna be for everyone - cutesy (even dated) graphics, bad grammar in some of the menus, song selection that may not be for everyone and the way the gameplay itself is handled can be clunky at times.
But I still like the game! Here are some quick Pros and Cons bit before I go into a bit of detail.
Pros:
+(-)Catchy-tunes (Songs might not be for everyone though.)
+Can be lots of fun with friends
+Lots of thought put into idle animations in lobby
+Emotes are pretty cute
+Clothing is cute for what's out so far
+Relationship system where you can be the same gender
Cons:
-Notes may not always match up with beat
-Fever mode can sometimes be the opposite of rewarding (all notes turn the same color, which can be a hassle since I use color to determine what note is which arrow key)
-Cash shop can be ridiculously expensive, there's not even a perma option for some items which is annoying
-Spacebar notes exist
Now for the more detailed bits!
The first thing I'll address is the note system - the core of gameplay. There's no option to switch keys to make things easier to read for you, which I'm okay with, but if you're from other rhythm games like Stepmania where you can customize your keys, it can be a bit hard to adjust. Currently, the most annoying thing for me are spacebar notes. Spacebars can easily make or break your score and a lucky wow or a 90% can ruin everything when you're competing with your friends. The spacebar is a whole 'nother game mechanic you need to learn. Of course, I'm exaggerating, but it can be infuriating at times. Back to customizing keys - I really wish you could since the positioning of your hands pretty much demands you have only one hand on your arrow keys and one hand on your spacebar at all times. Unless your fingers are long or you're really fast at moving both your hands from your arrows keys to your spacebar, you'll have to get used to playing with one hand for arrow key notes.
The second thing I'd like to address are the songs. Personally I think there are songs for everyone but it's mostly a mixture of pop among other things - like I mentioned before, the songs won't be for everyone. If you're picky about what you play or listen to with rhythm games it's definitely gonna be a hit or miss.
The last thing I'd like to address are the game modes. Some game modes (although I believe it is just one game mode, and that would be Meeting party) can be locked out if the female/male ratio isn't the same in a lobby, which may force some people into observer. But other than that, there's actually quite a bit of modes to play which will keep you busy for a while - but for the most part you'll likely be playing team survival or classic.
Overall, there's a very limited amount of replay value depending on what piques your interest the most in rhythm games. For myself, the game has a lot to offer - the ability to play with friends, dressing up your character and some pretty good songs! However, that won't always be the case for everyone.
I have a few suggestions which I'll quickly list.
+Have an option configure arrows keys to other keys
+Have option to disable fever mode turning all notes the same color
+Get rid of the gender restriction on Meeting Party
+Allow more clothes to have permanent as an option when buying
+More ease of access to items in the store with Beat
Hopefully this review was helpful! Have fun playing lovebeat!

Wakfu features a turn-based strategy combat system. It plays a bit like Fire Emblem or FF Tactics, but where you control 1 character. Obviously, you can form groups with other players and play with them.
Like any RPG, there is a level-up system, but thankfully, it doesn't really feel too grindy or mindless. Leveling up is quite fast, and you have to think about which spells you're going to use in combat, and focus on those spells. You can attribute stat points and customize your character the way you want, according to your playstyle. There are over 15 completely unique classes, each with many different possible builds.
Then there's the Ecosystem. In this game, most plants and monsters don't just respawn automatically. People have to "replant" them. This adds an extra layer of interaction with other players as a community.
Wakfu has very charming visuals, something you rarely see in MMOs these days. The music is pretty good too overall.
There aren't really any quests after the starting area, but in my opinion, this is a good thing. The game doesn't force you to do specific things in order to progress, and it encourages you to explore, make friends and just have fun. There might be moments where you feel like you don't really know what to do next, though.
Also, the entire game is free. I know it's hard to believe, but there's no catch, really. You have access to everything that really matters in the game for free.
So yeah, if you're looking for a solid MMO that isn't afraid to innovate, go ahead and give this game a chance!

Me and my Skype friends love playing Jackbox Games. We are now pleased to have The Party Pack 1, 2 and 3 in our collection of things to enjoy doing together.
As with the original Party Pack, all of these games are played with shared view of the host's display, using smartphones or other input devices to play through jackbox.tv. Only one player, the host, needs to own the game.
The most reliable stand-by and favourite of my group. Players are provided with two prompts and write responses to them, and each prompt is given to two different players. Then, each prompt is displayed and all other players, plus members of an audience if you have one, vote on which answer was better. Get all the votes for a Quiplash and extra points. In the final round, everyone is given the same prompt and has three votes they can give to anyone else's answers. Unfortunately, some of the prompts occasionally leave us uninspired and bored.
Just like the original, but with a new set of ridiculous trivia knowledge. Make up something to fill the blank in the bizarre fact, and compete with other players to be the most convincing and guess the truth.
It took us a while to figure out how this worked, but it has become a favourite. At the beginning of the game, everyone draws two pictures from given titles which will be content for the game. One at a time, pictures will come up available for auction, and each has a hidden value for which it will be resold after the auction. You will know the value of three art pieces... But only by title. You have to guess which picture is which. When someone else buys a picture you drew, you get half the money for it. Aside from that, you can take out loans from Predatory Loans, an unscrupulous bank with a bucketload of absolutely hilarious marketing jingles. This will give you more money to bid with, but you pay 150% back at the end of the game when you collect the money from your sales.
The presentation of the game is amusing, and it plays awful tricks - the titles of different works are very often designed to produce images that could be confused with each other.
A tangled logic puzzle for up to four players which clearly takes inspiration from Keep Talking and Nobody Explodes. In this game, each player has clues about how to disarm a bomb, and one or more have the buttons they can push to do so. Instructions become more convoluted as you progress through the "days" of your story as a bomb diffusing intern, and will begin overriding one another. This game accomodates smaller groups, but the intellectual challenge is awesome if you have a few friends who like logic puzzles and are feeling alert. The balance between taking enough time not to make a mistake, and going quickly enough to beat the timer is a tough one to hit. The extra time you didn't take in the challenges is your score at the end of the day.
Probably the weakest showing in this party pack, at least for us. Each round, whoever is judging chooses one of the game's prompts, as you might in Fibbage. Each player is then presented with titles for a bunch of sound effects and has to choose two of them to respond to the prompt. You don't get to hear the sounds before you select them, so the outcome can be surprising. The judge then chooses which combination fits the prompt best. First person to three points wins. It's not a bad game, but is somewhat less involved than the others and has a degree of randomness.

New features, new games, new music, let's get this crapshow over with. (By "crapshow", I mean my neck aching as I type this review up.)
FIBBAGE 2: This is a lot like Fibbage XL, and I said that it was great, but this version has 3 new features. First, player avatars. Not only are they eyes instead of lights, but you can pick which sound effect you want! Now, I won't have to worry about being stuck with the fart noise! Second, more prompts. Well, duh, new prompts are always welcome. Lastly is the De-Fibrillator. I HATE this thing. It's supposed to eliminate all of the answers, except for the truth and one lie. That seems alright in smaller games, but what if you have a full party? Yeah, everyone gets one, but it's still really O.P., which is why I don't use it. Besides that, this was a pretty nice sequel that gets a thumbs up from me.
EARWAX: Apples To Apples with sound effects. No, really, it is. While the 6-sound library for each player can be a bit annoying sometimes, the sound choices are great, with my favorites being "'Wow' (Male)" and any toilet-related ones. Those always seem to win... I'm calling it right now, if Party Pack 4 came out with Earwax 2 and included more sounds, people would LOVE it.
BIDIOTS: I'll be honest... I don't like this one that much, and neither does my brother. I think it's trying to be a spiritual successor to Drawful, but this one is just complete GARBAGE compared to Drawful, which is probably why Jackbox Games made Drawful 2 instead of Bidiots 2 AND made it separate. The gameplay is really confusing, I get screwed over, even without someone using a screw. What I mean by this is I LOSE MONEY. While the ever-changing Predatory Loans jingle and the critic commentary are great, the game seems really lacking compared to the rest in this pack. Just skip this one whenever you boot up the game. And no, watching people play it on YouTube does NOT make it better.
QUIPLASH XL: Clearly the best game in the bunch. The soundtrack is such an earworm, the characters (I'm gonna coin the term "Quipsters" for these little guys) are clever, with my favorites being Light Blue, Green, and Yellow, and the prompts are amazing. I really have no complaints for this game. My only suggestion is to not play it with boring scumbags. Play it with family and friends, y'know, the ones that are actually funny?
BOMB CORP.: This game's art style is AMAZING. I love modern games that use a pixelated design, like Shovel Knight, Pony Island, or the Death Minigames in Five Nights At Freddy's 2. The humor is great in this game, and the teamwork aspect is cool, very different from the other at-each-other's-throats games in the packs. My only problem is the concept of the game. Yes, it's fun, but it just seems like a smaller version of Keep Talking And Nobody Explodes, another fun co-op game on Steam. No, it doesn't have comedy or filing names, but it still has more to it than cutting wires. I'd see someone playing a round or two of this, but you're probably better off with KTANE...
And that's it. This is a much improved game. There's a bigger demographic, spreading to live streamers, there's more games to play, and there's more of a mulitplayer focus, only including one game that supports single-player (Bomb Corp.), while the last one had two (YDKJ 2015 and Lie Swatter). I would definitely buy this if I were you.
GAMES RANKED FROM WORST TO BEST:
Bidiots
Bomb Corp.
Fibbage 2
Earwax
Quiplash XL

I've been playing M&B since before Warband and still do. I pulled a lot of hours in retail version, before purchasing WB on Steam and never regretted spending money. Crazy, right?
So the vanila itself is fine until you get used to the game. It brings up lots of recognizable weapons and armor design from the most popular cultures of Medieval period to choose from. It gives a satisfying feeling, when defending a wall among your men bringing down scores of men. It's a great feeling to outflank your enemy that surpasses you in quantity (nearly most of the time) with a solid Knight charge. To capture an annoying lord that has been pillaging your village over and over and getting ransom for him. To either become a marshal and bring forth the lords, or try to start your own Kingdom, which is a difficult task at the beginning. You will end up sooner or later (after a hundred or two hours), realising that challenge is basically gone, since you've cracked the mechanics and finally got everything right and start thinking there is nothing more the game can show you.
And then you find mods.. Bryttenwalda, Europe 1200, 1257 AD, MP Mount and musket, CRPG, and coop like Nord Invasion and many more, like roleplaying Persistent World. With new features, reworked morale, recruit system. Completely new and quite accurate maps with a lot more Lords, towns and Castles to play through.
It's hundreds of hours of fun for such a small price.
And then, there are payed Add-ons, basically mods going in a full fledged release. Not all of them are definetly flawless, they carry many bugs in them and some additional work is always required, but that is only due to the engine problems.
The engine itself is very old now and is not suited to work out so many scripts in huge mods like the 1257 AD I mentioned earlier. All of the new features are difficult to implement properly, especially there are problems with Spawning and Path finding, with high-end machines dying with 600-700 hundred men fighting on the field, with crashes and stuff like that.
Still, it's one of the few games I so highly will and do support with my money, getting all the add-ons.

DISCLAIMER: Although it says 4.4 total i have invested much more before it went on steam (I have been playing this since beta). I picked up the steam version for my newer system during a sale.
C:MANO is not so much as a game as a simulation and in one of the best the market has to offer. Including a extensive database of weapons, ships, aircraft, land units, satelites and much more, as well as endless combinations of scenarios in which you can apply these platforms (some, like air defense networks, airbases and sats can be imported premade making basic scenario creation a cakewalk however you can fine tune to an incredible degree, down to the amount of bullets in an aircraft's magazine in flight of 200). IF creation is not for you there are many premade scenarios (the community scenario packs are free and easy to import) that are a blast. The immense detail and meticulous maintanence of the databases and core game engine justify the high price tag IMO.
HOWEVER: This sim is not for the faint of heart or the faint of wallet. The game is demanding, although my desktop's 6600k can keep things stable most of the times (there are no saftey stops for overloading the program, if you try and process 13 concurent nuclear detonations, the system will try to do it, exaust your resources and crash), my laptops broadwell i5 struggles and flounders under any but the most simple scenario. A high performance CPU, SSD, and metric buttton of ram is an absolute must for this. The sheer amount of things being simulated is immense and can bring most systems to thier knees. Also, there is no easy mode outside the tutorial. You will be micromanaging hundreds of units in real time (the pause time button is your best friend).
In short, if you have a system that can run it, and you want a simulation game in which you can model any modern engagement from anti piracy operations to all out nuclear blitzkrieg, this is the game for you. If not, look at the wargame series or somethine else that is easier to manage and run. If you think you're up for it, youtuber Baloogan does an indepth series of videos with the game and you can learn a lot.

Would love to recommend this game. If it were less than $45, I would. The developers clearly put a lot of work into ensuring the subject matter is detailed and accurate. They put less work in the design of the user interface and game engine. The developers need to get more experience in game design or need to hire additional developers with more expertise in this area. If they did so, CMANO would totally be worth the premium price they're asking for.

I use this game to simulate WW3. Yes, it's that detailed. It's wrong to call it a game, this is an actual simulator that strives to be as accurate as possible. It's Professional version is used by the military and think-tanks to run simulations. Having this on your computer 30 years ago would have landed you in jail, this is probably about as accurate and realistic you can get without a Top Secret clearance. Just about every kind of naval and air weapon system since the beginning of the cold war to the present day are simulated to a very high degree of accuracy with real-life calculations. It's easy to simulate anything from a small-scale dogfight between a few fighters to a massive air/naval battle between carrier groups. I've made a scenario that literally features all of the nuclear air, sea and ICBM forces of the US and Russia. The performance takes a nosedive when you start having thousands of units because of the sheer volume of calculations the game does, but it's still insanely impressive. This isin't a sim for causual gamers, only HARDCORE military simulation fans will enjoy this.

First things first, I would say that CMA/NO sits right on the line separating what is a game from what is purely a simulator, and that should be taken into account for anyone considering purchasing it. Secondly, yes, it's $80, I got it for 60% off and it is commonly at least half-off during major steamwide sales. As with any game, I would recommend it be bought on sale.
One common concern about CMANO is bugs, which frankly I have experienced very few of, I would say around 1/100 of the scenarios in game that I have edited/created have wound up bugged and/or corrupted beyond fixing. In my own experience with the program I would not list bugs as a major problem, although of course I cannot speak for everyone
The program takes an enormous database of weapons platforms, systems, sensors, etc, and models at the very least a rough approximation of their publicly known capabilities, takes a range of variables, and rolls the dice regarding how these systems successfully or unsuccessfully function in whatever scenario they are being used in, (ex, It determines whether or not a surface-to-air missile successfully hits its target, is spoofed by countermeasures, or simply misses). This sort of dice-rolling (literally called that in the program) is an issue for some (primarily concerned about just how "realistic" the results of this actually are) and is often combined with concerns about the limitations of the scripting in-game. These concerns and complaints are completely valid, although I implore anyone to find a program at the scale and complexity of CMANO that is wholly open ended and with all possible variables as seems to be desired that can be acquired without a government license for a price tag under $200.
------------------------------------------------------------------
TL;DR
Pros:
A simulator without easily accesible peer, and the only of its kind availiable on steam.
An absolute dream for those desiring and/or interested in this kind of simulator
On sale during the major sale cycles on Steam
Still actively updated, particularly the database, but---->
Cons:
Expensive, clearly.
No free demo
Bugs may be an issue for you
Although I don't take issue with it, the UI simply sucks.
<----any new major features are probably going to be DLC (as is sadly expected of most games nowadays)
Meh:
Performance (Framerate) isn't a steadily flowing creek, and probably won't be regardless of your specs, if this is a problem for you, its a Con, if not, it isn't.
Enormous learning curve, some hate em, some like the challenge, I am one of the latter.
----------------------------------------
All in all, I enjoy it very much, haven't bought the LIVE DLC scenarios, don't think there is much of a need to. I am a junkie for this type of stuff, and having got the game 60% off it is worth every penny.
If the price is your #1 sticking point for trying it out, I recommend the standalone DLC Northern Inferno, $20 regularly, and less than $20 on sale, It's a single standalone"campaign" in the game that is useful to see if CMANO may or may not be "your kind-of game"
ps. if you buy it, don't forget to download the platform descriptions and pictures from the website, helps a lot with familiarity and makes things more enjoyable.

CMANO is a sandbox of military simulation and fun. Ever wanted to pit a flight of F-16's against, well, anything? This is your game. You can lay out complex missions, watch as the AI executes it all, or micromanage each individual jet. The database alone is monstrous, covering almost everything you can imagine from 1946 up to hypothetical future aircraft.
One of the more pleasant parts of the game is the interface is fairly simple. So instead of fighting to learn the interface you get to fight the scenarios. Sonar, radar, and emissions are all modeled correctly. Some scenarios can have a steep learning curve, but once you realize that you need to think like a real commander and learn the methods, things tend to work out.

. I've got hypothetical conflicts galore, and the community is really robust. Well worth the cost for a professionally developed and supported piece of software.

I want to be able to recommend this game for its gameplay but can't because it is so buggy and its user experience is beyond awful.
I love the concept. Command is a game that gives you:
- Complex strategic pictures to play with (while you concentrate on supporting that Marines deployment in Tripoli, are you not forgetting the long-range aviation threat over Albania, or the Soviet naval group steaming past Crete?);
- Lots of uncertainty that creates nail-biting action (there is nothing quite like the panic that comes from detecting a submarine already in torpedo range of your carrier group, or a stream of anti-ship missiles headed your way from a direction you were "sure" there were no enemy forces);
- A real sense of achievement (OK, beating that final boss in that other game is rewarding, but nothing like saving Iceland from a Soviet invasion without losing any major ship).
Command is not a beautiful game. It's basically coloured dots slowly moving across maps. As far as I'm concerned, that's how it should be; like chess. Other naval strategy games try to look nice, but fancy graphics only distract from the gameplay. So, kudos for that. Still, I would have liked the game to do some storytelling. For example, when you end a scenario, you're given a prompt: "this scenario has concluded, you will be presented with an evaluation". It's quite a let-down after a large battle. I understand it's supposed to be a simulation game, but I still feel it doesn't do justice to the sunken ships, thousands of people who lost their lives, perhaps the nations that rose or fell that day.
However, the real issue with this game, and the reason why I can't recommend it, is its programming. It's ridiculously buggy. I don't finish most games because the non-stop stream of bugs and unexplained slowdowns and "pauses" frustrate me too much. It isn't helped by a user interface that's by far the worst of any program I own. Simple actions require dozens of clicks, everything is confusing, key information is hidden in remote menus, mission planning, which should limit the need for micro-management, ends up creating death-traps for beyond-stupid “AI” units... it's a joke. I wish the (obviously amateurish) developers would hire real software engineering and user experience experts to fix the game and give it its real potential.

Ah, Party Pack 2, Easily earns the #1 Spot in order of favorite pack out of the three. This pack's filled with gems, and honestly, there are more games that I'd give a higher rating here than in 3 and 1 combined. Each and every game in this pack gets a high rating from me. Let's begin, shall we?
Bidiots - 9.3/10 - Bidiots is my 3rd Favorite Game made by Jackbox, with first being Tee K.O, and 2nd being You Don't Know Jack. Bidiots is an absolutely hilarious take on art auctions. I have no clue what I'm doing, and neither does anyone else I play with, but it is oddly very competitive and addicting. Draw 2 Drawings based on silly prompts you're given (much like Drawful), and then let the auction commence! Each person has an art professional on their team that will tell them three paintings worth a big sum of cash. But since this is Jackbox, you've gotta try and guess which of those paintings you're seeing at the moment, or if you're not seeing a valuable one. Are they saying the beer bottle painting is worth a good sum of cash? Haven't seen a beer bottle and you're over halfway done? Shucks man, that beer bottle you're looking for could've been that♥♥♥♥♥♥♥looking painting you didn't bid for 10 minutes ago! We're not done yet though. The host has a hilarious British accent, this game takes the Screws from You Don't Know Jack which you can use once per game, forcing the person you use it on to bid on artwork. Best of all, there is a loanshark company in this game with the catchiest jingle you've ever heard. Dammit Jackbox, I played this game for the first time in December, and I still have the Predatory Loans Jingle in my head! Anyway, this is an absolute masterpiece, and it takes the cake for this pack with Earwax JUST behind.
Earwax - 9.2/10 - Earwax is incredible. Your goal in earwax is to take turns judging the other players on the sound combinations they choose. You're given silly prompts such as "What ItsLeAshton does in the morning.", and "Batman on the toilet.", and you're given about 8 Sounds at random to choose from. You must choose a combination of 2 sounds that fit the prompt the most. There are over 500 Prompts, and at least a good 150 Sounds. The first to 3 Points wins. The gameplay itself is one thing, but the biggest thing that gives this game such a high rating in my book is the incredible replay value. I could replay this game for MONTHS and not get bored of it, and I feel that everyone I've played with could easily say the same thing. This game leaves me redfaced due to laughing lots as well. Laughter IS the Best Medicine. If you want to live a long life, play Earwax or any other Jackbox Party Game. A gem of the pack for sure.
Fibbage 2 - 8.6/10 - I will not go into too much detail here, as I've already stated tons about Fibbage during my Fibbage XL Review for Jackbox Party Pack 1, but Fibbage 2 is basically an upgrade with more questions, a few jingles, and Defibrilator, which allows you to narrow your choices to have a better chance at guessing the truth.
Quiplash XL - 8.0/10 - Quiplash is a genius game. Quiplash XL includes all of the prompts from the original Quiplash, the Quiplash DLC, AND over 100 More! In Quiplash, you're given 2 prompts such as "Make up a swear word.", "A good reason to travel back in time to 2 weeks ago." and "A great use for a spaghetti noodle.". One other person will get the same prompts as you, and after everyone is done filling out their prompts, everyone's answers to the prompts will be pitted against each other and everyone votes on the funniest answer. It is the first Jackbox Game I discovered, and is still one of my favorites. It has a great replay value, and tons of hilarious prompts, AND a hilarious host, Josh Schmitty Schmittenstein.
Bomb Corp. - 6.0/10 - Bomb Corp is honestly the most unique Jackbox Game there is. It has a storyline. You are an intern at Bomb Corp, a Bomb Making Company, and you have many problems to face. Start with defusing bombs, then filing explosive cabinets, then defusing bombs with manuals written by CHILDREN, then solving explosive keypads, then making coffee, then fixing a copy machine, and THEN delivering an ALIEN BABY! This game is really amazing, and has a comedy line the whole way through just like You Don't Know Jack that keeps you reeled in.

## Old Rythmatic Feel With a Grandiose New Style
I feel like I need to preface this review with the following. I received this game after meeting the developer on Reddit. That may not seem important right now but we'll get to that soon enough. Rythem games are nothing new to the industry, specifically after the explosion of Guitar Hero and Rock Band games from the late 00's. As much as those games have lost their way recently it's hard to deny their impact on the genre as a whole despite titles like Space Channel 5 and Amplitude having existed before them.
Orbital X is more akin to something like Amplitude though. It features throbbing techno tracks and a rail system with persistent obstacles that need to be avoided. Kind of like those temple run style games that litter the App store and Google play but not ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and with no microtransactions. In short, they can actually be completed without having to drain a bank account. That's not to say the game is without it's series of power ups. By reaching different scores you can unlock different planets from our solar system that act as your player character. The power ups range from score multipliers to extra lives with varying degrees of usefulness.
Like I said, it's really just another rail runner game and while that may be true, there's a bright side here. This game rarely feels frustrating even when you've been playing for awhile. The first time I opened it up, I played for close to three hours nonstop. While extended periods of play are nothing out of the ordinary for me, that usually stems from my own pathological obsessions. When it comes to Orbital X, I can play it for hours at a time because it's just a fun game that presents a solid challenge. Don't take this to mean that the game is without its faults but the fact that this entire game was created by a single person is almost enough to allow you to over look those problems.
## Solid Design With Minor Flaws
These problems aren't exclusive to this title and these shouldn't be seen as a reason to not play the game. Orbital X has a very unique color palette and that palette is changed periodically to a photo negative when you pass through a portal. This on its own is not particularly a bad thing but when you mix it with the disorienting movement of moving side to side and being repositioned every time you enter a new portal, it can become a problem for some people. The tracks can also offer viewpoints that are less than ideal at time, especially when the screen becomes black and white and objects can be difficult to differentiate from one another. I can attribute more than a few deaths to the fact that the screen is always moving slightly when the track itself is also twisting. A lot of that can be attributed to my own stupidity in most cases but that's beside the point.
The colors in this game are half past nauseating sometimes but I still can't stop playing it. The game has three main stages, each with a different color set and level of difficulty. Of course I can only assume that one stage is different from another because as I've said before, I am the worlds okayest gamer and this game is very challenging. Suffice it to say, I never make it very far but I enjoyed it regardless.
## A Winner That Should Be Played By Everyone
Even if you're not a fan of these types of games, Rail Runners not Rhythm games, like me, I would still suggest you play this game for awhile. When a game is under three dollars and you still don't at least give it a chance, that says a lot more about you as a person than it does about an independent developer. Like it or not, games are difficult to make and even more so when you are a single person taking that task on. It's people like this man here that keep pushing the industry forward by focusing on quality rather than monetary gain. I can see several ways the creator could have monetized this game and flooded it with microtransactions but he decided to take the high road and create something worthwhile.
Check out orbital X on Steam. It's cheap and it's even on sale right now. You, as a reader, gamer, and member of the Game Raven community literally have no reason to not try this game.

This was my first computer game I've ever played and it has aged extremely well.  Don't worry about not playing the first one, you can pick this game up and play it without any problem as the first game was MUCH more lax on the story side of things.  This game is the definition of what it means to be a classic.  As is often the case with Bioware games, the writing is fantastic with comedy being seamlessly interweaved with the high-paced action game that it is.  The level designs do not lack for anything.  They really make you think since every room is like its own puzzle.  I remember when I was young, around 9 or 10, I would be stuck on some rooms for days before my tiny brain put together what I needed to do.  This was an era before I was even aware I could google game walkthroughs, but I loved figuring everything out.  The boss fights are epic, with each boss seeming like a more complex Legend of Zelda boss fight.  Finally, what REALLY sets this game apart for me is the sheer amount of secrets in the game.  This game is from a time when designers could throw in a secret room you accessed by stumbling across an invisible bridge over a never-ending pit or running towards a section of wall that seems slightly off-color from the rest.  They reward you with items, health, or perhaps a joke room with a poorly photoshopped picture of the developers' faces over some cartoon characters.   Either way, these secret rooms do not detract anything from the experience, and they're a real treat to find.  This is a game that does not hold your hand and try to steer you to progress.  No, this game sits and waits for you to progress, expecting you to know what to do or to take as much time as you need to figure it out.

Tldr; L4D with rats.
Game is fun, but unlike L4D (where the in-game AI ramps up difficulty based on how well you're doing) this pretty much roles a dice at regular points. I suspect it'll get a bit of a rework over time, but at the moment it can seriously over-ramp the difficulty for new players making some levels fairly unplayable on one run, and then really boring on the next.
Notable example: At one point after 3 of us had been playing (on easy to learn the ropes) we get a swarm, 2 rats dragging off the other human party members and a bloody ogre beating on the only other member capable of helping (the AI was off killing something else it had found at the other end of the map, or staring at a wall) all at once. This happened on “easy” mode btw – where your end rewards are fairly unlikely to be good! I can’t help but think if the AI makes multiple boss/special rolls, that that should somehow adjust the loot (i.e. use a score method).
Oh the bot AI is terrible, seriously - it's like a dizzy kid with ADD on speed "oh look a corner, I'll stare at this while 2 members of the party die next to me" or "I'll just run off back down the streets we came from 20 minutes ago to fight an NPC no-one else gives a s****e about… Maybe I can get killed!". If you know ANYONE to take those NPC slots - buy them a copy of the game, *seriously*; even if they are the sort of person that dribbles in the microphone and needs a helmet when walking about the house – they will definitely be more competent than the in-game AI.
Anyhow - that sounds like a rant, it’s not :) If you liked L4D, it's likely you'll appreciate this - especially if you liked beating the zombies with melee weapons and like the possibility to actually block. Just avoid NPC party members – those are the worst bit.
There is some character progression and a sort of 'random roll for personal loot' thing that happens at the end of levels. The loot you get can be for ANY of the characters you have (1 of any of the 4 PCs) which means this may turn into a bit of a chore if you only really connect with one character. Thankfully you can melt loot down for upgrades / another chance at loot.
Minor gripe: Progression like this tends to create elitist idiot syndrome. So far I haven’t seen that (mainly cause I play with good friends) – but I suspect “online experiences may differ”, so it’s best enjoyed if you’ve got a few friends to play with.
Another minor gripe: for some reason turning off the music in the game doesn’t stop the music on the debriefing screen, so if you use teamspeak – you’ll probably spend the last bit unable to hear anything anyone’s saying.. The only 'fix' is turning down game volume, and then it's possible to miss audio clues in the missions.

Sorry to say, but it's boring as hell right now. The game has good potential, certainly more than Dirt Rally, and I may revisit the review at a later date, but it's just not there yet.
I do acknowledge that the underlying physics are better and more realistic than in Dirt Rally and RBR, but there are simply too many crippling flaws that take away from the overall fun factor of the game. Each and every one of these issues on its own would be somewhat understandable, but the infinite rear grip, the atrocious default setups, the overly reactive weight transfer relative to any serious sim title and how insanely much it's focused on the front, RWDs being broken in general etc all add up, and the end result is not pretty in the slightest.
As well, while I can understand the continued focus on Rallycross, a number of other major elements of the game, such as Landrush, the Your Stage mechanic and the overall team management currently all feel like elements that were tacked on for no real reason just to make the game seem more complete at first glance than it really is. Baiting out good early reviews for more preorders? Wouldn't put it past CM, sadly.
Landrush: Why? Why is this in the game? The cars are unique, but they don't particularly handle well at all even with the correct setups, and barring the fact that they run on gravel, they are completely out of place in a game centered around rallying, especially with the current multiplayer system. Why bother with any of these instead of doing Rallycross? Even the number of tracks is utterly laughable.
Your Stage: I get the need to come up with a backup plan after losing the official WRC license (and for that and other reasons the FIA deserves all the criticism in the world), but in practice it just throws the same sections at you over and over, so much so that the stages ultimately end up being almost as easily memorized as the ones in Dirt Rally. The only difference is that, instead of regurgitating everything from your mind all at once and being able to memorize even the perfect overall line everywhere, this is more like using flash cards to study for an exam, with the exam literally just being a random assortment of those cards being thrown at you one after another, with awkward, overly long and overly straight transitions in between any of them. Add to that the sheer lack of environments (5 as opposed to Dirt Rally's 6) and you end up basically seeing it all within the first 20 hours of the game, if not less. With another 20 you've already mostly figured out how to take them all regardless of the car you're driving.
Team management: At first glance it's quite good. However, not only is there absolutely no depth to it whatsoever past the first couple of hours (seriously, you just make your livery, occasionally go back to change sponsors, then do a slightly improved version of the staff hiring system from Dirt Rally - that's it, you don't have to care about anything else), but it also puts off both more casual players who don't want to have to deal with this AND simracers who would rather just focus on the driving, without it being any fun for anyone (like me) who does actually like having something like this. And no, you lose too many credits by skipping any of that, so it's not an option.
As a whole, the game is simply struggling to offer much in the way of enjoyment for any longer than a few hours right now. If you want to get it, wait for a patch and more content instead. Then again, seeing as this is a numbered title in the series, I don't know if there's much I expect from CM anymore.
Potential alone can't carry a game, and neither can more realism make up for crippling flaws or a sheer lack of enjoyment. Why play something if you're not going to have fun with it? Dirt Rally was frustrating at times and it's got some seriously unfixable flaws, but at its best it was a hell of a lot of fun. Dirt 4 simply isn't. I really hope CM will address these problems and add more content at a later date, but right now I think my time would be better spent on other titles.
The saddest thing of all? Rallycross is the best part of the game. A rally game.

I've been a fan of the DiRT series for a long time, ever since Dirt 2. So I will break down what has improved and not improved over the series, many people compare this game mostly to Dirt Rally from what I see.
Overall, Dirt 4 is a huge step in the right direction. They brought back landrush, rallycross has 5 tracks and a large variety of cars, historic rallies and regular rallies have a huge emphasis.
CAMPAIGN: To most, the campaign looks very short, which there isn't that many events. (About a dozen for historic rallies, and rallies), and 5 for landrush and rallycross. But as you progress these events, they get much longer, I have over 40 hours and haven't finished the campaign, level 43 at the moment. There is also a triple crown section as you complete the game which is a huge campaign event and you unlock higher difficulties.
WHAT CHANGED:  Also, unlike Dirt Rally, many people did not enjoy how it was a hard core simulator, but those who loved simulation had a huge enjoyment on how well it handeled and how punishing it was. Dirt 4 also has a difficulty for gamers, so you can enjoy with arcade physics. I only played simulation, and I think the handling is like Dirt Rally but improved, especially the tire, weight of the cars, and tarmac physics improved. Although, the game took away hillclimb, and it does not have as many discplines as Dirt 3 and Dirt 2. I still miss Raid SUVs and Trucks, trailblazer, and other events that took place in those games. Dirt 4 has a massively improved repair system and you get to manage your own team with their own skills and real people, as you move up you can build up your team. Chief engineers have to assume what to fix and engineers start off slow, and your agents only get small sponsors. Also, you can upgrade a huge variety of facilities that give you bonuses and help you grow your garage and team. DIrt Rally had a repair system but you could only hire a few engineers and manage them and improve the skills, and condition of all parts was listed as a percent, not nearly as in-depth. Dirt 3 and previous to that had no repair system. Damage system is also much improved.
DAMAGE PHYSICS: Something I always felt was amazing about the Dirt series was the soft body physics. The physics are determined by every impact and the car reacts to that. Cars have a lot more proper dents, scratches, fiberglass and carbon fibre holes and cracks, and even many parts flying off or breaking all together. Many people DO NOT understand that these are licensed cars, so the damage physics have to be limited so they don't appear in the interior of the car. There are times though where the physics do react a little odd and if you have very heavy damage on your car the damage gets limited at how far it pushes. Every main component of the car as you'd expect will break and wear overtime.
Vehicle Upgrades: Something new to Dirt 4, as you upgrade the facility you can unlock Grade D,C,B, and A parts. (A the best). The higher quality parts are much more expensive and take more time to repair, but wear down much less quickly. This is useful for longer races and such. Didn't really see any performance differences between the parts, they're only meant for strategey.
AI: I'm kinda mixed on this one, and this is where I see all of the complaints. (I used the 2nd highest difficulty, demanding). Which once you complete one of the sections of the campaign you unlock the "Brutal and fearless AI" which is harder than the highest. But anyways, sometimes the AI can rubberband or be super challenging at times. In some races, I could barely keep up with the AI, in some, it would slow down a whole bunch on turns or straights, and I'd win by 30-60 seconds. Also the AI can be unreasonable at times, it doesn't slow down on water, in landrush the AI is extremely aggressive, rallycross it seems better than DIrt Rally.
The cars: There's only a few more than Dirt Rally, and missing some from the previous Dirt 2 and Dirt 3 games. Overall the cars got a huge texture and interior refresh and look better in most details and exterior things. They also handle better overall. As move to the older cars with more horsepower, they are much more difficult.
Tuning: A big change for Dirt 4. Dirt 4 has extremely precise tuning. Although, the skill of your chief engineer will decide how precise you can be. You can tune camber of wheels, all of the differential parts, engine gears, brakes, etc. For many cars it varies, more modern ones usually have more tunable components. You can also save tune profiles. In previous Dirt games you could tune as well but was very broad and didn't really impact much. Many people have complained the default tunes cause the cars to be slightly understeery. In rally cross, I always made my gears shorter to give me an acceleration advantage.
CONTENT: A mixed bag. The game features 5 rally tracks (For historic rallies too), 3 landrush locations and 5 rally cross locations (3 of which from Dirt Rally). The tracks have a junior and full circuit and sometimes a clubman circuit and can reverse too. There's around 50 cars. The new stage generator adds quite a bit to the game, but many players including myself have found many simular sections in the game and sort of a deja vu system. The game also has a HUGE amount of challenges in joyride and a new Dirtfish school which is a huge playground where you can do whatever. You can also generate your own tracks. Here is my question: Even if there was maps and tracks from previous games, bring them back too! Adding a lot more reused content is a lot better than cutting down on it.
STAGE GENERATOR: It's a really cool and simple feature. You can adjust 2 sliders for your complexity and length. Most stages range from 2 miles up to 10 miles and complexity makes the turns and bends more common and difficult and adds in more obstacles. Many stages do have similarities though.
WEATHER: The weather system is the best it has ever been. You can completely customize the time of day, and what weather. There's rain, snow (with varying intensity), fog, mist, dry, and much more. The weather completely changes the cars handling and visiability too. For example, in Spain when it rains on the tarmac, braking distance is longer and the car slips a lot more. Many tracks where it previously rains will leave puddles and such on the next stage. Weather can also be on different sections of the track. Overall excellent and very detailed. The sunsets are especially beautiful and night driving is a lot of fun.
DIFFICULTY: There's a lot of customization. As mentioned there are simluation or gamer modes. Simulation handles like Dirt rally but better, and gamer is similar to Dirt 3's handling, but of course revamped and tuned to be better. Incase you didn't know, Gamer is supposed to be arcade handling and makes it easier, simulation is supposed to be realistic and hardcore. There's a huge variety of settings you can customize which adds bonuses to how much you earn. AI difficulty, traction control and other electronic controls, transmission, wipers, cameras, and much more. I had everything turned off for me, damn was it hard. I used an old xbox 360 Controller which it works pretty well. I also have a cheap Thrustmaster wheels and pedals which it worked pretty well, you'll have to set it up to your own preferenes though. Wheel setup was an ease.
GRAPHICS: Big improvement over Dirt Rally, but the foliage doesn't look that good. Textures and lighting are hugely improved. Dirt 3 and Dirt rally can look better in some places though. Lots of detail in the car interiors and on the track. Crowd also looks very well done. Shadow and object pop-ins are quite obvious though. Game runs well at 4K nearly maxed out for me. Look at profile for specs.
I recommend you pick up this game if you love Dirt or if you want an excellent offroad racing game. Codemasters are releasing patches based on people's feedback. Still a few minor bugs.

Because DIRT Rally is a challenging experience, while DIRT 4 is a medicore game.
Seriously. I wasn't expecting some intense sim, I was going into pure fun, but I'm having little of it. Codemasters are trying something new with every DIRT installment, putting something new in each one. Sometimes it's a hit and miss, like infamous Gymkhana in DIRT 3, which was actually well executed, but large group of players (including me) hated it.
DIRT 4 actually is trying to play safe and there's actually little of variety here and its main focus is on the rally. There is also Land Rush and Rally Cross, but they don't take that much time in the Career Mode as the Rally challenges. If anything is new here is a new type of a car - a crosskart, that can be driven in Land Rush and Rally Cross challenges and... uhm... it's the weakest part of the game in my opinion.
The whole handling system seems to be refined but not advanced compared to DIRT 3 (DIRT Rally aside). And it's weird, the rally cars have more weight and seem to be a little glued to the road. It needs a while to getting used to. On the other hand trucks, buggys and crosskarts seem to be very loose on the surfaces and it's very easy to spin them out of control. Still nothing you cannot get used to.
But the main problem I have with DIRT 4 is a lack of variety. Interesting part is - I didn't know DIRT 4 have random track generator before I played it. I was suprised that every stage is different and yet it feels oddly the same. And there's the problem with that randomness - after just a couple of hours into driving you'll start noticing repeating patterns and whole sections of the tracks. It gets so bad, that at some sections of the stages I felt like I was litterally driving in the loop. It gets very repetetive and boring.
And there's nothinh new to see actually. We get Michigan, Australia, Wales, Sweden with snowy tracks and Spain with asphalt tracks (the least intresting location, BTW). Nothing that we didn't see before in previous DIRT games, right?
In Rally Cross and Land Rush it's even a bigger problem when you championship is two stages and you get to drive twice the same stage, only second time with one ore two laps more.
And because of that the graphics also doesn't look very appealing. Not the most important part, but it's cool to play a game that looks cool. After couple hours of driving, you start recognizing turns, corners and terrain around them, so there's not much joy to your eye. Car models are fantastic though, with some really great damage system - every mistake leave a dent in your car including damaging components inside it.
Managing your team and garage and menus, also gets boring after a little while, going through the menus over and over after contracts with your sponsor or engeneer expired is not fun.
I'll try to squeeze some more joy out of it, but so far I'm not impressed. I would recommend it only after some major price drop, fur now it's not worth it.

Been a gamer my whole life, and as a military veteran, I enjoy mil sims quite a bit when done with detail. I went into this with some excitement, ready to dig in and make this a 'Study Sim' similar to how much I enjoy DCS World for its complexity.
Honest review:
Fairly disappointed. The complexity seems to be mostly found in the difficulty of managing the very awkward text based interface(the display screens look more like raw database output than anything you would see in a military scenario), instead of a realitic or immersive form of complexity. And then the rest - parts where I expected more content - just seem shallow, not complex, and even money-grabbing, to be honest.
As a fan of Dangerous Waters and other strategic milsims of that top-down type, I thought this was more of the same, with many more units. On paper, that is what this looks like. The Steam store page makes it look like that.
In reality, this is pretty much LESS of the same, so to speak. I am trying to play this more - maybe they really hid the features I am missing here?, but its really not holding my interest and it feels like work, it is not engrossing.
Compared to Dangerous Waters, this is like that, but then start removing things. There is no sitting at the stations to man them yourself, hear what they hear, take sensors through their logical functions, find that submarine YOURSELF, all the FUN, ENGROSSING PARTS. None of that. There is the same sensor(as a game object, but not literally seen or operated), and some dude says he found the sub and you choose to attack it, but all that is text on the screen feedback or at best, new icons or circles on the map. Nothing tangible to dig into.
Compared to Dangerous Waters, this is like that, but then take away the 3D view. They did not model the equipment in any way I can find. Those icons on the map are all you get. I know DW didnt have great graphics or animations or effects, but the effort made to let me SEE what I am doing makes a difference in situational awareness.
The supposed upside of this would be that it has SO MANY MORE MODELS than DW, and it does. That falls apart very quickly though, when you realize that means MORE LINES IN A DATABASE, and not much else. No equipment to operate in any tangible way, no manual tasks to do in a realistic way simulating how it works in real life at all, nothing. Just more text than the other guy. That rings VERY holllow to me.
When you take away the skill-based ability to see, operate, and successfully use a simulation of the equipment, what you are left with is a 'Simulator' - where the AI does most of the work , everything is too automatic and simple, and the map and text are very hollow and seem a lot more like an alpha prototype engine for a future simulator, than a functional simulator realized.
Last but certainly not least, there is price. I am a 'Binford model' guy, and if you don't get the reference I mean, I buy the best one, every time. I want something that will last and has a solid warranty behind it. I will always pay more for quality. But I do that not because my money means nothing, I do that because I am looking for QUALITY. And the price of this is BAD. Far beyond BAD. When you have some simple icons, text menus and a database of theoretical specs for lots of equipment, there is really only so much work you did in making your game. Thats just the reality of it. Eighty Bucks is a joke . I got this for Twenty Five on sale and man, I wouldn't do THAT again. I really don't feel like even hardcore milsim folks would find this a good deal at Eighty. no way.
But it gets worse - this game is LONG on DLC and not afraid to push it. The first 21 maps you can load in SP are all DLC bait. Each prompts you to make an additional purchase of twenty or more to add to your eighty you already, honestly.... wasted on this database dump of a 'mil sim'. I can't honestly use that term to describe this, because its got lots of Mil but they didnt really try to Sim any of it.
Lesson learned on this one - its too late for me to return it. But the lesson would be: mil-sim realism doesn't mean much if its at the cost of pretty much all other features like ACTUAL simulation of equipment or letting me visually see the toys I am putting into use.
Highly un-recommend this. No idea what they had in mind, but it feels like they missed their mark wide left, or maybe they just know they are fleecing people for way more than the game deserves. That last part might be more likely than you think: I get the impression this above AAA price is an attempt to fund turning this prototype database modeler/engine into an ACTUAL GAME in Command 2 when it comes out.
