I picked up 40k Regicide for two reasons. The first is because I love the 40k universe, and the second is because I want to support the devs (Straya represent).
I wouldn't say I'm disappointed but I definitely was not grabbed by the game.
Yes, the game is more or less chess with Space Marines and Orks, with light turn based tactics gameplay sprinkled on in the Regicide mode. If you don't like chess then you probably won't like 40k Regicide. Fortunately I do enjoy chess (not as much as I used to though, chess club kid here, no really) and I can't wait to play this with a friend or two.
The visuals and audio are nice and hit all the right 40k notes, but otherwise aren't spectacular, the gameplay is, as previously mentioned, chess, but the light tactics gameplay (which takes place after your chess move) allows you to change up the game in ways that might pull you through if you suck at chess (chess club kid who never payed attention here, no really) which is nice, but it's not enough to make the game stop being chess.
If you like to play chess then pick up this game, if you're a big fan of 40k then I'd recommend waiting for the campaign to be released in its entirety (not out yet, and the first injection will be 15 out of the 50 promised missions) because from the teasers and interviews it looks like it's going to be pretty cool. If you fall into both of these camps then you can safely grab the game now, and if you fall into neither then just give this one a miss.
For what it's worth you are getting your money's worth here, and even more when the campaign releases.

Ever wanted your own naval ops command center? Look no further my friends. The breadth and depth of this title is staggering, and I wouldn't have it any other way. This is pretty much a sim I've always wanted my entire life and I didn't know it till now. But be warned, this is not for the feint of heart.
If Paradox grand strategy games or Ageod and HPS wargames are too much for you to handle, this is certainly not for you. If, on the other hand, you are a fan of those titles and want to take it up another notch (or three!) give this sim a look. I've been a fan of both turn-based strategy and real time strategy games based on historical military engagements played on the PC since the late 1980's, and I have to say that "C:MANO" is a fantasy come true. I tried playing Harpoon before, but for some reason, its user interface kept leaving me frustrated and I didn't feel immersed in my encounters because of the struggle I had with the UI. C:MANO's user interface is better, and more intuitive, and right after I bought it I was able to immediately play and enjoy a scenario without reading a document or manual. The unit/weapon database is astounding in depth and surprisingly updated. It truly is a fantasy sandbox for anyone wanting to see how a scenario involving a particular set of units would play out. I recommend this game to hard core real-time real world military simulation enthusiast who will not be turned off by the fact that the game doesn't have much "Michael Bay" effects in it--only serious number crunching and fantastically accurate outcomes of scenarios and engagements. Two-thumbs up.

Once in a while, a simulation or game comes around so complex it almost becomes a hobby in itself to learn it properly. War in the East by Matrix Games in one such game/simulation. DCS World is another. Command: Modern Air/Naval Operations is almost one too. I have to be honest though, when I got it I was pretty much able to get a game going rather quickly thanks to right-click menus and some quick reading of the manual. But to truly master it will take years.
Command, or CMANO, is nothing short of an ops room simulation.
Equipped with a database containing a mass of platforms spanning from the 50’s up until the near future is a sandbox within which the player can explore a multitude of historical and speculative scenarios. It is relatively scaled back in terms of visuals and sound, NATO symbology representing the various ships and aircraft in any given scenario, the playground is spread across the globe with audible warnings of hostile weapons releases and the roar of missile launches being the peak of the audio experience. This is a hardcore simulation. A simulation that turns into a sandbox for all those what-if’s or for recreating history. It’s an impressive achievement by the developers. Highly recommended for the Harpoon crowd.

A sniper's narrative:
My company and I had just fought a harsh battle against the allies for a town, we won, but at a costly death count. We pushed them all the way back to a bridge which was a snipers dream, plenty of perfect shots, if we had dreams. After the short skirmish for the bridge, the enemy fell back to a medium sized cottage at the end of the bridge, I was no help as the only way to clear them and push further was a snipers nightmare of close encounters inside a building with no support. Soon we pushed them from their entrenched location at the cottage to a small farm shed, lots of trees, plenty of cover and hiding spots, I went undetected. After killing many men who had not realized the importance of keeping your head down they fell back to a mansion like building that the small shed must have belonged to. As a woodland hunter of men, this was easy and simple, my job was to cover our left flank and snipe anyone who decided to push from the position of the mansion. Simple for a sniper of my qualifications, however somehow a couple of them ambushed my position, I don't know how. A good distance from immediate support I decided to ditch the rifle and switch to my pistol and make a run for it, I made it, barely. However now I had a dilemma, they had my rifle, and them being inexperienced with it could not hit moving targets, that did not stop them from taking a couple soldiers by surprise. I grabbed a spare rifle and went to work of hunting those that had hunted me. They didn't stand a chance, they were easy to find, being inexperienced in the sniper trade they had held my position, they were all down before even one realized where the shots had come from. Feeling that I had eliminated the threat to my hide I went back to my original position if not pushed up further as my troops had gained some ground, same task as before kill any who attempted to flank and those who could be taken down. Four soldiers came for me, I was only able to react in time due to the clumsiness of one, their plan was to surround me and take me down with a quick blow to the back of the head, so as nobody in my immediate vicinity would hear the gunshots and come to my aid. Smart plan, but the supposed knockout man was too hasty and I heard him just in time to dodge the shovel he swung at me, I turned around and as the shovel was rather unwieldy he could not recover, I shot him point blank with my rifle, he was dead before he even started to fall, his haste was his squads downfall, as they were a decent distance away, one was 25 feet away, another a mere 20 and there last man a manageable 30 feet away, the closer two were from the same direction, the further third was to my left at the time, I was able to recover fast enough to get two shots into the man who was 25 feet away, two shots to the chest from my rifle put him down for good, his friend who was now a mere 15 feet away as he had closed some distance, began to fire, I took cover from the incoming fire behind a tree and pulled my pistol, it only took three shots, when I went behind the tree he pushed too fast to flank my left, I took him down when he was 10 feet away, he was still running. His unsuccessful flanking maneuver was what allowed me to see the third member who had just started setting up to start laying fire on me with his rifle, he was a lot more accurate than his late friends. He was 20 feet away, that zone of fire where the pistol is too inaccurate to make the shot, the time it took to get back to my rifle was just long enough for him to start his barrage of well-timed and well placed shots, I peeked around the tree to use the rifle, he hit me in the arm, just a flesh wound however it put the rifle out of my ability to use, the pain would make me too inaccurate and he had hit my main support arm so as even attempting to aim the rifle would be impossible in my current state. He thought I was worse off than I was, he pushed carefully, checking to see if I would make a move every 5 feet he moved up, I made my move with my pistol when he was still moving at 7 feet away, I had to use my left hand, which was not my primary go to when it came to accurate aiming and fire control, and I managed to spray my pistol in a hastily aimed pain filled barrage, firing all five bullets that remained in the clip, I hit him with only two. One to his left shoulder and another to his chest, right side, he went down hard. I reloaded and aimed a shot at his head and fired to make sure he was not faking, he was not. We won but at a cost, I fully recovered and went back to sniping poor inexperienced soldiers, sadly not everyone had such small easily dealt with wounds.
Thus was the battle of a small town that was known as a tactical chokepoint due to its bridges being wide enough to move armor and supplies up further, would us having this town win us the war? No, not directly, but indirectly maybe, one can only hope that those soldiers died for the winning side, and hope that their sacrifice lead to victory. It is the task of the survivors of war to not only remember the dead, but to fight for them as well, and if possible even win for them.
This is how I play Heroes and Generals. You don't have to be as dramatic as I am about it, but it allows you to build your own narrative and stories. I like this game a lot and of the 62 hours I have played at this moment an estimated 40 hours are fought by my sniper. Great game decent graphics, and honestly I love it a lot, have fun and no matter the side you choose I hope to see you on the front lines.

Far Cry 3 comes in the acclaimed series starting with the original Far Cry, which was for its era a pioneering game. The third entry is a first-person shooter that combines elements of the original open-world of Far Cry, a huge variety of side quests a la GTA, with small touches of Tomb Raider and Assasin´s Creed.
It manages to surpass the original in every aspect and manages to become a reference for this game kind.
Pros:
+ vast environment with tons of quests to do and places to explore by climbing, paragliding and swimming
+ excellent graphics, effects and animations
+ memorable villains and some very interesting secondary characters, all presented through well-thoughout dialogs and a main story with shocking and mature-oriented moments
+ variety in arsenal, different play styles from stealth to full-gun blazing
+ nice music (especially at the very end :)) and sound effects
+ game duration can be tuned according to player, most quests are optional; tons of achievements and tasks for the completionists
Cons:
- some quests can become a bit repeated towards the end, same for the environment which always remains jungle-like
- some parts of the main quest do not make a lot of sense.
- music beat can be a bit distracting in some battle moments
- second island is perhaps less interesting and challenging than the first one
- connection to uplay is obligatory to play even if you open it through steam
All in all, a real gem and a must-play action game that defines the standards for the genre. This is how sequels should be made.

Vermintide is a hack n' slash Left 4 Dead w/ loot & fantasy trappings. The core gameplay is great, cutting down giant hordes is awesome. But the game falters with its reliance on RNG elements.
Firstly, the loot system relies on literal dice rolls. Weapons & gear aren't handed out based on your accomplishments or progress, rather difficulty setting & item pick ups in a level effect your random chance of maybe getting something good. This leads players to not play for fun. Instead they try to abuse & exploit the system or ai & find easy ways to beat levels just for the slim chance at getting some decent equipment. There's literally no reason for this system other than to pad out the game.
Secondly the AI that controls the enemy spawns (the equivalent of L4D's "director") is clearly much dumber. L4D's director was programmed well enough to take balance, location & level pacing into account. But here the director seems to be more RNG based. Aside from the scripted areas for Rat Ogres to appear, it's a dice role on what will show up where. I've had my entire team wiped from multiple assassin & packmaster spawns. Especially at the end of a level the "director" tends to just hammer you with hordes & specials in an attempt to kill you. And if you die you get an insulting amount of crystals (crafting materials), like 8 or so, which really doesn't make up for wasting 10 or 20 minutes on a doomed run.
It's fun for a L4D rip off but its abuse of RNG can really waste the players time, annoy & infuriate. It relies on these elements to pad the game out. If that bothers you, or if you value your time, give this game a pass. But the core of the game is good & the flavor of the game, the character banter, the setting, that's all good.

Hmm... What to say about this game...
Like Warhammer?
Like Left 4 Dead?
Like 4 player co-op?
Have friends to play with?
Like PvE?
Hate rats?
If you answered yes to any pair of these, you'll probably enjoy this.
These pairings pretty much sum the game and gameplay experience up.
1. Vermintide is pretty much Games Workshop's Warhammer spin on Left 4 Dead.
Everything from the hordes, through to the Specials. With an End Times twist.
The only real difference being a Class base to your heroes. Each with a specified weapon set (no weapon swaps/pick ups), which you can edit at the beginning of each map, if you don't do so at the Tavern (lobby) between missions.
Also, ammo is somewhat scarce, so the combat is predominantly melee based.
2. The game is a 4 player co-op, with 5 playable characters.
Each has his own pros and cons, gameplay-wise.
When playing with less than 4 players (full lobby), AI bots will fill the role of your teammate(s).
Unlike other 4 player co-ops, teamwork is a lot more vital to mission success. Not only when dealing with the Skaven in numbers, but also completing objectives.
You can play solo (with AI "assist" - I used that term loosely), but it is not recommended above Normal difficulty, and once you get downed, it's very likely to be a mission failure.
3. As stated, like L4D, this game is PvE.
Your adversaries being Skaven, the Ratmen.
Seeing as Fatshark are such big (self-admitted) L4D fans, and took A LOT of influence from the franchise - can you call it a franchise, if there's only two of them? It's not even really a series. Might just go with a "duology"... Anyhoo... - I wouldn't be surprised if one day they decided to turn the tables, and let players assume control of the Skaven Specials, a la L4D.
The devs did a great job on this game.
The maps are large, the load times are fast, and there is no latency between transitions to new area.
*Note: once you progress to the next area, you can not return to the former, so it'd play to utilise any pick ups found, etc. before moving on.
There are hidden areas on the maps, so it pays to explore, if you have the time to spare. Also, through experience, you risk the chance of triggering a horde if you hang around too long, so be warned.
Weapons and customisation is a bit of a touchy subject with this game... I'll just say that it leaves something to be desired.
I understand the justification for the system, believe me, but when trying to create replayability factors for a game, let it be based on the gameplay experience itself (which this game definitely has), not and RNG reward system.
In my opinion, this is the only point this game falls short on.
That said, nobody's perfect.
I would definitely recommend this game, and see myself continuing to play it regularly in the foreseeable future.

This isn’t Dirt Rally 2.
You need to give it some time to get used to it, but it's a great addition to the DiRT franchise.

Even though it may not seem so at first glance, DiRT 4 is perhaps the most ambitious entry in the series.  Overall, it is a pretty great product and shows a clear path forward for the franchise, although there is plenty of room for improvement and it is unlikely that anyone will be totally satisfied by what is on offer here.
DiRT 4 attempts to be a product that caters to both the newer sim-friendly fans of DiRT Rally as well as the more arcadey fans that enjoyed the other mainline DiRT games.  It is extremely difficult to cater to two wildly different styles and sets of demands in the same game without massively compromising both experiences.  What DiRT 4 tries to do is akin to putting Call of Duty and ARMA-styles of gameplay in the same game while keeping things fun and engaging for both styles, and keeping that in mind, DIRT 4 turns in a superb result here.
The fans of the original DiRT games, who are more accustomed to arcadier handling and a larger variety of event types, may find themselves wanting here sadly.  The main event of DiRT 4 is rally on increasingly tight and technical tracks, with Rallycross and Landrush being the only diversions from it.  Fans of the originals who just liked slipping around in a bunch of different disciplines without worrying all that much about perfection won't have that variety on offer here when compared with previous entries in the series, the rally may be too flavorless and difficult, the absence of rewind may be frustrating, and the handling may still be too unforgiving.
The sim-friendly fans get the better deal out of this, in my opinion.  With the simulation handling, we have a largely improved showing over DiRT Rally in my opinion, which was a bit too slippery and had overpowered braking.  While this game currently has a bit too much understeer and collisions aren't punishing enough, it clearly improves over Rally with better tarmac handling, better grip on gravel, more accurate braking, and a better sense of momentum that has meaningful consequences.  Its worth noting that too many reviews on here just stem from the first hour of the campaign, which has you in a vehicle with a ridiculous level of understeer that isn't representative of the rest of the game.  Taking my favorite car from Rally (the '95 Subaru) feels better and more realistic to me in DiRT 4, even if that "realism" means sliding less.  Each car and class of cars feel distinct and unique.  The classic Mini is a nice even training car, and the RWD cars will leave you wondering what sadist came up with the idea to do something so nasty to people.
The other big innovation is YourStage, which is a random rally track generator.  This is a huge benefit for the game because it makes each track unique and unpredictable, although there is clear room for improvement.  Each of the 5 locations in the game have different sets of "blocks" which can be randomly formed together depending on length and complexity sliders.  The game then takes that course and does some variation on the surrounding envornment.  It's a great system, but there are a few drawbacks.  First off, while the results do look quite natural and nice (I've never seen a result that was unnatural or outright broken), there is a step down from DiRT Rally both in terms of visual fidelity and in terms of unique track design.  You won't have anything looking as good or as unique as Greece or Monte Carlo (?) in Rally, however DiRT 4 makes up for that at times by having a large variety of dynamic weather enabled here that can look great and be surprising too.  Second, there is a lack of variety in the "blocks" available in each location, meaning that you may have the same turn or area repeat several times in a stage, which can be distracting.  Third, aside from having a competing car crash on the track ahead of you, there is very little that is randomized on these blocks to make them different, such as bumps, slopes, or other alterations that would really beef up the randomization.  The end result of YourStage is that instead of memorizing entire tracks, you are largely memorizing individual turns or sets because they will show up more often than they ideally would.  It's still a great system, but it could've been a lot more with, say, an additional 33% more "blocks" per location and a system that added more unique features to those blocks.
Graphically, the game looks quite good.  While some of the texture work and foliage is pretty weak (the foliage in particular could really use a higher resolution option on PC), the game can look quite striking when it plays to its strengths, like the lighting and weather effects.  Going around a hairpin and seeing dirt you kicked up 15 seconds ago still be in the air is a great touch.  The sound is fantastic, with plenty of incidental detail when driving and solid voicework.
The campaign is solid enough, with the main hooks being the building up and staffing of your team and leveling up.  You sign contracts to get staff and sponsors, and as you level up and can afford more, you can get upgrades and better staff that give various bonuses, including ones that vastly increase the ability to repair effectively during rally events.  You can keep taking sponsored cars which are always provided in exchange for a significant cut of your winnings, or you can buy and race your own cars, which can be purchased new from a dealership or used, which gives a good deal of choice that isn't usually apparent in many racing games.
Multiplayer is good but has some issues.  Aside from a lobby-based versus multiplayer where the host has a lot of control, there are two limited-time events: a tiered competitive versus system and a series of various no-restart single-player leaderboard events that payout based on your performance relative to other competitors.  The latter is really fun because there is no way to escape catastrophe aside from quitting (and losing any potential payout) or just pushing through.  The tiered competitive mode is flawed because everyone starts out on the bottom, and only the top half gain any points to advance through the ranks, while the lower half lose points.  Also, while the leaderboards are cross-platform, the multiplayer isn't, which means that there is a pretty fair shortage of players.  There won't be a lot of lobbies open, and the competitve ladder is pretty much DOA from my experience.
While it is a pretty solid package overall and it does a great job of merging the wants of the two sets of fans the series has, the end result is a good title that has a fair amount of room for improvement regardless of which side of that divide you fall on.  There's a lot of good work in this package and deserves more love and attention than it seems to be getting currently, even though it's likely that a good chunk of what is on offer won't be to your liking.

DIRT 4 is the ideal rally simulation with genuine unpredictability and lasting value. It is not a sequel to the energetic DiRT 3; it's a refinement of DIRT Rally with a few throwbacks to the older games in the series. It is mostly a strenuous rally simulation that rewards time and effort, with a near endless number of procedurally generated rally stages. The mixed assemblage of hairpins, hills, and hazards produces a few similar corners, but it's still a great addition over a limited number of unchanging tracks. The career progression is excellent with a small amount of team management added for good measure. The non-rally modes, Landrush and Rallycross, pale in comparison although are not without their moments. Joy Ride might be Ken Block screaming at Codemasters to let him back inside, but it ultimately proves to be a minor distraction. The multiplayer side of things is quite good, and the online challenges will keep you coming back for more. Taking into account all of these pieces, DiRT 4 is a superior rally game to DIRT Rally and its additional content is marginally stronger. With the success of DiRT 4, Codemasters will likely continue pushing rally to the fore, and I am excited to see what road lies ahead.

Did you love Final Fantasy tactics?
Do you love that feeling of accomplishment despite the hellish pain of constant death that rivals even Dark Souls? Do you love deep tactical rewarding strategy based combat?
Then Wakfu will probably be the game for you. On its cute and pristine exterior, there's a huge amount of depth and punishing dungeons and temples. This isn't your average MMO, you wipe in a temple that can take nearly an hour to complete? Well that's too bad, you'll have to start from the very beginning. This isn't some game you can get away with spamming. Positioning, timing and execution is key. Even basic battles against mobs have a strategic depth to them that feels foreign to an MMORPG.
This game runs on turn based grid combat, you level your character like any other in an RPG, however each element has its specialties. Fire is typically AOE (area of effect) , Earth is typically direct damage, Water is usually healing or mobility debuffs or buffs with some damage mixed in. Air is usually knockbacks or line telegraph attacks. But that's only typically, each class feels extremely different. From manipulating time, to picking up your foes and tossing them, to entirely relying on lady luck in combat. Wakfu brings a whole new fresh style to combat that I've never experienced in an MMO before.
Words of warning, if you like questing, you'll find it extremely lacking on quests until you reach the out-lying islands of the nations of the World of Twelve. However they continue to work on updating the game with more quest lines that guide you into areas. I say your first real challenging quest chain is on the Wild Estates, where a mixture of puzzle solving, challenging battles, even sports and an Indiana Jones style hunt for an artifact will take center stage. Did I mention its really hard? Because, it's really bworking hard!
There's a large slew of crafting professions, an entirely player run economy, and the most challenging PVE MMO experience I've ever had. As for the PVP I haven't experienced too much of it. It depends on the server you join but the economy has been somewhat at a standstill and it's more likely you will get trades from your haven bag or face to face than the market. Kamas, the games currency aren't all that hard to get however, especially considering you can mint them yourself.
Wakfu is a beautifully designed, deep and well made game that is literally the most challenging experience I've had in an MMO, rivals even what I experienced in my days of EVE in terms depth of combat. There's really a whole slew of possibilities you can approach a battle based on your class and playstyle, those possibilities yet nail biting, hair pulling difficulty is something I do have to admit that I love. We need more games like Wakfu, not MMOs, just games period. This game is the XCOM: Enemy Unknown of MMOs, it's about as tense too. Give the game a shot, add me on Steam if you'd want to party up, don't be afraid to ask questions to the community either, they're quite understanding and helpful, there will be a few bad eggs I'm sure.
In closing, Wakfu is a generously made game, with a lot of love and hardwork put into it, down to the extremely artistic style handcrafted areas, and lovable design

I would recommend this game, but there are certain things about it that different kinds of gamers may or may not like, I'll try to sum up some of the specific qualities.
1: Like most MMOs it's a long grind to the higher levels, but it doesn't feel like you're doing the same thing over and over, generally you get to go through different dungeons and fight new monsters the more you level so you aren't always doing the same thing.
2: You have specific skills you can build, everything from Farming/baking to being a jeweler there's lots of stuff you can do other than punching monsters faces all day, you don't absolutely have to if you're the kind of person who just likes fighting, but it can be helpful and even fun to learn these skills, some sidequests involve using these skills as well.
3: There is a story to the game but it's really not the main focus until you level up drastically, but even so there are plenty of other things to occupy your time in this game, really half of it feels like you're making your own story with other players, which moves me on to the next topic.
4: Politics, yes I said politics, there is a political and economic system in the game world that is run by the players, you can vote for elections or even become governer yourself, laws are set to keep the economy well (or to leech off of other players if they're a dirty politician) not to mention if you break the law you will be labled at a ciminal that other players will attack, and if you are caught then you will have your character sent to jail, also laws are in place to keep the ecosystem in order, which once again moves me onto the next topic.
5: Ecosystem, yes there's indeed an ecosystem in this game, you want wood? Plant some trees but don't cut too many down, want to hunt some monsters? Make sure too many of them don't get killed but also don't let there be too many ect ect. There are generally laws in place to help keep it balanced.
6: Character Classes, there are a total of fourteen different classes to choose from "Damage dealers tanks and healers oh my!" There's tons of variety in terms of how each class plays, each have their own mechanics making none of them truly "useless" Yes there's one that's overpowered but even that one has a down side, so in terms of classes you won't be dissapointed.
So if the things I just mentioned sound interesting and maybe even fun I would highly reccomend trying this one out, it has a beautiful art style and TONS of content to keep you playing!

I prefer games like war games like Hearts of Iron, Supreme Ruler and the ilk.  This game is not like those except in the broadest terms.  Those games have some complexity, but they aren't too difficult to figure out... they are intutive, for the most part, this game on the other hand is not.  My opinion may change if I ever take the time to get a complete understanding of it, but at present that seems a daunting task. The tutorials aren't very good and the graphics need updating.  I normally don't care too much about graphics, but this game seems to be lacking them almost altogether.  The price of the game is too high in my opinion.  I think the game is so high because of all the research involved.  Having a large database is nice, but I think the first goal should be playability.  The playability for this game is woefully lacking.  I wish I could trade this game in for another... they make a game that I think I would enjoy much more (War in the East). I bought it on sale for $59.99 (normally $79.99) and can already tell that it really isn't a game for me... and have only put in a couple hours or so. BLUF: This is not a "game" in so much as it is the best simulator of modern air and naval combat I've ever come across.
You may want this game if:
you seek the highest realism and detail possible in a warfare simulation.
you enjoy commanding huge forces and using them in complex actions.
you enjoyed reading Janes encyclopedias as a kid (or adult).
Do your research before buying this. This is not for anyone that is a casual gamer, or thinks they can easily transition from an RTS or grand strategy game to this. This may as well be running on a pentagon computer as a simulation to game out attack strategies for the next major war. There is no "gameyness" here. Everything is modelled to the Nth degree. Radars, radar signiature, electronic countermeasures, nukes, weapon systems, sonar and sound propogation including CZ's, effects of weather... literally untold effort over years was poured into this, and not a minute was wasted on 3D modeling and lighting effects. The end result: You are the commander. You know what your ships and planes look like, you've spent decades around them. You've spent years training for a war you hoped would never come. Now, it is time to put the forces of your nation into action. This is the command center, and it looks like one.
I can't reccommend this program enough.

CMANO is one of the greatest simulation games out there for those who are interested in military hardware. From it's seemingly endless and detailed military database to it's many scenarios that cover a period from 1945-2020 this is a military armchair generals wet dream. The game mechanics include a serious sensor/weapon gameplay in which an intricate amount of calculations are made akin to an actual military grade combat simulator. You want to see what happens when X forces attack Y area that has Z units? You will get a pretty accurate picture of how it would end up with this game.
In addition the editor seems to be a endless toolbox where you can exercise your dream military engagements and even create campaigns with some effort. There is a great deal of tools like triggers, events, scores, weather, time that help you create whatever scenario you dreamt of. The editor is where most of my time went to I tested hundreds of military hardwares in different situations. To give a few examples the S400 vs F35 or DF21D vs Gerald Ford Class Carrier. Both tests ended up having very interesting results.
There are some obvious downsides namely being the UI and Performance but those are not distruptive to the experience and have been improving ever since it's release with 9 big patches released so far. Kudos to the developer team for their continuous support of the product. As of the writing of this review I think the game has gotten very smooth on these two weak points.  In addition to those points I have to say out that the visual aspects of the game are weak since it features a world map but it maintains the modern Command and Control Center operator feel which is crucial.
If you think the price curve is too high for CMANO go get Command: Northern Inferno it's a smaller scale CMANO that features a 1975 Cold War turning hot campaign that will teach you how to play and will give you good a taste of the game mechanics.
In Conclusion I give this game 9/10.

This is one of my top 3 favorite games. Why? Well, here are some pros and cons:
+Depth
This is something inherent to any good sim. To simulate a proper environment, the game must allow one to interact with the world to a huge extent. C:MANO excels at this. You can manage aircraft loadouts from a huge variety of options, decide the speed and height/depth each unit follows. Weapons can be fired automatically, but also can be manually fired if the player prefers an exact amount. Want your units to fire more AMRAAMs at targets automatically? If so, you can tweak that with an extensive ROE/EMCON/whatnot menu. This governs a variety of things from the use of nuclear weapons and evasive manuevering to what radar/sonar/ECM profiles your units follow. This can also be set on a unit to unit basis.
+Editor
This is where I spend most of my time. While the game comes with a large variety of scenarios and the "Community Scenario Pack" contains enough that you will never finish them all, sometimes there are places where the player wants something else. Want to have a fight between two opposing carrier groups or test that weapon system against another? Well, you can do that. While I typically prefer to make shorter, less intricate missions, there is a scripting system in place for all of your more complicated ideas.
+Database
This pretty much goes hand in hand with the editor. Without both, the game couldn't really thrive. Really, I am constantly surprised at how many systems are there. From supercarriers and hypothetical aircraft to obscure coast guard helicopters, the game has it. Ohh, and if it doesn't, it also has a huge weapons database. Want to give that arleigh burke a laser? Well, its pretty fun.
+Active Developers
Something I find great about C:MANO is that, despite the release being, in my opinion, worth the money, the devs have continued to update the game, adding features that I never knew I would love.
+Realism
Realism is obviously going to be inherent in this type of game, but realism does not make a game great. However, when the other, above things are considered, it adds a lot of extra value. The effort they put into the ECM and Radar systems are truely astounding. It adds extra meaning when your aircraft have realistic sortie rates and your weapons have the proper ranges. It allows C:MANO to be beyond a game, and be a sim where one can learn about many technologies from the early Cold War to the near future.
+-UI
From a quick glance, it is easy to call the UI ugly and overall of poor quality. Sure, there are some things that could use improvement, but the UI is ultimately very functional. I actually like how it looks because it gives the impression of a more realistic program, something a more gamey UI could not provide.
+-Learning Curve
That is one of the concerns about the game. Having a steep learning curve can be very annoying to new players and can easily scare off potential customers. However, while a difficult learning curve is hardly ideal, it is all but necessary in a game with as much depth as C:MANO. I recommend jumping in and playing one of the "First Contact" scenarios a few times. Sure, you will get demolished for a bit, but thats they way I figured out how to play, and I found it quite fun, slowly getting better.
-Land Combat
Land combat, if you couldn't tell from the game's name, is a very weak part of the game. Infantry platoons are always unable to kill anything before running out of ammo and vehicles behave in an unrealistic manner. As I have heard said before, land units in this game only exist to be targets. Another huge failure is the inability to disembark land units from landing craft, helicopters, and aircraft. Many scenario authors will teleport/create ground units to simulate this, but it is always very artificial and restricted. However, as I said before, the dev team is very active, and I wouldn't be surprised at all if land combat was fixed later.
-Price
Okay, the $80 price tag is very steep. However, I absolutely believe it is worth the cost. There isn't another game like it, and it is truely a gem. Also, I would like to point out that many people spend $60 on games of *much* less quality every year.
I think its also reasonable to point out that Steam Refunds exist.
Anyway, I think the last thing I should point out is that C:MANO isn't for everyone. It is a very time consuming game and even some of the shorter scenarios are quite long. Even if you do have an abundance of time, any possible enjoyment could be taken away by its slow pacing or lack of visuals.
Thanks for reading this, good luck with your decision-making. :)

Regicide mode, however, pretty much only keeps the movement and "capturing" of pieces chess-like. In this mode you have abilities, unit actions along the lines of snapping off some shots at an enemy unit, throwing grenades, or going to ground. Also including amazing animations and badass killcams! (Watching the Librarian turn an enemy unit into a fine red mist never gets old.)
The graphics and audio are top-notch, each unit has it's own unique lines and actor and the models themselves look exceptional!
In all, I could probably continue rambling on an on, but, to sum it up? This game is incredibly fun, and I highly recommend it!

Hmm... What to say about this game...
Like Warhammer?
Like Left 4 Dead?
Like 4 player co-op?
Have friends to play with?
Like PvE?
Hate rats?
If you answered yes to any pair of these, you'll probably enjoy this.
These pairings pretty much sum the game and gameplay experience up.
1. Vermintide is pretty much Games Workshop's Warhammer spin on Left 4 Dead.
Everything from the hordes, through to the Specials. With an End Times twist.
The only real difference being a Class base to your heroes. Each with a specified weapon set (no weapon swaps/pick ups), which you can edit at the beginning of each map, if you don't do so at the Tavern (lobby) between missions.
Also, ammo is somewhat scarce, so the combat is predominantly melee based.
2. The game is a 4 player co-op, with 5 playable characters.
Each has his own pros and cons, gameplay-wise.
When playing with less than 4 players (full lobby), AI bots will fill the role of your teammate(s).
Unlike other 4 player co-ops, teamwork is a lot more vital to mission success. Not only when dealing with the Skaven in numbers, but also completing objectives.
You can play solo (with AI "assist" - I used that term loosely), but it is not recommended above Normal difficulty, and once you get downed, it's very likely to be a mission failure.
3. As stated, like L4D, this game is PvE.
Your adversaries being Skaven, the Ratmen.
Seeing as Fatshark are such big (self-admitted) L4D fans, and took A LOT of influence from the franchise - can you call it a franchise, if there's only two of them? It's not even really a series. Might just go with a "duology"... Anyhoo... - I wouldn't be surprised if one day they decided to turn the tables, and let players assume control of the Skaven Specials, a la L4D.
The devs did a great job on this game.
The maps are large, the load times are fast, and there is no latency between transitions to new area.
*Note: once you progress to the next area, you can not return to the former, so it'd play to utilise any pick ups found, etc. before moving on.
There are hidden areas on the maps, so it pays to explore, if you have the time to spare. Also, through experience, you risk the chance of triggering a horde if you hang around too long, so be warned.
Weapons and customisation is a bit of a touchy subject with this game... I'll just say that it leaves something to be desired.
I understand the justification for the system, believe me, but when trying to create replayability factors for a game, let it be based on the gameplay experience itself (which this game definitely has), not and RNG reward system.
In my opinion, this is the only point this game falls short on.
That said, nobody's perfect.
I would definitely recommend this game, and see myself continuing to play it regularly in the foreseeable future.

This game wears it's inspiration on it's sleeve - it's so much like Left 4 Dead you'll find some of your old techniques work just as well in Vermintide.  It's basically the same mechanics - fight of hordes of cannon fodder npcs (in this case, Skaven which are ratmen) while keeping a sharp eye out for special Skaven that seek to pin and separate members of the group.  It even includes "boss" fights in the form of a Rat Ogre (think of the L4D tank) and patrolling teams of StormScaven (that can be avoided like the wandering witch from L4D2 - it's really better NOT to fight them)
That being said - the game is more melee focused than range focused.  So depending on your blunderboss or crossbow for most of your work is unwise - it's best saved for special situations.
There are 5 classes in the game, each with their own distinct personalities and weaponsets.  Each class has several weaponsets of their own which have their own attack animations and various strengths and weaknesses.   some are better at handling large single targets, some are good at cleaving large numbers of foes, others are better at blocking or knocking down foes.  There's bound to be a weaponset that suits your playstyle.
The game also has a random loot system and a leveling system.  All the leveling appears to do is give out free weapons at every level and unlock maps and features in the Inn (which is more or less the lobby).
The Loot system is very interesting.  You see, you get to roll 8 dice at the end of a SUCCESSFUL run.  The default dice have a 1 and 3 chance of giving you a point.  The number of points you get determines which loot on the random loot table to your right you get.  The more points you get, the better the loot.  The harder the difficulty you set for the mission, the better the loot table you get.  You can further increase your chances in the roll by finding certain dice in the level.  Each special die you find replaces one of the 8 dice you have.  These dice have better chances of rewarding a point.  Ones you find in chests, for example, give you a 50/50 chance of getting a point.   There is Tomes you can pick up (each level has 3), these tomes give you a dice that gives you a 66 percent chance at a point.   The catch?  you need to give up your healing item to hold it.  There's also a skaven you can find and kill (but he runs right into a horde) that will drop you a loot die.  Finally, there's two skaven grimoirs you can find that guarantee you'll get a point - but the cost is your potion slot and 25% of your team's health - additionally if you drop the grimoire either purposely or by dying - it's lost for the rest of that round and cannot be recovered.
So as you can see, the game actually ENCOURAGES you to explore rather than just rush through everything and rewards you for taking that additional risk.  Greater risk for the chance of a greater reward.
As for mechanically, here's how it breaks down
DIFFICULTY
In all difficultys, the higher you go the harder the Scaven hit and the better your loot table.  However there are additional things to consider
Easy and Normal - No difference other than the above
Hard - You start with no Heal items.
Nightmare - Friendly fire is turned on for ranged weapons and bombs.
Cataclysm - Friendly fire is ramped up.
GRAPHICS - Spot on.  I have no complaints about it.  The game is absolutely pretty to behold.  Only complaint I have is that I think a little more work could of been done to make the player characters easier to make out in the middle of the chaos.  Otherwise they did great.  They really nailed it your first person animations.  The way blood flies in relation to your strike helps build the immersion.
MUSIC - fine at first, but gets a bit repetive.  I've tried turning it down, but doesn't seem to help.
SOUND EFFECTS - spot on and satisfying.  When steel meets blood and bone, there is little doubt of what's going on.  Additionally, the sound idenifyers of the special and boss ratmen are hard to miss once you know what they sound like.
COMBAT MECHANICS - the melee combat is fun and serviceable, but just clunky enough to annoy you from time to time. You have stamina which is spent for blocking and pushes and comes back at a reasonible rate.  And the block works as it shoud.  But it's really hard to get a feel for the reach each weapon has, especially in an online environment with a weak host.   The distance each strike reaches is just inconsistant enough for you to notice.   Don't get me wrong though, it's good enough to be fun.
AI - This is probably the games biggest weak point.  Pathfinding for the NPC's is based on the strength of the hosts CPU.  Weaker computers give you some really wonky pathfinding.  Some of the later maps you can really see the difference.  And the bots?  Barely usable.  They tend to get stuck if there's a special Skaven behind you.
Overall?  On a 5 star scale this game is a solid 4 stars.  If i was grading it, I'd give it a 85.  It's a considerably above average game with solid mechanics.  It's only let down with some shoddy pathfinding on a few of the map.   At the price they're offering, it's more than fair.  I recomend this game.

Hydrophobia: Prophecy is an interesting concept that fails too deliver on serveral fronts. The story revolves around Kate Wilson a security agent on a massive ship named "Queen of the World". The homeworld (presumably Earth) lacks resources too sustain human populations; a lucky few live in luxury on the Queen of the World out in the ocean. The cruiser is attacked by a terrorist oragnization known as the Malthusians, a not so clever reference too economist Thomas Malthus. It is up to Kate and what is left of the security forces too navigate and salvage the sinking ship.
Where Hydrophobia fails is in exectution. The game is near impossible too play with a keyboard and is very difficult too use a controller as well. The puzzles are relatively easy, as the game itself always points you in the right direction. The voice acting is absolutely atrocious. The voice actors have no emotion in reading a poor script, which eventually grates on the players ears. Nobody talks like they do in Hydrophobia, in some circumstances it was humorous, but overall really detracted from the overall game. Terribly adapted Japanese animes have better lines then this game. The more I found myself playing the game the more I wanted too turn it off. The pretty water and occasional shootouts do not salvage this game. I can only recommend purchasing this game if it is on sale with a huge discount. Even then you are not missing out.
-Alex

I have to remember to review this game as a Dirt game and not a Dirt Rally game. I was super excited to play with different cars on unique tracks with the same handling characteristics and physics as Dirt. However, it seems that's not exactly the case.
When I first heard about this game, I thought you'd be able to ramp down the arcade of it all and make it really feel like a Dirt Rally experience with an arcade surrounding. Sadly, the arcade feel pokes through more than I would have liked. There's a disconnect between me and the car that doesn't exist in Dirt Rally. I feel like I'm controlling a 3D object instead of a car with real physics simulation. The feedback through the steering wheel feels good at first, but the car doesn't exactly do what I tell it to do based on my input. I feel like I'm wrestling with the programming of the game instead of the weight of the car.
The tracks aren't bad but they are very bland. Sure, Dirt Rally would have you playing the same locations over and over with the same exact turns, but there were specifics to those turns and how the car handled over them with bad camber turns and inconsistencies in the road. In Dirt 4, I'm pretty sure I'm seeing the same exact turns 2 or 3 times within the same "auto generated" track, and not just by the turn itself, but trees and other objects are identical to the point of where I ask myself what lap am I on, then I realize it's a sprint run.
The sound is not all that great, again, comparing this to Dirt Rally. The cones must be made of some high density metal in this game because it makes so much noise when you crawl over one at 2 miles an hour. I played around in Dirt Fish Rally open area to test the small details of the game and accelerating at .1mph makes the tires screech, so not exactly true to life. I get it, it's not a simulation, it's an arcade game with sim options, but still, attention to detail should exist regardless. There's too much music, too much crowd, too little focus on what's important at times, driving. The woman's voice for turns can be really annoying, especially when she tells me how great I am, just tell me the turns and be quiet. Again, all of this is a comparison to Dirt Rally.
The graphics I feel are worse than Rally, detail was put into things that don't matter. I don't care how many and how good the people look at the start or finish, keep the detail in the road and audio, since that's where the immersion should be. The reflections are nicer, which is good but the track detail definitely took a hit.
Overall, not a bad game. Just don't do what I did and expect a longer and more in depth version of Dirt Rally. This is Dirt 3 with the arcadeness of it all turned down by around 15% with “rally stages”. I will say though, the joy ride part is good fun.

I’ve been waiting for this game for 6 years. I’ve only played for 15 hours now but somehow I already felt the urge to write my review and help DiRT4 achieve a ‘Positive’ overall review score. I truly think it deserves it.
I almost got caught up as well in this nonsense of ‘I wish this game was more of DiRT3 / DiRT Rally’. To me the latter was far too difficult; instead I really liked DiRT3’s Gymkhana (!), though DiRT3’s rally stages were much too short for my taste. DiRT2 was a sweet spot.
So what have I gotten in DiRT4? To me it’s a nice blend of DiRT3 and DiRT Rally mixed together.
After DiRT3 we already got DiRT Showdown (120% arcade) and DiRT Rally (pure sim hardcore). Now we can finally decide for ourselves how much assist we want. There is a gamer mode for arcade fans and simulation mode for more skilled players. Gone is the ‘Whoa, dude!’ flavor of DiRT3. Overall interface experience leans toward the more ascetic DiRT Rally and that’s a good thing.
Car models are pretty detailed. They get dirty along stages nicely. The environment is upgraded as well. Birds fly right before your eyes, drones film your journeys. Graphics may not be perfect but it’s fairly decent.
There aren’t many countries present. Instead you get Your Stage® which will make the game even more playable and last longer than it would with more locations but of stages identical every time you use them.
Upgrading your facilities and your team is a great touch. Same with car repair and tuning possibilities. Car selection is nice. Around 50 varied machines. The pre-order Hyundai R5 drives great, just don’t forget to earn the money and buy it!
No rewinds? You get used to it really quickly. Ultimately you can always restart a stage if things go wrong. No flashback functionality means you need to be truly fearless ;-)
All in all DiRT4 is the bomb. Everything that’s best from DiRT3 and DiRT Rally rolled into one. 9/10

Dirt 4 is a very enjoyable game. If you played the old Colin Mcrae games then blasting through the Australia stages will bring back fond memories! This game has been compared directly to Dirt Rally and both improves on certain aspects and falls back in others. For example if you enjoy the single player campaign then you will appreciate the career mode having more features like team building, sponsers and team liveries. The stages the game generates have a decent amount of variety and look good. Some sections of track are reused but generally it is a step forward for rally sims.
The rally physics have come in for some criticism (right so) for being too understeery and not allowing the player to steer the car with the throttle. I hope Codemasters patch the handling to fix this as you can't dial out these issues entirely using setup tweaks. Braking distances have increased and you will need to have some finesse to stop the car effectively with ABS disabled. The cars drive nicely, have a more solid feel than Dirt Rally and still put a grin on your face. The tarmac physics in particular are a step forwards and the cars feel more connected to the road.
The Rallycross cars are a treat and powerslide wonderfully providing captivating racing. Dirt 4 is at its best when you drive these monsters. As the official FIA RX game I hope to see more of the rallycross circuits come to the game via DLC.
Landrush and stadium trucks are entertaining enough but feel like a bit of an after thought and don't offer a great deal of content.
Overall if you enjoyed Dirt Rally or previous Codemasters Dirt titles there is a lot to like here. The soundtrack, while I am sure is not to everyones tastes, adds to the game. The game plays smoothly on my system and it detected my steering wheel and seperate pedals and shifter with no additional configuation required. I have not experienced any crashes or game breaking bugs either. One last little nice touch they have added are some random events like competitors jumping the start in RX events, AI crashing in rally, drones or helicopters flying overhead as you speed along, animals crossing the stage or your car having some unexpected failure. These things add nicely to the immersion factor.

+ Good handling
+ Good career progression
+ Daily/Weekly/Monthly events are fun
+ Rallycross is excellent
+ Lots of handling settings offering a lot of variety
= Graphics aren't the best, but good enough imo
- Not that many cars
- Procedurally generated rally stages is a nice idea, but executed poorly with not enough variety, so you end up seeing the same sections of track repeating quite a lot
- Rally pace notes need a proper overhaul. The procedural track generation isn't helping either
- Inconsistent AI
Overall i still recommend this game, as the gameplay is a lot of fun. But certain rally stages can get very frustrating with bad pace notes, so beware.

Door kickers is a game about kicking doors and shoot up the place...no really it's pretty much that. The game has you planning and executing plans from a top down view in which you can setup your teams of Swat officers and plan their route to breach, bang and clear the mission. Want to deal with a room full of enemies watching the doors? Simple you can set your 2 teams of officers to each door and have them kick the door in or blow the door open, then flash and start shooting everyone dead. It feels wonderful.
==========
The Good
==========
1. Gameplay - Having this feeling of being a swat team commander or a tactical planner is rather fun but also difficult as you must plan every step to ensure the mission goes to plan. You have to adapt to the situation because if you don't you can get your team killed or a hostage. Lucky the game gives you many options to do your job, you can customize your officers giving them from aggressive equipment such as riot shields, grenades, breaching charges and your weapons of choice from SMG to shotguns. However you also can go in more passive using stun grenades, tasers or even take everyone out quietly with silencers to make it as if you were never there.
It goes the same with planning the mission, you can plan every step, every choice such as blowing up a door, using flash or grenade or just kick doors. You can also set it where you can play the mission yourself having full control over each unit in real time or you can set everything up with waypoints and execution orders (they allow you to set up when to breach or move out or hold a location) and simply watch your plan come to life.
2. Levels - I found the level designs rather fun and enjoyable. You have levels with multiple floors, some with windows in which sometimes you have a sniper element that can help take out targets for you. And on top of that you can use their ingame map editor to make your own crazy missions. There are also a lot of missions to play through and 3 stories to go through with the cool element of if you lose an officer...they stay dead...no replacement making it a bit more challenging.
=======
The 50/50
=======
1. Difficulty - There are times where missions can feel very difficult and needs the best plan or just luck to win. This can be annoying at times but overall it helps fuels the challenge of being a tactical planner. For example there are missions where you must save a hostage and disarm a bomb however if you plan the mission poorly you can end up having a hostage shot or the bomb going off before you reach it...making timing everything. So expect to re-work your plans over and over.
======
Overall
======
It's a fun police type tactical shooter for those wanting to either take control of each unit and do everything real time or be a planner and watch your plan go to work. There is again a lot of customization and maps to play to keep you busy and most of all a lot of enemies to deal with.
Perfect illustration of how naive and wishful planning can often be.

This is an entertaining little casual strategy game. It's a bit like Frozen Synapse, but without turns. Instead, you have the ability to control one of your team at a time in real time (not generally recommended but sometimes it's just more convenient) or pausing and drawing up a detailed plan.
For planning you drag a footpath, and set waypoints. Waypoints occur any time you want to do something other than keep walking. For example, you can change or lock facing, hold position and fire until your cone of sight is clear, toss a flashbang, perform some form of breaching maneuver, or collect evidence. You can also set up to four 'hold' points--very useful for keeping all your team working in unison.
In the beginning, you'll probably use none of that and just drag your squad members around, but if you want the best results, you'll learn to use and execute plans. It's much easier to clear a house with a team working simultaneously like a tidal way flowing through it, each member clearing their sector and relying on their teammates to do the same, than it is to try and move them one at time, no matter how good your leapfrogging skills are.
In a sense, the midgame moves from a strategy game to more of a puzzle feel. This is becuase once a map is generated, it remains the same, so you can grind on it until you get a plan that works as well as you want it to. It's a very satisfying feeling when you get a multistage plan to clear a building and can do it all in one go, triggering phases as you go. A skilled player will spend the bulk of their time in planning mode. A masterful player will not only spend most of their time in planning mode, they'll only use it once at the beggining of the mission.
It feels like it was ported from a tablet game. The biggest reason it feels like that is that all levels are on a single screen--though some missions have multiple levels (floors). This means that no matter how big a level is, there's no scrolling around the map, and no need for a mini-map. It's all handled by scaling the sprites instead, so that on a simple small map, everthing is bigger, and on the largest maps, everything gets a bit small, and there is no option to zoom in. That can make certain forms of breaching a door more difficult to plot because sometimes waypoints will end up so close together it's hard to get the right one. This mainly happens to me when using a shieldbearer to kick down a door, take a step into a small room that's probably empty anyway, and back out. It can be done, but sometimes it's a bit fussy to get it done.
The structure of the game is a bit odd. You are forced to grind a bit at the beginning on single missions before campaign mode unlocks. This works in your favour though, as the prescripted single missions gradually increase in difficulty, but don't penalize you if someone get injured or killed during the mission. In a campaign mission, the injured require time to heal, and dead remain dead--though it's completely up to you whether or not you want to accept those results or not. You can always choose to restart the level and try again.
Your plan will remain intact by default, and you can tweak it so it works better.
Tweaking a plan is where the game falls on it's face the most. Some adjustments can be made cleanly, but others will wipe out every step past the adjustment. Further, some waypoints are harder to revise than others for no discernable reason. Chiefly, if you have a waypoint to wait for a signal to continue, you can't delete that waypoint until you toggle the signal at that waypoint off.
To clarify, lets say you have a plan laid out and at a certain point you want a member of your team to wait for an "alpha" command. This would mean that they would execute every command up until that waypoint, and then hold position until you hit the "A" or "1" key. This would be done by right-clicking the waypoint, and clicking the "A" button on the submenu. Every other command on the submenu can be wiped out by deleting a waypoint, but a waypoint to wait for a trigger like that cannot be deleted (in spite of being able to right click it and select "Delete Waypoint") unless you first right click it and click the "A" on the submenu again.
It can be frustrating if you haven't figured that out--and it's something the game does not tell you.
The upgrading system is a bit of a joke. As you do missions, your team will rank up, and once your team has ranked up enough, new jobs and campaigns become available. Further, as you complete missions you earn stars to use to unlock new guns and equipment. But XP and stars are easy to grind for thanks to a very simple random mission generator that gives out more or less the same rewards, regardless of the actual difficulty of the mission--at least as far as stars are concerned. No mission yields more than three stars, no matter how difficult or complex the map. This means you can grind through maps containing one or two small rooms, stuffed with easy targets and three star them every time with very little effort. In an hour or so, you should be able to unlock all the jobs, and all the equipment you find interesting.
There is also a sort of "talent tree" called doctrines. As your team levels, you gain points to spend, but there really aren't that many things to spend them on, and they're all or nothing, so in the same time you unlock all the jobs and all the equipment you want, you can complete the entire doctrine tree. It's busywork more than an accomplishment.
There are also some menu... quirks. If you watch a replay, the only way to get back to selecting missions is to back out to the main menu again. This isn't that big of a problem though, because after a couple replays, you won't use that function very often.
The replay function has two significant flaws beyond the menu issue. The first is that to watch a replay is to save it--there is no choice in the matter. The second is that there is no apparent way to watch the replay without the plan marks. I don't want to see my waypoints in the replay, I just want to watch my team flow through an enemy stronghold like a force of nature. That isn't an option, which cuts into the uh... replay value of the replay feature.
It's not a AAA game, and it isn't trying to be. But for what it is, it's satisfying (provided you aren't paying full price). I didn't (and wouldn't) pay $20 for it. I wouldn't be happy if I'd paid more than about $10.  It's not a bad game, just overpriced IMSO.

Yes, Ylands is very similar to Minecraft, but there is much more to it that make it a much more interesting and absorbing game.  There is a great deal of depth to this game which makes it fun and challenging.
After over 100 hours playing on one map, I am finding my frustation level is getting higher than my enjoyment level and I will likely play the game less until some issues in the game are resolved.  A key issue is that it takes scarce resources to acquire critical scarce resources to move into the higher levels of the game.  And this effort requires increasing amounts of time engaged in repetitive activities which become frustrating and unrewarding.
For example, I was just slain by a mutated bear that was likely protecting an area of valuable scarce resources.  With my death, I lost weapons, armor, and other resources, many of which were created with valuable scrace resources.  In order to recover these items and continue my quest I have to return to my home island, which takes several minutes, gather more resources, build new armor and weapons (which aren't as good as my lost armor and weapons), return to the other island, find my way into the cave of the mutatated bear, and hope I won't be killed again by the mutated bear.
These types of efforts can be enjoyable for a while, but the time and repetive effort becomes quited frustrating after a few times.  But, one needs to persist in these types of efforts if one is going to advance to the higher levels of the game.
I have great hopes for the game, but will likely play a lot less frequently untils the developers resolve some of these issues.  So, yes, buy the game if you enjoy Minecraft type games,  But be aware that the game will become less enjoyable as one reaches the higher levels.

At $80 I am relunctant to recommend this game but I will.   I paid full price for the game and I am satisfied.    It took me a few months to convince myself to purchase the game at full price so now I am committed to getting my money out of it.
Cons:
Price - It is very expensive for a game.   They are going to limit who buys or even considers this game because of the price... but maybe that's what the developers of the game want.
Land Units - The game is called Command: Modern Air/Naval operations.  It's not called Command: Modern Air, Land and Naval operations,  I get that.   BUT,  really... you can't have marines, navy seals and other infantry units in the game and then put almost no programming to make the units useful in a scenario.   You can add marines or seals to an aircraft for deployment but you have no easy way to get them off the aircraft.   You have russian, UK paratroopers that you can select for a scenario but no US AB units.  You can't add specific infantry units to an aircraft for deployment.  The land units move around the battle field like aircraft in some cases.   Land unit gameplay could be better with a little tweaking.
Pros:
The air and naval side of the game is detailed to insanity.   You have to know your unit capabilities and weapon load capability to make it work.   If your jets fly over the enemy airfield and nothing goes BOOM... you did something wrong.  Check your weapon and load specifications.  If you are at 1000 feet but the weapon requires 10000 feet to be released.... it won't fire (lesson learned).   The game requires more then just a point and shoot mentaility.    You need to plan it out,  understand your unit and weapon capability to be successful.
I won't go into submarine warfare part of the game because at this point I don't know what I am doing with it.   The details of the submarine gameplay are again, INSANE.
Scenario editor -  I love messing with the scenario editor and trying differnt event triggers and actions.  It's also a great way to learn more about units and weapons capability in the game.  The editor is what makes the game for me.   Most of my time in the game has been messing with the editor.    You can literaly build any operation or battle in this game.  The only limitation is your imagination and time.    Somene posted the game is 60% research,  30% scenario creation, 10% gameplay and that is about right.
This game makes you want to learn more about operations,  units and weapons.   It's required.
Support - I had an issue with one of the scenarios and support was there to help.  I'm always relunctant to contact support for any game because I know in most cases customer support is not a reality... but in my case the technician gave me a solution to my problem immediately.
This game has a dedicated development group that is constantly updating the game and listens to the players.
The game overall is a fun game to play.   As I learn more I'm sure it will get even better.   There is a learning curve and it will take a lot of gameplay to really understand all the mechanics in the game,  I just hope I have the time to commit to it.

This is how CMANO works:  You start off playing a Scenario (Which is usually a battle that lasts anywhere from 6-24 hours) and are typically given either aircraft stationed at airbases and/or surface ships or submarines that loiter in the ocean.  Before assuming command of your assets, you are given specific Objectives. (Destroy an ICBM Silo, escort a friendly Cargo ship to a specified waypoint, achieve air superiority etc…)  You will then be responsible for developing a strategy to achieve victory, which will entail analyzing your forces’ capabilities via the software’s massive database.  The maximum range of an F-15E’s Radar, the Passive Low Frequency signature emitted by an Oscar II SSGN, or the Cruising Speed of the Daring-class DDG, are examples of the data metrics that you may scrutinize.  (Make no mistake, CMANO is 90% planning and 10% doing.)
Once you’ve deployed your assets, success in every engagement will be governed by your ability to properly execute specific tactics, such as: winning long range air engagements against 4.5 Generation fighters, stalking a naval task force with an SSN, or executing SEAD operations against advanced SAM systems, such as the S-400/SA-21.  The Scenario will conclude once you’ve either completed your Objectives, or run out of time.  You will then be given an evaluation of your performance.
**A quick word on the oft-mentioned database: It is arguably the most extensive non-governmental repository of data on every conceivable weapon of war designed by man since the conclusion of the Second World War.**  Enough said.
Over the past year, Command’s interface has gone through numerous revisions both in terms of appearance and functionality. You can now for example, maintain the altitude above ground your aircraft will fly at, irrespective of changes in terrain elevation.  This would allow you to keep your F-16 within a MK 84 JDAM’s minimum release altitude of 10k feet AGL, irrespective of changes in terrain elevation.  Other welcome additions include: allowing players to finally determine how many weapons they have allocated on a single enemy target without doing too much clicking (This change finally came one year after I pointed out this flaw in this review!), frequent updates to its already massive database, a new look for its GUI and numerous other additions that would be too onerous for me to report on, due to space limitations.
However, there are certain other ‘changes’ that make this software UTTERLY FRUSTRTING to use. Reasons that are unbeknownst to me, the game displays as default the range curves for radar and weapons used both by yourself and the enemy, EVERY TIME you load up a new saved game. This dramatically slows down performance and fills your entire monitor with dozens of circles and rectangles.  You are thus forced to fix this mess, by going through Command’s tedious menus, whenever you load up a new saved game!
The Rules of Engagement window has been filled with so much superfluous content that any beginner will find it almost impossible to understand. There is also still no window that streamlines the activity data of what all of your air or naval assets are doing, so you are forced to remember off the top of your head lots of very minute details: which aircraft is still being shot at by what enemy plane, which of your ships are firing SAM’s at which aircraft, or which submarine still has its Active Sonar turned on. Remembering so many details becomes impossible on the large scenarios.  The game physics also has serious flaws: Just to name a few bugs, aircraft tend to be shot down by missiles that fly at completely different elevations and their turn speed seems strangely unaffected by changes in altitude.
All things considered, even with its flaws, I believe this game will give its very small target audience (service members and hardcore military enthusiasts) hours of enjoyment and learning.  I would therefore be happy to recommend it.

Many, many years ago, a few of us young farmhands got paid $20 to shoot the rats killing chickens and such at one of the local barns. We stayed up through the night and into the wee hours of the morning blasting those terrifyingly vicious demons into a fine red mist.
Fast forward 12 or so years, and here I am paying a little less than what I earned that night to upgrade to the Collector's Edition of this game, just so I can ironically stay up all night blasting rats into the wee hours of the morning.
I have no regrets about either one of these situations, because frankly, most rats are really evil little creatures. But also because FatShark is a responsive and obviously hard working company- to the point where they fixed a "minor engine issue" even after announcing that they were on holiday.
In regards to canon, I've been a fan of the Warhammer franchise since the tabletop's popularity in the 90's, but had since stopped playing anything from it. This 'gateway game' lured me back in with familiar lore and concepts- and got me playing the digital side of the franchise (to which I also have no regrets).
Generally speaking, the gameplay and feel is very smooth and fluid. It is really satisfying to make a spot-on kill, or mow down Slave Rats with a two-handed hammer. This game allows you to feel really in control of your character, and bringing out the best in them is up to you. That being said, once you get into a groove- your pulse really starts to pound with adrenaline.
The banter between the characters is fun and often informative, and the game keeps you on your gaurd even on Normal difficulty, with excitement to be found often right up until you dive onto the wagon to escape.
I've altered this review heavily over time because FatShark responded to the community and added mini-bosses, tons of new maps, new weapons, new techniques, more ways to get and change items... and so much more. I really can't say much negative about this game, as my previous complaints have all been hammered out.
All in all: my only hope for this game is that they keep expanding it, keep adding new enemies and weapons, and just keep that ball rolling until they blow our asses out of the water with an amazing sequel constructed from all their hard won wisdom.
Now come kill some rats with us- you won't regret it.

First things first - Please DO NOT LISTEN to those people on the interwebz that say this game is another W40K trash game like that heretical Storm of Vengeance. Or those people that aren't satisfied because its just a CHESS game with W40K skin. NOOO. Warhammer 40000 : Regicide is more than chess.
At the point I'm writing this review I played a short session of Regicide before going to sleep and HOLY ♥♥♥♥ BISCUITS I am amazed by the quality of graphics and animations. Take note that this game is still in early access, so it still got many bugs here and there and some features locked for now. So far it has two game modes - classic chess (no need explaining this one, it plays just like real life chess except the pieces are W40K characters) and Regicide mode.
Now ladies and gentleman, Regicide mode is where things get interesting. Ever played XCOM : Enemy Within? Regicide mode has that game's feel. It's still chess (with the usual piece movement and kill the king rule) but throw in some XCOM strategy elements and voila - u get Regicide mode. During your turn, you get to move a piece first (using standard chess movement rules) and after you move a piece, you can spend initiative points for your army to execute various orders - like shoot, hunker down, use an ability etc. After u ran out of initiative points then its your opponent's turn. In Regicide mode each piece have stats (like HP, attack etc, the usual stuff) so it's quite different from your usual chess game.
The main piece of the cake IMO is the kill animations. The devs really put in some good effort into animating those miniatures from Games Workshop into awesome 3d models that kill each other in gory, violent and khorne-approved ways. And surprisingly enough the graphics are quite demanding, which means that this game, with its high-quality graphics - proves that the devs didn't make this game just for fast cash grabs or to spit in the faces of fans - they are really making a high-quality, high-production value W40K game, which is what we fans been craving all these years (after the destruction of THQ). Give these guys from Hammerfall a chance (its their first project!) and I'm sure we will see MOAR good W40K stuff in the future. Plus the devs are really friendly and respect their customers!
Being a W40K fan, not buying and playing this game is just HERESY.
