I like it, it has this cute unique charm that you don't often see in free to play's. The gameplay has very much depth on comparable terms to when ragnarok was popular before transitioning to 3D. For somebody who has watched the show on both seasons, I can say this is very faithful to the wakfu IP, especially if you like old video game references and culture.
It is a very artsy game for something than runs on java and is sprite based.
The game itself is very hardcore in terms of rpg's where you need to number crunches and research on having the ideal build for character’s. The gameplay is more forgiving in a sense compared to the old days where everything was un-killable without organized efforts. It is sandbox but it has some sense of direction, every so often you will get a quest giving you an idea of what you should be doing at this point.
However the professions in the game and the drops give it a very strong grindy feeling, but it doesn't hurt so much because of how easy it is too grind. They give you several options and ways on how to level professions so you don't get bored or annoyed instantly.
It's very easy instead of being this long gradual process, not to mention how fast you can level up. In each battle they give these conditions in the upper left which are rule sets, and if follow them no matter how confusing they can be you will get some insane bonuses. Me and a buddy have been playing this since Friday, and we reached the 30's bracket with just 6 hours of game time each day in-between this game and dark souls. And we came from games like WoW and Guild wars where everything was boring and repetitive.
These rules are unique challenges and make everything more challenging because we are purposely putting handicaps on ourselves to get the best rewards. And the xp and drop rates are astonishing if you follow through, I used to beta test this game back in 2011 before they came to steam and I dropped it because of how much of a chore everything in the game was.

This may be one of the first games I played where they made the environment an integral part of the game because when you cut down trees, harvest plants, or kill mobs. These things don't respawn. You have to do your part and befriend nature by collecting seeds, planting trees, and breeding monsters so you can the players around you have access. You get rewards and points by helping the environment and give your character a reputation on how helpful you are to the people around you.
Everyone is rewarded for not being selfish and increasing this collaboration between people.
The last part I’m going to cover is the politics system and how it affects people who join nations. The people in seats of power are given the reasonability of making sure everyone in their territories is looked after. They spend their cash and collect taxes to buy bonuses which apply to everyone in their nation and their lands by having increased drop rates, more natural resources available to use, and giving access to dungeons that are not normally open for everyone. They also organize the pvp structure for the lands and against other nations.
They pass laws protecting the environment and reward those who plant and expand dwindling resources. And give people titles for those who go out of their way to give security to the people that serve their realm. Everyone has a part to play to guarding lands against thieves and invaders, to distributing crafting materials and giving to the less fortunate or under leveled.

Okay, so two quick things to mention from what I've seen in other reviews:
One: This is NOT the revolutionizing 3D Sonic Game that came out on the Gamecube. This is the sequel to the TRUE revolutionizing 3D Sonic Game on the DREAMCAST, which was by the same name without the 2.
Two: All the DLC does is unlock the bonus feature of 2P battle that was introduced in the re-make on the Gamecube, so there's nothing really lost by not getting it unless you have two controllers and want to play with somebody else in this glitch-fest.
Anyway, as for my quick little review. While the game itself is stellar, or should be, the PC port is a hunk of dung that I'm glad I didn't buy for it being Sonic Adventure 2. I luckily got it as part of a bigger bundle, and honestly the levels and controls are extremely glitchy on this port and I find myself dying many times because of hitting invisible walls, having my speed inverted, falling through ground, or just plain having my screen turn black for 10 seconds while the video dies despite the game continuing on, which ends up desyncing the audio/video.
As much as I really, truly want to recommend this game, after playing a little bit of it, the glitchiness is just too much to handle. I'm going to try playing some more later, but honestly it's hard to play a game you love when the mechanics of it are as broken as this. If at all possible, play the Gamecube port, and/or the Gamecube port of Sonic Adventure (DX). I'm honestly not sure if it's worth it to play this if you've never played Sonic Adventure (2/battle) before since I feel it will leave a terrible impression upon the two games.
tl;dr
The game itself is amazing, but the engine is broken on PC. People who think this is the ground breaking original 3D game are ill-informed.

First let me say:
DiRT Rally was NOT a sim. It a) overdid the new tires-dig-into-loose-surfaces mechanic, it b) didn't touch many simulation topics in regards to power delivery and tire mechanics (very noticable on asphalt) and c) it didn't actually simulate the motorsport with all its rules.
DiRT Rally was a game, not a sim. Was it as hard as sim? No, but close... much closer than any Codemasters game before. But the as-difficult-as-the-real-thing part was a mixed bag - on the one hand it was hard because it didn't care to compromise realism for approachability on the other hand some of the things that it simulated badly made the game even harder than real life rallying (this of course goes both ways, other undersophisticated physic-simulation aspects made the game easier).
Now to the real DiRT 4 review:
DiRT 4 is not a sim, it's a game. The physics are
sophisticated than DiRT Rally's, especially in the parts that made DiRT Rally inaccurately harder than it should have been.
+ much improved tire simulation on non-loose surfaces (but compared to actual sims it's very "sim-cade", it's still a much improved estimation of how a tire behaves close to and over the limit)
+ suspension geometry now accurately modeled and influencing the Force Feedback (same idea that actual sims have about FFB, not just self-aligning torque from known curves, but considering levers of the suspension)
+ improved angular inertia (weight distribution felt when the car is rotating)
+ accurately more noticable difference in grip between dry loose-surfaces and wet(heavy/soaked) loose-surfaces
+ improved aero modeling (but not as noticable as the Codies think it is)
+ part wear not from direct damage is noticable (and can be improved through more high quality car parts)
- all the estimated constants in the physics simulation seem to be more on the forgiving side
devs made the physics "best case scenario" instead of "best educated guess after intensive research"
- the loose-surfaces all feel "deep"... it's hard to describe: think of a loose surface as a puddle of standing water, DiRT 4 feels like there is no aquaplaning ever and the tire always reaches somewhat deep into the puddle
what else is easier:
- the courses are a lot less technical and 90% of the time also wider (although, that the track limits are often on a slope, is easier and harder at the same time, it's less "terminal", but it sends you spinning or jumping into a barrel roll easier)
- damage influences the car less
- damage is way easier to repair and takes way less time to repair (it's a bit of a joke, like the devs made the gamer-handling rally-damage and repairs and then had no time to put the sim-damage-repair system into the game)
- after driving through water splashes are gone within 2 seconds without using the windscreen wiper
- it's easier/faster to earn money to buy cars
- the AI difficulty (their stage timings) is FAR easier. I almost always win on the highest difficulty ("tough", not sure if another one is unlocked after finishing the game) with all assists and stage-restarts turned off
biggest issue for me is the "my stage" track generator. It's fun, but very limited, after 10 hours you definitely notice corner combination de javus, I assume after 30 hours you've driven every corner type that is in there for 20 times and know "ah, this is gonna go like that and I take it like this", same feeling you had from driving a DiRT Rally stage for 10 times and then again after 2 weeks off.
Now some positive things
regarding gameplay directly:
- on PC the game
look better than DiRT Rally, graphic effects (like rain, dust etc.) look better and especially the lighting looks very natural, the suede of the steering wheels in the right lighting conditions is the best looking in ANY game today (and I've played and seen the GT Sport and Forza 7 interiors!)
- the sound is as good as it was in DiRT Rally and in some respects even better, but not all cars have improved and not to the same degree either
-
, a good balance between the clean low-profile DiRT Rally and the
of DiRT 2. This goes for the menus, the intros, the career and team management as well as the incredible soundtrack (it could be more tracks, but what is there is very awesome!)
- the replays do a far better job than in DiRT Rally and you can choose to see only helicopter footage and silence the co-driver calls (turn of music or choose the exact song you want)
- the co-driver calls are more accurate, what is called out as a "5" will never be a 4 and the timing of the calls is more consistent than in DiRT Rally (I assume in DR we all soon stopped complaining about the co-driving effing us over, because we memorized the especially bad calls after the third time or so and knew how what was coming)
some final little goodies:
- after finishing a stage, you can check on how your opponents did. "Wait, wasn't Vatanen in the lead, now it's Kankunen, what happened to Vatanen?" and then you can check in the split-timing table what happened to him, if he had turbo damage or a flat tire for example... and see in what position he is now.
- for the english language you can hire a older male co driver who seems seasoned and "pro" or a younger female co driver who does just as well but delivers the notes with more fun, a little less serious (feels like she signed up for a charity-rally with a famous driver just for the fun of it)
I could still list some minor issues, like for example that the pause-button on my wheel is fixed and can't be assigned or that the non-automatic windscreen wiper option does nothing (bug) ooor that the onscreen-steering-wheel has some added oscillation affect and is not a 1:1 presentation of my irl steering wheel (think "virtual wheel is on a torsion spring"), but those are very minor issues, some of which will get fixed soon, I'm sure.
Now, do I recommend this game? YES, I do(!) ...but if you have DiRT Rally and not completely overplayed that game and if 50 bucks are a lot of money to you, you should probably wait with the purchase for a sale.
Either way don't be close-minded about this game and you will have a
of fun.

TL;DR (at the top!) ... 7/10.  Good exploration game but I find it lacking long term playability.
If you like sandbox/exploration/crafting games then this will definitely occupy for for a while.  I've played aound 40 hours and about now at the point where there I'm not motivated to play again.  I'd also say that about 5-10 of those hours have been spent in game but actually browsing the Wikipedia page - read on for more explanation!
Positives
---------
* Exploration is good/fun - first your island, then other islands
* House/base building is flexible and more interesting than Minecraft.  It's a bit of a timesink though because it's tricky at points
* Lots to craft, hundreds/thousands of items.
* You'll be up and building a base in no time at all
* Boats/cars/transport all craftable ... although cars etc. have no real use as islands are a bit small and too rocky.
* Nice little "surprises" on most islands. Won't spoil the fun ... but it's nice when you find them.
Negatives
----------
* Inventory management. Too many items, constantly dropping stuff, inconsistent stack sizes. Even crafting 20 chests and you'll still be running out of places to put things.
* Crafting. No idea why the "tech tree" is hidden. Just drives to you the wiki to work out what is needed. Seriously hope they change this... I was super glad I have dual screen setup for this game!
* Light.  It's so dark at night (and in caves) and the light is so poor that it's hardly worth going out at night. And you can only hold 1 item at a time (i.e. torch) ... so cave exploring is not fun (ambushed by creatures).
* Base building.  I built a boat and put my "base" on there ... islands are too small and too far apart for me to make a large base on just one island.
* Hidden stats. Is iron armor better than Leather armor? Is one type of sword better than another? Who knows!
* Boats are slow.  I guess it's kinda realistic ... but 5/10 minutes to move between Islands is a bit of a pain.
* Multiplayer. I know it's early access... but I put 6 hours work into a server and it was wiped due to a very minor update. So I wouldn't touch it for now unless you're OK with waking up one day and all your work is gone/done.  I know this needs to happen ... but if /every/ update wipes servers then I don't think it's worth playing at this time.
All in all I would say I enjoyed the first 10-20 hours of the game ... then kept playing to see what else was there ... and then now I'm thinking "why bother playing?"  It somehow doesn't drive me to keep playing like Minecraft or Terraria would.  Ultimately, however, it's still early access and I think it has good potential. That said ... I paid the same for Minecraft and Terraria .... so I'm kinda discounting early access since other completed games cost the same.
Would I recommend it? Yes.  Would I say it's something you could sink 50+ hours into and play day after day? For me, no.

The Open World:
This game seems like it could be awesome, but then it turns out to be a major letdown in almost every possible way. After going back and playing Crysis and Crysis Warhead, this game seems to somehow have taken similar graphics, location, combat and game play, then downgraded it. Sure, it has open world free roam, but every location looks like the same tropical fantasy land with flashing plants and crates. I want something that feels half-authentic. I played a few hours in and I regret my purchase.
Hunting/Crafting:
You have to kill golden tigers and reptiles to craft leather bags? Whatever happened to using real equipment? It just creates a bunch of tedious time wasting going out chasing animals down with AKs and a machete. Now, to restore health and make your way through the game, you have to craft a bunch of syrettes by hacking at every glowing plant in your path and then micromanaging your inventory space.
Combat:
The gritty kills and recoveries from the previous game are all but gone, you simply put on a bandaid or go for cheesy daisy chains of machete rushes behind enemies who are clearly deaf (which happens to be as good as it gets). There's almost no way to openly maneuver, you just hold down one spot and regenerate like a troll.

Let me just start of this review by saying this, the games in this pack are so much better than all of the games from pack one combined. While Part Pack 1 was carried mostly by Fibbage and Drawful for me, I feel that all of these games are superb in one way or another! I will be giving this game a score out of 20, with 4 points for each game seperately! These are in no particular order so lets get started!
Bomb Corp:
So I don't know how many of you have played the game Space Team on your phones, but this game is very similar to that game. In this game everyone recieves instructions on their phones about what wires to cut on a bomb that is on the screen, what instructions to ignore, what colors change and many more aspects. This is a very fast pased game and it is really fun to play with other who don't have much gaming experience because I feel that they will like this type of game seperatly compared to traditional video games.
3.5/4
Fibbage 2: I'm gonna be honest with this one. If they made the original perfect, than this game is beyond perfect for anyone! I'm sure that you have all heard of fibbage so I won't go into the details on what its about however there is a new rule to the game that might change up how you get some points. Its called the DeFibulator, and what this does is it narrows your choices down to 1 truth and 1 lie. I love this addition and it is a great way to mix up the gameplay, but keep it familiar so that veterans of this game will still have a lot of fun!
4/4
Earwax: Going into this pack I felt that this game would be worst game in the whole pack. I mean a game about sounds doesn't exactly sound like the most fun game to be honest. However, I'm glad to say that I was suprisingly wrong! This game is an absolute blast! Basically, its sort of like fibbage where someone chooses a prompt and each person answers on their device. However, in this game you try to form a small story by chosing two sounds from the six that you see on your device. Its clever, the sounds are really good and some of them are actually spot on to what they would sound like today, and I love that some of the prompts even bring in player interactions such as, "The sound of Bob waking up in the morning." Its a great edition that I'm really happy to say is one of our favorites!
3/4
Bidiots: Ladies and Gentlemen, the cousin of my favorite game from the last pack, Bidiots. If you remember from last pack, there was a drawing game called Drawful. It was a plesent game and it was really easy for the yonger audience to pick up on. However, it seems that they have completly switched up the forumla in this one and decided to go and make this game a bidding game. So Everyone starts out by drawing 2 drawings. Then the "Auctioneer" will auction off each and every drawing. Now the goal of this game is to have the most money by the end of the round, and the best way to make money is by buying art. Now the trick is to outbid everyone else, buut you don't want to go over the actual price of  what the painting is worth, because then you will lose money. You gain tips from your "Art Buyers" on your phone and they will tell you what to do relating to the current picture up on the TV. Its a clever game that has a lot of twists and turns. It is a little bit confusing at first, but other than that this game is a huge blast!! I do consider this game to be the weakest in the group, but all of the games are really fantastic in their own way, so I still love you bidiots!
-2.75/4
Quiplash XL: This is probably my favorite game in the bunch. Never have I seen so many laughs out of any game, and I love Quiplash because of this reason. So this game is compilled of three rounds (Just like Fibbage). Where you will be given two questions on your device and you will answer the questions with either funny, truthful, or down right stupid answers that will try to get the audience to vote for your choice. Once all of the responses have come in, then each of the questions will appear on the TV. Each question will have two answers and everyone will vote on their favorite answer and the players who answered the question will recieve points based on how many other players/spectators choose their answer. This game is absolutley amazing, and is by far the bset game in the batch!

So I got this game after watching a Let's play of RoosterTeeth like a year ago. I don't play this game with friends and I've only played Escape mode. I enjoy playing because it's challenging. You get a very limited amount of ammo even on normal difficulty so you need to make every
count. I like the variation in armory like having a Scar 20 or a M4a4 (if I'm not mistaken), revolvers or colts and also crossbows and compound bows!
Some positives and negatives from a solo player perspective:
Pro's:
- Challenging
- Great maps
- Great assortiment of guns
- Good voice acting (altough sometimes repetitive)
- Maps last between 30mins to 1 and a half hours
- Objective rotations (sometimes objectives are different than the last time you played)
Con's:
- Buggy AI (zombies stay in a crouched position, don't die or simply demolish you)
- Flashlight is too bright!
- Objectives can sometimes be hard to spot or hard to get to
- Accuracy of weaponry

Hydrophobia is ultimate a tech demo for the realistic water system with particle physics, fluid dynamics (or simulation thereof), and beautiful graphics. You play "Kate", a system engineer on the Queen of the World, a floating arcology (giant floating city) that was being attacked by nihilistic terrorists who want to unleash a nanobot plague and kill all the humans so the planet can start anew. As Kate, you survive, hack your way through the ship surviving various challenges such as fire,electricity, and water. Kate's spelunking, cliff-climbing experience comes in handy as she climbs, jumps and swims through various levels while combating these terrorists who wants to annihilate mankind. The game gets extremely buggy near the end, with disappearing objects and disappearing bosses. It is short (I finished in merely a few hours, and I'm a slow player) and it is an experience, albeit, probably not one that needs to be repeated.

A mixed bag that attempts to build on the strengths of the original but seems to struggle against its own design. I love how much larger the new maps are but that is also one of the games biggest issues; Much of the game is spent shift-looking far ahead of you to line up the perfect shot while hiding behind cover because a missed shot means a counter-shot from off screen can kill you. Too many of the maps were a complete joke with you spamming walls of shotgun fire off screen in the hopes of killing stuff (and actually succeeding) and rewarding you with a huge combo or punishing you with a bullet in the back from off screen. I guess rooms made out of entirely glass were popular in the 80s because there are also tons of windows this time around, meaning enemies from outside of your vision can shoot to kill from multiple rooms away. Melee is usually an option but with long corridors and tons of breakable windows its often unrealistic to melee everything everytime.
If the game was in a different engine (with some kind of first person option) or had a zoom feature I would've really loved this and it would've felt like a significant improvement over the original. New characters, bigger levels, more weapons, and a psychedelic story are great and all, but when the core gameplay is this frustrating and unwieldy it is difficult to recommend. If you enjoyed the original its worth picking up but I wouldn't recommend it for newcomers to the series despite being completely seperate from the original (outside of lore).

Despite the reviews that have averaged around 64/100, the game itself must be looked at not for its longevity or story.. It needs to be looked at for it's signature greatness: Realistic water physics!
Seriously, for a indie title like this that was created by a handful of developers, it is very very hard to imagine why the hell many AAA title game developers with a extremely high budget can't pump out the same, if not better of a water-physics game!
So simply put, if you don't understand what makes this so unique, here it is:
The water is very dynamic, and uses Cosine trig functions as a basis for the water's modelling.
The water uses many properties from real physics: Room 1 has lower water level, Room 2 has higher water level.. Door opens between the rooms, and Room 2's water flows into Room 1's water until it evens out.
Even more exciting: When water flows into a room, waves will come through, pushing your player away, and the water smacks up against a wall them moves in the opposite direction.
The water in this game can be manipulated too. If you shoot a glass window with a room full of water, the window will burst and in comes the massive amounts of water. The game is just pure awesome JUST because of the great water physics modelling. Everything else about this game is mediocre, and I can't justify paying full price ($15.00) for this game. I got it on sale and could justify the sale of ($7.00) or lower.

I will only recommend this game to people who have waited a while for a new rally game.
Cons:
- Physics. This games physics is absolutely terrible. I have managed to do a 7x barrol roll and I only had to repair my cars chassis.. For 2.52 minutes. Puncturing a tire and losing the rubber isn't that big of a deal either apparently  as it was possible for me to still finish first on the stage with approx. 5 km left with a 89 % difficulty.
The repair part in general is unnessesary. I have not once had to spend more than 18 minutes on repairing my car. It would be a nice feature if you had to make decisions on which parts you should repair and which you shouldn't.
- Interface. The interface is kind of messed up as well. You have to leave career mode and go all the way out to the main menu in order to buy cars for your career. It feels like the interface could be streamlined a lot with some few tweeks here and there.
- Gameplay. There's quite a few weird details in the gameplay. If you are racing in Wales you may see a flock of rabbits running out in front of you car where in Sweden it may be crows flying out in front of your car. Also. The drones on the track is kind of wtf to me.
Another thing that annoys me is the rain/snow on your windscreen. It looks absolutely terrible.
After each stage you also have to waste around 7 seconds driving to a racing marshall to stop the car and you can't really control your speed anyways as you are slowed down if you cross the finish line too fast.
- Track layout. I noticed this when I was racing in Sweden. It feels like the tracks are quite similar. It feels as if the same track parts are used. Kind of like trackmania if you have ever tried to make a track in that game. This part is especially noticable in the hair pin corners.
Pros:
- Audio. The engine sound is amazing and so is the sound of your tires racing across the gravel and especially the snow.
I'm a really big fan of the soundtracks in the game as well although some of the songs have been used before. I'm looking at you Fifa.
- Handling. It's a very easy game to pick up and mistakes are very forgiving. This can both be a pro and a con but for the average Joe I think this is a pro.
Conclusion:
I don't feel like I have paid for a game that costs 54.99€. It would be a good game for half its price but it's too lackluster to be a AAA title in my opinion.

NOTE: This is a review on the STEAM version of the game and how I feel the game from a PC perspective and not a mobile perspective. There is no difference from the steam version and the mobile version but there are some things that look good on a phone or tablet but not so much on the PC. If this was a review on the mobile version then I would definitetly recommend this game.
Now as the game is still open beta, there are many things to be added and polished on (like levels, maps, shops etc) so I can't talk about the lack of content but instead I will mention the things that I feel are weird in the PC or things that should be added or modified.
The UI - It shouldn't come to a suprise that when you make a cross platform game between PC and mobile, there are gonna have to be corners cut. In this case its the UI. On mobile, the UI looks great and makes sense but on the PC, it just looks cheap and unclean. Preferably if possible, adding an option to switch between tablet UI and PC UI would be amazing. The UI also lacks alot of small yet needed details like specific HP, MP, and XP numbers.
Friends/Party System - While there is an friends list system, there is no party system. You can use the summon code (which is a bit buggy at times. I was stuck in loading) to play on the same channel/map but there isn't a real party system. so you can't see their HP/MP bar without clicking on them. This may not be as big as a problem now but in the future when there are healer classes, it would be extremely difficult to play as you can't attack a monster while keeping tabs on your friends HP at the same time.
Weapons/Classes/Stats - There are 4 main stats in the game; HP, MP, Attack, and Defense. The class you have on only affect your skills and nothing else. "Daggers" gives the most Attack of all the weapons, "staffs" give the most MP, and "swords" give the most Defense. Here's the problem. All the classes are equally tanky. I have played all the classes besides Guardian and I have noticed little to no difference in survivability. Being tanky isn't going to help when you're playing a Rogue or Mage because that's not what they do, and Warriors are suppose to be tanky, but do a bad job at it because there are no skills to help him be tanky. In fact, I would say Mage and Rogue are more tanky because they have defensive skills (Mana Sheild and Stealth). This makes Attack the most valuable stat for doing the most damage. AQW was really customizable because there was no restriction on what weapon you could use. You could be a Mage and use a hammer, but this only worked because every weapons attack stats were the same and the attack stats are mainly determined by the enchant. In AQ3D, each weapon has different stats. Attack determines how much damage you do, and that's the only real stat you should be going for as Rogue or Mage. Even Warriors should build this over Defense tbh. "Daggers" have the highest attack making the "daggers" the only viable weapon to use for high DPS. This takes away a lot of customization (plus it looks weird for a mage to use a dagger as a weapon). Some solutions to this would be adding more stats (like LUK for Rogues and INT for mages) or making it like AQW where all weapons have equal damage and the stat's are based off enchants.
Again, this game is still in beta so it is expected to be some flaws but there is a lot of potential in this game. With some things added and polished, I can see this being a very fun game

Having never been a Left 4 Dead enthusiast, it didn't mean too much to me when I was told this game played like Left 4 Dead. I am, however, a Warhammer enthusiast, and I am pleased to tell you that this game stays fairly true to the brutal, unforgiving nature of the franchise.
You play one of five heroic figures, each just different enough from the next to provide a noticeably different experience.  The controls are pretty intuitive, combat is quick and fluid, and the weapons are beautiful.  They even have a specific keybinding to "View Weapon," at which point the character will take the weapon and hold it up, as though inspecting it.  Done in first person, this provides a pretty good view of the weapon itself.  As far as I know, there isn't really a point to doing this other than to admire the detail the developers put into the weapon, but I love that they made this an action in the game.  You can also view weapons in your character's inventory screen, in a more nearly traditional way.
The game rewards you for completing the mission, and basically only for completing the mission.  There are tomes and grimoires you can pick up, which are essentially treasure items, but you only get credit for carrying them with you if you successfully complete the mission.  It doesn't matter if you kill one hundred thousand vermin, or not a single one - you get the same reward for completing the mission either way.  I like this aspect of the game, because it drives home the fact that you aren't really here to soldier it out against the Skaven - you're part of a strike team, an elite infiltration squad, and if you can't complete the objective, nothing else really matters.  It also helps less competitive players feel like they did something other than just hold the door open for the guy with the blunderbuss and the two handed hammer.  For those more competitive players, you still get the glory of seeing your name at the top of the stat list at the end of the mission.
As far as how the game actually plays... if the trailers don't paint a pretty enough picture for you with the entrails of your enemies, I'm not sure I'm a better artist.  The combat does remind me, in a number of ways, of how Skyrim plays.  It's first person, you have a melee weapon and a ranged weapon, and ammunition is pretty important.  Timing is important.  Blocking is important.  Aiming is less important, because as the name implies, there is a veritable tide of vermin surging forward more often than not, and there are times that it takes significant talent to miss a shot.  Inventory-wise, you have a health item slot, a buff potion slot, and a grenade slot - that's it.  While to me it at first seemed a little too spartan, it turns out that this setup is generally sufficient for what you need to accomplish.
While there is no skill-point system, you do get bonus loot for leveling up.  You also get loot for completing missions, and sometimes a consolation prize even if you fail.  If you looted chests and/or found tomes or grimoires, you also get a better chance to receive better loot at the end of the mission.  They harken back to Warhammer's d6 origins when you literally roll on a loot table for your reward, and it is very nostalgic.  I wish I had a little dice-rolling tin like they do....
It also cannot be stressed enough the importance of at least pairing up, if not traveling as a group of four.  Sometimes special Skaven units will tackle you and render your hero helpless, and one of your friends has to pull them off of you.  This is probably my least favorite part of the game, as it seems a just a little ridiculous that your hero cannot extricate himself from some of these circumstances, and it sometimes seems to artificially bolster the need for teamwork.  That said, it's also just as well if someone wants to be a jerk and run ahead/lag behind/yolo solo.
The characters are also very chatty.  It adds a great deal of personality to each of them, and some of the lines are just great.  The voice acting is very good, and the litany available to the characters is impressive.  Never a dull moment with arguing elves and dwarves about!
I don't really have a lot of negative to say about this game.  I practically had to max out the mouse sensitivity to give it the handling I was looking for, but that was easily resolved in the in-game options menu.  The lack of a "sprint" button is a little disappointing, but generally you don't have to worry about it very much.  The level design can also be very confusing for me sometimes, and once I was stuck in a single zone of the map for maybe 5-10 minutes, looking for the way out after having run past it a dozen times - but that could be just me.  On the other side of that argument, it seems even more like an actual part of a city, which may or may not have been exceptionally well planned out.  The level of realism in the game is pretty good.
I would certainly recommend this game to probably anyone who likes FPS-type games, or the Warhammer universe.

Let me say one thing real quick, I LOVE THE GAME! Why did I not recommend the game? It was given the Uplay treatment... If you don't know, Ubisoft puts a service in their games called Uplay which is essentially Steam (actually, it's almost the exact same thing) but it transfers cross-platform. Sounds pretty good right? Be able to keep multiplayer progress, achievements, and even your bonus content through Ubisoft's cloud network? Ever hear the phrase, "Everything good comes at a price?" Neither have I, but it's relevent now... Uplay though amazing on paper, is pretty much (if you're on Xbox) a second fee to pay for a game... Not for their service, nope. PER game! This means (like in my case) that if you buy a second hand copy of the game and the person who owned it before you used the code that came with it, you have to buy another code. Be careful with older Ubisoft games though, as their multiplayer servers are usually empty or closed all together, ultimately screwing you out of the price of the code in the end, and they get extra money... You're probably thinking, "Well, you bought the game on PC from Steam, you shouldn't have any issues!" Well, no. I did buy it on Steam, but the thing is it doesn't work. The Uplay servers are down, and I don't think they're coming back. What's the problem with this? Well, I had to switch computers since my last one is being repaired (by someone that is mechanically unskilled but that's a story for another time), so I had to reinstall Far Cry 3 and Uplay. Last time I had the game I remember having issues, but now that the servers are down, I can't sign in. I could use Offline mode, but I haven't signed in on this computer yet, so my username and password isn't in the computer. So basically, all I can do on PC is use the map editor since that's a separate program (which to be perfectly honest, I use more often anyway)...
So in short, unless you want to use the PC's updated map editor exclusively, for pretty much an FPS creation program (which it would be easier to just buy one or learn how to make one yourself), the PC version of Far Cry 3 is practically useless if you wish to do anything else. Want to play multiplayer? Nope. That's in the main game. Want to play the story mode? Nope. Also in the main game. Want to play for some achievements on your Steam account? Nope. You can't open Far Cry 3 if you just now bought the game (or in my case, swapped computers), so you're not going to play the game...

This game, man...
tl;dr at the bottom
The Hotline Miami series is definitely one that you need to play in chronological order to fully understand the greatness of it - this game is an excellent, excellent,
follow up to the original Hotline Miami. It's just that, though - an excellent
. If you're interested in getting into this series, definitely start off with the first game.
I'm someone who actually prefers this game to the original, however. If you played the first game, the levels are more similar to the biker levels after Jacket's story wrapped up than the original Jacket style. If you haven't played the first game, stop reading this review and go play the first game because at this point in time this review is worthless to you.
In short, though - less focus on masks and varied gameplay styles and more focused on characters. It's less open ended as a result of this, and while removing the Jacket style in favor of characters with set abilities for each level is something I'd normally cry heresy over, this game manages to execute it extremely well to the point where I didn't even care that I wasn't given a huge variety of masks to choose from and had a lot of gameplay freedom taken away. This sounds much worse than it is, trust me - this game hits the nail on the head with what it's trying to do and it's excellent as a result.
It also is a lot more difficult than the first game, I think; the levels are larger and there can be a pretty serious loss of progress once you get towards the end and die, as opposed to the original's tendency to have smaller levels. As a result, there is a lot more enemies. There's also less masks, as I noted earlier, and that can create a handicap for those who relied on certain masks in the first game and being able to have more variety.
It's as violent as ever, thankfully. This game pulls no punches in how graphic it is, and it benefits from as much for certain. One of the things I love about both games of this series is that it gives me an outlet to battle stress by allowing me to vent my psychotic urges to just beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of anybody I can. Much blood, very graphic executions (except for evan lol), but I might just give the first game the edge in the gore and violence department if that much is your thing.
As for the story, it pieces a bunch of the events of the first game into context and gives them meaning, as the first game could be pretty incoherent and schizophrenic with the story it tried to tell. It was an effective stylistic choice, for certain, but this game serves as providing context for the events of the first game and it's why I'm telling you to go play the first game if you haven't played it yet. This game expects you to know the first game. Back on topic, though - the story is surprisingly powerful in this game. From memorable characters such as Richter to Beard to the Fans, it manages to show just how ♥♥♥♥ed up everything is in a way that has a lot of powerful moments. I don't want to spoil anything, so I won't go into any plot details, but the story is fantastic and surprisingly gave me the feels on a few occasions.
Lastly, the soundtrack - it's as ♥♥♥♥♥in' as ever. Seriously, the soundtrack is even better than the first game and can hit like a truck. This is seriously one of the greatest soundtracks in any game ever and I can totally get behind the soundtrack itself costing as much as the game -
tl;dr - this game expects you to know the first so go play that if you haven't already. If you have, there's an excellent story being told here alongside some absolutely amazing gameplay and one of the greatest soundtracks you'll find anywhere.

NOTE: This is a review on the STEAM version of the game and how I feel the game from a PC perspective and not a mobile perspective. There is no difference from the steam version and the mobile version but there are some things that look good on a phone or tablet but not so much on the PC. If this was a review on the mobile version then I would definitetly recommend this game.
Now as the game is still open beta, there are many things to be added and polished on (like levels, maps, shops etc) so I can't talk about the lack of content but instead I will mention the things that I feel are weird in the PC or things that should be added or modified.
The UI - It shouldn't come to a suprise that when you make a cross platform game between PC and mobile, there are gonna have to be corners cut. In this case its the UI. On mobile, the UI looks great and makes sense but on the PC, it just looks cheap and unclean. Preferably if possible, adding an option to switch between tablet UI and PC UI would be amazing. The UI also lacks alot of small yet needed details like specific HP, MP, and XP numbers.
Friends/Party System - While there is an friends list system, there is no party system. You can use the summon code (which is a bit buggy at times. I was stuck in loading) to play on the same channel/map but there isn't a real party system. so you can't see their HP/MP bar without clicking on them. This may not be as big as a problem now but in the future when there are healer classes, it would be extremely difficult to play as you can't attack a monster while keeping tabs on your friends HP at the same time.
Weapons/Classes/Stats - There are 4 main stats in the game; HP, MP, Attack, and Defense. The class you have on only affect your skills and nothing else. "Daggers" gives the most Attack of all the weapons, "staffs" give the most MP, and "swords" give the most Defense. Here's the problem. All the classes are equally tanky. I have played all the classes besides Guardian and I have noticed little to no difference in survivability. Being tanky isn't going to help when you're playing a Rogue or Mage because that's not what they do, and Warriors are suppose to be tanky, but do a bad job at it because there are no skills to help him be tanky. In fact, I would say Mage and Rogue are more tanky because they have defensive skills (Mana Sheild and Stealth). This makes Attack the most valuable stat for doing the most damage. AQW was really customizable because there was no restriction on what weapon you could use. You could be a Mage and use a hammer, but this only worked because every weapons attack stats were the same and the attack stats are mainly determined by the enchant. In AQ3D, each weapon has different stats. Attack determines how much damage you do, and that's the only real stat you should be going for as Rogue or Mage. Even Warriors should build this over Defense tbh. "Daggers" have the highest attack making the "daggers" the only viable weapon to use for high DPS. This takes away a lot of customization (plus it looks weird for a mage to use a dagger as a weapon). Some solutions to this would be adding more stats (like LUK for Rogues and INT for mages) or making it like AQW where all weapons have equal damage and the stat's are based off enchants.
Again, this game is still in beta so it is expected to be some flaws but there is a lot of potential in this game. With some things added and polished, I can see this being a very fun game

Game is getting a lot of unecessary hate. I personally think it's great.
Physics feel much better FOR THE MOST PART than DR (I am a fan of that game). Cars feel heavier and you can throw their weight around, and they don't launch into the air badly over every small bump which makes it much more realistic.
Actually, the only complaint about the physics is that the back of the car needs to slide more... it's just a bit too grippy so it *seems* like it's been dumbed down for cry babies. It hasn't; it's just the rear has a bit too much grip which CM have addressed in a video and it may be fixed. Cars feel much better on tarmac now too.
Force feedback feels great too, much better and more refined than dirt rally.
Graphics seem to lack in some detail like textures, but car modles, track/road detail, lighting, rain, and general particle effects have GREATLY improved. As an Aussie myself, I can confirm that the Australian stages have authentic australian lighting and it really feels like I'm speeding through the outback.
Haven't tried landrush yet, but RallyX is fantastic too.
Track Generator is also really nice. Setting the length slider to the max and then turning down the complexity gives some very fast, satisfying stages in Australia. Haven't tried the other areas yet.
Performance seems a bit funny though, I've had some weird stutter here and there, and I can't max it at 3440x1440 and hold a consistent 60fps with a single gtx 1080. Haven't tried SLI yet so will update the review when I do.
Overall rating would be a solid 7.5/10.
Lost 2.5 points for what feels too much traction at the back of the car on loose surfaces. That said, I've never driven any of these rally cars in real life so I can't really compare, but from watching videos of how the cars behave and then watching Dirt 4 replays, it just looks like the cars regain grip way too fast at the back.
So the final verdict? Great game, worth your time if you like rally, and it will be getting a lot of playtime out of me.

We host parties every month or so, and tend to have two groups of people show up - my friends, who are mostly gamers, and my partner's, who mostly aren't. We have a pair of TVs set up in the lounge for mine to play on at these parties, and the rest tend to play Cards Against Humanity or socialise elsewhere in the house.
I was immediately impressed by how quickly both groups sat down in the lounge to give the Jackbox a go when I first bought it yesterday. We started with a round of Fibbage 2, which was loud, funny and silly enough for everyone to feel comfortable giving it a go without having to feel like they were joining the 'gamer' half of the crowd. Since you're controlling the games from your phone, nobody has to feel like they're out of their comfort zone with an Xbox controller or constantly waiting for a turn with a gamepad. Both the gamers and non-gamers in the group were able to play together, which is a really hard trick to pull off.
The games in the pack are varied enough to keep things interesting, and none of them are disappointing. I will say, though, that while the bomb disposal game is still pretty hilarious and engaging, it is a LOT harder than the others - the story mode is purely cooperative, and it can be a lot harder for less engaged players to feel like they're contributing. It also supports fewer players, which ended up cutting our playtime short in favour of the other titles.
I tried really hard to find a deal on this game before I picked it up, but I'm pretty happy with the $25 I paid for it in the end. We're going to be cracking it out again in the future, and it's a safe and reliable option for crowds who aren't necessarily full of gamer types.

Jackbox over Google Hangouts lets us share laughs with friends all over the country, no matter where they are. Our group looks forward to playing the Party Pack 2 multiple times per week (along with the first Party Pack) and it's always a great source of entertainment. This is highly recommended and well worth the small price of admission for the amount of value that your group will get out of it.

ZUP! is a little 2D physics puzzle game series that would be totally unnoticeable among peers, has it not been for the infamously ridiculous amount of achievements it has.
But let’s start from the beginning. Gameplay is as simple as it gets. You have some squares that either stay, move, represent “you”, represent place “you” need to get, and – hence the title – explode. Essentially, picking up right thing to explode is the main way to solve puzzles in this game. And since the number of possible items to blow up rarely exceeds a dozen – you will hardly get stuck on any particular level for more than a minute.
Note, that with puzzles that simplistic, the mental reward, the proud feeling of “I did it” will be passing at best. If saying “I solved all puzzles in Braid without looking up hints” will probably raise some friends’ eyebrows in well-deserved awe, saying the same about “Zup!” will keep those eyebrows in question as still as the level of your IQ after playing this game.
Having said that – I don’t mean to say that the game is bad. It can still provide quality entertainment for dull moments in life, like, when you stuck in the airport for an hour, or sitting through stakeholders meeting – anything that would otherwise be filled with endless crushing of candies.
Now, elephant in the room: achievements. Game developers apparently saw the excitement the puzzles produced in players, or rather, the lack thereof – and found a skillful way to compensate it. Or, should I say, overcompensate – since “Zup” series is now responsible for about 98% of all the achievements I got, and even future years of gaming would hardly bring this number to anything lower than 90%.
Is it good, having thousands “free” achievements? I don’t know. It is definitely not for everybody. Having that many achievements has its “oh you played THAT game” vibe about it. But here the solution is simple – just stop caring what other people think. And after playing ZUP! you’ll have all letters you need to reflect this in your achievement showcase.

I recommend this game, but beware that matchmaking is poor in certain regions. I live in Asia and can never find games. If you are going to get this game, bring friends or do not bother at all.
That said, the game does have surprising depth for the price and genre. At least in the beginning, there is a "correct" way to play each character that synergizes with the characters strengths. The playstyle becomes altogether different and team composition needs to be tweaked accordingly.
Aside from this, there are two things to note. The game is definitely a gear grind. If you dont like that, avoid it at all costs. Also, sometimes with latency the hit detection becomes a little questionable - you will swear you hit things but it just wont register.
Otherwise, the art direction, level design and all other aspects of the game are great and I highly recommend it. Just wish the multiplayer were more accessible.

Hydrophobia:  Prophecy (Dark Energy Digital, 2011)
I've completed Hydrophobia: Prophecy and had a great time doing so.
It's true that this was originally meant to be the first game in a trilogy, that it had major problems upon release, that the rest of the trilogy was scrapped and a new version of this game created that incorporated (some) content from what were meant to be the follow-ups, and that it has since appeared dirt cheap in numerous bundled deals and on Steam.  But don't let any of that distract you from what is now, today, a polished product that is genuinely fun to play.
In short, Hydrophobia:  Prophecy is an action-adventure game with strong platforming elements, set on a huge ocean liner, or rather in the bowels of a huge ocean liner.  The gameplay is fairly standard.  You are able to shoot, with a variety of different projectiles at your disposal, but it's not a shooter by any stretch.
The level design is great, the controls work, defeating enemies and overcoming environmental challenges feel satisfying, and as mentioned above, the price is likely to be right regardless of where you choose to buy it.
SCORES
Graphics - 82 %
Water effects are brilliant;  the main character has terrible hair though (plastic dreadlocks on what is otherwise a gorgeous model), which I found somewhat distracting throughout.
Sound - 70 %
It works;  nothing particularly noteworthy though.
Execution - 75 %
The game, in this iteration, is a good execution of its core concept.
The storytelling via cinematics and viewscreens placed around the ship is effective.  You dislike the bad guys;  though sadly their politics are never as deeply explored as it could have been (likely owing to the trilogy being scrapped).
The free running-style gameplay and acrobatics work and never pose any problems, such as unexpected falls or missing jumps because of problematic surface detection.
One does feel that the setting (a huge ocean liner) could have been more interestingly presented, and it doesn't feel all that much like you're inside a huge ship on the ocean (regardless of copious amounts of water).  Again, it is likely that this concept was originally meant to be explored further.
The water manipulation powers from later in the game also feel a bit tacked on, as they obviously were, considering they weren't meant to be in the first episode at all.
Addictiveness - 80 %
I wanted to continue playing, and I did, and I pursued some achievements, and I enjoyed myself.  That sentence has about two "ands" too many, but hey, the game is a bit like that.  You never know if you're close to the end and you don't really care.  It's fun getting there, and that's mainly what matters (in my opinion).
Overall - 75 %
It's cheap.  It's good.  Buy it if you're into third-person exploration games with some shooting and a lot of acrobatics.
The achievements all appear to work, which I know is important to some people.  There are collectables, again, if that is your sort of thing.  I just wanted a thrilling experience with an unsual setting, and I got what I wanted.
I'm looking forward to doing another playthrough at some point.  And that's really the best recommendation there is.

While the TR-ish foundation is there, the puzzle solving, jumping and climbing, and combat, all of these are under utilized and so sporadic that most of the time you're just left to play in the water, which is the main focus of the game anyway. This is a great title. It goes on sale often, so you can defintely pick it up cheap. I'm typically only interested in co-op, so I solely played each of the maps on Escape mode. The game nails the tension that horror games need to nail with the darkness and soundtrack, and the need to pull up your phone to figure out your next step keeps you on edge. Additionally, the zombies are tough, and you'll need to make your shots count (by aiming for the head). The shooting doesn't feel bad at all. You can't just spray these zombies down, as a general rule. The issues I had were mostly dealing with connection. Even after forwarding all appropriate ports, my friends had difficulty getting in my games. They were able to get in my game on one occasion, but unfortunately, we were all slaughtered by the same player-controlled zombie (even when I had disabled the "player zombie" option). This brings me to my second gripe - the player controlled zombies themselves. Though I appreciate the desire to keep downed players involved (both with spectator roaches and player-controlled zombies), the zombies themselves are extremely strong. They still go down quickly if you aim for the head, but I think the player should be notified loudly if a player zombie has spawned, perhaps even with a text overlay in the corner of the HUD. It's just too easy for a player to join the game, die, and then ruin your team's run without you seeing them coming. However, despite this, I definitely enjoyed myself.

In Far Cry 3, you play as Jason Brody, a man who got lost in a tropical island along with his friends, with all of them being kidnapped and spread around the Island, with the main goal being to take down the evil rulers of the island and free his friends.
To this day, 5 years after release, the graphics are still superb. No way to complain about them, they are fantastic. The scenery is beautiful - I love tropical islands myself, and the scenery is perfect for me. The weapons are great and look great, and have good phyics. However, the game is too easy - you take 1,000 shots to die (hyperbole), and you can get a virtually infite amount of healing from syringes that you can carry with you, since you can continuously pause and craft more should you run out, and they take about a second to deploy for a full heal.
The story is great and intriguing, and the missions are not very repitive. This is a stealth-based game, and stealth is a very common mechanic you have to master. One way of stealth in this game is to crouch behind enemies then stab them, then hide their bodies. You can complete missions, capture outposts, and reveal Radio Towers which highlight the map.
In this game, there is no need to buy weapons, except for the last weapon unlocked at 18 Radio Towers revealed (It has to be bought), as weapons become free by revealing radio towers. The only purpose for money is to essentially buy ammo (which is not needed, and a luxury), and to buy the final weapon, which is a very, very good weapon, better than all the others.
It's a good game, I recommend it. Play it on hardest settings.

This is a tough one.
If you haven't played HM1, don't buy this. Play the first one and then decide, honestly I think it's still better.
HM2 carries over some of the charm we know and love from the first installment of the series but still makes slight changes in level design that change gameplay fundamentally.
Going 'Melee only' is a lot harder now than it used to be, as the game encourages guns and combos more than its predecessor.
The experience changes drastically because of this, as it makes the game a lot more strategic and tactical and gives up some of the flow I loved in the first game.
Often times you will find enemies (with guns) far away from you and will die to situations that are simply impossible to survive without knowing what waits for you behind some long distances. These enemies will be impossible to kill without stopping or slowing down to press shift to look further out, which heavily influences flow.
Without giving anything away I can tell you that the story will now have you play a multitude of different characters which means that choosing a mask rarely happens at all and usually without a lot of variety. This isn't something I miss too much though, because the unique character designs really manage to make up for it.
I'd say the game is inferior to the first one in very many ways, but that doesn't make it a bad game at all, considering just how amazing Hotline Miami was for most people who played it.
The story good enough and still manages to keep some of the 'what is happening?' confusion you might have felt during the first game alive.
All in all I would probably recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the first game. If you're sceptic, try to pick it up on sale.
If you feel like the first game lacked a bit of strategy, then there really isn't a whole lot for you to think about. Buy it.

ZUP! is a little 2D physics puzzle game series that would be totally unnoticeable among peers, has it not been for the infamously ridiculous amount of achievements it has.
But let’s start from the beginning. Gameplay is as simple as it gets. You have some squares that either stay, move, represent “you”, represent place “you” need to get, and – hence the title – explode. Essentially, picking up right thing to explode is the main way to solve puzzles in this game. And since the number of possible items to blow up rarely exceeds a dozen – you will hardly get stuck on any particular level for more than a minute.
Note, that with puzzles that simplistic, the mental reward, the proud feeling of “I did it” will be passing at best. If saying “I solved all puzzles in Braid without looking up hints” will probably raise some friends’ eyebrows in well-deserved awe, saying the same about “Zup!” will keep those eyebrows in question as still as the level of your IQ after playing this game.
Having said that – I don’t mean to say that the game is bad. It can still provide quality entertainment for dull moments in life, like, when you stuck in the airport for an hour, or sitting through stakeholders meeting – anything that would otherwise be filled with endless crushing of candies.
Now, elephant in the room: achievements. Game developers apparently saw the excitement the puzzles produced in players, or rather, the lack thereof – and found a skillful way to compensate it. Or, should I say, overcompensate – since “Zup” series is now responsible for about 98% of all the achievements I got, and even future years of gaming would hardly bring this number to anything lower than 90%.
Is it good, having thousands “free” achievements? I don’t know. It is definitely not for everybody. Having that many achievements has its “oh you played THAT game” vibe about it. But here the solution is simple – just stop caring what other people think. And after playing ZUP! you’ll have all letters you need to reflect this in your achievement showcase.

Holy cow! Zup is just sooooooo good!
This game will draw a line. A concrete line between before Zup! and after Zup!. The feeling you get for completing levels is just pure fantasy. You fill up achievements faster than you can drink beer. You feel good about yourself by just clicking squares. Seeing some explosions. Going forward.
Buy it. Play it. Uninstall it. Never look back. Good decisions don't need rethinking.

Having finished all of the single missions and all of the campaigns, both in Normal and in Iron Man, I believe I'm in a position to write a few things about this game. I don't usually write Steam reviews, but Door Kickers is a special game that deserves recommendation. As someone who is very interested in tactical gaming, the top-down tactics offered by this game are very enjoyable.
The game gives you control over a team of SWAT operators and tasks you with defeating the bad guys and completing missions such as rescuing hostages, arresting a suspect, securing evidence, preventing escape of the suspects or escorting a VIP. There are different ways to play the game, but the way I play it (and I guess the most obvious style of play) is real-time with pause. The way I usually do the missions is like this: I draw actions for my troopers, let them play out those actions, pause, assess the situation and then plan my next move. You can also play the game in 100% real-time or even prepare the entire mission in the planning phase if you want. It's a lot more difficult and challenging to do, but the option is there. There is no 'true' method of playing the game.
It's a challenging game. The guns are deadly. That goes both ways. If you don't want any of your troopers to get killed in one or two shots, you better make sure that you watch your sectors and assume that there is danger around every corner. The game mercilessly punishes you for your mistakes, but the rules are fair and if you lose a trooper it's almost always due to your own mistake.
Perhaps the greatest compliment that can be given to Door Kickers is the fact that a number of real-life tactics can be applied to it, and that these are often the most effective. The best way to clear a simple room is the way real operators often do it: stack your troopers near the door, open or breach it, throw a flashbang (tip: use them excessively), enter the room, establish points of domination along the nearest wall(s) and let your troopers shoot all of the bad guys in their own respective sector. Take a look at the top-down illustrations in
. Some of the tactics that are shown in that chapter actually work in Door Kickers. That is an impressive feat, and it highlights the developer's understanding of real-world CQC fights and tactics. Because of this, Door Kickers is arguably one of the more realistic small-scale tactics games there are.
It's not without flaws. From time to time, your troopers will make a stupid mistake which may get one of them killed, such as when they accidentally throw a grenade against the wall instead of into the room. And they cannot perform certain basic tasks like leaning and crouching, though that might have been a design decision. But overall, the controls are very fleshed out and the game is very enjoyable to play as is. It allows a certain degree of freedom in how to approach each situation: your stealth approach doesn't work? Kit out your team with harder-hitting assault rifles. Can't prevent a hostage execution in time? Try a different route or be more aggressive. Having a lot of trouble eliminating an armoured tango? Invest in one of the guns that offer better armour penetration. Or just throw more flashbangs. More flashbangs are always good. Some of the equipment that works in certain situations will not work in other situations, and vice-versa. All of the equipment in the game has utility, although some are more useful than others.
Door Kickers 2 is currently in development, but the first game is still very much worth buying and playing. If you're looking for a good top-down tactics game, look no further.

This is a tough one.
If you haven't played HM1, don't buy this. Play the first one and then decide, honestly I think it's still better.
HM2 carries over some of the charm we know and love from the first installment of the series but still makes slight changes in level design that change gameplay fundamentally.
Going 'Melee only' is a lot harder now than it used to be, as the game encourages guns and combos more than its predecessor.
The experience changes drastically because of this, as it makes the game a lot more strategic and tactical and gives up some of the flow I loved in the first game.
Often times you will find enemies (with guns) far away from you and will die to situations that are simply impossible to survive without knowing what waits for you behind some long distances. These enemies will be impossible to kill without stopping or slowing down to press shift to look further out, which heavily influences flow.
Without giving anything away I can tell you that the story will now have you play a multitude of different characters which means that choosing a mask rarely happens at all and usually without a lot of variety. This isn't something I miss too much though, because the unique character designs really manage to make up for it.
I'd say the game is inferior to the first one in very many ways, but that doesn't make it a bad game at all, considering just how amazing Hotline Miami was for most people who played it.
The story good enough and still manages to keep some of the 'what is happening?' confusion you might have felt during the first game alive.
All in all I would probably recommend this game to anyone who enjoyed the first game. If you're sceptic, try to pick it up on sale.
If you feel like the first game lacked a bit of strategy, then there really isn't a whole lot for you to think about. Buy it.

MILD SPOILERS: I go over some of the game's mechanics and similarities to Left 4 Dead, which it is -heavily- based on.
I don't find all that many games very addicting or legitimately entertaining,but this one is among the few (proportionately speaking). To keep it simple up front for those TL;DR people, if you love or even like Left 4 Dead, I think it's a safe bet you'll enjoy this game (and if you don't, just refund it).
You probably notice from gameplay videos how similar it is to L4D, and it has so many of the same mechanics (inventory with two weapons, a healing item slot, support item slot, and throwable item slot, as well as countless other things), so much so that I at first thought it was made by the same devs as the games feel nearly identical.
I'd rate it better than L4D, it's different, yes, but it is also better imo. What does it have that L4D doesn't?
-Leveling
-Weapon keeping and upgrading
-Interesting loot system
-Five characters, where for the most part, they have varying playstyles, where in L4D, a character is just a skin.
What does it have that L4D does?
-Glowing character outlines through walls to find your team if you get lost
-When your life runs out, you need to be helped up by a teammate before the enemy kills you.
-When you do die, or a friend dies, you can be rescue or rescue a friend later on in the level by freeing them.
-Elite enemies, remember Boomers, Hunters, Spitters, Smokers, Tanks? This game has rat versions of those.

There's more, but you get the idea, it's great, includes a free DLC with 40 weapons -and- some other goodies. On top of that, the devs have plans to extend the game greatly with expansions and free content, including but not limited to having new enemy races (i.e. not just rats).
Cons?
Well, I'd say the maps feel shorter than L4D's maps, but I believe at launch, this game has more maps to play than L4D did, so take that into mind, and the possibility of future content.
The bots, they are problematic. They've gotten a lot better though, they'll still make stupid decisions now and then, like taking healing kits when other bots or you are more damaged than they are (but they also heal you with their kits if you are hurt badly enough to make up for it).
The bots used to have a bad habit of chasing elite enemies rather than helping a defeated player back up, leaving them for dead. They don't do this quite as much anymore, I find they're much more dependable now. I can reliably beat one of the maps on the 2nd highest difficulty with nothing but bots, so they've improved.

Okay lemme get the one ridiculous, stupid, and enragingly awful feature out of the way: the loot system. It sucks - really, really badly. I don't think it is humanly possible to devise something that should be awesome and rewarding in a way that could be any worse than the loot system in this game. It really is very bad.
The way it works is you are given 7 dice. These are not dice that have numbers on them; they either increase a point on your loot, or they don't (so, in other words, they have either a 0 or a 1). Normally, you have 7 dice that have a 2 in 6 chance of landing on the 1. However, there are 3 types of dice that you can find to replace some of the normal dice.
You can find "loot dice" by exploring the maps, but the presence of these is totally random; they have a 3 in 6 chance of landing on the 1. Or, you can find hidden tomes that provide a 4 in 6 chance; these take up the health slot in-game while you're carrying them, so one person has to neglect any health potions or health kits while carrying the tome. Finally, you can find grimoires that always roll a 1. However, these take up a potion slot (potions can be used to get either temporary strength or speed, and neither are incredibly useful) but more importantly they take away 30% of your entire team's health.
There are usually about 3 tomes and 2 grimoires in every map; that means that if you have found them all (they are somewhat hidden) and you are carrying them all, by the end of the map you are missing 3 potential health items you could carry and your entire team's max health has fallen to 40% of what it is normally.
At the end of the level, the dice are rolled and your total is added up. The number of dice that landed favorably get you to better, higher-quality loot (even if you roll none, you still get something, which I guess is nice). Furthermore, playing on a higher difficulty increases the quality of potential loot. For instance, playing a map on normal lets you get one of either a lot of whites or some greens or a blue on the highest roll; on hard, the same map provides the chances of either a lot of greens, some blues, or an orange on the highest roll.
So here's the one reason that more than any other this loot system sucks. I was playing a mission on hard (I was playing with a new guy, and there's an appreciable difference between normal and hard, so we really had to work at it). We found two loot dice, three tomes, and a grimoire. It takes a lot of effort and time to do all that, especially on hard. I complete the mission, I roll a 2, and I got a green item. That means for a lot more time, difficulty, and effort, I got the same loot that I would've gotten doing the same mission on normal and ignoring the tomes and grimoires and if I got a decent roll.
When I play and get loot, instead of feeling rewarded, I feel
. It's horrible and stupid and I'm honestly not sure how anyone could have possibly let it into the game.
Especially because the rest of the game is just good fun. There is intersting loot to be had, and there are ways to craft it even if you do only get loot that you hate. The new Sigmar's Blessing content makes the game much more fun and the loot much more interesting, and I'm under the impression that the developers are going to continue giving out more free content. That's awesome!
The melee combat feels awesome, and the ranged combat is pretty cool. The special rats all feel like an afterthought and don't really belong. Often times several assassins or pack rats (I don't remember their actual names :P) will appear at the same time and wipe out the whole team (this is the equivalent of several teleporting hunters and melee-smokers that you can't shoot, in L4D terms). The pack rats are especially odd because they work by hooking you with a long pole, and dragging you around. You can't do anything about it, and your teammates' best weapons are in melee. Because there is no sprinting, the result is a bizarre chase while they try to catch up to the rat, who is only slightly slower. It doesn't change the dynamic, or make you switch positions, or anything like that; it's just kinda annoying and feels out of place.
Rat ogres and poison globers also feel pretty out of place. The ogre essentially just requires being hit a lot, and in my opinion they take waaaay too long to die. Not fun, doesn't change the tactics really, just kinda is annoying and can sometimes wreck a half-hour progress for no avoidable reason. The globers throw poison at you to try to cause you to disperse, but the maps are clearly not designed with this guy in mind; the result is extrememly annoying and not fun or interesting. The same is not true, however, for the assassins or ratling gunners, which are genuinely fun and require a bit of changing tactics.
Overall, I feel that the way the different "specials" spawn is just slightly off. You can go a long time without any showing up, and all of a sudden you get swarmed by two gunners and three assassins. Sometimes, on normal, an entire mission would go by without any ogres (thank goodness). Other times on normal, three appeared in the same mission.
The fantastic melee and the interesting later-on loot make up, however, for all these gripes. The loot system is infuriating, but I usually just remind myself that I'll use it primarily just to make the gear that I want. Grab friends, play it. Despite all this complaining, the rest of the game really is fun enough to make up for all this.

Hey friends, just thought I'd share some of my thoughts.
Time played: 4+ hours
I was pretty reluctant to buy this game, as I already have DiRT Rally, and there have been mixed reviews, but so far I have been really happy with my time playing this game.
Graphics 8/10
Music 8/10
Sounds 10/10
Difficulty 7/10**
Overall 9/10
Ok, so where do I begin... This game is really pretty pleasant, no matter what reviews you see. When you first start you get an introduction that lets you choose between a more arcade style of racing, or the simulation style. Being someone who had clocked plenty of hours on DiRT Rally I chose the latter. After a race it recommends a difficulty for you, myself being pro.
Modes: I played a few different modes in the first few hours: the tutorial (wow!), rally, joyride, and competitive.
-Tutorial: This is great. As someone who played the previous game (only somewhat successfully) this was really nice. Whether you are new to the concepts or not the practice is really helpful.
-Rally: Oh yeah! This time around you don't have to start in a 60's car. That fact alone makes this so much better. I am also really pleased with the setup for the career, it just makes sense.
-Joyride: If you're into gymkhana this could be for you, the smash attack and time attack modes are pretty fun.
-Competitive: While I only did one race here, it was pretty fun to rally against others in real time, also came out with a win!
Pros: Fun, realistic, rewarding, great team management system (something the previous game really needed), great atmosphere.
Cons: None so far. This game has been really good.
I would totally recommend this game. I'm four hours in, but that's just the surface. Cheers!
