I've played through almost the full career mode for modern rally (there's still Historic rally, landrush, and rallycross left) and I love this game. I doubt anyone who says this game is too easy has actually played it on Sim settings with all assists off. I'm going to need to buy a stress ball because of this game. 9.5/10
More details:
It feels different than Dirt Rally, but that is not a bad thing at all. The cars have a proper feeling of weight, the FFB is really good, breaking distances are more realistic and overall the driving feels more realistic. Slightly too much grip in some corners, but the developers have noted the criticism and said they will be trying to work on it. Even with that negative point, the driving feels great, tarmac is especially good.
The career mode is so fleshed out compared to it's predecessor, there are many customization options for your own team and there's definitively incentive to play the career and not just do free plays.
The damage simulation is much, much improved. You can have break issues, engine misfires, gearbox problems, lights flickering etc. happening to you in the middle of stage if you haven't been keeping your car repaired and upgraded. You can upgrade individual parts, a higher rating means it will hold up longer, and it does make a difference. There seems to be engine wear simulation, if I am costantly reving my engine through a stage, downshifting to early and hitting rev-stop or redlinig a lot, the engine will wear quickly and you will actually notice having had a loss of performance the next time you drive the car after being repaired.
Your Stage is a neat feature, I like it so far. It doesn't provide as much detail as hand-crafted stages, naturally, but it does give you a new map every time and keeps you on edge, teaching you to value your co-driver. Sometimes I feel like I can recognize corners and sections, but overall every stage is different and feels rather new. It would be nice if some more corners and tiles were added in the future.
Giving you the choice between 2 different English-speaking co-drivers, as well as several other languages, is nice. One problem I've had is hairpins and acute corners being called too late after high speed sections. I adjusted the pace-note timing in the settings to a bit earlier, and it made it better, but this could use some tweaking from the devs.
There's a lot to be said, but I really like the game so far. If you liked Dirt Rally, you will like this game too. It is NOT easy, unless you choose to make it easy for yourself.

Wakfu is a turned based MMORPG, that has interesting graphics, music, so on and so forth with things that've already been touched on.
Lemme tell you about the part of it that really makes ME excited. Wakfu really tried to build a world that was entirely dependent on the people who play it. So, right off the bat? There are zero NPCs, aside from the occasional quest giver. That means if you're looking to sell your♥♥♥♥♥♥ you better start up a stand. There's also an Ecology system that effects monsters and gathering nodes (trees, plants, ore, etc.) wherein, if you kill too much, or take too much, it'll actually GO AWAY. It's up to the player to repopulate these areas by planting things, breeding animals and generally working with the "Wakfu" of any particular area.
Some other notable parts are as follow: Player elected governors, citizen points that can effect how the world treats you (Wanna be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, be an outlaw and go to jail? Hell yeah you do.), instant player housing (Haven bag) that... also works as your store, a place to decorate things, a place to put gathering nodes and so on. There's also huge maps, the ability to spec into every kind of profession, interesting character classes that have little to no over lap as far as utility... I mean, come on!
I'll admit I'm pretty stoked about this game. However, it is definitely not a game for everyone. The combat can be pretty off putting, and it's generally not as fun of an experience if you go at it alone. But, if you're the type of person that really likes to see a game take some amazing steps for MMOs, you might wanna give this a shot.

First I should point out a misconception I had with this game that led to a negative review at first. This planning in this game is really not designed for you to make a perfect masterplan for each mission in one go. In my first hours of the game I was making long elaborate plans but elements of chance make this really unreliable. You can run a perfect plan one time and then run the exact plan again but maybe a shot will miss or an enemy spawns in the wrong place and that run is completely ruined, so you just restart over and over till it lines in your favor and that is not a fun way to play.
Sure the game gives you the tools to make a masterplan like that but the inability to edit any of that plan without almost completely redoing it should be a sure sign that that is not the intended way to play.
Once I dropped making plans and instead ran a little, paused, worked a bit more, etc I enjoyed this game much much more than at the start.
One other thing is that the game really needs more non-lethal tactics, I recently took down a dificult 22 enemy level with only the tazers but ooooh many was that janky. When lots of enemies are tazed in a row the pathfinding makes it that you can only pick up one of them at a time, meaning I had to always have somebody on guard for when the other guys stood back up, and sometimes it didnt register that I was arresting them and then they got stuck in the throwing grenade animation for some reason?? Overall the game really doesnt seem to expect people to play this way which makes me wonder why they included the tazer at all.
Other than that it's a lot of fun and thats about all there is to be said.

For a sequel it does what you'd expect from one: To take the original game and expand on it.
Pros:
More challenging than the first game.
There is now an indicator in the top right hand corner of the screen to tell you how high your combo is.
Lots of new characters with unique play styles for the player to adapt to.
Because it isn't centered around an insane soldier with P.T.S.D. it has a more natural and understandable story that wraps up some unanswered questions of the first game, while at the same time having a story that will only make sense if you pay attention.
The soundtrack is bigger and better than the first with returning and new artists.
Still provides the simple yet challenging gameplay of the first game.
Cons:
Single sections of levels can feel way to big for comfort, the first game had lots of small environments to provide a good chance to go reckless and go on an insane combo streak. With these mostly bigger levels it feels as if you have to play it safe, or take the higher risk of dying by going reckless.
Besides the levels being very big, there are lots of enemies, so single sections can last a long time (especially on hard mode).
The enemy's situational awareness can sometimes extend outside your vision leading to lots of cheap feeling deaths when killed by that one dude with the shotgun you literally couldn't see. (This flaw also can be a fault of the bigger levels)
This is a sequel that Hotline Miami fans will enjoy, if you haven't picked it up now you probably should.

This isn't an MMOFPS, fights are limited to 32 players. Pet-peeve of mine, MMO should mean MASSIVE numbers of players in the same environment.
The RTS side drives the usually-unbalanced games where one team gets more resources and vehicles than the other. The "Staged" or training battles give both team lots of resources. That would be nice, except one team usually dominates the sky with planes that are hard to shoot down and deal lots of damage. Granted, they are hard to pilot... But the AA guns cant be resupplied other than by destroying them, they turn very slowly and deal low damage.
Physics are very, very simple. Jeeps are hard to drive in a straight line. There is so much lag you can't be a gunner in someone else's vehicle. The lag spikes make aiming on the move impossible. And that's with under 70ms of delay.
You don't unlock classes without paying money or grinding days upon days of playtime.
Vehicles are unbalanced between factions. And again... grind grind grind. The US doesn't get a fighter plane. Just a heavy fighter/bomber.
The maps are massive... with very tiny capture points in the middle of wide, open expenses you can never cross on foot without getting sniped.
There's 2 modes of play, long range and short range. Middle ground doesn't really work. You can try being stealthy, but crouching slows you WAY down and you can't go from prone to crouch.
The "Fun grind" includes making 3500 credits for a 30 minutes game or 5K credits for a 1h+ game. Fire 20 rockets and pay 10K credits for ammo. Yes, ammunition costs credits. Repairing your guns cost credits. And there are no fast way to make credits. You get some more credits the higher your character is ranked, but games usually take 30 minutes. Some skirmish end more quickly, maybe 20minutes.
There are advantages to paying money. Like skipping 100h of gameplay, or getting a 2nd perk for your characters. There is no way to get a second perk with credits.
There's been some updates, but some design flaws are never corrected. ( Why can't I change my load-out when in a squad with friends? Why can't I join a match in the same assault-team as my friends? )
Game requires lots of teamplay... no ingame voice chat, no quick-messages, and the chat window is TINY. Whistling can only do so much.

Free to play, fun to play! World War 2 is a popular theme for many games, but few offer such quality as this game. Considering it currently does not cost anything, it is definitely worth the time to try it.

The Heroes part of Heroes & Generals reminds me of the very first Call of Duty multiplayer. You have a limited supply of options with weapons for either faction you choose, the battles are cheap, yet you get very involved in them, there's a lack of communication between members in the staged (matchmaking) games, and you're allowed vehicles to drive around and shoot from. H&G incorporates a currency system, and you get paid a certain amount depending on your rank and how long you've been in the battle on the ground fighting. The basic weapons you start out with are just above 10,000 credits, but the ones that you unlock later on in the game, are in excess of 100,000. That is 10x the amount and time you just spent to earn up for that measly Grease Gun or MP34 you now own! There are several career paths you could choose from once you reach certain levels, and those cost credits to enlist into. For example, the tank crewman costs 22,000 credits, and the pilot costs 18,000. Let's start with the vehicle pricing! All vehicles, no matter which one you choose, will always be above 10,000 credits. The basic tank that you unlock after becoming a tanker is around 50,000 credits. For planes, I don't even want to know what they cost! Simply put, this game almost forces the impatient players to become Pay to Play players. Everything is unlockable through not paying anything, but it'll take 3-4 months to just get to the higher rankings and unlock the better equipment. The game revolves around currency.
I'm not into the rankings to allow me to access the Generals part of H&G, so I cannot review this aspect at this time. I do know that War Bonds (other types of credits you earn from participating in battles) come into play to supply ground troops with reinforcements, which are greatly needed at certain times; the number of tanks provided; the number of planes provided; and the number of infantry vehicles are provided. The Generals can give orders to attack other areas.
You have two types of games to join in H&G: Staged and War.
In Staged battles, your battles that you choose to participate in will not affect the outcome of the war and the faction that you chose. You earn generally less credits, and these games take greatly lesser amounts of time. You only are allowed to participate in skirmish matches until you reach level three, but by this time you've racked up a good supply of credits and experience. In these matches, are where you learn to play the game and learn to utilize your career path specialties. There is little communication between players, and either a team is very successful or a big catastrophic failure. Rarely will you see two teams of equal value in a staged battle.
In War battles, you get the option to choose at random or a very specific battle to participate in. You choose a faction, Russia; USA; or Germany, and fight for these countries. You're given a map of Europe, and your faction will be Blue, and the enemy faction will be Red. You can see which cities and towns, and routes you control. Battles will be flashing on your map, and you can click on these battles to participate in them, whether it be a Battle of London, or a battle of a small-german village. Whoever can control 12 major cities wins the War of Europe.
There are two types of modes of which you can participate in: Skirmishes and Assaults.
In Skirmishes, you fight to control three different and all neutral points at the beginning of the game. Whoever can hold two or more of these points for the majority of the game will win. It's straight and simple. Mostly seen in staged battles.
In Assaults, the main objective is to capture points in a city, forest, airfield or village and to control these points. You can be on the defending side, in which you defend generally two points out of a certain number of points for a given period of time until the end of the game. By this time, you will have won. But, the defenders cannot lose one of these two points, for they will have to work to regain this position and to hold it for an extended period of time. If the positions are held, the said area will remain claimed to the defending faction. For attackers, they start out with usually one or two spawn points, always on the outskirts of the forest, town, airfield, or village. From there, the attackers must push back the defenders to their main two points they must control. This is where the most resistance usually comes into play. The attackers must take these two points the defenders hold to win the said area for the attacking faction.
Overall, this game, for the strategical part of it, is why I continue to play Heroes and Generals. I dislike the amounts of credits you have to build up for everything, and the amounts of experience you need to build up to unlock careers and items and new ranks, but in the end, I believe it is worth my time and effort for a fun, and ever-changing and evolving game!

Players must work together to protect civilians and help them escape once the rescue vehicle arrives. Once you approach the location of the civs, zombies will start hording around the house. I've played every Dirt game and most of the preceding series. People are taking dumps all over this game because it's not Dirt Rally. Well, it isn't Dirt Rally. Pure Rally mode isn't necessarily as good as Dirt Rally, but Dirt 4 is the successor to Dirt 3, and in that respect it's a good game.
The addition of procedurally-generated Rally stages is pretty outstanding and makes for more longevity potential than Dirt Rally had. It also means the graphics don't look as good as Rally, which is a shame.
That said, I took the time to tweak my settings to get it to feel right on my Logitech G920 just like I did in Dirt Rally and it feels great to drive in simulation mode.
Nothing revultionary here, but the variety of rally tracks along with the other game modes makes it worth a purchase if you're into the genre.

Dirt 4 is first a rally game, harking back to Codemaster’s earlier Colin McCrae titles, but it takes lessons from Dirt Rally and the various Dirt and Grid titles to become what I feel is the best non-F1 title Codemasters has ever produced (I'll withhold judgement on the F1 series until I've played it). People who were daunted by the simulation aspect of Dirt Rally need not fear here: the game offers two handling modes, one being a development of Dirt 3's model and the other being an improvement over that of Dirt Rally. There have been accusations flying around that the simulation aspect of the game has been "dumbed down", but I feel this is simply a knee-jerk reaction. There is a lot more depth to the way weight transfer works this time around. The car feels as if it's ploughing trough a loose surface rather then sliding on top of it, and a lot of aspects that Dirt Rally did not model, such as how the car behaves in puddles, can catch you off-gaurd here.

In terms of sheer variety, Dirt 4 outpaces Dirt Rally by a very significant margin. Aside from the larger variety of cars and disciplines, the your stage feature does mean that there are no stages in the career mode repeat themselves. You do occasionally see the same corner popping up (betrayed by some distinct feature), but it's a significantly better variety then Dirt Rally offered. Whilst there is an occasional gem hidden between the oysters, the stages lack the distinct notes that Dirt Rally offered by giving you some of the most iconic rally stages in the world.

Even if the road itself is featureless, the event doesn't have to be. You'll find cars on the side of the road, the occasional wildlife or overzealous pilot getting in your way. Additionally, whilst in Dirt Rally you'd get the occasional flat tire, Dirt 4 has you picking up a variety of gremlins, some are the result of sheer bad luck, and some are the result of hasty repairs (the latter being a lot more severe). Dirt Rally sometimes had your opponents shuffled down the order due to grating brakes or slipping clutches. Now this can happen to you too.
Over Dirt 3 and over Dirt Rally, the career mode in particular has improved significantly. Dirt 3 was simply a succession of challenges, some of which you had to do even if you did not like them (The Gymkhana tutorials in particular have disappointed many players). Dirt Rally, on the other hand, was just the same championship repeated over and over again, increasing the difficulty whilst you tried to grind enough cash to buy a car with modern suspension. None of this is present in Dirt 4: You can set your own difficulty straight of the bat, the events at the start focus on beginner cars, and there's seperate tiers for each discipline. If you enjoyed Dirt 3's less serious Gymkhana or DC Challenge events, they're hidden under the "Joyride" section in the menu and they're free to do at your leisure, not impacting the career at all.
Aside from the four disciplines, Dirt 4 has a progression which involves how much other teams like you and you building your own team. The structure is reminiscent of the first GRID, but it is more open: Now each event can be completed by either driving for another team, or by buying your own car and running it by yourself. Teams can grow to like you, giving you better offers each time you are succesfull in meeting their goals. You can then invest the money you earn in your own team and buy cars for events no team is offering for. You can play it the other way around too: Focus almost entirely on developing your own team but taking the occasional drive for another team if you can't afford the car you want to drive, or if it isn't available for sale (as all the older cars have to be bought second hand, and the market isn't always offering). The variety of ways to participate means that there is hardly a necessity to grind towards the things you want to do, which was an issue in all the previous games. The achievement here is that it manages to do all this without robbing you of a sense of progression.
All in all I think it's a significant improvement over both Dirt Rally and Dirt 3, and fans of either (or both) will find this a welcome return. Don't hesitate picking this up at a price you feel comfortable with.

The loot system is horrifyingly bad and the special rats feel a bit out of place, but otherwise the game is incredibly fun. You'll love this game if you like at least 2 of the following: Left 4 Dead, fun melee combat, satisfying decapitation, or the thrill of turning garbage loot into slightly less bad loot until you get the really special and amazing stuff.
===
Okay lemme get the one ridiculous, stupid, and enragingly awful feature out of the way: the loot system. It sucks - really, really badly. I don't think it is humanly possible to devise something that should be awesome and rewarding in a way that could be any worse than the loot system in this game. It really is very bad.
The way it works is you are given 7 dice. These are not dice that have numbers on them; they either increase a point on your loot, or they don't (so, in other words, they have either a 0 or a 1). Normally, you have 7 dice that have a 2 in 6 chance of landing on the 1. However, there are 3 types of dice that you can find to replace some of the normal dice.
You can find "loot dice" by exploring the maps, but the presence of these is totally random; they have a 3 in 6 chance of landing on the 1. Or, you can find hidden tomes that provide a 4 in 6 chance; these take up the health slot in-game while you're carrying them, so one person has to neglect any health potions or health kits while carrying the tome. Finally, you can find grimoires that always roll a 1. However, these take up a potion slot (potions can be used to get either temporary strength or speed, and neither are incredibly useful) but more importantly they take away 30% of your entire team's health.
There are usually about 3 tomes and 2 grimoires in every map; that means that if you have found them all (they are somewhat hidden) and you are carrying them all, by the end of the map you are missing 3 potential health items you could carry and your entire team's max health has fallen to 40% of what it is normally.
At the end of the level, the dice are rolled and your total is added up. The number of dice that landed favorably get you to better, higher-quality loot (even if you roll none, you still get something, which I guess is nice). Furthermore, playing on a higher difficulty increases the quality of potential loot. For instance, playing a map on normal lets you get one of either a lot of whites or some greens or a blue on the highest roll; on hard, the same map provides the chances of either a lot of greens, some blues, or an orange on the highest roll.
So here's the one reason that more than any other this loot system sucks. I was playing a mission on hard (I was playing with a new guy, and there's an appreciable difference between normal and hard, so we really had to work at it). We found two loot dice, three tomes, and a grimoire. It takes a lot of effort and time to do all that, especially on hard. I complete the mission, I roll a 2, and I got a green item. That means for a lot more time, difficulty, and effort, I got the same loot that I would've gotten doing the same mission on normal and ignoring the tomes and grimoires and if I got a decent roll.
When I play and get loot, instead of feeling rewarded, I feel
. It's horrible and stupid and I'm honestly not sure how anyone could have possibly let it into the game.
Especially because the rest of the game is just good fun. There is intersting loot to be had, and there are ways to craft it even if you do only get loot that you hate. The new Sigmar's Blessing content makes the game much more fun and the loot much more interesting, and I'm under the impression that the developers are going to continue giving out more free content. That's awesome!
The melee combat feels awesome, and the ranged combat is pretty cool. The special rats all feel like an afterthought and don't really belong. Often times several assassins or pack rats (I don't remember their actual names :P) will appear at the same time and wipe out the whole team (this is the equivalent of several teleporting hunters and melee-smokers that you can't shoot, in L4D terms). The pack rats are especially odd because they work by hooking you with a long pole, and dragging you around. You can't do anything about it, and your teammates' best weapons are in melee. Because there is no sprinting, the result is a bizarre chase while they try to catch up to the rat, who is only slightly slower. It doesn't change the dynamic, or make you switch positions, or anything like that; it's just kinda annoying and feels out of place.
Rat ogres and poison globers also feel pretty out of place. The ogre essentially just requires being hit a lot, and in my opinion they take waaaay too long to die. Not fun, doesn't change the tactics really, just kinda is annoying and can sometimes wreck a half-hour progress for no avoidable reason. The globers throw poison at you to try to cause you to disperse, but the maps are clearly not designed with this guy in mind; the result is extrememly annoying and not fun or interesting. The same is not true, however, for the assassins or ratling gunners, which are genuinely fun and require a bit of changing tactics.
Overall, I feel that the way the different "specials" spawn is just slightly off. You can go a long time without any showing up, and all of a sudden you get swarmed by two gunners and three assassins. Sometimes, on normal, an entire mission would go by without any ogres (thank goodness). Other times on normal, three appeared in the same mission.
The fantastic melee and the interesting later-on loot make up, however, for all these gripes. The loot system is infuriating, but I usually just remind myself that I'll use it primarily just to make the gear that I want. Grab friends, play it. Despite all this complaining, the rest of the game really is fun enough to make up for all this.

Early Access review:  I hate to have to put a reminder for every EA game I play, but this game is actually in Early Access.  You will find bugs still.  The game may not run perfectly on every seetup (it runs more than fine on my now aging $800 PC, but every setup is different and you know how these things go).
So now on to better things.  The game is pretty decently fun.  The amount of things you can make is fairly crazy, along with how you can build stuff up the way you want exactly.
When you start off it's going to look like an Island simulator where you're stuck going through early age weapons, tools and things.  It will be like that for a long while.  Eventually you get to where you can make dynamite, guns, even cars.  You advance through the ages as you play along and find more stuff.
It looks realistic at first, though there is this weird power source you find on these islands that's not in the real world, and it also can infect some of the animals that are close to where it exists and change them a bit.  This power source is what lets you start to make the more advanced stuff later.
There is potion making with all sorts of strange effects.  I haven't got into that part of the game much yet myself, but have heard all sorts of weird things about the things people are finding out potions can do.
You can switch back and forth from single player into multiplayer, though I can't comment on that either as I've only been doing single player so far.
I find the low polygon look to be interesting and different, and it's still somehow pretty looking at the same time (just look at the screenshots above to see if that appeals to you or not).
I really like the ship building part of the game, you can build some pretty massive ships up and keep building things onto them and turn them into moving bases and more.  It's all just up to you on how much time you're willing to spend.
One thing they definitely can and do need is a better way to sort the lists of things you can make.  There are just so many things to build....  Sooooooo many.  After just a few hours it has turned into this immensely huge list that keeps growing and growing still.  While you can type in a search world to find some stuff quickly and there are a few sort categories, they need to do a bit better on both breaking the categories down and letting you search things in the text box based on what they do rather than just their names.  I love that there are so many things, it's crazy and fun and gives you a great many options.  Yet there are so many they need to tweak the sorting system a bit somehow for sure.
My game doesn't stutter or anything and I've not hit many bugs.  There still are some there yes for sure, and some can be pretty bad if they cause you to lose your ship, though if you're lucky you can still go out there and find it.  If you fall off your ship with the sails down and it keeps going and doesn't hit an island to stop it, I'm guessing you'll be stuck building a new one as your spawn points get set at islands and not on your moving base (It would be nice if they let us build an item that could select our spawn point and we could put that on our ships, but as of now I haven't seen anything like that).
The basics of the game start out like any other survival game only in a more realistic setting (at first).  It's like you got stuck off on an island present day only with an odd power source somewhere around.  The elements, nature, animals, food, these are the things you fight for survival.  Not zombies, skeletons, undead, etc (again, you do fight slightly mutated animals later because of that weird power source, normally down inside deep caves).  But the way it progresses through so many different cool things to make it sets itself apart.
The paranoia over collected data is pretty much nonsense.  They removed the tracking to watch where people are buying the game from (so that they could watch to see what sales and promotions were working) because of people whining about it (not that there was really anything wrong with that but they still removed it to make the paranoid people happy), and the other data file that lets them see where and what people are dying to in game and such to help them with tweaking can be turned off if you don't want them to know this for some reason.  It's basic data a great many games collect, and yet they removed one and the other is optional.  I'm very happy with the Developer response, I'm not the least bit concerned nor do I feel spied on.  A little paranoia is good, but some of these people are just going overboard.

Having played 28 hours of this game, I've decided to tell you why I think that this game is worth every cent.
Obviously, It is absolutely imperative that you play the original game
playing this one.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number is a game developed by Dennaton Games and published by Devolver Digital and serves as the sequel for Hotline Miami, a
and one of the most critically aclaimed indie games of all time.
The game takes place after, during, and before the events of its predecessor and manages to maintain some of the frantic action that popularized the first game, HOWEVER, Wrong Number is much more story focused than the the original and serves as the developers way to tie up loose ends.
The gameplay retains certain aspects of from Hotline Miami but the levels are designed in such a way that you have to cower in fear behind each door and wait for the perfect moment so as to not get either snipped by a shotgun from across the map or spotted through a window.
I, like most people, didnt enjoy this kind of level design, because there are enemies outside your camera's range who can react faster than you and end what seemed like a perfect run.
One of the aspects the latter didnt retain from the former was the melee combat. In this game, melee combat was somewhat nerfed, making the melee swing slower and the and the range smaller.
One of the most controversial characteristics of Hotline Miami 2 is its relatively large cast of playble characters. But Haplop, how could more characters equal less fun.
Well for starters you have more characters but less unique playstyles. There are 27 masks each with their unique gimmicks and playstyles opposed to the 14 characters of Hotline Miami 2. Whats more is that there most characters dont add anything new, here's whats new.
Remember the Richter and Aubrey mask from the previous game? They now grant no special abilities.
There is also a character wich instead of killing can incapacitate and disarm foes for bonus points.
You also get to play as a soldier wich can switch between a knife and one of for weapons ( a rifle, a shotgun, a sniper rifle and a flamethrower) but cant pickup any other weapons.
The soundtrack is just downright beautiful featuring the works of El Huervo, M|O|O|N, Perturbator and many other independent artists, it can go from slow and melancholic to full on assault in seconds and it really does not only live up to the standards set by the previous game but somehow also manages to surpass them by a pretty big stretch.
Not only that but the audio in general is really descriptive and the mushy sound of grey matter splattering all over the room does add to the gory factor of the game, wich by the way, makes great use of the Hitchcock effect (google it)
The sprites may seem a bit, how should I put it, wonky (?) at first but after playing through it you realize that it is one of the best way to convey to the player the setting of Miami's 1980's.
Overall the game in itself is great, the gameplay isnt as satisfying as that of the 1st game but the story is beautifully written. Its a much more down-to-earth game and the story always has you feeling sorrowful and melancholic while still keeping you interested and engaged as you watch this immensely dense plot unravel before your eyes while you cant really do anything about it.
I guess that that is what really gives you a sense of accomplishment, once you manage to get the bigger picture that is.
So...

A hostage crisis in the suburbs. The troopers move up to the entrance cautiously, wary of potential threats in the vicinity.
You stack up against the door. Your teammate moves to the front, his Kimber drawn. You have the advantage of marksmanship, training and skill and you both know it. But you are still up against many.
You take a deep breath and blast off the door handle with your Mossberg. the door swings open and your teammate fires 3 well placed shots. A body hits the ground.
"THE COPS ARE HERE" rings down the hallway and you hear the mulitple doors opening and closing.
Your heart pounds furiously.
No time or chance to back down, and you charge into the lion's den, sending the first hostile you see down with a single blast of 00.
Simply put, this game is like Rainbow Six from a real-time-strategy/top-down perspective, where you control SWAT troopers as they conduct raids against criminals and terrorists.
Each game is highly lethal, and most demand a certain time limit to be met, most of which happens to be a minute or two. Every move you take requires very careful planning.
Is there a blind spot unaccounted for?
Is there someone covering me?
Is someone's line of sight blocked by another, possibly endangering both?
Your operators are well trained and will easily take down multiple hostiles at once, but they aren't God. A single fatal mistake in planning or an unprecendented move by a hostile will more often than not lead to their swift and violent demise, whether it's a burst of MAC-10 fire from the side or single 7.62mm round from a AK-47.
In a game where every second counts you have to get used to controlling every operator at any point in time. Watching flanks, breaching rooms, using tactical manoeuvres to clear, all have to be done in a single fluid motion.
On drug busting operations prepare to launch a 6 man offensive on an entire port, where you have to simultaneously control all your fireteams and keep them alive, and secure the evidence before the cartel gets a chance to destroy it.
Your classes are clearly defined.
The Pointman, who is extremely mobile and deadly in tight spaces but will easily get swamped by numbers.
The Assault, who can both be a close quarter fire-hose with a submachine gun for laying accurate and well controlled bursts or a mid-range specialist with an assault rifle, dishing out accurate semi automatic fire that stops people in their tracks, but lose your close range mobility and versatility.
The Breacher who can blast doors open and engage multiple enemies with buckshot but quickly get outgunned at mid-ranges and risk collateral damage from the pellet spread.
The Stealth who are good mid range specialists who will put hostiles to sleep silently but will lose their edge in closer engagements.
The Shield who can block most incoming shots but can only use a pistol and may not have the mobility in close spaces or the accuracy for long escort missions.
Skill is required to make the best out of every trooper you train for every situation and make sure everyone comes out alive.
You spend more time planning alone than executing, and you will get frustrated sometimes from the frequent restarting but every completed mission grants a never-ending sense of pride.
PROS:
1. Excellent AI. Troopers are not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and will react to defend themselves and hostiles will actively flank and investigate sources of noise.
2. Tight map design that pose a challenge to players
3. Customisation is well-controlled and delivered with a clear focus on maximising the trooper's usability on the field over the simple mindless pimp-your-gun-to-be-special attachment chucking we see in many other games
4. Price. I got this on sale for a measly 3 bucks and it's been worth every penny.
5. Comprehensive controls and a decent How-to guide for quickly jumping in.
6. Minimalistic UI that tells you what you need and what you need alone and great graphics.
7. Immersive atmosphere that gets your heart pumping every time a raid is initiated and keeps you coming back for more.
8. A decent bare-bones progression system that rewards you with better troop quality for future raids but doesn't go as far as to become a grindfest.
9. As if the above aren't enough there is workshop content with plenty of diversity. Want a new scenario? Try a pirate ship raid. Want to satisfy your gun fetish? Get mods that increase the number of weapons available at your disposal.
CONS:
1. An unforgiving currency (star) system that renders you in a tight spot if you make a costly mistake in your investment, where you potentially lose the ability to progress yet are unable to earn more to buy the gear you need.

I've been a longstanding player of Artix Entertainement games. This is a big step up from a company that previously released only 2D flash-based web browser games.
Firstly, I'll state that the AQ3D project is aimed at being played cross platform; PC, mobile phones & tablets. It's also run by an independant company with just under 50 or so staff members, who are also still maintaining and monitoring other AE games. (AQW, DragonFable, etc.)
As others have mentioned, this is in an open beta stage. Take this into consideration if you feel frustrated with how the game feels for now. Some things may work, while others won't.  I've been playing the game since it's tech demo / alpha stages, and it's come a long way.
Now; down to business. I'll be taking pros and cons based off of what I said earlier about the project.
Pros:
-Simplistic UI for cross platform appeal. It's very simplistic and transparent. It could be worked on a little bit for PC players but aside from that it's nice.
-Supportive Staff. Artix Entertainement are probably the pinnacle of game devs who will listen to their fans and take suggestions. A good few former fans of the games actually ended up being part of the AE staff into positions such as concept art, music production, cutscene animations, etc. They also take their playerbase very seriously. So seriously, that Adam Bohn, AKA Artix turned down a written check $84 million offer for the company back in 2007. You can count on them to have your back if you know there's something wrong going on. They are the most transparent bunch of guys and girls I've ever met in terms of game developers, and they're very open to players about what happens behind the scenes.
-Fun humour. The humour that AE has put out through the years has always been a G-rated sense of humour, as their games appealed to a younger audience. Expect 4th wall breaks, cheesy jokes, and almost unbearable puns.
-Fantastic story development. I've seen people worried about storyline issues, but that won't be a problem. AE has had no problem delving into intriguing and at times very dark story-telling. Their narrative process is very good.
-Fantastic content timed releases. For the last god knows how many years, AE games, specifically AQW, have constantly delivered content each and every single week for the last 7 years in a row. Expect ALOT of stuff in the coming releases.
-Simplisticly designed. Graphcs, AI, designs. All very good and very simply designed. You don't need a powerhouse pc to run this game.
Okay, time for negative.
Cons:
-Grind, grind, grind! Expect the grind to be insane in this. From levelling up, to getting gold, questing, etc. If you don't mind grinding for hours, then you'll disregard this point. AE games are very farm-heavy, but if you want to get that item/level you always wanted, there's no doubt you WILL reach for it.
-Awkward camera controls. (PC ONLY) I'd preferr to have my characer walk in the direction in which my mouse is pointing, and have the camera follow them. There should be a supported mouse format IMHO.
Points outside of pros/cons
-Is the game P2W?
Not necessarily. While currently Guardians (The Upgrade status in AQ3D) have access to exclusive content, that's what they're getting for supporting the game. You can obtain high-level gear, but not without taking the time to do it. Also, the way the system has worked for the last 7-8 years is that the weapons you buy through microtransactions are pretty much cosmetic based.  The point difference would very, very mininmal to a level 15 bought weapon compared to a level 15 earned weapon, so no. Future released classes MAY be bought through microtransactions, but there'll be a way to earn them too. It's not at all pay-to-win
-Max Level Already????
For now, yes. However over the years the level caps have always been slowly scaled upwards in tandem with the level of content that AE releases for their games. You might be the max level of 15 now, but who's to say that the cap won't be increased when it comes out of open beta.
-Microtransactions WTFFFF
This has always been a split decision point on me. In some points, the microtransactions for secondary currency has been a staple in AE games, however as they are an independant run company there are times when they'll need to support their server costs, so microtransactions WILL be present.  However the deals offered are pretty bloody solid and you're not really encouraged to buy Dragon Crystals. At the end of the day it's your choice if you buy them or not. Whether you want to buy it or not is up to you. See my earlier point on the Pay2Win statement.
All-in all, it's a classic AE game. However it has an ideal and bold potential, considering where it's trying to reach for the market. I expect it'll do very well for mobile/tablet gaming. The fact that as a player on PC, you can play with someone using  Android devices, and soon to be iOS devices is very heartwarming to see something truly cross-platform.
**Edited for punctuation correction**
It's everything I expected out of an open beta and more. Can't wait for future updates!

Dirt 4 is first a rally game, harking back to Codemaster’s earlier Colin McCrae titles, but it takes lessons from Dirt Rally and the various Dirt and Grid titles to become what I feel is the best non-F1 title Codemasters has ever produced (I'll withhold judgement on the F1 series until I've played it). People who were daunted by the simulation aspect of Dirt Rally need not fear here: the game offers two handling modes, one being a development of Dirt 3's model and the other being an improvement over that of Dirt Rally. There have been accusations flying around that the simulation aspect of the game has been "dumbed down", but I feel this is simply a knee-jerk reaction. There is a lot more depth to the way weight transfer works this time around. The car feels as if it's ploughing trough a loose surface rather then sliding on top of it, and a lot of aspects that Dirt Rally did not model, such as how the car behaves in puddles, can catch you off-gaurd here.

In terms of sheer variety, Dirt 4 outpaces Dirt Rally by a very significant margin. Aside from the larger variety of cars and disciplines, the your stage feature does mean that there are no stages in the career mode repeat themselves. You do occasionally see the same corner popping up (betrayed by some distinct feature), but it's a significantly better variety then Dirt Rally offered. Whilst there is an occasional gem hidden between the oysters, the stages lack the distinct notes that Dirt Rally offered by giving you some of the most iconic rally stages in the world.

Even if the road itself is featureless, the event doesn't have to be. You'll find cars on the side of the road, the occasional wildlife or overzealous pilot getting in your way. Additionally, whilst in Dirt Rally you'd get the occasional flat tire, Dirt 4 has you picking up a variety of gremlins, some are the result of sheer bad luck, and some are the result of hasty repairs (the latter being a lot more severe). Dirt Rally sometimes had your opponents shuffled down the order due to grating brakes or slipping clutches. Now this can happen to you too.
Over Dirt 3 and over Dirt Rally, the career mode in particular has improved significantly. Dirt 3 was simply a succession of challenges, some of which you had to do even if you did not like them (The Gymkhana tutorials in particular have disappointed many players). Dirt Rally, on the other hand, was just the same championship repeated over and over again, increasing the difficulty whilst you tried to grind enough cash to buy a car with modern suspension. None of this is present in Dirt 4: You can set your own difficulty straight of the bat, the events at the start focus on beginner cars, and there's seperate tiers for each discipline. If you enjoyed Dirt 3's less serious Gymkhana or DC Challenge events, they're hidden under the "Joyride" section in the menu and they're free to do at your leisure, not impacting the career at all.
Aside from the four disciplines, Dirt 4 has a progression which involves how much other teams like you and you building your own team. The structure is reminiscent of the first GRID, but it is more open: Now each event can be completed by either driving for another team, or by buying your own car and running it by yourself. Teams can grow to like you, giving you better offers each time you are succesfull in meeting their goals. You can then invest the money you earn in your own team and buy cars for events no team is offering for. You can play it the other way around too: Focus almost entirely on developing your own team but taking the occasional drive for another team if you can't afford the car you want to drive, or if it isn't available for sale (as all the older cars have to be bought second hand, and the market isn't always offering). The variety of ways to participate means that there is hardly a necessity to grind towards the things you want to do, which was an issue in all the previous games. The achievement here is that it manages to do all this without robbing you of a sense of progression.
All in all I think it's a significant improvement over both Dirt Rally and Dirt 3, and fans of either (or both) will find this a welcome return. Don't hesitate picking this up at a price you feel comfortable with.

Disclaimer : I really love warhammer so I may have a more forgiving outlook on the game becuase of my love for the franchise. This experience comes from playing with friends to dropping solo with bots and with random players on Nightmare difficulty ( the 2nd to last hardest difficulty ).
Things I will answer.
1st: What are the mechanics of the game and how do they contribute to an enjoyable experience.
2nd: Community , is it Toxic or friendly?
3rd: Is it worth it?
For those who dont have much time I will simply tell you its a fantasy L4D with magic , swords and lots of dead rats. If you enjoyed L4D you may find a new game to play here and that you could try it out for and hour but if you dont like it then refund it.
Now to the questions...
Mechanics...
yourself and three others form a party of four seperate characters to take on the Vermintide , a horde of ratmen come to destroy your town. The first of these five classes I will go Into is the Soldier , he is mostly a melee character wielding either 2 handed hammers or swords to a mace and shield or sword and shield combo. The soldier usually will be in the front of a party and try to bash the mobs and tank it for the team. While most characters can also do this , the soldier and dwarf have access to shields that allow them to block and bash more often then their counter parts.
Next we have the dwarf who plays very much like the soldier , however the weapons at a dwarfs disposal very a bit from the soldiers , for instance while the soldier can have a repeater rifle the dwarf can get flare guns that light up mobs of rats setting crowds ablaze.
Then we have the mage ( My personel favorite ) This class is a power house that must manage their magic in the form of a heat management style where if you generate too much you will die but if you keep it under control you will kill EVERYTHING!!! ( insert power level joke here ). The mage has access to large AOE spells or very powerfull single target spells that can make or break the game depending on who uses it. The mage also gets a sword to help them ( I recommened the fire sword ).
Onto the Elf , Do you like fast weapons? Do you like bows? Do you like heat seeking arrows??????? Then here's the class for you!!! Behold my bow that never misses its shots, I found a Bow that has heat seeking arrows and its great. The elf is however a great character for killing the trash mobs , the bows help a lot ( just like most secoandary weapons ) to kill the bigger more prominent foes so save that ammo for something tough.
Last but not least the Witchhunter , This guy is great if you're looking for some gunplay , sporting duel pistols ( flintlocks actually ) and either a zwiehander or a sword and pistol. This guy is great for range firepower on a single target ( pistols with pierce would be awesome Fatshark! ) or you can get a repeater rifle for him aswell and use that to murder many rats. The pointy hat is also pretty great.
Onto question two. Is the community "Toxic".... Kinda .... Ive been kicked simply becuase I wasnt level 100 ( which means nothing but you played the beta and had a lot of time on your hands ). Most players hate the grind like myself but becuase of the loot system , ( after each mission you roll dice to get loot , doing objectives gets you more loot such as tomes or finding dice in chests or of loot rats ) Players usually try to do all the objectives and most of the time a party will die trying to do most objectives and this has made my experience crap.. I'd rather pump out 3 matches on normal then try to roll for one good weapons becuase I can just craft weapons from the basic tier up.
People in this game will boot you simply becuase they forgot to put the group on Invite only , people will boot you becuase you use a mic or dont use a mic. Experience's may vary....  My experience with people on Vermintide is VERY negetive... some of you guys might find great people but I ended up just running with bots ( which has gotten me far more loot then running with people on my end of things ). Its better to simply complete a mission then risk lossing it and wasting 30 minutes of your time.
Complaints/cons: This game is brutal and I wish there was a moment where rats were not always coming at you even on easy. For some reason during my experience I encountered hordes far more often then people I watched on twitch.
This game doesnt really have a tutorial... It just kinda throws you in and points at stuff but sticks you with other players while you try to learn the game.
Finally is Vermintide worth it??? Yes it is worth it but I would buy it and try to play with friends.

The game is very early access so if you are fine with lots of bugs then the content is more than enugh to keep you playing for hundreads of hours. That said I cannot stress enugh the very early access nature of this game. You can and will lose all your progress if you expirance a game breaking bug and there are a few.
Some of the things in this game that keep me playing:
Exploring is actually fun. The devs put all kinds of interesting stuff both on land and under water but even in the air and under ground. I was digging a hole in the sand to make glass and I just randomly found a cannon ball. I was sailing across the sea and saw something floating. I stopped my ship (which I built myself) and it turned out to be some cloths. but under water in that spot I found a crashed plain with some loot and stuff inside.
The building system allows a lot of freedom with free placement and grid based but at the same time this level of complexity makes building things a bit of a pain but the devs included an editer that has tools that make creating artworks like casles and cities a lot easer if you are more into the building aspect and not so hot on the survival part. You can creat custom maps and games and upload them for people to use kinda like mario maker.
The crafting system works by crafting things to unlock other crafting things and exploring is encuraged by makeing some recipes only unlockible by finding things from other ylands.
Currently there are no npcs but there are animals to hunt and horses to tame.
Again if you are fine with bugs then I really think you will enjoy this game if you enjoy games like minecraft (there are basic 'red stone' like items in the game but more to be added)

This is the 3rd copy I have now purchased,
3 steam accounts , 3 copys of Ylands,  great holiday fun.

-This review is of my early impressions of the game seeing as I have only sunk 3 hours into it so far-
-I have only slept 2 1/2 hours in the last 48 hours so if this isn't as well written as it could be, please forgive me-
Ylands is a simple game on the surface. At first glance, it appears to be one of those "Mine, Chop, Craft, Build, Progress" games that are like a time sink for anyone interested in that type of content. As one of these people, that appealed to me right away and had me biding my time until I had the cash to dole out on this game.
(Like any person anxious to get into a game, I skipped over the codex/tutorial and thought it wouldn't matter. Give it a quick read before progressing past it upon loading your first character on a map)
-My First 3 Hours-
The first few minutes were spent familiarizing myself with the controls and navigating the beach I started on. This quickly turned into my attempting to punch a tree, and then realizing, after half a minute of bare knuckle brawling with a palm tree, that I had to go through the crafting menu of the Inventory and get tools to get any legitimate work done.
In a minute I stood on the beach, flourescent red hair and moustache glistening in the wind and began digging into the earth to start a base of some kind. I've always been a fan of underground bases, so I thought that would be the best course of action. In short order, don't. Not until you've gotten a few wall torchs and have a flint lighter. The main reason behind this is that the natural lighting in the game isn't as good as it COULD be. The natural light doesn't filter in through a hole some, casting shadows. It is like a stagnant entity barrelling down from above and the slightest movement under dirt or stone will cause a deep green color to fill your screen. (This also happens with the darkness at night. While the torchlight looks absolutely wonderful in the night, they don't cast nearly enough light to make them worth using around a base/home)
After nearly five minutes of mining underground with stone tools that I interchanged as often as they broke, I found myself at an impasse. I, for once, didn't want to build underground anymore. Taking the materials I got (stone, dirt, sand from the beach), I walked back up into the light and began trying to terraform the beach to make it nicer. This turned out to be a horrendous mistake, as the beach soon became an entirely foreign land, filled with jutting spikes of sand and dirt that wouldn't place flat. (I, in my 2nd full hour of playing, would later realize punching the ground is the best way to flatten the ground. That is, if it weren't for the imprecise hitting. That'll be saved for a later section)
Then came the waterfront. The ocean water didn't flow into any of the divets in the ground that I made at the edge. If I added dirt or sand, it went around it just fine, but taking anything away would leave the water looking like a newly generated modded minecraft world. It just wouldn't flow.
So that world was scrapped and my character went onto greener pastures. A brand new world and beach brought new problems. Over the rest of the 1st hour and first fifteen minutes of the 2nd hour, I spent carting back logs from felled trees and slowly building an elevated log house. No roof yet, as straw roofing costs too much for getting so little in return. The grind to even build the small home was bad, especially since I had to skirt around the rainforest edge lest I be mauled by a panther.
At the tail end of my 2nd hour, I had learned I needed to get Clay and Iron, in that order. Getting Clay was the most taxing, annoying part of my playtime so far. This consisted of crafting up nearly a hundred arrows and venturing across the island in search of a clay deposit. This journey took me through high mountain peaks, dense rainforests, a box with a smiley face on it, and several leopards and panthers, all of which were hard to get rid of. The reason wasn't my poor aim, no, the problem was that the arrows I fired had a roughly 33% chance to stay stuck in the air. Only after the arduous fight did I find the clay. Even then, I only found out it was clay after mining three or for times at it. Was it worth it? I don't know. I stopped right as I returned home with a full inventory so I could write this early impressions/review.
-The Problems
This game suffers from some problems. Any game in Early Access does, no exception. The few problems I've encountered weren't horrific, but it did lead to some minor annoyances. The list of problems is as follows:
1. Grinding for Hay to make straw blocks is hell. While you can go around areas and start picking withered plants up from the get go, it is demoralizing when you go to craft straw blocks and it takes 5 hay to make a single 1x2 block. At least when you chop up a log you get five seperate pieces to build with, but the hay? One.
2. Arrow Freezing. As I said about the arrows, about 33% of the time my arrow would freeze as soon as it left the bow, sticking in place like a knife stabbed into a table.
3. Water. The ocean doesn't flow into any holes made on the beach and stays still like a freshly generated minecraft world.
4. The lighting is too dark early on. Torchs do almost nothing in the night, everything gets this deep green color, and digging into the ground far enough to change the light will make you see NOTHING.
5. Imprecise mining, chopping, swinging, punching. Come on. How hard is it to get your fist/pick/axe/mace to hit where you target? I can't believe how many close calls I had while fighting panthers and leopards with my mace since it would hit everything EXCEPT what I target.
(The previous #5 problem was solved once I advanced further in the game. An Iron Shovel flattens the ground when you use it.)
-Conclusion-
Despite the few problems I've come across in my short 3 hours in the game, I did find myself enjoying it quite a lot. The art direction is cartoony in a good way, the lack of blood (that I've found at least) makes it suitable for all ages, and regardless of the grind to get 5 hay for a single 1x2 straw block, the grind to get everything else made me feel like I deserved everything I got. This game will undoubtedly get a good chunk of my time until I can get some of my wishlist games bought during the upcoming Steam Winter Sale.

I saw this game on steam and was like "Hey, the reviews don't sound too bad". And then I started it...
First let me tell you, I'm not a fan of strategy RPGs, where you have to position your character and such. Maybe this clouds my judgement, maybe not.
I opened the game, and had the choice to do just the tutorial after a few MB downloading (which is a pretty nice feature!). I then proceeded to wait for the game to finish loading. Since it took more than a minute, I just restarted it. And it loaded instantly. Then I had to give my acoount a name. Well, seems like "God" is forbidden in your account name. The game doesn't tell you however. It just tells you "This name is forbidden". Nothing more, nothing less. After a few tries I finally found out, that "God" isn't allowed, so I took something else. The game asks me if I want to play the tutorial. I did, and I regret it. In the tutorial you are asked to gather and plant seeds. Gathering is easy, but the planting... Imagine a field full of flowers and quite a few spots with just grass on them. You can only plant seeds on grass obviously. The game thinks so too... or not. "The area is full", "Ecosystem: bla bla, try killing some monsters" are the messages I get. Well, ok. Let's kill a monster. The game doesn't give you an option to do so though.  Tired of this, I deleted my character, so I could pick the name again. And finally could play it, after ignoring all the bugs (also ignoring the fact, that no sound played, another bug).
The classes seem to be fine and fun. I have only tried one class, however. So I guess I can't really tell much about it. The GUI seems pretty nice. Big screen, almost nothing on it. I guess that's pretty good, I missed the minimap though (Dunno if you can activate it somehow). Finding out, how the "Quest Compass" works, I finished a few quests and leveled up. The game yet again tells me something "Don't forget to spend your points!", or something like that. However, this is only something you can do on level 5 and later on, because then you unlock something, where you can actually spend points on leveling up.
After finally reaching level 5, I decided to stop playing. I still don't know how I level skills or how I even get them. The game doesn't tell me either.
Maybe if the game fixes some of the bugs, I will give it another go. But as of now, I can't recommend it due to the bugs and the innovative GUI.

One of the real surprise packages this year, Vermintide is a must play to any fans of the Warhammer Fantasy Universe or even Fantasy in general. The Game offers a combat system which feels some what similar to left 4 dead but with it's own unique twist on it so don't think this is a left4dead game with a Fantasy skin over the top. The enviroments are very well done and offer pleasing eye candy and the use of darkness present in all the maps only adds to the atmosphere. The game isn't easy either and encourages the players to work more as a unit together than as seperate entities, once a level is completed you can play again on a harder, more challenging dificulty. The characters are very well rounded and offer a unique playing experience individually (apart from the witchhunter and imperial soldier who feel very similar).
There are some drawbacks however...the game does get quite repetitive and you do find yourself grinding the same missions in the hope of getting better gear on the dice rolls, and it is extremely frustrating when you don't get gear for your character after completing a 30-40 minute mission. Another thing this game lacks at the moment is a Horde mode as well which would so benefit this type of game. It would add hours onto the playability of the game. Finally if you are going to get this game, bully your friends into getting it like I did, it is way for fun with your mates who you can communicate with rather than 3 other screbs but don't tell them I told you to do it XD.

When I saw that there was a new game for Adventure Quest, I was stoked. Playing the original AQ was part of my childhood, it was something I looked forward to, especially with great devs behind the game, thinking so I delved right into this game.
. . .
It's a mess.
Granted, this is indeed "Early Access" and is in open beta, but for what it has so far, it's not worth it.
First off you have the typical copy and paste quests, what might that be you ask? "Kill 10 Blue Eyes" "Collect [x amount] from [Blue Eyes]", "Go to [location] and [left click]" etc. It's the epitome of repetitiveness, and the XP you are rewarded is a complete joke.
You will hardly find a challenge in this game, even if you are solo playing it. The enemy designs are ok, mediorce, the boss designs? Literally the Destiny treatment aka "Make a common enemy larger and slight differences and slap it as a boss".
Defeating an enemy/boss does not feel rewarding at all. A large majority of the time you get a drop from a kill which is then used to craft armor/weapons etc. I like the idea behind it, but simply farming enemies/bosses by all means does not feel rewarding, especially for how easy they are, and how minimal you get, or end up with eventually.
There are 3 starter classes, you got the Rogue, Warrior, and Mage. They all fit their roles, but one thing that stands out for the Rogue is that, well, when he enters stealth, everyone can still see you, enemies included. Perhaps a bug but that's something to mention.
Combat itself is kinda clunky and could use work. You only have 5 attacks really, your main spam-o-fest button and the rest "special", so there's no differation at all.
There is also a 4th class, "Guardian" which is just a Paladin really, which is locked behind a $20 paywall (or $50 if you want the bigger pack). I'm completely fine with this option, the devs do need to make the grub after all for a F2P game.
There are dungeons in this game as well, and you get a Dungeon key once every 3 hours. So when you enter a dungeon, you might think it'll que you up with 2 other people, correct? Nope, throws you in, even alone. Most of the time I've been in dungeons, the other two people that were in, were afk beyond 20 minutes, and still didn't move. You then leave and are prompted with a message clarifying your progress will be lost if you leave. Gee, thanks for reminding me that there isn't an auto-kick feature, and due to that I lost a key because of random people afk'ing.
There really isn't too much to say about this game, the combat is clunky, limited options, repetitive quests, no challenge, game doesn't feel rewarding, no party system, entering a dungeon is a cluster ♥♥♥♥, barely any mentionable content, etc. The only thing worth mentioning is that the community is very friendly and helpful.
I do greatly hope this game will improve with time, but as of right now, there is just so much better than this. At best this is just a go-to game when you have literally nothing else to play, filler.

At first, don't listen to the 1-2 hours played negative reviews.
After 20 hours I feel quite confident to say that it's a great game if you enjoyed Dirt 3 a little bit more than Dirt Rally.
I personally always play with a pad so Dirt Rally for me was not enjoyable because I couldn't drive in a straight line. Although I've read that some Dirt Rally veterans like Dirt 4 more, most seem to agree that Dirt 4 is a tad easier.
D4 offers you two handling modes which is great. The randomly generated stages are... sometimes on point sometimes a bit boring. It's not perfect at the moment, I get some moments where I think "wait that part was there one minute ago" but it's not often.
After the introduction you can start your own rally team. Give it a name, colour and hire engineers, PR managers and different co-pilots and spotters. It's really cool to see your own team winning. Money you earn can be used for different things so a little bit of foresight is key.
Historic Rally and normal Rally both are really nice because you are more or less forced to drive many different classes of cars which leads to much variety.
Rallycross and Landrush are loads of fun, if you can accept the very very agressive AI. Sadly not all circuits from WRX are included and EKS's Audi is also not in the game.
All in all a great game, if you turn any assists of and use the simulation handling I bet you can also be satisfied if you're a Sim racer.

Was a heavy critic of this game, tried it through Family Sharing before buying, bought it after a night of playing.
Surprisingly, a very good game. The handling is different to Dirt Rally as much as as Dirt Rally's handling is different to RBR. I never drove a rally car, or any car in the last 15 years, so I can't say which one is more realistic, but I can say that they (RBR and DR) are very different in handling and fans of their respective games will fight over it until they break their keyboards. Most people just enjoy both games for their respective merits, though.
Performance:
gtx980, i7 6700k, 16gb ram, new-isn HDD. 75fps on ultra, no issues what so ever so far. I realize some people have problems, but I'm lucky.
Handling:
Anyway, back to D4. I didn't feel that rally handling was easier or harder, in general. It's harder to lose traction on gravel which makes driving on it easier and harder - depending on what you're trying to do at the moment. Driving on asphalt is much harder, at least for somebody who thought it was the easiest thing ever according to DR. Crashed many more times in Spain than in Germany.
Stages:
Mixed feelings. Generator is better than expected, and certainly not what early refunders said - there are plenty of hard technical spots, you just have to get out of the rookie championships. The game generates easier stages for those. I feel like the proportion of long stretches and narrow technical paths is about right and differs between each stage. One can be a nightmare and another a cakewalk. Still, having fully custom made stages like in older games would have been better. Keep the generator, but only to extend replayability. Having stages longer than 16km would have been nice, too. Just generate a longer track, how hard can it be?
Everything that's not stages or handling:
Objectively better. Career is more in-depth. You can race for other teams, have positive or negative relationships with them, buy your own cars (used or new), sell them on auctions! Customize your team's livery and colors and stuff. Repair is more in-depth, too. You can clean your car which costs time but makes diagnosing more reliable - mechanics don't magically know what is broken. You can take a quick look or do a full examination of the part. Repair times are not certain, it can be a bit shorter or longer than expected. A lot of stuff can get broken on your car, much more detailed than in DR. A lot of stuff can happen on the stage, too! A helicopter flying too low stirring up dust! Can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥ A car crash ahead, tech people signalling you by waving and placing bright signs on the road! Idiot drone pilots giving you a mini heart attack when they fly too close! Weather can change during a single stage, you can find fog patches, etc.
There is probably much more stuff that I forgot to tell about, but I believe that this game, even if you get it for rally and nothing else, is a worthy successor.

I’m changing my positive review to a negative one. Played it a little longer and it’s an average game.
It seems that people who liked Dirt 3 expected it to be similar and people who liked Dirt rally expected it to be the same. Well it’s neither. I have waited for this game for a long time and had high hopes. I love Dirt rally, it’s punishing, winning is impossible but driving is very fun. It lacks difficulty settings and a better career mode so my wish was so driving still would be fun and sim-like with proper career and difficulty settings. Dirt 4 add these. Dirt 4 at times feels more difficult to drive, sometimes physics feels good and sometimes it feels…strange. Yes it feels different than Dirt rally, but it’s not a bad thing and it’s not an arcade game. The good thing about Dirt 4 is that anyone can enjoy it – from casual players who like more arcade racing to hardcore sim fans, it’s all up to you what assists to use. Dirt rally didn’t have these, assists did almost nothing and there was no difficulty setting. So in the end I’d say Dirt 4 can be more fun. Physics has more variables, the handling model and physics are more complex but I don’t know if this is right. On gamer mode everything is fine, cars are easy to drive, it’s how it supposed to be. But simulation mode is much more difficult than Dirt rally. In dirt 4 you constantly must fight oversteer and understeer. 4WD cars feels strange. They’re very difficult to drive, they oversteer and understeer badly. How is this possible? Well if you come slow into a corner it understeers, if you come faster you can’t control the sliding and end up in the trees. Push the throttle a little and you’re sliding, touch brakes and you’re sliding. Worst thing is you can’t control it, you don’t know what the car will do after you do action x. But many cars feels pretty good.
There are several modes. Career where you compete with AI players in few disciplines, rally, buggy races, historic rally and rallycross. As you progress stages get more difficult, cars get more powerful and game becomes more challenging. Driving in fog for example is crazy, but not very realistic and gets old very fast. All the fun goes away when you can only see 10 meters away.
AI is broken. Sometimes it’s very easy, sometimes it’s good and sometimes it’s unbeatable. By saying that I mean AI sets the time which is above the world records of real players.
It has online mode where you can compete with 7 other players in a rally. There’s also daily/weekly/monthly events which are quite fun, you get only one chance to do them right, if you fail you must wait for the next event to start. There’s also a rally school where you can learn the driving techniques and just drive around learning the handling and controls of different cars. Online mode pro-tour is absolutely idiotic. Every time you finish you get or lose points. You need points to advance to the next tier. If you lose points you go down a tier. Now there are two problems. First is that same players compete in different tiers, which means low tier players compete with high tier players, so good luck climbing up the tiers. And like it’s not enough there are only few people playing online. I’ve played for several days and every day there’re the same players again and again. Another problem with Pro tour is that you lose points if you finish low. So if there’s 6 players and you finish 5-6th you lose points. Now where’s the problem? If you come 4th and two players quit use lose points. Nicely done Codemasters – punishing people who are trying and not giving up because others leave.
You’ll race through different locations like Michigan, Australia or Spain. But i hope to see more locations later. They’re all look and feel different but I’d like even more variety.
What’s new is that stages are randomly generated so they should feel new every time you drive. Memorizing stages in Dirt rally is not fun. Yeah they are better but after some time it gets boring driving on the same stages over and over again. Well, in Dirt 4 stages get boring even faster. Today I’ve three identical sections IN A ROW! Are ♥♥♥♥ing kidding me? And even if all the sections in a stage are different, you get to know them fast. Every stage feels the same, there’s no variety on corners, you know every corner and what to expect. So it’s similar to Dirt rally, but Dirt rally at least has different kinds of corners, every corner feels different, in Dirt 4 there are same copy pasted corners on every stage, it’s even easier to memorize the stages on Dirt 4 than on Dirt rally. Auto generated stages my♥♥♥♥♥
Graphics are pretty good. Cars are pretty and environment looks good. At time it may look worse than Dirt rally, but it has more little details. Performance is good, I get stable 60fps most of the time, but had to lower some settings, because on some stages it dropped to 50 or so. It definitely looks better than Dirt 3, I don’t  know what those people who say Dirt 3 looks better are smoking. All the older Codemasters games had that stupid color filter which I truly hate.
Beware achievement hunters. Achievement do not work in this game. Codemasters are such good masters they can’t even make the achievements work.
And lastly - why they took out the workshop support?
In the current state i can recommend this game only if it’s on sale for 75% off. Both casual and sim friendly but it feels like early access and just a base of the game. The game is still fun to play but it needs more updates.
