Alien Robot Monsters is a fairly generic tower defense game.  Enemy robots have some entrance points, and you have to prevent them from reaching the exit points.  When you kill an enemy, you earn scrap, and the scrap allows you to build and upgrade your towers.  After each mission you earn up to 3 stars, and you use these stars to purchase global upgrades for your towers.  If you've played a few tower defense games, then this description should sound familiar.
But ARM has a few things going for it.  It includes over 20 towers, including tesla-like cannons, sniper perches, fire bunkers, and barracks.  Each tower has a tree of unique upgrades that you can buy for it, and some of the upgrades unlock new towers.  So you might start with the basic barracks (which produces regular soldiers), then upgrade it to an armory (with heavier soldiers), and then upgrade it again to a heavy armory (with even heavier soldiers).
Some of your towers hit all enemies in range, some can hit anything on the level, some can slow enemies down, some can hit ground forces only, and some can hit air or ground forces.  There are lots of towers to choose from, which gives you lots of ways to play each level.  Unfortunately, it takes almost the entire campaign before you unlock everything (which is listed as a "feature" in the game's description), but this slow build only hurts the game.  ARM is most fun when you have everything available.
Enemies also come in a variety of shapes and sizes.  Some are fast, some have shields, and some buff their allies.  There are also special boss creatures for each of the campaign's five sections.  But sort of oddly, the most annoying enemies are the flying ones because you're not given a dedicated anti-air tower, and you just have to make do with your other towers.
The campaign that comes with the game consists of 37 levels.  There are any difficulty settings or game modes, so once you beat a level with 3 stars, you're done with it and there isn't any reason to try it again.  About 10 of the levels are tough and might take you an hour or more to figure out.  The other levels are pretty straightforward, and you can probably beat them with just about any strategy.  But in all, it took me about 20 hours to complete the campaign, which isn't bad.
ARM is has a polished presentation and a friendly interface.  It also allows you to see the exact numbers of your towers, which is nice.  It has a few bugs (the Field Recovery upgrade didn't do anything for me), but it's still playable.  Overall, the game is effective, and it's pretty cheap, and it's worth playing.

If I could describe this game, I'd describe it as eating your fifth least favorite candy,
It's not the "worst" thing you've ever tried, and it's certainly something you can tolerate in large doses for a while but eventually you'll reach your limit a little earlier than you would with an average candy you like.
Here's a quick summary if that metaphor derailed my review:
The biggest pro to this game is by far the voice acting, I absolutely love the dialogue they gave to the towers upon clicking or upgrading them, some are clever puns, others are just funny bits and pieces. The graphics are fairly nice to be honest, the biggest issue with them is I feel the style is a little too.. cartoony when you really focus on the enemy or friendly units. Besides the art style being a little wonky I'd say the colors and general appearence are very good. The music didn't hit any keys with me personally but I think it's worth a listen to anyone else. The real tragedy of this game is it's not that intuitive but I'll give a more detailed explanation after I cover this biggest feature.
GAMEPLAY:
Ah yes, the gameplay. Well to begin, it starts off pretty bog standard for a Tower Defense game, I mean they're not reinventing the wheel like Kingdom Rush did with towers being shut off or destroyed mid battle, but they sure toss their hat in the ring trying to mimic every now and then some unique patterns of enemies, for example: You may have some troops who have good anti armor weapons, and most of the level you've fought armored enemies, but then suddenly just at the end of a level you'll get an enemy who provides a force field to grouped enemies around them making you mostly ineffective, now that's not an exact example of actual gameplay but it is a similar generalization, you'll find yourself going through the standard Tower Defense "Build this tower and spam the others" to win most of the time, but then you'll need to readjust your strategy mid way through sometimes.
The bigger issue I have with this game is the upgrades outside of a level, it's again bringing up similarities to Kingdom Rush, where when you've completed a level "for example" without taking any lives lost, you'll recieve 3 gold stars for completing the level, now outside of the level you can upgrade various stats for towers or abilities. The big issue is, by the time you reach the.. I believe 20th or so level, you realize how unfair those upgrade prices are, you can do every side mission flawlessly leading up to a level you just can't pass and you'll still not be upgraded enough for your play style to beat it by bashing your head until you get through it, like I said this game is very unintuitive, you're supposed to complete each level in an almost "Exact" way, with the exception fo the first 5 levels if that.
My personal beef outside of the problems I've already mentioned is the difficult spike. I bought this game ages ago and played it as far as I possibly could, I reached the, I think, 1st or 2nd of the robot city area of the map, but I simply couldn't get passed it, every strategy I tried failed, and due to how obscure this game is at the time of it's release I couldn't find any walkthroughs, and so naturally I was left with an impassable level. In other words, if you find a level you can't do an exact remake of what the developer did, you're essentially boned since most of the later levels are very linear. Forcing you to take action in very specific ways, and if you deviate at all your chances of success are hindered massively.
With all of that said, I'd give this game a 5 out of 10. It's average, the annoying unintuitive level design, the art style, the forgettable music (at least to me) really make this game go from a really good one, to a barely above average tower defense game, personally I'd only recommend it if you're itching for a new tower defense game in your library.
... also the sound design is alright, but the gunshot sounds will get on your last nerve eventually, especially the outpost tower's rangers.
[This was all my opinion, feel free to disagree, and if you feel this review wasn't very well focused, I agree I know it isn't. Currently the time is nearly 5 A.M. or 05:00 and I've been awake since all day yesterday. Not asking for you to excuse me, just providing you with an explanation for any errors.]

projectiles have a constant horizontal velocity and a constant vertical acceleration (on Earth the value of this acceleration is 9.8 ms-2).
newton's first law of motion states that an object will stay at rest or continue to move at a constant velocity unless acted on by an unbalanced force. the red block provides an unbalanced force which causes the yellow and blue blocks to accelerate.
newton's second law of motion states that when an object is acted on by an unbalanced force it will accelerate. this acceleration is directly proportional to the unbalanced force and is inversely proportional to the mass. as the red block causes the yellow and blue blocks to accelerate the acceleration can be calculated using the equation: a = Fun / m
newton's third law of motion states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. as the red block exerts a force on the yellow block, the yellow block exerts an equal and opposite force on the red block.

I've bought the game after some hesitation because I read Porhammer's review and I thought I'll give it a try. Now I am demanding refund.
Just so you know what to take from this review. I play rally games since early 2000's on both wheel and Xbox controller and I love DR and don't really like Dirt3. So you may be asking what did I expect from the Dirt4, right? Well, you may recall this statement:
"If you loved the challenge of DiRT Rally, then you can switch to the Sim Handling mode and have an experience that is even closer to the real deal than we managed to achieve with DiRT Rally".
-Codemasters Chief Designer Paul Coleman-
That made me look forward the D4 launchdate like a small child. I like the RPG format of D3 and I missed in Dirt Rally. I thought why not? I may be the best rally game ever, with the ability to switcxh between punishig handling model of DR and simplistic ad frankly terrible driving model of D3.
Weeell, It didn't happen. So let's see what i like and what i don't like but remember I may be a bit pedantic so don't take me 100% serious.
I like:
-The RPG elements of the game are just amazing. I love the Service Area, the on-stage events, starting order etc. I love It.
That's what I missed in DR. That's what i coveted more than my next breath.
-The selection of cars is tremendous.It ranges from 60s to 2010s and thats more than I can wish for.
-Nicky Grist returns. Do I need to say more?
-Dirt academy. I love the free roam area. Another thing I missed in DR.
-Your Stage. I am a bit crossed on this one because since I heard that YS is a thing I thought: "Damn it, another procedural generated fiasco". I mean Procedural generation is amazing but no-one can ever thing that you will get such a detail you got from DR stages (Which is one of the main things why DR is a legend). The thing with rally sport is that the stages are not just plain and simple pieces of tarmac/gravel/snow placed in a field. Special Stages are designet to be the twistiest or quickest and most interesting roads in the region. With rocks scattered around them, weird crests, broken pieces of tarmac etc. Your stage is just like building Lego railroad. You've got your bits and pieces, some straights, few types of corners and may have hundrets of those and Yes, you can create almost indefinite amount of variations but they are all gonna be the same and all gona suck after two drives. First of all, I have played Dirt Rally for a short time, and i found that a bit too challenging
This game is for the people, who liked Dirt 3 and Dirt Rally, it is basically a mixture of the two. By choosing Gamer, the game feels more like Dirt 3, a bit less realistic I might add. But if you choose Simulation, you will get an experience similar to Dirt Rally, but not as unforgiving.
If you're a hardcore Sim Racer that loves Dirt Rally, maybe give this one a pass, but if you're like me, and can appreciate when a game is realistic while not being too hard, then definitely give this game a shot

These are my impressions after about 9 hours of playtime.
I absolutely love this version of DiRT. It combines elements from DiRT 2, 3 and Rally so well and makes something a little bit different. I can easily recommend this to any rally or racing fan in general, but I can also recommend it to sim racers.
The career mode has been excellent so far. There is plenty of content to go through and none of it feels dull. The inclusion of other various modes like Joy Ride and Your Stage as well as all the multiplayer content will give this game a ton of replayability.
This game has gotten a lot of flack for its physics, but they're actually better than DiRT Rally's physics. I loved DiRT Rally, but I always felt like the cars were way too easy to slide and control a slide with. Now the cars have more weight to them and improved aerodynamics so you don't get those random mid-air turns like you did before.
The only real issue I have with the physics at the moment is the excessive rear grip in cars. It shouldn't be that hard to get a RWD car tail happy, but it feels like something is holding the back end for you. DiRT Rally had a very similar issue to this and it was patched so I hope they do the same here.
The visuals have noticeably improved as well, despite what others may say. The main thing I've noticed is improved lighting, reflections, and crowds over previous titles. The crowds are very graphically intensive so I recommend turning the setting for those down to medium-ish (turn off Advanced Blending as well).
Overall I would give this an 8/10 so far. If they fix the issues I have with it then I will happily give it a 9/10.

I'll keep it short and sweet:
+ Great and satisfying melee combat with just the right amount of depth (you're still fighting a massive hord here, don't  expect graceful parries and pirouettes).
+ Set in Warhammer world and very immersive, game's atmosphere is really fitting and WH fans will be right at home here. If you hate Warhammer or its aesthetic though... well, you'll hate it here aswell.
+ Loot system. This is your character progression part of the game. It's not super important, but you'll want to participate. Depending on what type of player you are this can be a good thing or a bad thing. Recent patches added new ways to recycle your items, so even when RNG doesn't favor you you still feel like you're progressing.
+ Developers are nice and do listen to the community.
+ Difficulty. This is a difficult game. But I think that various difficulty levels do a good job of catering to everyone. If you want you can just have a good time feeling like a dwarf/elven/etc. god of death and destruction as rat bodies pile up left and right. Or if you really want to challenge yourself you absolutely can.
- This game is something of a diamond in the rough. Performance, bugs, etc. vary from player to player.
- Grind. It is possible to grind in this game. It's not something you have to do (or even should do), this game is much better when played from time to time or with friends... prolonged grind will burn you out very quickly. Hence some of the replayability issues mentioned in some reviews. Imho this game has great replayability as the core gameplay is very solid, but if you grind you may feel that way soon. So if you have addictive personality this game might not be for you.
+/- This is a a multiplayer co-op team game with all the perks and problems that brings. It is NOT a single player game. Yes, there are bots and yes, there is something of an overarching story but you will have a very bad time if you want to treat this as singleplayer/solo experience.
Worth every penny.

The core gameplay concept is the same from Hotline Miami 1, you move around and kill people. I will say that there are places where HLM1 did better than HLM2 and vice versa.
For starters HLM2 actually tried to tie in a story.... in fact 8 of them. You'll play as a movie actor that has a dark secret, Jake's story of how he ended up where he ended up, Beard/Soldier's Hawaii war adventures ft. Jacket, the fans who are a group of 5 that go on killing sprees for the hell of it, the son of the Boss from the first game, Manny Pardo and the Miami Mutilator, an author named Evan and last but not least Richter from HLM1.
Some of the characters have their own special abilities so it adds to a variety of gameplay, however this was already done in HLM1 via the mask choices. Some notable ones are back such as Jake's killing throws and Tony's killing punches. Actually let's talk about Tony for a second, in the first game Tony was an excellent choice due to the fact that you could kill enemies without a weapon and still be able to bait with gunfire. This second ability was removed in HLM2. No longer can Tony pickup weapons, he can punch fat people and execute them but you are now forced to play at the game's pace if you chose to play as Tony. At least there are plenty of better choices in the Fans group.
Moving along, let me discuss some cons compared to the first game.
- Executions are extremely long. This makes doors a powerful foe.
- Tony, poor Tony.
- For some reason, you start to shoot slower after every Combat Shotgun shot. Does not happen on Double Barrell.
- Dog AI is sometimes completely broken.
- The AI in general seem a little dumb down.
To make up for it, the story is good (or I can even say there is a story). Unique gameplay on certain characters. Hard mode introduced and it plays sort of like a puzzle mode. Making your own routing for the A+ achievement was a lot of fun, it made getting the Genocide achievement tolerable.
In terms of the audience, I would say HLM2 is geared towards casual play and not speedrunning. The RNG is really bad, enemy placement can change on restart, their pathing can change, you can survive up to a full shotgun blast and the maps are really open.
Despite some nuances I still found it enjoyable to be able to 29/29 it.

Some people mentioned that the art in Tiny Guardians resembled Kingdom Rush quite a bit, which was most likely intentional on the part of the developers. The game's mechanics were still fairly unique, of course; it didn't take the formula wholesale. That's something this game did. But cribbing from something doesn't necessarily mean your work is going to be bad, and Alien Robot Monsters is a pretty good title that adds to that formula. The game starts off in a colony-era sci-fi setting, where a contingent of space marines have been deployed to investigate an inhabitable planet. Unfortunately, you aren't the only ones attempting to colonize it, and shortly after landing the troop finds themselves attacked by...well, you read the title. Time to defend yourselves.
If you've played Kingdom Rush you'll get the hang of this pretty quick, and it might not jump out at you at first. You start with only one tower, a Depot of rookies who are armed with simple machine guns. Not long after you get the Tech Lab, who can fire slower bursts of lightning for bigger damage and armor-piercing. These are your two core units, which you can build into a ton of other things, depending on what upgrades you buy on them. Adding an extra soldier to the depot for example, allows you to make it into a marine barracks, your first blocker unit, while increasing range lets you make it into an outpost, a more straight tower upgrade. Likewise, you can make the tech lab into the science lab, a more powerful AOE tower, or the satellite uplink, which shoots at one enemy for high damage, and has infinite range. Every tower has three particular upgrades to it, letting even the earlier ones feel like they have a lot of impact while fully kitted out. The game also has a fast forward button, which it's cousin lacks, although that's in exchange for any hero units, which you won't find here.
That all said, there are some problems. By the end of the game you'll have so many paths you can take towers down that you might find yourself forgetting what upgrades are necessary to get the one you want. You can look that up in levels, but it's still a bit bothersome at times. Speaking of upgrades, one un-intuitive thing is that while most don't carry on to the next stage, some do: adding an extra man to the depot is advised even if you don't want a barracks, since the outpost will have only two members in it otherwise, and the tech lab's range upgrade extends to the science lab. By the end of the game I also found that I had so many options it was difficult to discern what would be useful, since enemies can have both armor (blocks bullet weapons) or shields (blocks science weapons), and can come in some difficult combinations. There were some I just never used much. The upgrades you can buy with stars also feel a bit lackluster, and maybe not as helpful as they were in Kingdom Rush.
Aesthetic-wise I find the game quite nice. The B-Movie inspired enemies all look appealing and satisfying to blow into scrap, while your attacks have some real punch, particularly at the end. Every tower has voice clips for when they're built and upgraded, which have a bit of that old RTS charm to them. The game doesn't take itself very seriously, which you could probably expect by the title.
I beat the campaign, did the optional levels, and unlocked all the achievements in about twenty-five hours, so it's comparatively a bit short. But ARM is well-paced, and constantly gives you new things to play around with, as opposed to so other games in the genre where you unlock your full arsenal and still have most of it to go through. If you've done everything or nearly so in Kingdom Rush and want more like it, or just want something different to it, I think it'd be a fine addition to your library.

A mobile TD game that has serious issues with providing too little information to decide correctly.
This is yet another mobile tower defense game. You can tell by the fact that you cannot play with a keyboard, only with a mouse, and that the UI is huge.
But that wouldn't be a big problem in itself.
Imagine that you're playing a complicated version of rock-paper-scissors with more elements. Say "armor-shield-groups-robots-grenades-stun-fire-lightning-laser". But there are two problems:
First, no one explained the rules to you properly. Was it stun trumps armor and robots, laser trumps shields, grenades trump groups but only if they are non-robotic? Have fun figuring it out without any real feedback.
Second, many attack elements are hidden behind others (the game has only two basic towers which you then transform into completely different ones, quite an interesting idea) and there are blind upgrade paths that silently set you back. Was it grenades upgrade to fire, lightning to laser, but don't forget to skip the side upgrade of a higher range or it will be lost and you won't have enough money? You must uncover and remember rules such as: The extra soldier transfers to the outpost but after that it is lost. The extra range transfers to the science lab, but the double chain doesn't transfer to the laser.
In October 2015 the developer promised to update the in-game descriptions to include this information but it's still missing. So your only option is to guess.
Ultimately there are too many good TD games to bother with this one. If the developer updated the in-game description, I would give it my reluctant recommendation, but as it is:
Not recommended.

Overall, I'd say its a great game, would recommend supporting AQWorlds by purchasing a membership to get a early access code to the game. I can see a bright and clear future planned ahead for the game and hope the devs never give up and achieve the games full and true potential.

In some ways, this is a fairly "ordinary" FPS, but apart from the fairly fun "e-vision" mode you get from holding your tablet in front of you, this game is just great for the water effects, and I don't just mean visual effects, but the sensations of wading through water and being outmuscled by the water in just the right manner whether it be by calm waves or a deluge.
Someone just *really* went to town on making realistic water.

This is something like Dead Space (you 're an engineer and wander all over a ship fetching things and offing bad guys) and something like Mirror's Edge (female PC, lots of climbing, red pipes).  But the best part is the water.  The ship is flooding, and the ship has some amazing fluid physics, and makes use of water in interesting ways: swimming, flooding an area on purpose, drowning enemies, a wacky water attack.
It's short, and there are some story issues (you don't get the water power till just before the end, and the enemies are repetitive), but it's a fun idea and the price is right.
If you have a good enough computer to run it and not look and perform like crap, its a good game.

(This is a review of the game itself. I am not able to rightfully judge the quality of this PC port, as I have not played either of the original versions.)
This review is coming from someone who has never been a fan of Sonic and who personally didn't think that Sonic Adventure 1 was great, even as a kid.
It's difficult for me to honestly confess how I've never played this game before. It's not that I didn't like the first game, but I just never got around to this one. Now that I've played it for almost 2 hours straight (I can't completely review it, but...), I honestly was not amazed at all.
The controls, in my opinion, are downright way too slippery during Sonic's/Shadow's sections, and I'm probably one of the few who actually prefer Knuckles's/Rouge's stages (EDIT: NOPE NEVER MIND. The pyramid Knuckles stage has permanently changed my mind. That's possibly the worst thing in this game.). First of all, Sonic's stages typically somehow end up with me careening off of a cliff even though I was definitely not meaning to do so; even in planned sections, with stages like Green Forest inside of the speed sections in the hollow tree logs (I managed to, I guess, be tilting the control stick lightly, and I can never get Sonic/Shadow to run straight through it, but it feels as if one small mis-nudge of the control stick, and I am careening upside-down and falling through the ceiling, without being able to really control Sonic/Shadow). Knuckles/Rouge controls just fine from what I've played (depending on the stage) and is definitely the most stable of the characters, but I personally dislike his/her stages still... But, nothing can compare to how much I absolutely hate Tails's/Eggman's levels. They are bland, slow, repetitive, boring, and enemies pop out of nowhere will little to no warning in various stages.
(Edit: I've done two play sessions now. It somehow got worse during the second play session. Sonic's fight against the boss inside of the pyramid really sucks, in my opinion, since I already dislike Sonic's controls, and I now have to deal with slippery controls and jumping on small platforms that retract into the boss. Knuckles's pyramid stage also really sucks, but the boss is actually pretty good for Knuckles. I like how there's some good challenge with that particular boss. Then I got to the first Tails level in space, and I gave up. In addition to disliking Tails's stages already, now I have to play them by avoiding shooting things that you can accidentally lock onto, while shooting things right next to those. ALSO THAT LASER SOUND. I gave up, sorry.)
I no longer recommend this game, at least on PC. Something about the controls, especially in Sonic's/Shadow's levels, are very slippery (at least with playing this PC port with my Xbox 360 wired controller), and I didn't have much fun with the things that I did play. Perhaps the GameCube controller's slight indentations on the analog stick might make the controls much less slippery.
I'm not here to say that this game is better or worse than the first, however. I've not played the first in a very long time, and I doubt I'd appreciate it very much either. I give this game a 5/10 from what I've played. To be honest, I think I prefer Sonic Lost World to this (not trying to anger anyone, I'm just being honest). At least in Lost World, there's no Tails/Eggman or Knuckles/Rouge stages, and I feel like I can actually CONTROL Sonic.

The infamous question posed at the beginning of Hotline Miami 1 never really got the attention it deserved. While the first game was great, it simply didn't have as much narrative and depth as the sequel. And that's only the first thing that sets Hotline Miami 2 above its predecessor. But we'll come back to that.
Let's start with the first two things you'll notice about the game; visuals and music.
The visuals are all spot on. Every background and color scheme has a purpose, even if it isn't obvious exactly what it is at first glance.
And the music. This may just be the best video game soundtrack I've heard, and that's just listening to the music on its own. When blended with the visuals and storytelling, it takes on a whole new life.
And that brings us to the storytelling. I'm not sure what made the developers want to make something so different from the first game in this regard, but it was a fantastic decision. The stories of each character slowly become intertwined with each other as the story of the game unfolds. You learn not only of the events that led to the first game, but the results of your actions in the first game. Not everything will be apparent right off the bat. Hell, my first reaction to the ending was "That's it?" But as I sat there and the memories of each game came back, I could only appreciate what the writers had done.
And lastly, gameplay. Honestly, there isn't much to say. They kept everything we loved about the first game and just added more depth. More characters, more abilities and more diverse enemies. The level design was a step up as well.
This game may just be the first 10/10 gaming experience I have ever had, and I would highly recommend it to anyone, especially fans of the first game.

Pretty good game, with some nice changes and slight improvements over both Dirt Rally and Dirt 3.
First of all, Dirt 4 is not to be confused with 'Dirt Rally 2' while in several ways they are a very similar game, there are quite a few subtle changes under the hood that will make Dirt 4 feel completely new and put you back in your place and make you feel like you can't drive a shopping trolley properly.
Also, I'm not much of a reviewer so forgive me if my review is poorly formatted and is a little all over the place. I just typed it up as it all came to mind, so I probably have missed something important....
Now, onto the good stuff...
I play Simulation style with all assists off and with XB1 controller.
This is not my first Dirt game, I actually do sorta know how to play a Dirt game... poorly...
I am still getting a feel for Dirt 4, so my review could change in the future as my skills improve.
Handling is a bit different in this game, although it's very hard to describe. most of the vehicles overall feel slightly 'heavier' and I would say behave a little more out of control at any given moment, perhaps it's me still getting a feel for how the physics are and the handling in general.
Overall I would have to disagree with the community on this one, Handling has improved over DR and is much more in line with 'Simulation', it's way harder to get into that sweet spot for your super sweet power-slide around that hairpin now and shifting your weight around does feel better than ever before when you can get everything flowing just right.
The audio is pretty good, I would find it more comparable to Dirt 3 than DR. a nice mix of tracks that do a good job of adding a little bit of flavor to the games menus.
While on track the audio is just as good as it used to be with some very nice new sounds for various mechanical failures and bumping into objects.
Your co-driver sounds fine and isn't as robotic as many would have you to believe.
Multiplayer has a much needed boost in game modes over DR. Only minor issue I have here is I would love to see multiplayer rally stages with a staggered start, like how it was done with Dirt 3.
Other wise the changes here are very welcome and should have some good hours of fun with friends with some of these modes.
Single Player is much more like a 'Dirt' game where you have to progress though pre-made championships to earn the right to race in more championships. Overall the single player is much faster paced than DR's is with a much more rewarding results at the end of your event, and a much more accessible way to manage and organise your own racing brand. Cars are cheaper to buy and you will have more money. Can't really complain about that.
There are many new little cut-scenes during these end of round celebrations that I feel do add to the game in a very nice way.
Graphically The game looks fine to me, and I can't really agree with the comments about it being a 'downgrade'. I play my game with a mix of high and ultra settings for the most part with a very good FPS. I do however have some minor issues with FPS dips during some scenes (mostly rally-cross type events) to around the 40-50's. Not really ideal and hopefully we can get some more performance squeezed out of the game with some future game updates and GPU drivers.
To summarise it's a pretty solid entry in the series with some great improvements over Dirt 3, but only very minor improvements when compared to Dirt Rally.
While I still have alot to learn about this game once you really give it a chance you can start to appreciate some of the changes and how they have improved the game overall.

I played over 1000 stages on dirt rally and bought nearly every car.  So I had to pre-order dirt 4 and guess what... IT'S ACTUALLY IMPROVED!!  Every single aspect of dirt!!  Highly recommend. See more below.
First of all the simulation handing is better than dirt rally.   Feels better, more realistic... like I can feel the road and connect with car way more.  Weight transfer is good, etc.   You can also actually feel stuff with the car WAY more like when you enter a gutter or hit a curb, etc...
Also the stages...   Love the tarmac tracks.  I've played some tarmac tracks where you drive through a small town!!  So cool!! I also had to pass a broken down wrx from the rally in front of me when I was in a FWD kit car... kinda cool there is a little cone.  Also sometiems the reply drone is like right in front of car is scary!  And you cant just go balls out at the end, since you now have to drive and stop at the marshall.
Tuning is so much better as well.  You get save slots for each stage type and the options are far better.  Can also bring more than one spare tire or zero if you want.  Repairs are more important: have to do quick inspects to get accurate repair time.
Career mode is actually good, with some intro and tutorial stuff for newbies.  Freeroam,  joyride, and gymkhana dirt 3 bonus material type stuff...  Team management and sponsor management actually matters too. Also you can pick your livery... yes!! Team Poptarts... here I come!    I have yet to try other game modes but soo cool so far.  But looks like you have to choose how to spend money early on to make the most of your career.  You can upgrade your facility for different thing or give engineers perks, etc.  Can even negotiate salary or sponsor bonus too!
There was a daily challenge multiplayer event where you did a few stages live against other people with limited tune time.  I thought that was cool.  Apparently you get some online skill group ranking?  IDK still new to me.  I've only done rally and some gymkhana.
The graphics engine is crazy better than dirt rally too... game looks pretty good even with lower options.  Prob need a really good rig to max this game out.  The fog is pretty freaking dense.  I found trees, objects, and advanced ambient occlusion to really kill fps. Just put anistrophic filter and texture to max, with some MSAA, and it doesn't tax your PC much. I am able to max out a 144hz g-sync monitor e.z. if I lower some stuff down from high/ultra.
Few small changes could improve the sponsor or facility page, like listing requirement of the price on the quick notes on the right instead of having to select each one to see if you're are elgibile.
Anyway... once I changed FFB, controller bindings, difficulty setting, and found a good graphic setting this game is great!!   Just wish it supported SLI already.  Still better than previous dirt!
Ok back to Dirt 4 for me!  I recommend you buy this now!  See you online.  Cheers!

This review has been written after roughly 5 hours of game time.
For those enjoying the more 'sim' experience of Dirt Rally, this may be a bit of a let down. Even in its "simmiest" the game feels arcade. FFB isn't crisp and feels dampened and simplified. The rally stages don't look or feel authentic, no builder would construct road in such cambers and angles. But hey ho, we have more open track selection, at the cost of the stages feeling like they're from Colin McRae Rally 2 or 3.
The career is fun, as long as you don't mind the arcade railroading it offers. Also, for me, coming from Dirt Rally I wished I could kick the whole tutorial. To my relief it wasn't too long.
Graphics are fine, although at points feel bit coarse and generic. Feels that this game has been made with console performance in mind.
Verdict: Console rallying in the proud arcade tradition of previous DIRTs (excluding DIRT rally). You have been warned.

I'll keep it short and sweet:
+ Great and satisfying melee combat with just the right amount of depth (you're still fighting a massive hord here, don't  expect graceful parries and pirouettes).
+ Set in Warhammer world and very immersive, game's atmosphere is really fitting and WH fans will be right at home here. If you hate Warhammer or its aesthetic though... well, you'll hate it here aswell.
+ Loot system. This is your character progression part of the game. It's not super important, but you'll want to participate. Depending on what type of player you are this can be a good thing or a bad thing. Recent patches added new ways to recycle your items, so even when RNG doesn't favor you you still feel like you're progressing.
+ Developers are nice and do listen to the community.
+ Difficulty. This is a difficult game. But I think that various difficulty levels do a good job of catering to everyone. If you want you can just have a good time feeling like a dwarf/elven/etc. god of death and destruction as rat bodies pile up left and right. Or if you really want to challenge yourself you absolutely can.
- This game is something of a diamond in the rough. Performance, bugs, etc. vary from player to player.
- Grind. It is possible to grind in this game. It's not something you have to do (or even should do), this game is much better when played from time to time or with friends... prolonged grind will burn you out very quickly. Hence some of the replayability issues mentioned in some reviews. Imho this game has great replayability as the core gameplay is very solid, but if you grind you may feel that way soon. So if you have addictive personality this game might not be for you.
+/- This is a a multiplayer co-op team game with all the perks and problems that brings. It is NOT a single player game. Yes, there are bots and yes, there is something of an overarching story but you will have a very bad time if you want to treat this as singleplayer/solo experience.

Very solid tower defense. Most levels are challenging and you have to try many different strategies before you find one that fits. The progression is not immensly original but at least it's decently interesting. You get more stars if you ace a level. You can then spend said stars on a dozen different upgrades - all resettable at the click of a button. So you can change up your strategies a lot and it gives you a strong incentive to go back and clear earlier levels 100% to give you a better chance at the later ones.
As the sucker I am for achievements I enjoyed how you can complete pretty much all of them in one playthrough. (So yeah maybe a bit on the easy side.)
* The controls and UI feels like a bad port from a mobile game. The tapping (upgrading towers, troop rallying) and swiping (map scroll) would make sense on a tablet or phone but feels stupid on PC. There are also many missing keyboard shortcuts and nothing is rebindable. This is easily my biggest gripe with this game.
* I have found no way to see what in-game upgrades carry over when you evolve your tower into a new type. Range upgrades sometimes carry over and sometimes not. Amount of marines in a tower sometimes carries over and sometimes not. Even if you learn with time you'd still expect to be able to see what active upgrades a tower has (in the tower stat screen perhaps?). This is inconsistant and very annyoing early on.

Hydrophobia: Prophecy is 3rd person survival-horror style action-adventure game. While the PC keyboard/mouse controls are fine, the game also has platforming elements, as well - so, I wound up using the X360 Controller for this one.
While the graphics are not spectacular, they are good & do get the job done just fine here. The water looks stunning. The voice-acting is good, though the story could use a little more kick & depth to it.
The water in this game is its own creature, as it will effect the environment & its surrounding - especially since feels like it has weight to it. Using the environment for combat is another thing that makes this game stand out, since you really don't have very many weapons or skills at your disposal...until later on in the game.
When it's all said & done, Hydrophobia: Prophecy is a pretty good start to what looks to be a series that could have a lot of potential, if they keep on building on the nice foundation that this game actually sets.
Grade = B-

Okay, so here is my review of AQ3D. I go into several aspects but you can find the opinion below.
First of all, I'd just like to address something:
Noting this fact is important before going in. It means anything they try is experimental and will require feedback and work. If you go into this game as it is right now, you will need patience therefore as things are worked upon. I post this on the release on Open Beta, so if you are reading this in the future some things may well be addressed by this point.
AQ3D is a free to play game, with a one time upgrade, Guardian, that unlocks the Guardian Class and some exclusive features like the Guardian Tower. Most aspects of the game can however be played without a Guardian Upgrade, and no important features to the game are currently locked off by it. There is also a secondary currency in the form of Dragon Crystals, which are used to skip or speed up crafting times, buy potions (pro tip: you can also earn them in game in areas) and buy access to Dungeon Keys when you run out of all of them. I find the in game prices of Crystals reasonable in some places (100 DC gets you a full 20 dungeon keys for example which is 20 runs, and the option to buy them only appears when you run out) and not so reasonable in others (some items). Buy with caution as always. (Another pro tip: if you have the items to craft a item, but want to speed it up, craft the item and then pay to speed it up rather then just paying for the item. You will save half your DC.)
Combat right now needs some work. There are 4 classes: Mage, Rogue, Warrior, which are all free to play, and the Upgrade Exclusive Guardian, which requires a one time fee. Each has 4 skills and these skills are used to kill things. SImple. The problem comes from lack of variety in combat currently. Looking at future promises for the game these skills will apparently be morphable for various tasks, and in the most recent Design Notes (Which I recommend looking at on their site for the latest news if you are interested in this game) point out they are considering feedback on this matter. Expect some changes.
Crafting is currently a simple affair. You kill foes for items to craft things, and then go to the relevant NPC to make them. All crafting items have a timer on them that ticks down no matter if you are in the game or not, and you can claim items from your menu rather then going back to them (So if you don't want to wait in game for 4 hours, log off, go for a nice walk or something, and come back 4 hours later and it will be there for you). You can also choose to buy the item outright with DC if you don't have the crafting items, or if you do you can craft them and pay to speed it up. Drops in my experience are fairly plentiful so you should not have issue gaining them.
Right now there is not a lot of content. There will be enough to keep you busy for a while, but you will run out. The Halloween event will come out soon (Which as a holiday event will not stick about probably) and the Dragon's Liar is planned for November. Content will probably come slow, since again this is their first foray into 3D. Be aware of that when playing.
Usually, I enjoy the dialogue of AE games, but the tutorial has a lot of cringeworthy moments. I enjoy fourth wall breakage as much as the next, but the tutorial has way too much of it, especially one moment that made me cringe for all the wrong reasons. You know which bit staff. Be warned: puns, forth wall breaks and other such things of that nature will apply. However, I did find the writing of the game improves after that point,
I can only give my own experience here. From what I have seen the community is fairly helpful in game, and the staff are (generally) kind and helpful. I have heard the odd bad story about some, but have not experienced it myself. I find that if you are polite and helpful when expressing opinion or asking for help you will have a good time.
Personally, I believe that what they have right now is a fairly solid basis for the game, but that is all it is: a base. There is a long way to go and many more features are planned before it becomes a full game.
I would recommend giving the game a go since it IS free, the download size is quite small, and most systems can run it, but keeping in mind that the game has yet to find it's feet, it's staff and content are few and will be updated slowly, and this is their first 3D game. Keep those caveats in minds and I think you will have fun.

'Alien Robot Monsters' is not just a tower defense game. It is the most diffucult tower defense game ever. I doubt that there will ever be a harder tower defense game than 'Alien Robot Monsters'.
In principle the game is fun and comes with the typical addiction tower defense games offer. Graphics are fine and the music is very good. Towers and enmies are interesting. And although I really like tower defense games 'Alien Robot Monsters' was a rather painful experience.
The problem with this game is that it only allows one solution. You have to play maps again and again and again to find out which setup works. IMO that's not how a tower defense game should work. If you look at 'Defense Grid' you can use tons of different approaches to beat maps. 'Defense Grid' does not let you down. It allows you to experiment and reach your goal with different strategies. This is not the case for 'Alien Robot Monsters'. There is only one way and you have to find it in order to collect three stars on a map. It's like a racing game with 200 different cars but all players select the same car because it's the only car that allows you to compete with other players. Try 'The Crew' to find out more.
I consider a game a good game if it's fun. 'Alien Robot Monsters' caused me far too much frustration to recommend the game. Since I do not want other players, especially not friends of mine, to go through the same painful experience, I can not recommend the game. There are very many other tower defense games available that simply do better than 'Alien Robot Monsters'. But if you feel like Superman or like playing single maps for hours again and again, go ahead and try. You have been warned.

Alien Robot Mosters is a towed defence game that has been extended into multiple evenings worth of fun in planning, optimising and executing the kill-alley operation in order to prevent those waves of mechanical monstrosities from getting their hands on your  settler population. Game presents a steadily rising challenge with tower choices where there are no universal winners in lane clearing power thus requiring experimentation and adaptation for each level if you want to get through all levels undamaged.
Each tower is sufficiently different from another and in some cases even benefit from manual control from the user as in the case of redeployable marines and their derivatives. There are multiple cases where the optimal solution consists of re-prioritizing their focus in mid-level. Upgrading towers doesn't simply increase damage and range, but ofter changes completely the mode of operation. A great example of this is that one upgrade path from the tech tower is a satellite-based weapon that shoots any targets from off-map. There's also units that are resilient or weak to certain types of damage.
In many strategic games the main focus is in gameplay leaving visuals and audio as secondary, but in developers of ARM have not taken a shortcut here. The soundtrack is great, I like the voicing with the humour it has, sound effects are lively and the semi-retro 2d graphics fit the game perfectly.
My verdict for ARM is that it’s a solid tower-defence which doesn’t try to be all around revolutionary, but does everything it strives for with top-notch quality without compromises.

This is a summary of my review video, which I encourage you to watch if you are looking for a more in-depth review.
Attack of the Alien Robot Monsters is a futuristic tower defense game with a 16 bit look and feel, where you fight against hordes of Robots in order to save your colony.The story does exactly what it needs to, tying a purpose and progression with the enemies and troops to the game. It is more minimalistic, but fits in well to the game.  The interface is sleek and simplistic, One minor issue I had was that you could only increase the time of the round x1, where it would have been nice to have a x2 option. Another small gripe would be that there was no way to tell what type of creatures would be coming up in the next round. It was a bit annoying, as it didn't give me time to prepare for what was coming, and increased my chances of having to redo the level not out of enjoyment, but out of frustration. The two most important factors to consider in a tower defense game are the level design and the tower defense layout, which go hand in hand with each other.

Level Design;
This was done extremely well in this game. Magnificent, even! They did an excellent job of designing each level so that it challenged the player, and accommodated the increase in towers and attack strength as you progressed through the game. I never felt that I was replaying the same levels over again, which is hard to find in tower defense games.
Tower Design;
This game requires a certain knowledge of what each tower does, and a tactical knowledge of where to place them. The towers are interchangeable, and as you  increase in level, if you want to, you can change the towers to a completely different style. There are large tech trees in this game, with a large variety of different types of towers that you can change to to battle against the different types of enemies. Each individual tower also has a decent selection of upgrades that do an excellent job of increasing the power of those towers.
There are marine style barracks and outposts, some of which are more powerful than others, which i go over more in my video review. There are also more tech lab style outposts, which offer air assault units (which I found to be largely useless due to poor AI). The variety of attack/ dps/ armor units give more options to defend against different attacks. While there are towers that are stronger than others as the game does suffer from a power creep issue. Although it still comes down to the right placement of the towers on the map. The enemy offers a large, diverse variety of units, that have certain buffs that you need to be ready for.
Bosses
The bosses are also large and varied, and may require you to replay them. The enemy troops synergize well with each other, more than your towers do with each other. Each level is based on a 3 star rating; the stars can be used to purchase upgrades. You need to have an understanding of tower defense games when you play this game, as it does not start at a noob level, but has a higher entry difficulty bar. The game starts at a moderate level, but quickly increases to a veteran level, then hardcore. You do feel a sense of progression due to this, and the end boss really requires a tactical eye rather than just relying on the skills you have acquired up to that point. The game never wasted my time, which I appreciated.
Summary
At the end of the day, the towers may have some issues, but the enemies and levels that you face rotate so that you constantly feel challenged, and keeps you on your toes. The balance between the ascetics, the gameplay, the mechanics, and how it all works together there were no issues. I didn't feel like it wasted my time, or that the hours spent in this game were for nothing.  I can absolutely recommend this game for those who have a base knowledge of the tower defense genre. There is a tactical element required for this game, and this game shines in that respect.

EDIT:  In case you forgot, Codemasters had promised us for the last several months that this would (in simulation mode) be a propper sim.  I was convinced that they were telling the truth.
------------
It gives me a ton of pain to do this, but it's only fair.  I'm sad to report that, despite everything they promised about this game, it has somehow managed to disappoint on every level.  I'll be focusing on gameplay.  I have only tested 'sim' mode.
--Graphics
If you were expecting the DiRT 3-level graphics we were all hoping for, this game will fall short.  Not only do they not compare to DiRT 3, they actually look worse than
.  How did they manage?  Its really THAT bad.
--Handling
You may remember the great debate about DiRT Rally's handling model.  Most hardcore sim fans agreed that, while it wasnt detrimental per se, it had significantly more grip than it should have.  So what did Codemasters do?  They made it even more gluey.  Its absurd. In sim mode, all assists off, you can take grade-3/4 turns in Wales at 80km/h without the slightest break of traction. Why?  It actually feels like the car is fighting you.  The lateral grip is so strong that, if you try to do donuts with the
RWD Opel Cadet, the car will simply squeal around in large, oversteering circles.  Power slides are nearly impossible unless you're going over 120km/h on a loose surface.  How, with the supposed help of Petter Solberg and Kris Meeke, did they pass this off? It feels like an early alpha test.
--Stages
If you got bored with the handful of tracks in DR like me, 'Your Stage' probably sounded amazing. Like the key to thousands of hours of playablity.  But nope.  Its basically a bunch of turn templates that get snapped together at random.  Sounds great, right?  Well, no.  I'm eight hours into this game, and I can honestly say I've seen a lot of clear repitition.  Instead of memorizing whole stages, you now memorize the bits and pieces that make them up. They might be different, but they don't feel unique at all.
Other bits:
- No multiplayer (or singleplayer) staggered starts like we begged for.  Watching the car in front of you go does a lot more for immersion than you might think.
- The damage system has been expanded upon, but still very poor.  The effects of a crash are in no way realistic.
- Team branding is cool, but extremely basic.  You pick one out of (eight I think?) patterns and four colors.  And that's it.
- Non-racing immersion is there, but lacking.  At most, you get to see your generic team standing around your car, a comment by your co-driver before they count you down, and you get to slow down for the marshall.  Nothing else.

Summary: Melee-only runs aren't exceptionally viable, music and story are good, gameplay is rage-inducing but is a satisfying, trial-and-error experience.
This game doesn't cater at all to melee only runs. There are enemies that can't even be killed with melee weapons and the map layouts are made with ranged weapons in mind pretty much exlusively, though each that I've played IS possible to beat with only melee weapons minus the particular enemies who are unkillable with melee, but definitely feels more difficult than it should. A lot of this game brings the phrase "style over substance" to mind with things like the graphics making it hard to makeout what certain objects are, if an enemy is dead, if a wall is partial, complete, or no cover at all, and just gets messy when there are a lot of things in the same area at a time, usually when there are a lot of dead bodies lying around. Other things that make me think of it are execution moves that take three swings to kill a downed enemy even though you can kill them in one hit while standing (otherwise I would say it adds to the challenge), the music getting EXTREMELY LOUD on one level in particular for no reason other than to try to highten the mood of a level designed for a duel gun wielder, who you're stuck with, though you can waste all of your ammo and go melee, when I just want to sneak around and kill enemies.
Stealth is not an option in this game. ALL enemies have eyes in the back of their head but cannot see more than so many feet in front of them (right...). They also have the fastest reflexes imaginable which was a problem in Rainbow Six Vegas 2 where I would try to sneak around and stealthily execute enemies with a silenced pistol, so you can't rush them. You have to sit back, wait for them to come close to a corner, poke in, kill them and run back to cover, bait them out (which is made more difficult by the fact that they have super human reflexes and SPOT-ON accuracy, making it extremely hard to dodge. It's also not helped that you can't see very far ahead of you even with the shift key, and enemies tend to come into your range of view just in time for them to shoot you before you can react), then do the poke in and out move, throw something at them run up to them and kill them, or bait them, THEN throw something at them.
Another thing that is annoying is that you're struggling to pick up a desired weapon when there are more than one in the same place. I ALWAYS want melee weapons for obvious reason, so I think there should be a feature to prioritize which weapons you want first. "1. Melee 2. Shotguns 3. Rifles" for example. I also get annoyed with doors because I just want to run through them, kill someone and run back, but they knock enemies over which I don't want to commit to an execution so I just have to go back and waste time. I honestly can't think of a solution for this other than making instant executions. I feel that would help the melee game a lot overall as then I could throw weapons more effectively to then go and instantly kill them. Again, I do understand that it's supposed to add to the challenge but it's just another thing that makes melee really hard.
The enemies are really inconsistent with their intelligence level. They can react with those reflexes I mentioned, but seeing dead bodies don't process in their brains at all, and they have such short attention-spans, I'm surprised they could keep jobs as guards.
The music is good. Moving on. The story is actually pretty good and somewhat engaging. It isn't something I just want to skip over like in the first game where it was so much less coherant. It's still out there and bizzarre but it works well in this game with more parts that are a bit grounded in reality.
So back to gameplay, Hotline Miami 2 is mostly based on trial and error. Not being able to see far in front of you and enemies being so reflexive seem to kill off any ideas of playing purely reactively as most of the levels just can't be ran through so it's definitely a game of planning and execution. The controls are also kind of awkward and didn't seem to be helped with switching to a controller as I'm always getting stuck on walls, missing an enemy by a foot, or walking through doors when I don't mean to. In addition, I constantly miss enemies by a pixel with is so annoying. It'll appear that I'm swinging right beside them and nothing happens but they turn around and kill me. Enemies also seem to kill you from behind them with melee weapons, which I don't even understand.
My last criticism (though a lot of these are just preference) would be that you have to start from the beginning of the chapter if you save and quit instead of being able to start at the beginning of each room which is where you start after each death. It's hard enough the first time so I don't want to have to replay a room. With all the aggravation, and this is one of the most rage-inducing games I've played, you might wonder why I would even bother playing it and why I even picked this one up after the first. I spent a lot more of the first game with ranged weapons and didn't try to go all melee from the start (which I have with HM2 and have beat every level so far only killing enemies with melee minus the unkillable, with possibly a few unnoticed exceptions that got killed with a gun). But even that way, the game made me rage madly. The reason I keep playing is because how satisfying it is to beat a level especially since I do it only with melee, which reinforces my feeling that there should be a challenge mode with melee only.
If you've even beaten a really hard game, you know the feeling. It's also one of those resentment things, where you're determined to beat it or beat it in your way, like on the hardest difficulty for instance, refusing to make it easier. It gets to the point where you ask yourself "Well, why do something that makes you angry?" but I don't feel anger is necessarily a bad part of playing games (see AVGN) and the reason I play games that make me angry is that the ones that I am the most invested in carry a lot of weight and tend to make me react the strongest which make them the most memorable. I could just not care and the games wouldn't make me angry at all but then I wouldn't really get anywhere and would have no goals.
I know this isn't intended as a stealth game, so I can't complain that I can't sneak behind enemies and back-stab them, (and actually in the first one, even without a weapon you could execute an enemy while standing), but making the enemies have less SUPER-HUMAN reflexes would help a lot with melee. I don't see why they wouldn't consider people trying to go for melee runs. It seems so obvious considering that there a melee weapons that can instakill an enemy at all and melee runs seem like such a good potential for challenges and achievements. This review has mostly just been about that aspect and it seems a little critical and like that's a big flaw, but I'm just pointing out how it could possibly be made better and what makes it hard to do that sort of run.
A lot of the things that make it hard to do a only melee run, are what make the game what it is and I could see where changing those things could give a very different, possibly undesired experience. It's really just something to consider. Either way, I love these two games and recommend buying them if you're okay with old-school challenge including lots of trial and error.

While comparisons to the Left 4 Dead series are inevitable and deserved, I believe this game adds enough to the formula to make it an excellent and unique experience.
Let's break it down.
- SAME: L4D "pattern" of play.  Take a group of 4 players, have them travel through a level and sometimes complete objectives while fending off hordes of baddies.  There are special baddies that must be dealt with using teamwork since they will be able to pick off a lone hero.  There are consumables in the level that can heal damage, blow up hordes, and give you back ammo.  There are different difficulties which basically lessen consumable spawns and make the enemies hit harder.
-DIFFERENT: There are five playable characters, and they are more than cosmetically different.  Each of these characters have their own selection of melee and ranged weapons, most of which are unique.  This lends to a sense of selecting a "class" when you select a character.  But since you can change your loadout depending on what weapons you bring, you can certainly tailor the role you want to play in the party.
-DIFFERENT: Loot and earning it.  At the end of the level, you roll dice to get better gear.  You can earn more dice in a level by completing the level in a more difficult manner.  How?  Collecting tomes and grimoires hidden in the level.  Tomes must be carried instead of healing items, limiting the amount of healing you can bring with you.  Grimoires must be carried instead of stat-boosting potions, and they also lower the maximum health of the entire team.  If a player dies while carrying a grimoire, it is lost forever; tomes are simply dropped.  The more you can complete a level while carrying, the better the chances of good loot but the more risk and difficulty.  It's a fantastic tradeoff.
-DIFFERENT: Emphasis on melee combat.  Melee is a bit more complex than L4D.  Normal attacks and strong attacks, different attack characteristics with different weapons, blocking and pushing with stamina, quick-dodging, and headshots... melee feels extremely gratifying and a little more skill based.
-DIFFERENT: Legit warhammer setting.  The level designs are beautiful, the characters are flavored with background animosity, and the enemies you fight are legit units in the Warhammer Skaven army miniatures game (even if you can point to exact mechanics from L4D).  Skaven fight like they should, in overwhelming numbers and with scary cunning from all directions.
This is good stuff and should absolutely be enjoyed with friends if you enjoyed L4D or similar games.

The first question I asked when I first heard about this game was "Does the lore matter?". Though the lore is there and it is fun to explore if you are a big Warhammer fan you don't need to know it to have a blast in the game. If you wish to play this game to learn the lore though, it is there.
This game has a playstyle very similar to Left 4 Dead 2, and you may dicredit this game for closely resembling if not copying that series. Though seeing as not many games are FPS melee horde I think it deserves a pass.
This game offers about 10-15 missons all of which get harder as you go on. Personally I haven't beat the final boss because that misson is just way too hard without friends. Some have complained that a lot of objectives in the missons are just rehashes of objectives from previous missons. Yes, you have to move black powder a lot, but the difficulty and lnviroment are so different that you soon ignore the "Oh wait, I have done this before". I personally believe that the different locations you explore and the just shear fun and challenge is enough for hundreds of gameplay.
Now, the loot system. The loot system at first was kind of a joke, but with the latest updates it added a big variety. The way you aquire loot is 2 ways: Leveling up and completing a misson and rolling dice. The first one is pretty self explanitory, but the second. If you were to complete a misson without doing anything extra you get to roll dice that only have a 1/6 or 2/6 chance of rolling a face side. If you roll a face side you go up the loot chart wich gets you better loot. Though as you complete a misson you can pick up risky, but rewarding tomes and Grimore. These are hidden on most maps and take place of potions and healing supplies in your inventory. Grimores reduce your health by about 33% for each one you have and this applies to your entire team, but you will get a dice at the end that ALWAYS rolls a side. This basically makes you think in a "risk vs. reward" way. As for types of loot it goes White (common), Green (uncommon), Blue (rare), and Orange (legendary). With each tier you get a ability that you can upgrade to unlock legendaries of course have 3 abilities and have better stats, but they are harder to upgrade.
This game is unique and such a blast even by yourself the one huge downside that could be a deal breaker is that if you lose connection to Steam while in a game with other people it instantly kicks you and the people playing with you get locked in some dumb blackscreen. Though this is rare to happen and can be avioded it is by far the worst and most annoying thing that can happen.
[9/10] Though this game isn't blowing up the media it defenitley does what is does very well and with friends you can easily get a hundred hours out of this game.

Full disclosure: I was provided a review key by the publisher.
This was an interesting title both to play and review, and the game left me surprised if feeling somewhat mixed. Obviously it has a low price point and can raise concerns about shovelware - I can definitely say that yes, this feels like a game a human being put effort into and thought through rather than shoving out as a cash grab. It feels like Alien Swarm without a budget.
I'd like to note that I played on easy, not because of challenge but because of a curious achievement which required you to beat the game on easy before doing so on a higher difficulty. What I noticed eventually was that a number of enemies were bullet sponges for the equipment you'd have at the time. Obviously this is fine for boss battles or certain climax fights, but at times it leaves you feeling somewhat weaker than you should. A small balance patch improving the "gunfeel" would elevate the combat (and therefore much of the game) - as is it's typical of the genre. However sometimes the combat felt excellent (usually during bosses/climax fights).
Which brings us to the other half of the game - puzzles. Puzzles are a hard thing to do right; especially in an action genre like twin stick shooter. This is where I feel I might have enjoyed the game a little more on a higher difficulty to make certain puzzles a little more fatal, because once you figure them out, you're effectively done with that puzzle. These have singular solutions, and that does reduce replay value (which isn't great considering the achievement design encouraging players into an easy difficulty and sometimes uneven gunplay). If you pick it up you should probably consider a higher difficulty, as I was able to effectively just blitz through certain damaging puzzles that probably should have killed me easily.
At the same time, I do have to applaud the developer for the sheer variety of puzzles and scenarios the game puts you through. The game packs in a lot of variety, far more than I was expecting from a title at this price, and I'll admit that finishing an aggravatingly long sequence with chainsawing a long-term nuisance was far more satisfying than I expected. Not all of the puzzles are winners (early puzzles are barely puzzles at all), but they are memorable and different.
Variety is in fact the big saviour of this game - there's a little bit of everything in this game, even Limbo-esque spiders. The game also feels better in later stages, as that first stage has to essentially serve as a tutorial and an actual level at once.
Graphics aren't going to impress anyone, but more importantly they're easy to read and understand what is going on. Sound design is isn't going to wow you and the guns sound weak, but the worst I could say is that it gets the job done. The engine seems to be from scratch. The plot is about on the level of a Saturday morning cartoon and the translation is weak at times, Levels are definitely huge, but on the linear side of things.
It was a difficult game to review because for every negative there'd end up being a big positive, and some of those negatives can be fixed. I intend to go back and finish the game (once). There was an odd but distinct feeling I had which brought me back to renting SNES cartridges from a video rental store as a kid. It was the feeling of a game not being great but not being bad and having enough novelty and fun that I wanted to keep going rather than simply quitting.  It's that weird nether realm of a "good" 6/10. With some minor fixes it'd be a solid 7.

It’s a real shame that Trigger Time has gone completely under the radar. It’s a story-driven top-down shoot ‘em up that should hold mass appeal to action gamers. However, almost a full week after its release it has yet to be reviewed on Steam. It Is my hope that providing this review I can help start remedying this and that more eyes get on the game.
Instead of a traditional view, I want to provide my insight into why I believe the game hasn’t received the attention that it deserves. I’ll start by outlining what it isn’t and then diagnose what it is holding it back in my opinion.
Trigger Time has been released at a very low $4.99. Therefore, it can’t possibly be the price that has deterred games from purchase. There is a substantial amount of content within the game for players to spend several hours playing through the entirety of the game.
The game features 9 levels. What is most pleasurable about this content is that the levels are significant in size. Further, they are entirely unique. Throughout the time that I spent playing the game I never came across repeated content. The developers lived up to their main design goal which was ‘never to repeat things.’ Further, each level feels completely unique unto itself while also providing just enough synchronicity for it to obviously be the same game.
The game is literally teeming with enemies, physics puzzles, and hazards. Each of these requires active thinking as well as the obvious action to conquer.
My favourite component was the gravity gun. There’s an interesting puzzle when you first get the gravity gun. The first part is learning the basic mechanic. You must move a pile of rocks to enter the next area of the level. You then enter an area with quickly respawning enemies. At first, I killed the enemies and wondered why I couldn’t progress further. I soon realized that to progress you must pick up those rocks with the gravity gun and put them into the path of lasers. Once the lasers are deactivated the gateway clears for the player to progress. Puzzles such as this are indicative of the entirety of the game and the constant thinking-action challenges presented.
Each level has a boss fight. The boss fights are challenging and require different strategies to defeat. The variety here is exactly what I was hoping for. Each demands a minimum amount of skill to defeat. However, the player should have theoretically acquired those skills throughout the game. There’s a feeling that you’re never thrown in at the deep end and expected to have picked up those skills from prior experience. This makes the game a reasonable gateway into the genre for new and younger players.
The one distinct complaint that I have with Trigger Time is that the default setting is only 1280 x 720 windowed. This means that the game was not even close to being full screen for me when I first started the game. When I decide which games, I am going to stream I usually choose them based upon the default settings. Games that are windowed and don’t take advantage of full-screen functionality are the first that I decide against streaming.  However, the default options can be changed through the options menu and you can select the 1920x1080 as an option. It should be the default.
Even still, this is more of a personal gripe than it is a reason for purchasing the game. And it doesn’t give an actual account of the game’s actual presentation. The truth is I’m a fan of the overall presentation of the game. The retro graphics are a wise decision for the game’s genre and theme. The sound is also quite fitting and much more than suitable.
I quite enjoy how the story is presented to the player as well. Although the term ‘cutscene’ inspires fear into players I quite enjoyed the periodical cutscenes. They appear at somewhat regular intervals throughout the game and keep the game flowing. Instead of just being a dull and meaningless game. This provides Trigger Time a positive point of difference between it and many other similarly priced genre games. I’m glad that the story brings the game to life because it creates much more of an experience.
The overall problem that I can identify with the game is that it isn’t entirely unique. There are many other games like it on the market – both that are inferior and superior to it. I often look for games that are unique unto themselves even if they’re aligned centrally to a given genre like this one is.
As much as I enjoy the mechanics and the games’ features I don’t think that there is anything here that I haven’t experienced before. There are things Trigger Time does better than other titles, including some selling at much greater costs, but there’s nothing here that I haven’t seen before.
This means that as much as the content hasn’t been repeated that there are times where the player will feel a sense of déjà vu. This isn’t a bad thing If you’re a genre addict but for those seeking entirely fresh experiences may not have a reason to purchase the game.
Unfortunately, another reason holding Trigger Time back from becoming a popular title among the Steam faithful is its lack of Steam Trading Cards. With the announced changes to games being admitted into the Steam trading card program indie games such as Trigger Time may be the games to pay the biggest price.
Now before I explain my reasoning, don’t get me wrong. I understand that there were many shady developers out there that abused the system. All you had to do to earn a quick buck from Steam’s trading card program was to release an asset flip or worse and add trading cards. You could give out plenty of keys to bots who would farm the cards and put them onto the Steam marketplace. Those developers would earn more money from the marketplace than they did their abomination of games. It’s good that they’re gone.
However, with the limitations put into place, some developers such as Shephf Games who would stand to benefit by this feature may be losing out on key sales. There is a portion of the Steam player base who will purchase a reasonably inexpensive game for the cards. They’d play the hell out of the game but understand that they would be getting a slight discount on the game as they’d quickly sell the cards away.
It is my hope that devs who do make good games that have clearly had a lot of time and effort put into their creation are able to benefit from the full array of Steam’s features. It would feel like a defeat of the system if 90+% of the game’s sales were through bundling. The reality is devs get about 10 cents per copy that way. Great for the player and great for the bundle sites but not so great for the developer looking to make enough to not have to worry about where they’ll get the money for their next game.
Trigger Time does, however, come packaged with Steam achievements and utilizes the Steam cloud. These are two handy features that help raise the value of the game in the eyes of Steam players.
Trigger Time is among the first indie releases that will suffer from the inability to add trading cards until it proves itself as a worthy seller on Steam. As such it should be treated as a test case by Valve. What we have here is a game that is very much worthy of purchase and the time it takes to play through the game. The game doesn’t do many things wrong not compared to the forces working against it. However, at just $4.99 I can recommend that action fans pick the game up.
Rating: 7/10
