After 9 Hours I feel that I am ready to write this review.
DiRT 4 is Not DiRT rally. It is it's own game. The handling model in simulation is what you make of it. You can complain with the horde or you can take notice of the weighted feeling of the vehicles and the much better tire model. The cars still fight and complain with you as they did in DiRT rally. The main differences that I have noticed are the snap oversteer is not as harsh anymore and even with ABS off now it feels like the brakes are softer and a little more forgiving.
Career, no it is not real rally stages and that is fine. The build your own racing team concept is actually pretty neat. Expanding your facilities to be able to house more staff, vehicles and such. It keeps the playability of the game high. This career only holds your hand to an extent, it is up to the player to do more with the career. The game does not force you as you can drive for other 'teams'. Purchasing and upgrading cars is well built for a game with limited cars. The Dealership offers you new vehicles of modern day cars, and classifieds constantly have inventory shift with the older rally cars. (Keeps you on the look out for some of the more rare vehicles).
Since I am only 9 hours in I have devoted no time to the multiplayer. I may come back and edit this review at a later time with more information. I will say though that DiRT 4 still has the community challenges. Time attack still done the same way as in DiRT Rally.
My Verdict: If you love offroad racing this game is a must have. Beatiful to look at, and always keeping you on your toes. If you are a hardcore simulation fan like myself, don't miss out on this game. Yeah the horde will disagree, but Codemasters has really put a different type of game together with their most immersive career in DiRT history.

What I loved about Dirt Rally did not seem to make it over to Dirt 4. Car handling feels off, this in turns makes the new tracks feel even more claustrophobic (using a G27, sim handing and zero assists), Dirt Rally might not have been perfect physics wise but it felt like you were driving the car with any errors resting solely on your inputs, not vice versa.
*edit #1*
People are spamming a youtube link where the chief game designer behind Dirt Rally/4 goes into more detail on the changes and how they improved on Dirt Rally. But the giant asterik that people spamming this link (as some sort of justification for the changes) conveniently are leaving out is the fact he states that most of the feedback from real drivers was done for rallycross with only a bit of time on modern cars, leaving a giant gap of all the stuff in between just kinda existing. He closes in admitting they need to go over them but only if that means they will be done properly with validation by drivers who have actually driven them.
Career system overall is meh, all the extra stuff they added is pretty neat but within 10 hours  I have completed basically the majority of the rally and landrush on the hardest difficulty available. I consider myself a barely average sim racer at best but there is a problem when stage times I deem as below subpar are only 10 seconds off of a fast driver such as Porkhammer on the global leaderboards.
*edit #2*
-The update they pushed a day or two after release did some wonky stuff to the AI, they are now running times faster then what you see at the top of the global leaderboard (basically impossible to beat) and are over aggressive in rallycross/landrush, which is no beuno seeing as your vehicle will take alot of damage from this.
-The "your stage" gimmick is just that, a gimmick. The more you play the more you start reconizing corners over and over again.
-Co driver calls never seem to be on time (no matter how much you tweak it) or correct (the amount of times a 4/5 turn ends up being alot tighter or a 2/3 being more open leaves you feeling frustrated as all hell).
-Basically all of the default setups for the rally cars are bad, codemasters deem them as neutral so that everyone should be able to feel comfortable driving them and I am not entirely sure how they figure they did that. Rallycross was atleast decent, landrush needed minor tweaking.
I will continue to play the game with hopes that something comes down the pipeline from codemasters to remedy some of the handling quirks. At minimum Steam workshop for setup sharing needs to be implemented ASAP.
In closing, if you are new to the series most of the gripes should not bother you from enjoying it. I personally would have refunded it had I not gotten it for 30 bucks.

One of my most favourite tower defense games. It is in the puzzle genre within tower defense (as in you cannot place towers everywhere so you have to make good decisions and tactics are important). Difficulty is well balanced and its easy to get into. There are only some moments where the curve increases a bit but you can always ask for help at the forums (helpfull community and the dev too).
There are plenty of towers and lots of variety between them (for example there are towers that spawn marines which can actually stop enemies or e.g. have abilities like laying mines). There are plenty of maps (~35). Maps are not too long so it doesn't get boring. The enemies are also varied.
And finally you get 'star' points after winning a level which you can use for upgrades which give you a passive bonus on each map or give you an active ability.
I would give it a 9. Could be improved with even more maps :).

I'm a huge TD fan. I've played hundreds of hours in many games (gemcraft, defense grid, orcs must die, sanctum, Deathtrap, Kingdom Rush, dungeon defenders, etc) and always looking for a fun game.
I replay TD games tirelessly, trying new strategies, as a timewaster, what have you, but I put in serious hours into TD.
If you've played Gemcraft, my best analogy is that ARM is like the vision fields - where you essentially need to youtube the solution 1/2 the time. Limited number of ways to do the level and I really don't have the patience to try every single combination to try & find the magical solution - on the 3rd map no less.

You are trying to find a new planet for your civilization to survive and so you have found your way onto Planet X. There's one small problem, there seems to be robotic inhabitants that keep attacking you at every turn as you try to carve out a place to live, and of course build defenses to protect those who came with you.
I'm not going to lie, you're playing as the "asshats" in Alien Robot Monsters. You land on this planet get attacked and then you retaliate, that makes total sense, but then to go on the offensive and decide that you are going to commit basically genocide seems a bit rough.
Now of course we are talking about a fictitious world, and of course this is just a scenario to help you into the story of a tower defense game. In this game you will be unlocking upgrades to your towers, as well as upgrades to units that you'll be able to utilize later in the game. You are given specific locations where you will be able to place your towers, so even if you have extra scrap metal (that's the currency) that you could use to purchase a tower, once all the spots are filled you are going to have to either blow up an existing tower, or just work with what you have.
This game is quite challenging and you will definitely have to pay attention to what is coming at you down the predetermined paths. I will say that there is definitely a balance needed between what type of towers you have out there as well as the order in which you upgrade them. You're going to get a basic tower with two gunmen to start off but as you progress deeper into the game you're going to be able to change that tower into many different types of towers, some of them will have units that you'll be able to place outside of the tower to try to take on the enemies as they come. There will also be towers that will shock your enemies, literally, and though expensive, a very good addition to have on the maps to help you through some of the tougher spots.
One of the things I do like is the fact that there is a little bit of customization that is done between levels. You can decide how you use your victory stars. For each level you will get 1 to 3 for successfully getting through the level. Now of course you're going to want to have every level give you 3 stars, but lets be honest there are sometimes when you just misjudge the enemy and a couple slip through, ruining your perfect run on that level. Have no fear though you can gain those missing stars with a replay.
Anyways you will use the stars to upgrade damage by weapons, unit health, more scraps collected per kill, etc. I personally like to at least get the base level of each upgrade but there's definitely reason to try to max out one upgrade before giving the rest some attention, its all in the way you play, and I think for this reason it definitely caters to the player.
The graphics aren't going to blow you away, but the overall flow and design that you are presented with looks great. I do enjoy the fact that there are enemies of all shapes and sizes and that each out is truly different, be it in speed, attack, or durability. There's also bosses that you need to be concerned with, if you survive specific levels you will find, after the final wave, that there's one more monster that wants to destroy you, get through that and you're well on your way to victory.
This game can be your's right now on Steam, and if you are a tower defense type of person, this is something that you're going to want to add to your collection. So with that being said I'm going to give this game an 8.7 out of 10.

Some of my favorite gameplay changes:
— 90 FOV, finally!
— A completely reworked spawn system. It combines the best elements from spawn mechanics of Ostfront and RO2. You can select a spawn point by just clicking on it on the map screen. And this applies to MDVs: half-tracks show up on the map as spawn points.
— You can select the tank you want to ride from the list and spawn right in it. You don’t have to rush to the tank as soon as you spawn and then deal with a crew of random players who made it to this particular vehicle first. No more waiting for tanks to appear or for the annoying “Waiting for additional crew members” message to disappear. But you can still spawn as a crewman on foot and join someone else’s crew.
— Reworked stamina system and gunplay. You can sprint for longer, but changing stance drains your stamina. So doing the “whack-a-mole” thing by popping out of cover for a quick shot and immediately ducking again will tire you out. Dolphin diving — even more so. And it’s much harder to shoot when you’re out of breath: your weapon starts to sway.
— All vehicles now have rider positions.
— Improved hitbox detection on exposed operators of vehicles. E.g. I think you can now shoot everyone riding in a half-track as long as you can get an angle.
— Ammunition is now included in weapon drops, instead of being in a separate pouch. A downgrade in terms of realism, but these were really tricky to pick up.
— Wire-cutters and barbed wire that actually stops infantry, just like in Carpathian Crosses.
— You can drop and pick up binoculars.
— Windows users now run a modified RedOrchestra.exe that is “large address aware”; this eliminates crashes to desktop caused by the engine running out of memory.
And in general, the game looks and feels a lot more polished now. There’s a gazillion of little fixes and visual improvements. I can only hope that someone will update some of the old custom maps to be compatible with the new patch. And the Darkest Orchestra mod.

Ylands is a game made by the incredible Bohemia Interactive development team in 2018. It is like Minecraft had a baby with Totally Accurate Battle Simulator. It is a low-poly style game which looks incredible and I will go into graphics and optimisation later. Ylands is a First/third-person survival game with a lot of possibilities available to the player such as driving, wild-west action, temples with puzzles, sailing mechanics, crafting and cave exploration!
- It has a lot of gameplay packed for players and can keep players busy for hours, once they get a boat. The main aim of the game is to get enough equipment to escape the tiny island and go to hundreds of procedurally generated island. The game is not over yet. You can unlock new blueprints and create new items! Build houses! There is a lot of gameplay to keep you busy for hours and I personally find it very enjoyable. Being able to let your mind create whatever it desires makes the game special. The only reason why i don't play it is because of performance.
- At the time of this review, the graphics are beautiful but it is horrendously unoptimised. It does not run on my computer unlike AAA games (Arma 3) at anymore than 40 fps on 720p, although my monitor is 1080p. It is a bit of a pain but I am sure Bohemia will fix it by the end of Early Access the very latest. Ylands is an incredibly awesome game in my opinion and I highly recommend it. I recommend it to those who only have really powerful processors such as an intel i7 and possibly if you have a GTX 1060+ graphics card. I have less specs than those and can run it at 40 fps with stutters every now and then, which really frustrates me.
- The graphic style is well designed and pretty and reminds me a lot of other poly games such as T.A.B.S. It looks like a lot of detail has gone in but unfortunately, it is lacking some options of the graphics menu. You have no ability to disable shadows, only turn down the quality (which is hardly any different to highest shadow settings).
In conclusion, Ylands is an extremely fun game with a few flaws but I recommend it still. My vote is just over 50% of Yes therefore this game will be uprated. Hopefully Bohemia listen to my feedback and some will be acted on.

I'm mainly writing this review for the purpose of keeping people from reading the inaccurate and/or untruthful negative reviews left on this page either for immature spite, lack of information or to troll. This review is coming from someone who has followed the game since it was announced and read every design notes post.
PSA: This game has been in development for a fraction of the time other MMOs had been in. You're not going to get bug free, flawless gameplay and an amazingly integrated options menu so soon when such a small dev team is working on SO much.
Furthermore rest assured most problems with the game will probably be addressed before the game's full release which they've said is aimed for Summer 2017. (That's a LONG time to add it a LOT of features, content and fixes the game needs at this stage.
This is a Beta Test, not a demo like what most games' "beta tests" really are.
Not entirely sure why every person and their mother screams pay to win as soon as they see the dollar sign in a free to play game. In no way is this or will it ever be pay to win as the team firmly believes in earning over buying.
TL;DR I know as much as possible about the game at the time of writing this. (Open Beta release day) Now with all my banter out of the way, here are the classic pros and cons I could think of off the top of my head.
Pros:
- This game is FREE
- Runs smoooth: I own a toaster of a PC and run the game no problem.
- If you've played any previous AdventureQuest game, there is a lot of nostalgia to be had here.
- Characters and monsters are colourful, unique and interesting.
- From reading the design notes, you can tell the small dev. team is really trying to be innovative with many aspects of the game.
- The Dev. team is the friendliest you'll find in the industry. They're gamers, they know the good and the bad of MMOs.
-When they aren't having meetings on how to improve the game based on the criticism they receive, some of them can be found on Twitter where questions can be asked occasionally. They're a very vocal team. (One of their animators actually streams while animating occasionally)
- It's not Pay2Win. Currently the only class with a self heal is the paid Guardian class but as this is beta, that is subject to change soon. There are a handful of paid SHORTCUTS to get weaker gear faster but the best gear is free.
- If you have a problem with the game, save for a few things, they will most likely be solved by the time the game leaves Beta.
- The Grind: This game is going to be a great time-sink if that's what you're looking for.
- The dev team promises a story you'll actually remember which is rare for an MMO.
- Cross Platform: Many would call this a con and I'd say it's both a pro and a con. I've played the game on my tablet and it runs smooth as can be. If I were away from home and had the time, I love that I can login from a mobile device to do something quick and get off.
- VERY small download: This is because the game doesn't download map assets etc to your system until you have visited that area for the first time. This keeps the game from becoming too big for things such as mobile devices which have low storage typically. (Read more about that on the design notes)
- While classes only have 4 skills, the amount of classes that will be in the game for you to switch and swap through on a single character will probably make up for that.
- Rest assured this game will not go down the path of games such as TERA or Black Desert. They've got good heads on their shoulders and while they are a business, they aren't money-starved beasts.
- Artix Entertainment has been building successful games for longer than most companies that release MMOs. They know how to make a good game, they know what players want in their games and they're willing to put everything into making that happen. A lot of them are previous players of these games and love the classics like AdventureQuest as much as anyone else.
Cons: (Keep in mind this is the release day of Open Beta, not an accurate representation of the full game)
- Character customization (for now) is nothing special. If you've played their previous games, it's the same here.
- Classes only have 4 skills. If you're looking for a crazy in-depth class system like TERA, this is not the game. Though I must add Artix has stated on multiple occasions one of their goals is something like a skill tree for each class.
- The Grind: This could be a pro if you play MMOs for the grind like my significant other. As of right now, playing through the areas consists of fairly grindy quests that don't exactly make a lot of sense. I expect this to change by release for progression reasons.
- Communication: A lot of criticisms thus far (Combat system, class skills etc.) have been coming from a lack of information. This is not entirely the consumers fault, rather the team doesn't do the greatest of jobs putting everything you need to know as a potential player / supporter of their product in an easy to find place for everyone to see.
- The options menu for now is not ideal. Keybinding and interface keys are on their to-do list as well as expanded resolutions and more options in general.
- For now, cutscenes are still in development (like everything else) and aren't too in-depth or anything yet.
- The best content at the moment  (The dungeons) are only beatable after you play through the grindy areas to level up your character. That's to be expected but if you're just trying to experience the best part of the game right now, you're gonna have to put a couple hours into it.
- Dungeons need a lot of work. Some are too easy and sometimes you don't get the drops you need for the craft item you want.
- Currently players kiting is a problem in the later areas of the game, it gets frustrating.
- Cross Platform: Obviously as a game that is also on mobile, the mobile aspect of the game definitely limits some aspects of the game.
- The UI leaves a lot to be desired at this stage. I expect it to improve by release but so far it's nothing special.
- Graphics, animations etc. aren't the best in the industry because of cross platform but when push comes to shove, the game looks great while also running great - as opposed to something like TERA which looks phenomenal but runs poorly even on top end PCs.
- Like all games with proper Beta stages, you will see many bugs and probably see the game break right before your eyes. This is beta, it is to be expected.
- Gameplay can get fairly repetitive but really, that's something that can be said about the majority of games.
I've listed additional concerns I have discovered through playing through the game which I have put here if you are interested:
TL;DR: This game holds a lot of promise and if you have a problem with the game right now, it will probably be solved in the future. These devs want to see this game go as far as Artix's imagination can go without it being something like No Man's Lie.
-Will there be many classes? Yes, many many many classes.
-Will there be a combat system with more depth? Yes, that is very much planned.
-Is this game Pay to Win? No not in anyway shape or form and that's just that.
-Will this game take up a lot of space on my device? Heavens no, in fact their system of self cleaning to save storage space is genius .
-Are the puns, jokes, references and 4th wall breaks in the tutorial a bit cringe? Yeah absolutely but it's just a test, it won't stay that way and trust that with a T ESRB rating, you'll be getting more mature stories later on.
Hope this review helped someone and if you have any questions concerning this game I can probably answer them so find me on my twitter (in my bio) or comment on this review.
And hey, if you want this game to succeed, consider dropping $20 and supporting them, I can't wait to see how far this game goes.

Step 1
Cook the peas in boiling salted water for 3–5 minutes until they are really tender, then drain and tip into a food processor. Add the mascarpone, olive oil and seasoning and whiz to a rough paste. Transfer to a bowl and set aside.
Step 2
Preheat a griddle or grill until hot. Toast the ciabatta slices for about 2 minutes on each side, then drizzle with a little olive oil.
Step 3
Spread the crushed peas on the toasted ciabatta slices. Roughly tear the mozzarella balls in half and place on top. Sprinkle with the pecorino and drizzle with a little more olive oil. Grind over a little more seasoning and serve immediately.

Rating:
Graphics: 4.2/10
Audio: 4.4/10
Gameplay: 3.1/10
Overall: 3.9/10

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
Captain Lycop: Invasion of the Héters is a 2D twin-stick shooter space adventure. It's one of those games that are in the same vein as the old-school "Asteroids" title. The player takes control of Captain Lycop, who pilots a battleship and carries out missions for the greater good. Most of these missions involve taking out other battleships in a bullet hell-y style combat system. The game was developed by French indie studio; Aéronie, and it seems to be their first title on Steam.
--------
Although the graphics look dated, they also seem to be intended that way. The style choice invokes nostalgic memories of older similar games, and even the cut scenes that include rough shapes and polygons are reminiscent of older space titles. Specifically from the early Nintendo and PlayStation era. That being said, the the character design lacks more detail than it should, the faces are basically pixels thrown together, though they aren't seen often enough to consider it a major issue. The animation quality and particle effects are very standard, but they get the job done. These aspects are important in games such as these due to dodging, and differentiating attack types. The game offers a few different locations to explore, though the terrain does not change that much graphically. The game is not demanding at all and can run perfectly fine on any low to mid-tier set up.
--------

The game's soundtrack is actually quite decent. The music will often match the situation within the game, and during combat. There are a few tracks that will play consistently throughout stages and may not stick out during moments of intense concentration or battle. Other than the soundtrack, the rest of the sound assets throughout the game are very generic space themed noises, which is fine as it fits in with the game's motif.
--------

The game-play is very solid. The player pilots a ship through various stages trying to defeat enemies as well as manoeuvring around any environmental obstacles in the way. When the ship's hit points reach zero, it will explode and the player will have to restart from a previous checkpoint. The battles are difficult and are meant to be so.
There are a few abilities that the game will provide in order to assist with battling enemies. Players can fit their ships with different weapons that can be crafted with accumulated scrap metal. This metal can be obtained from destroying enemy vessels or terrain. There is a skill tree system which allows the player to research certain upgrades and technologies. This can give the player various upgrades to their ship, as well as new weaponry.
The player is also given a few default skills that can aid them in combat. There is a speed boost key that allows the ships to move more quickly and an ability that even fire weapons a little faster. The shield regeneration ability is also available for use in situations where the ship's shield is down or has taken heavy damage.
--------
The game is incredibly difficult. I spent about 20 minutes on the first stage alone, which is more like the tutorial. I know the game can be played with a game-pad though I found the controls to be a little difficult to grasp. I encountered the same issue with the keyboard and mouse controls, though eventually I was able to get used to them.
I do feel that the game lacks a save feature, as it only saves your game after hitting certain checkpoints, which are pretty spread apart. Though I guess that also adds to the challenge of the game (albeit making things a bit repetitive). [There has been a new difficulty mode added since this review was drafted, adding more frequent checkpoints].
I understand this game is supposed to be difficult, and targets an audience that enjoys that kind of difficulty. So although this game wasn't something that I personally enjoy, I can see how others might. I

Contagion isn't a bad game. It has a fantastic concept and it could be loads of fun to play with friends. Frankly, I wish there was a middle-of-the-road option, because I don't want to not recommend this game. But when it comes down to it, I'm going to have to say to pass. The main problem I've found is a lack of a tutorial of any sort. You're thrown into the game, and you better hope you remember what all of the controls are. The punishment for dying is also a little harsh. If you die in a server with player zombies enabled, you might spawn in a location that you can't get out of. Thus, you're stuck there until a player makes it there. And zombie mode just isn't fun. And if player zombies are turned off, you play as a supersonic cockroach after dying.
I'm not one to jump in and play in a random server, so I'm not complaining about the lack of community. Setting up a private server is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥though, mainly due to the fact that I have crappy internet and I would rather not pay to host a server for a game my friends and I might play once a month. That isn't the dev's fault, but just something that I'm not too big of a fan of.
Pros-
Gameplay Concept: Contagion's concept is great. It's actually not a bad game, but needs some serious polishing.
Guns: The guns in this game are great. I like the accuracy and sometimes the lack thereof. I also love the fact that you have to manually reload.
Variety of modes: Contagion has a lot of maps and modes, and that's always a good thing.
Cons-
Controls: The controls can sometimes be a bit wonky, and there are so many features that you have to remember a crapton of inputs. There's a steep learning curve for controls.
Death punishment: As I mentioned above, the punishment for death is far too harsh where it's quite easy for a zombie to kill you.
Melee combat: Close-quarters combat in this game sucks. It is just kiting back and forth, hoping you hit with it. It's not that hard to hit something with a wrench. You don't need to wind up every time.
All-in-all, I'd give the game a 6/10. It could definitely use some tweaking, and once that is done, I think the game would be fantastic and I would gladly change my review to "recommended."

Video review:
Japanese folklore has been an interest of mine for years now, so I was quite excited to try out Hyakki Castle, a tile-based dungeon crawler built around this folklore. The game actually does a good job at it as well, with the setting being the game’s greatest strength. However, this comes at a cost.
Hyakki castle does a great job of building a world around Japanese folklore. All of the enemies fit within this setting, from snake-human hybrids (known as nure-onna in Japan) to demonic fire wheels (known as wanyudo), every enemy in the game is representative of some aspect of Japanese folklore. The entire game takes place in an oddly constructed castle with several distinct areas, from the basement all the way up to the castle tower, a few boss rooms scattered in-between. The castle setting is very fitting for the types of enemies found throughout, with the colors and lighting often being darker, to elicit even a little bit of fear from the player. There were even a few times where I jumped from a yokai suddenly appearing before me (like when a wall suddenly grows an eyeball with a loud audio cue). It was quite a bit of fun exploring this setting and finding new enemies.
The leveling in this game is super quick, about once every 10-15 minutes. Leveling restores HP, MP, and hunger, so the super fast leveling is great. Each level adds a skill point to be used in each character’s skill tree, which is different depending on the class picked at the start. I went with three samurai and one miko (basically a priest, the one casting all the spells) and had each of the samurai go down a different path in the skill tree, with the miko focusing on healing magic. Due to the quick leveling, I never had to grind to unlock anything and was able to progress through the game without worrying about being underleveled.
Hyakki Castle’s most defining feature is the player’s ability to split their party in two, exploring the map as two parties, split-screen style. The mechanic itself is great and I cannot name another dungeon crawler that does this off the top of my head, but this game simply did not utilize this mechanic to its fullest. In fact, I rarely split my party as it made the game incredibly difficult, contrary to what the mechanic is supposed to do. Ideally, the split party would be on two sides of an enemy, the front and the back, as hitting the back of an enemy deals more damage compared to the front. Unfortunately, it is simply too difficult to manage the two parties, as one would have to constantly be dodging and the other would have to constantly be attacking. It also does not help that just about half of the attacks in the game can wipe the party in a single hit on normal difficulty. As such, dodging is a necessity.
I ended up never using the mechanic for combat and only using it when certain puzzles required it (like having to stand on two pressure plates simultaneously to open a gate). In most scenarios, it was even impossible to get behind the enemy, as they would be blocking a passage that is only a single tile wide, not allowing room for players to sneak around them. The whole splitting mechanic is completely useless when it comes to combat, but it did at least allow for some interesting puzzles.
Every time one enters a new floor, there is a designated save tile that allows the player to regen HP, MP, and save the game. Unfortunately, this is only at the beginning of each floor, so if one wants to save after exploring a floor for twenty minutes, he/she will have to either run all the way back to save or attempt to find the next floor. The problem here being that enemies often one-shot the entire party, forcing the player to continue from the last point he/she saved. This requires constant saving on the player’s part, running back to the save point several times while exploring the floor. Of course one could avoid doing so by simply dodging every attack and never getting hit, but that is incredibly difficult in itself. If save tiles could be offered maybe two or three times per floor, even without the HP/MP regen, a lot of time spent backtracking could be saved.
After a certain amount of inactivity (as in, not attacking or using any abilities), the character HUD is hidden. The player can keep moving, but the HUD would stay hidden. This was incredibly annoying, as I would often find myself in scenarios where I need to quickly be able to cast abilities or attack an enemy in front of me, but the HUD does not even show up when an enemy is right in front of the player until the screen is left clicked. Even when exploring, I want to be able to see the health and hunger levels of each of my party members, but having the HUD hide itself so often did not allow me to do so. I would usually end up just pressing tab to open the inventory, then immediately closing it to refresh the HUD whenever it hid itself. I fail to understand why the HUD even needs to be hidden in the first place. If a player wants the HUD to be hidden automatically, at least make it configurable.
It is 2017 and there are still games coming out that are locked at subpar resolutions. Hyakki Castle is locked at 720p, which is then stretched when played in fullscreen. The game looks decent enough, but it would be so much better if higher resolutions were supported. A 720p PC game in 2017 is just not acceptable anymore.
Hyakki Castle looks and plays great, but simply has too many issues to recommend to a general audience. What the game achieves in its setting design and leveling system comes at the cost of a half-baked “party splitting” feature, a frustrating save system, and a 720p resolution lock. If you are a hardcore fan of dungeon crawlers, then I would suggest giving it a try, but for the general audience I would suggest staying away.
Full review (including score):

It's too easy to say this is just Legend of Grimrock in a Japanese setting. While the two share a lot with each other at a core level, it's the tweaks Hyakki Castle makes on the formula that helps it stand apart from its peers. This effort to be more than its pack works both in, and against,
favor.
The standout feature is the two-party system the game desperately wants you to use, but you probably won't unless you have to. When faced with a puzzle or challenging foe, the player can break their party up into two teams of two or one team of three and a lone wolf who doesn't play by anyone's rules but his own. However, enemies hit very hard in this game, so your best, and very much necessary, means of damage mitigation is physically sidestepping your opponent's attacks. This can be hard to keep track of with two teams, at least far more than if you are just operating with the one.
There is a dissonance between the intended experience of the two-party system and its reality. Most players will lean more heavily on keeping their team together simply because it eases some of the tension, especially when dealing with more than just one monster. Puzzles make use of the mechanic, but by doing nothing more than having one group stand on a pressure plate while the other goes in search for the other.
The save system and the hunger systems are two aspects of the game that need major work. Saves can only be made at the entrance to every floor, requiring the player to back track through the dungeon if they want to save after an arduous battle. This backtracking is punished by the hunger system, however. With every step and action, the characters become hungrier and hungrier, until they become famished, causing their stats to suffer signifigantly. There's simply not nearly enough food on a floor to keep everyone from reaching the starving threshold.
Visually the game is remarkable, fully utilizing the monsters of Japanese myth and folklore with its smooth graphical fidelity. Though the game is darkly lit, it's still easy to appreciate the designs of the demons and ghouls that lurk the halls of Hyakki Castle. Despite its crushing difficulty and lack of polish in some areas, Hyakki Castle kept me invested almost solely so I could see more of the monster designs.
The average player will find 12-15 hours of playtime in
, which isn't too bad given the price and the game's overall quality. Still, this is a niche entry into an already nich subgrene of first-person dungeon crawlers. If you really enjoyed
then you should give this title a preview, at least.
+ Excellent visuals and monster designs.
+ Classic first-person dungeon crawling experience.
- Save system and hunger mechanic are devestatingly punishing, dissauding players from exploring.
- Two-party system is inherently flawed in a game where physically side-stepping is preferred over tanking hits.

So here's the thing, I want to love this game. It's a japanese themed dungeon crawler. However, its interface and UX design is terrible. Tons of really annoying things add up, like you press escape and cycle through to your map, then press escape to close it but that doesn't work. You have to manually click the X to get it to close.
It has a party splitting mechanic that seems like a novel idea, but you have to create your own hotkeys for it because who knows what Alpha 1, Alpha 2, and Alpha 3 buttons are on the key board? Also so far in the game all its used for is to push multiple floor panels at once. I'd rather throw an old school rock or drop a weight because it's less of an inconvenience.
Some of the sound effects are REALLY loud.
Some times the keys are unresponsive by design. You try to dodge an attack but the animation has already started so you gotta sit there.
Timed puzzles, at least the one I encountered, are one shot. There are signs everyone explaining the obvious but this one said that if I hurry I get a great prize. I knew exactly where to go when I pulled the lever but there were no sound effects to give you feedback that something was happening, like how every other game handles it, so I hesitated a bit. I ran over to the spot, gate was closed, ran back to the switch to try again, nope. That was my shot.
Also there are save spots points... why... I'm just knit picky on that point, they can do save points by design. All that UX stuff is pretty inexcusable though.
So why do I recommend it? Because underneath all the annoying stuff is still a fairly solid seeming japanese based dungeon crawler and I REALLY REALLY hope the dev actually plays their own game and fixes all the poor interface decisions they made. Who knows though.

This is one of the easiest recommendations I'll have to give. Alien Robot Monsters (ARM) is a really addictive tower defence game.
The goal of each mission is simple. Your base is invaded by swarms of enemy robots and you must fend them off by strategically placing various military towers and tech buildings in the area. The enemies come in a variety of shapes and sizes, as you'd expect from any tower defence game, each having their own strengths and weaknesses. Likewise, each of your buildings is made to deal with a certain enemy type better than with others. Getting overrun by hordes of weak enemies? Get yourself some mortar towers. Having trouble with armoured tanks? Build an orbital laser. And so on.
After completing each mission, you get a rating out of 3 stars. If none of the enemies got through your defences, you get full 3 stars. If some went through, you get 1 or 2 stars. If too many get through, you lose the mission. The stars are not just there for you to feel proud, either. They're used as skill points to purchase upgrades to your buildings. Hence there's a lot of incentive to do well on each mission and even a chance to replay the harder missions later in order to get a better rating on those.
Normally there's no way of knowing what sort of enemies to expect in each mission, so the latter missions often require a bit of trial and error and can be quite hard. Regardless, I'm having a blast with the game. Fun gameplay and a great presentation. What more could you want?
If you've ever remotely enjoyed any tower defence games, give this one a try. It's really cheap and affordable despite its high quality.

Hi, this is a simple game review.
So, let's talk about Zup!, and why I can't recommend it to others, despite its very low price.  First, let's get the positives out of the way:
-Wonderful, soothing music
-Simple, yet good graphics
-Interesting physics puzzles
-Easy achievements
All of this comes together to create what should be a nice, simple puzzle game.  After all, what's not to like here?  Well, in the end, it all comes down to the gameplay, and that is where Zup! just doesn't succeed.  This is primarily because simple and interesting doesn't necessarily mean good, and while I could see Zup's game mechanics possibly working, it doesn't work here, and it's all because of one thing: I'm just guessing.  Nothing about Zup! felt rewarding, and in something like a puzzle game, it's incredibly important that I feel accomplished after beating a tough level.  If you didn't see the trailer, Zup! bases its game mechanics around blowing up red blocks to propel your tiny blue square into a green zone, allowing you to advance.  However, I never felt as if I used logic or reasoning to solve the puzzles in the game; I just clicked red squares until I got something that worked.  After beating a game, you should feel like you were better at the game than when you started, and I can't say I improved at the game whatsoever from the first level to the last level.  Tack on the fact that I could complete this game in just 17 minutes, and you have an unrewarding game that you can complete in little to no time, the likes of which I cannot recommend.
FINAL SCORE: 4/10

I'm blown away by how poorly this game is being recieved by gamers on steam. I've been playing these DiRT games since DiRT 2 and have loved this series for being more accessible and fun than other games like Gran Turismo and was disappointed with the departure that was DiRT 3 and DiRT Rally. DiRT 3 had too much emphasis on doing stunts and incredibly difficult "Drifting" challenges along with a ton of events locked behind DLC pay walls that ruined the experience. And DiRT Rally was TOO realistic for my taste, with incredibly difficult handling and graphics that seemed reduced compared to DiRT 3 and even DiRT 2.
But DiRT 4 feels great. It performs excellent on my computer configuration with all graphics completely maxed out and zero compatibility issues with my XboxOne elite controller. The tutorials were very easy to follow and explained things about Rally racing that I never knew about before when playing the older DiRT games. The first event was challenging and the randomized track generator works great to help provide a different experience everytime to fans of Rally racing and best of all, this game features Trailblazer and Rallycross, two of my favorite events in this franchise.
I can understand racing fans beind disappointed with this game focusing on a more casual audience, but that's not necessarily the fault of DiRT 4 or Codemasters. The developers clearly made DiRT Rally specifically tailored towards a more hardcore audience and came back this year with a much more casual and accessible experience that I personally am enjoying. The graphics look much better than DiRT 3 (Despite what you'll read here in the reviews which is just ridiculous) but they don't look as good as games like Driveclub or Project cars so don't get too excited.
Overall I definitely recommend this to fans of the main series (DiRT 1, DiRT 2, DiRT 3) and just pay close attention to the features and videos that are CLEARLY LABELED on the store page before you purchase games...

Many were afraid this would be a sequel of DiRT3 but in fact it's an upgrade over DiRT Rally with the capability to offer casual gamers the arcadey side of rally while at the same time allowing the DiRT Rally fans to keep in the Simulation mode with improvements over DiRT Rally's physics.
This is definitely a fantastic game and worth the money and will surely consume lots of hours.
However, this game will sooner or later face the same problem that DiRT Rally did: lack of content. Only the developers can prevent this from happening, by adding more rally locations and by adding a couple more important cars to the classes, for example: Peugeot 206, Citroen Xsara and the Toyota Corolla.
There are a few other cars, such as the WRC class but since the crappy WRC 7 devs got the license, we can't get the cars nor the official tracks and that sucks. Hopefully one day Codemasters will be able to get the FIA WRC license which will allow them to re-add the official tracks into the cocktail and some official cars. This will also allow them to make a WRC mode like they've done with the World RX championship module, separated from all the other modes.
Anyway, this game is perfect and its only lack is the rally content. This game really needs - and already has the bases to support it - all the rally locations of the WRC calendar, such as Monte Carlo, Finland, New Zealand, San Remo, Corsica, etc. The physics are awesome and  the graphics too.
Also, the new multiplayer mode "Pro Tour" which is like a Fifa Ultimate division/tier ranking system is great for the competition, which will have up to 8 rally drivers driving simultaneously in a track.
A big thank you and thumbs up to Codemasters and I hope you guys keep releasing DLC with paid content so that we can keep supporting the game as you keep adding more content.

A little more tame in presentation compared to the Monster-fueled Dirt2 era. A little closer to Dirt Rally or the original Dirt, or the F1 titles in presentation style.
No TrackIR support at launch is a disappointement, especially when its a feature that's been present in many Dirt games, it would be less of an issue if that was a new thing for Codemasters to support.
A little heavy on the team micro management side, although none of it (so far in my career) seems necessary at lower difficulty levels (if you just want to drive...)
The Rally tracks are more on the simulation side, much narrower than what you would be used to if you are coming from Dirt2 and 3, they are slightly more challenging and require more nuanced driving.
The 3D modeling and rendering of the cars is top notch, while the track/environment art remains largely the same, which is not a bad thing. It's all very sharp. However, even with visuals set to Ultra, there's a little lack of depth in some lighting situations, like overcast or noon lighting, where everything just looks un-lit and its hard to tell where to go (of course, ignoring copilot info). Some GI, increased shadow distance, post processing could help add depth to the environments in future iterations.
Overall I still recommend the game. My main gripe in this list is the lack of TrackIR support which I hope gets patched at some point. I would love to play the game in cockpit view, but without TrackIR, it becomes a huge hindrance, and I have to settle with using Hood or chase view. Being able to look freely, having the head disconnected from the car's axis, being able to look into turns as your car goes sideways, to me seems essential in a game like this.

Best survival-crafting game evar!
Let's get some stuff straight right away:
Microtransactions... They are ONLY VISUAL and the reason the devs put it in the game at early acces is to show players from the start that: yes there will be microtransactions and no they will not make you win.
Love or hate it (I freaking hate microtransactions!) it's there...
Bugs: well of cause! It's early access! Now I have tried losing everything and sure, it's a pain, but not all game engines run smooth from the start.
I do however have great confidence in the devs. They run a very active forum and sometimes seems to fix bugs within days of reporting them. Updates are frequent and they plan to release late summer 2018.
Now for the fun stuff:
This game is awesome! I loved minecraft and I have since played Ark, 7dtd, space engineers, stranded deep, subnautica and a lot of other lesser known survival-crafting games... This one beats them all!
At first glance Ylands looks like a crossbreed between stranded deep and 7 days to die. Very similar mechanics and goal.
But the difference is that Ylands' craftable items list goes on where the others stop. And Ylands does not hide the good stuff behind and endless grind og super rare mats. Not at the moment anyway.
Often its more a question of having the recipe and the right tool and workbench for the job. Some of the later workbenches does cost quite a lot of mats, but in my experience the mats are available, you just have to go fetch.
The moment you fall in love with Ylands is when you craft your first ship. And I mean ship, not a boat or a raft... Well that too, but you can build a genuine ship. And on that ship you can build your chests and your workshops so you can craft while sailing. Suddenly you are not moving stuff back to your base, but rather moving your base to the stuff. It is ekstremely satisfying sailing around exploring and looting.
Another feature that really shines is the ability to "free place" just about anything, letting you place objects or displayed items exactly where you want them.
And these are only some of the currently implemented features. This game is far from finished. I can't wait to see how even more awesome this will become!
If you like survival-crafting, you won't regret picking up this game.

I've played and beaten Sonic 2, 3 & Knuckles, CD, Adventure 1 & 2, Heroes, Shadow the Hedgehog, Sonic 2006, 4 Episode 1 & 2, the DS version of Colors, Generations (including the Unleashed levels mod), and nearly finished Lost World, and I have to say... Slowly eroding nostalgia and stockholm syndrome are the only things that keep me playing his 3D outings.
You probably already know whether or not you're going to buy Sonic Adventure 2 before you read a review of it. You most likely played it when you were younger, or are a fan of later Sonic games curious about his past. Reading this might not change your mind, but I can assure you of one thing: This game has not aged well. Sound familiar? Sonic Adventure 1 is the same way, and many of its mistakes apply to the sequel as well.
Sonic Adventure 2 once again tells the story of Dr. Eggman's attempts to rule the world, and Sonic the Hedgehog and co.'s attempts to stop him. This time he's got a plan that might actually work - He's stolen Dr. Evil's "laser" from Austin Powers: The Spy Who Shagged Me and is holding the world hostage. What for isn't made clear. It's not money. He wants power. But what he plans to do with it once he has it isn't really addressed. Helping him is Shadow the Hedgehog, a genetically engineered super hog created by Eggman's grandfather, and Rouge the Bat, a government spy/jewel theif who doesn't know the meaning of "conflict of interest". The good guys just follow them around trying to stop them. No dreams or ambitions of their own.
The overall story, when written in a few non-sarcastic sentences, I really like. Seeing that story unfold is like watching a Mystery Science Theater movie without the riffing. The acting is either bad, or passable by accident (my favorite scene is when Eggman hurts Sonic, and Tails lackadaisically says "I will never forgive you for this"). It's also localized poorly. Often it seems characters are saying whatever is in their mind at that moment rather than having a coherent conversation. There are many instances of odd wordings and sentence structure. The technical issues SA1 had in its cutscenes have been reduced ever so slightly, but many still remain. Lip synching is all over the place. Characters talk over each other, and sometimes, themselves. They make odd movements while talking to one another. It *is* better than SA1, but it's not what I'd call good.
The game is separated into Hero and Dark storylines. There's no overworld this time, just cutscenes and action stages. Each side has three characters who are basically clones of each other. Sonic and Shadow run through linear levels quickly, with lots of platforming and occasional puzzle solving. Eggman and Tails use mech suits with guns to shoot their way through too-complex platforming stages. Knuckles and Rouge search for Master Emerald shards (or other items) in non-linear levels that quickly become too large for their own good.
Sonic Team did seem to learn a few lessons from SA1. Sonic and Shadow's levels are laid out like racetracks. Minimal side paths and long straight stretches where you can run freely. These are easily the most fun levels to play. Camera issues are minimalized by not having lots of corners and objects in the way. But they added some new design issues. Both can do a Light Speed Dash to zip along a line of rings. It helps you get around, but it shares a button with both a somersault attack and the spin dash move. There will be many, MANY times where you'll go to spin dash and will instead be flung at some nearby rings, or try to use some rings to get over a gap and will instead somersault right over the edge. Sonic also has a bounce move that shares the same button, so a mistimed Light Speed Dash in the air means instant death. Technical issues with basic movement are still shared with SA1 as well, so slight variations in ground height or angle will cause energetic spasms in your character.
Tails and Eggman play much like E-102 Gamma did in SA1. They shoot their way through levels, using a targeting laser to mark enemies for destruction. For some reason I don't mind the sound much, but it does make a high pitched tone whenever you do this, which will be all the time. The level layouts themselves are more complex than the hogs', and this does not work in their favor. Sonic is supposed to be about going fast, and the mech suits Eggman and Tails inhabit move slow. The later levels often have closed gates that you have to locate the switches for before you can proceed, which makes them take even longer. Basic movement is still riddled with technical issues. Early on you gain the ability to extend your jumps by hovering, but lightly brushing up against a wall will cause you to plummet downwards instantly, causing many accidental deaths. Camera problems are also in full effect when in tight areas. The camera does not get stuck nearly as often as it used to in SA1, but it often manages to find just the wrong angle for the jump you're trying to make or the enemy you're trying to target. That said, it *IS* better than SA1's camera. It feels like they actually played the levels and tried to choose somewhat reasonable angles.
Knuckles and Rouge's levels are scavenger hunting affairs that mirror Knuck's levels from SA1. These are my least favorite levels to play because of one stupid design decision: the proximity detector that used to show any item of interest in range now only shows one at a time. It artificially inflates the time you spend wandering around, and I hate it. This doesn't matter much for the first few levels, since they are small. But both of their final levels take place in space, and are huge. If you haven't been playing these levels since you were 13 like I have, you can easy spend 45+ minutes in them, going in futile circles until you reset the level in the hopes of getting better item locations (like I did when I was 13). The level designs are often confusing. One of Knuckles' levels takes place in an underground mine and involves changing water levels to open paths to different mine shafts. The tight spaces are great for getting the camera blocked in bad angles. Rouge's final level takes place in space near planetoids that will gravitationally attract you. It's like Mario Galaxy, but worse. Both characters are capable of gliding, and climbing on certain walls. There's a new attack in this game, the Drill Dive, that lets you dive downwards while gliding, and it's actually pretty good. It looks cool, can destroy enemies effectively, and lets you dig in the ground for items.
The Chao garden returns, and it has the same system as in SA1DX. I don't really care for the Chao garden, but it doesn't detract from the main game, so I don't mind it existing.
Upsides? Like most Sonic games, the music is pretty good. Live & Learn, and especially the vocal theme to Sonic's first level, City Escape, are songs I own outside the game. Sonic's Metal Harbor stage also has a ska-like track that is my personal favorite from the game. Even when not memorable, the stage music always matches the stage environment well. *Sometimes* the graphics can be impressive, mostly when they use actual photographs as textures, though the polygon count is still pretty low. The final boss battle, featuring Super Sonic and Super Shadow in space trying to stop a giant lizard from destroying the Earth while Live & Learn plays is genuinely exciting. If you really memorize Sonic and Shadow's levels, you can actually have some fun with this game. Their abilities make sense with the level design, even if they're all mapped to one button.
You already know whether or not you're going to buy this game. SA2 has more fun potential than SA1, but can also be much more frustrating. They both average out to being pretty bad games. I still play them, because I'm a true Sonc fan. I stick with him through the bad times. Nostalgia aside, I wish there were more good times to be had with him.

I'm really enjoying this game - the multitude of tower upgrades give this TD game a unique selling point. It's also got a lot in common with Kingdom Rush and that's no bad thing, e.g. in-lane warriors, missile strikes and para-troopers are similar to KR's knights, meteor strike and re-enforcements, but it's all sufficiently different that I feel that this is money well spent.
The pacing is nice, perhaps a little slow, but some of the linked tower upgrades are fantastic and the pacing might be required to introduce you to them. Linked upgrades mean that you don't just build, say, a flame-tower. Instead you build a MG-tower, upgrade its range, which unlocks a ranger tower. Upgrade the ranger tower with rockets and that finally unlocks the flamer. It's a neat system and reasonably logical so you don't have too much to remember. But it adds flexibility to your strategy overall.
If you like TD generally and you like Kingdom Rush especially, you'll love this - it's slickly done and dirt cheap for the quality on offer.
A few videos have noted that there's no option to change music/effects volumes, but you can at least togglel each on/off.

DiRT 4 is the follow-up to Rally's "grueling physics with some cars and tracks tacked on" in the form of an actual game, if you care not for quality of life features Rally will probably satisfy you just as well, if you're looking to simply have fun then 4 is prepared to deliver in spades. DiRT 4 calls back to the best parts of Rally and 3, offering you variable assists and difficulty to either help even the petrol-challenged finish in good shape or to provide a reasonable challenge to enthusiasts, a garage of cars to collect, varied events to blast through, and your very own racing team to manage.
DiRT4 presents itself confidently and comprehensively to players of any skill level, with a robust training academy that covers a multitude of key concepts you'll apply in actual races, optional gymkhana-like stunt courses, and well scaled career events that either ease you into the world of rallysports or give you a few milk runs to acclimate you to the new game's feel. Once you've had your introduction to what the game has to offer it has an interesting system of progression, rather than requiring you to saddle yourself with a single car and team or just picking a car of your choice out of the ether DiRT 4 has an actual garage of vehicles that you must stock using your winnings, or you can take a loaner car in exchange for a portion of your winnings.
The garage and its contents are part of the new team management features, where you are allowed to hire engineers, upgrade various facilities, select sponsors, and customize your team livery. The management features themselves feel well implemented, not taking away from the racing itself but rather contributing to DiRT 4's sense of persistence between stages and events, as sponsor stickers appear on your vehicle, engineers have tangible effects on your ability to repair damage between stages, only the "upgrade" system of exchanging repair times and credits in exchange for more durable parts feels superfluous. Also of note is the actual system for buying new cars, with you having to pull many vehicles from the randomly generated "Classifieds" where you are not actually guaranteed to find the car you want and all offers have further randomized upgrades, some coming out of the box with parts that are simply downgraded and some with top-of-the-line racing parts.
Anyways enough about management, the racing itself is very par for the DiRT course, although the game boasts procedurally generated tracks you will often encounter the same elements several times in the same stage, so while the variety is welcome you shouldn't expect too much. Assists can be turned off and difficulty raised before a race to increase your winnings, though you cannot swap between the arcade and simulator driving styles without a visit to the main menu, which is understandable. Each event gives you access to a service area at different milestones throughout the list of stages, giving you a chance to repair the damage that persists between stages, clear the mud off your sponsor stickers, and make adjustments to your tuning settings if the last stage showed them to not be to your liking. Rally events will involve over 20 vehicles, many more if multiple classes are involved, and generally function the same way they always have, the "minimap" is a line along the side of the screen showing your progress from start to finish and displaying a "ghost" of the current fastest time in the form of a white triangle also traveling from start to finish. After each event the game gives you a nice podium to appear on, tallies your winnings, deducts team-related expenses, and then applies "reputation" to your driver level, which is used to unlock new team management options.
At the end of the day the various management features are nice and all but are merely icing on the cake that is an exceptional return to form for DiRT, if you enjoyed DiRT 3 you will find much to enjoy in 4.

This is the first time I ever write a review on Steam. I felt the need to say some words about this game since there is an overflow of negative reviews from people with less then 3 hours.
The game is a true example what a survival crafting game should be. You start off on a remote island with basically nothing. You have to figure by yourself how to survive, craft and build. The game doesn't hold your hand. There is a codex that explains a few basic concepts of the game but that's it.
The game looks amazing. The animation style makes it a really relaxing game sometimes. The systems the guys from bohemia implemented are amazing. Dynamic weather that changes the gameplay 180 degrees. Are you on a ship in the middle of a storm? Waves keep getting bigger and the ship starts leaning from side to side. Are you caught in the middle of a snowstorm? 10 minutes outside fully dressed and you freeze to death, while all the objects around you are covered in snow.
I only played 10 hours in 2 days and I must say I barely scratched the surface of this game. Everytime you think you found all the receipes in the game, 20 more just pop up in your crafting tab. Resources are plentyfull and it is fun to just explore an island and find little signs of civilization: houses, deer stands, bandit camps etc. Hunting and fighting the wildlife is satisfying aswell.
The building system is done very smart. You can rotate an object on all axis and you can move it on every direction. The materials clip easily and the system is easy to handle. You can build a small hut in no time prividing you have the materials. The rest is up to your imagination. Mining is fun aswell since you can basically modify all the terrain in the game.
This game is more enjoyable if you play with other players online. Allowing 8 players co-op game has the potential to create a gigantic playground. Have 2 friends build a base on an island while the rest move up with the ship somewhere else. Establish supply routes or just have naval battles or try to invade each others islands.
As in Arma 3 the editor is so well-done allowing the player to reinvent the whole game. Place assets, modify the terrain at your liking and create the perfect scenario for you to play or publish it to steam for everyone to enjoy.
Yes being in Alpha the game is full of bugs and glitches. Some of which I encountered are as follows:
Camera locks when going down from horses, ships glitch out and the animation gets stuck, rendering issues on some island or all objects on an island not appearing properly until a game restart.
Leopards and sharks tend to glitch to the ground and their animation don;t change smoothly. They just collide around.
Game runs pretty decent on high on my rig ( i7-6700HQ, GTX 950M 4 GB,  16GB RAM) but from time to time on multiplayer games there are lag spikes and in certain areas the fps drops from 70-80 to 30 for around 3-4 seconds. So the game still needs some optimization but there transition from EA to full release is still 8-9 months ahead.
Overall I highly recommend this game in this state if you are interested in a open world survival and crafting game. The games offers thousands of hours of replayability and the editor allows for the  most imaginative people to create their own worlds. Attention to deatil is amazing and the relaxed visuals will make you fall in love with this game.

Call of Duty: Ghosts is the 10th game of the Call of Duty franchise and definitely the most controversial one.
This game also has controller support with aim assist enabled, so console players will be very pleased.
The multiplayer is the aforementioned reason why many fans loathed this game with passion. The reasons are:
They can be obtained through:
The New Prestige system is directly connected to Squad Points. Each player starts the game with 1 character (Squad Member). Each character can be leveled up to level 60. Upon reaching the 60th level, you have to use your squad points to buy another character. This character will be Prestige 1. When you reach level 60 again, you must unlock another character. This character will be Prestige 2. etc.    The thing with squad points is that they can be used across all Squad Members.. That means, that if you have enough squad points you can unlock literally ANYTHING you want to, making prestiging kinda pointless.
All in all, this game strayed a bit too far from the COD formula, trying to innovate but ultimately It kinda failed. It was still a very solid and polished game. However I don't recommend getting this game on PC. I deeply like playing it on my PS3 where I have reached prestige 1, the population is considerably higher and the DLC is much more active. But on PC, it is very much dead,

The campaign of this game is short and unmemorable. The dog is a gimmick that is only really used at the beginning of the game, with no real impact after that initial level. This is similar to any other Call of Duty game, there is the classic enemy due to pass events that wants nothing but total world control and revenge. Your character doesnt say anything, making his actions seem dull and emotionless. There are plot twists you see miles ahead of you, and the classic vechicle missions on rails with the "AC-130" mission popularized by Modern Warfare 1. The ending is a cliffhanger, but honestly I wouldn't want the story to continue because its so emotionless.
The art style seems "dull". Every color is bland and grey. Unremerable envionment with no color.
Every gun feels the same, the assult rifles all seem the same besides the firerate. The characters feel "cartoon-ish". I can't really explain this feeling, but play Modern Warfare 1 or 2 and you will know what I am talking about. This iconic hit marker sound in this game is the worst ever, it doesn't feel impactful and sounds like a low thud.
Can't really say anything, multiplayer on PC is dead for this game. Almost every other Call of Duty has more players than this one which is so sad. Modern Warfare 1 and 2, Black Ops 2 and 3, and even Infinite Warfare have more players than this.
I do not recommend this game. Even though I purchased this game for $10, it was a waste. The campaign is remarkably short, barely at even 4 hours. I couldn't imagine people actually paying $60 for this game.

To be honest I am a big fan of Hotline Miami 1 and was very excited for the sequel Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number. When Hotline Miami 2 did come out, I had very mixed feelings about it. Sure you were able to play as multiple characters in the game but it doesn't feel like Hotline Miami, to me at least. Hotline Miami 1 had this very fun gameplay where you had the OP Tony mask that speedrunners would use and the Peter mask which the Assault Chapter significantly easier. But somehow Hotline Miami 2 failed to recreate the same feeling we had when we played Hotline Miami 1. They were shoving the story to out faces and actually having us read instead of slowly piecing together what's actually happening in Hotline Miami 1, it felt like that they were too lazy to make a story in the background so they put the story in the front. It sorta ruined the mystery that Hotline Miami 1 had. There is also a lack of masks in this game. SUre you can now shoot from both sides with SMGs with The Son and Mark and you now have the ability to roll with Cory and The Son, but that doesn't really satisfy me as a fan of the franchise. In the first game there was an abundance of masks, there were also secret masks but in this game there aren't anymore secrets and there is a lack of variety in gameplay. If you compare both The Fans and The Son they are very similar. The Son can have the same ability of Tony where he can 1 hit KO people with one punch, he has Mark's ability where he starts out with dual SMGs and shoot from both sides and he also has Cory's ability to roll, with the only difference is that he starts with a Katana. The Son basically has all of the abilities of the Fan's excluding Alex and Ash's ability for obvious reasons. Alex and Ash are Two people in one character. Also the ending felt lazy. It felt like they had no more ideas and justt wanted to end the story there.
For Fans of the first Hotline Miami this will disappoint you
But for new comers to he series feel free to try this game, it does have its good parts.

I might change my opinion later on, if they update it some more and polish it further, but as is, I can't recommend this game. It's incredibly boring.

This game made me realise that the Sonic franchise really is in a pitiful state.

The game is split into two campaigns: Hero and Dark, with both being split into 3 gameplay types: fast paced running, shooting segments, and item hunting.
Sonic and Shadow's stages have occasional stops in their levels, but are generally fast paced and fun to go through and replay.
Tails and Eggman's stages are similar to Gamma's stages from Sonic Adventure DX; you basically lock on and fire at enemies while running. While fun at times, turning is slow and locking on emits a very high pitched sound.
Knuckles and Rouge's stages have you finding emeralds and keys in a variety of maps; however, unlike in Sonic Adventure DX where you could chase all the emeralds in the map, you can only go after one item at a time. The camera also takes a while to adjust to in their part of the game.
There is also an extra chao garden where you can raise chao pets, get animals and drives (capsules) from the main game to raise their stats, and have them compete in several competitions such as racing and karate. There are also several upgrades (some mandatory while others are optional) that you can find throughout the game that will aid your character's abilities.
Despite a few confusing parts in its story, I found it to be pretty enjoyable overall. Worth playing through at least once.

I reviewed this game years ago, but I'm rewriting it to be a little more informative than my previous entry.
is without a doubt my favourite installation in the Sonic the Hedgehog franchise, the amount of time that I spent playing this as a child on the Gamecube is impossible to measure. This game has higher replay value than almost every game I have ever played and the Steam Version only adds to that further, I'll elaborate a little further into the review.
This game offers the choice of playing the story out from two different perspectives, the hero side and the dark side. The story isn't anything overly unique, but a typical Sonic the Hedgehog scenario: Dr. Eggman is trying to take over the World with the assistance of two new entries to the series (at this point in tine), Shadow and Rouge. The World is powerless to stop them after taking over the abandoned space Colony ARK and reactivating a weapon capable of destroying planets, thus leaving it up to Sonic, Tailsand Knuckles to stop him.
The core gameplay consists of three different stage types:
- Action Stages: Play as either Sonic or Shadow in high-speed race to the finish levels overcoming numerous obstacles and challenges. Definitely the most fun of the three different stage types and the closest thing to the original Sonic feeling.
- Treasure Hunting: Play as either Knuckles or Rouge using hints and a radar to locate hidden pieces of the master emerald around various maps. This is a mixed bag for most players as it can prove to be frustrating unless you've played the levels before, but it breaks the ganeplay up nicely in my opinion.
- Shooting Stages: Play as either Tails or Dr. Eggman (yes, you get to play as EGGMAN in this game, why haven't you already bought it?) in a set of shoot-em-up style stages. Another nice addition to break up the gameplay a little bit and can be a lot of fun with the exception of a few stages (Eternal Engine, ugh), it's very satisfying to rake in a huge number of points and go for the A ranks.
The game unlocks some minigames as you progress through the story mode stages, Kart Racing and Boss Battles. Kart Racing is a nice addition, though admittedly nothing overly fancy, just a generic racing game with some unlockable karts, a throw back to Sonic Drift. The Boss Battles are as you'd expect, boss rushes for each story mode once you complete the stories.
Arguably the best feature of the game is the Chao garden. Chao are creatures that you can raise and train to play Racing and Karate mini games. What Chao themselves are is difficult to explain, but I've always seen them as virtual pets in the case of
, you raise and train them by collecting certain items in the main game stages and delivering them to the Chao Garden after obtaining a special key in the stages. There is a lot of depth and information to cover on this so I won't go into it any further to prevent a bigger wall of text, I suggest reading about them on the SA2 Wiki if you're curious.
Everytime you complete a stage or mission, you acquire an Emblem, of which there are a total of 180. Emblems are another thing that extend the replayability of the game as collecting them all requires completing different missions from different stages and achieving A ranks. They aren't mandatory for completing the game, but they definitely give you a reason to keep coming back for another round.
While a lot of fun, it is difficult to play the Steam version on a keyboard, this is a game that is definitely better with a controller, I strongly advise using an Xbox pad if you have one. The lack of online multiplayer is a real shame which is the only real fault that I have with the Steam version of the game, the oopportunity was there but it wasn't taken. Local multiplayer is available for the 2 Player Battle DLC, a must have for this game, very fun and competitive multiplayer gamrs to be had for all stage types with additional characters to chose from.
I will defend this game to the death against haters and those who don't appreciate it's replayability, however, one thing that has always and will always bother me about this game is the clunky camera. Many times have a been short of an A rank or even lost a life as a result of the camera glitching out. Thankfully this doesn't happen too often, but you will notice it upon a playthrough of the stories, particularly in the Treasure Hunting modes.
All in all, this game is worth every penny, it is practically given away during sales. If you're a fan of the series, I would strongly recommend playing this game of you haven't already, it's one of SEGA's best. If you're new to the series, it may be a bit unusual to get into at first, but I would still recommend giving it a try.
