Artix Entertainment, this is your chance for greatness. You know this. I know this. Let's cut the bullcrap and admit what you have, what you don't, and the amazing things you can add down the road now that your releasing on steam. You may have plans to do these things, or you may not. That being said, I would greatly appreciate it if you read this.
Things you've accomplished:
- True Cross-platform
- Map Layout (Includes Questlines)
- Dungeon System
- Classes
- Animation. (save for certain issues with the 104 bpm where it stops the animation of a sword swing midway through, I will assume your going to fix that so smooth sword swings remain) Major props to Korin on this.
- Communication. This is where you are the kings and queens of game development. Of every game developer I've had the pleasure of listening and talking to, ya'll are the most responsive to player concerns, at least with AQ3D. All I ask is that it continues, and Epic Duel or AQW doesn't happen in terms of balance. You've certainly learned many lessons from your 2 mmo's.
- Abilities. Four different abilites per class that look pretty, but functionally they are extremely repetitive. There's not much you can do to change that, what with this being an mmo, but just continue producing a wide variety of different switchable classes down the road and you should be fine.
- Graphics. For a mobile game, you've found a way to make it beautiful. Be prepared for the onslaught of elitists though. They WILL scream "this game looks like WOW, but with worse graphics" and other such uneducated drivel. When this game goes live, you WILL be torn to shreds over this, until people either wise up, or leave. In fact, put the fact that the graphics had to be toned down for mobile in the description. It'll help to keep the hounds at bay.
- F2P model. It's not P2W, which is very good, I do have some qualms concerning your f2p model when it comes to crafting though, as you will see in the "fix" section of the review. If and when you have pvp, I would prevent premium players from using OP weapons. Or, even better, make the Yulgar's Inn pvp a fistfight only, so it requires skill and dodging to win, rather than "who has the best stats in the game". In all honesty, the fist fight would probably be more fun. (You could use abilities too)
Things that you need to fix:
- Crafting. It's a nice concept, if not a grindy one, but in my opinion you should save the crafting for the dungeons, and let the normal areas have item drops. Biggest no-no you have right now with crafting is the wait times. NOBODY wants to wait 2 days to craft an item that is useless by the time they get it. Some will consider this P2W, and whether they're right or wrong, they are players you WILL most likely lose. Do what you need to do to keep the game balanced while maintaining a reliable source of income. I have ideas about that reliable source of income in the next section.
- Typos. Sweet mercy, the typos. You know professionalism is key, and not having typos in your game shows professionalism. I assumed they would be fixed by open beta, but apparently not.
- RNG bosses. There's a line between fun grind, and horrid grind. RNG bosses are that line. Just let the boss be there, every time it spawns. It makes life easier for everyone, and more fun. Remember, this is meant to be an MMO for mobile, with extremely CASUAL players.
- Balance. Again, this is meant to be a casual game for anyone to play. Artix has said that you should be able to play from only a few minutes (5-10) to pulling an all-nighter and still be able to have fun. Having monsters that can bend you over and kick you back to Battleon when they're the same level as you, or one level higher, will not cut it. The company has since shared their agreement with this line of thinking, and I appreciate that. However, this is a huge problem, and as such many would-be players have already left.
-Quests. The MMO genre is an old beaten horse in terms of PC gaming, and it takes something special to make an MMO stand out from the crowd. Do whatever is possible, and things deemed impossible, in order to introduce quest variety.
You have your trademark humor and cutscenes in the works, now all you need are quests that aren't either kill x of y, or pick up x of y and take it to z.  (This is the thing you're least likely to fix)
Offhand suggestion: Use those allied NPC's you've made to create battles like the intro area. Just make it so they're always respawning and fighting as soon as they spawn, and it'll help to create a more lived in space for your areas.
Things to make it more fun, and encourage longetivity:
- Steam Economy. Yes, this could lead to serious gold farming, but it would also lead to a much cooler experience. To prevent inflation, you could have a specific kind of currency that has a global cap, say 500 million. Each player is given an equal amount as they join the game until all 500 million are doled out. If someone throws it away, have a system that gives the currency to a player that hadn't yet recieved any. Those that couldn't get any, can trade items for it. The better the item, the more currency it would be worth. The worth of items in this currency would be decided by the players, and an entire economy would develop. Finally, you can connect this economy to the steam economy by having a certain amount of currency (50, 100, 1,000, 10,000, and so on) that a player is allowed to sell on the market instead of spending it. That way, new players (lazy players or veteran players too) can either buy the currency via steam, or they can earn it by getting items and then selling them at auction. My idea obviously needs fleshing out, and probably has a few holes, but it could work if done properly. A good economy means a good game, and trading is always a game within a game. It adds more things to do! :D (plus $ for you)
- Steam Workshop. Wether it be weapons, armor, dungeons, or even storylines, if you give players the assests and the ability to make it, it will make your job easier, the community benefits, and the creators can get a chunk of money from the items bought, or if its a map, you could allow people to buy some kind of map collection or map related item (like buying stamps for community maps in TF2). Obviously, there would be garbage and things you'd have to sift through, but TF2 is an excellent example of a good workshop. Currently there are 3, (count em) 3 different community projects, with new maps, weapons, cosmetics, and even game mechanics. If it's even remotely accesible, and you can find a way to foster a workshop community like TF2, then this game will have a lot more longetivity. Which of course you want.
(Yes, I understand both of these things require a HUUUUUUUGE amount of work on your parts, and they're obviously features that will be added after the game releases, but if you can do both those things and do them well, your game will be a much longer lived and better loved game. And isn't that what every game dev wants? To see their baby played years later? To see it all grown up?)
Conclusion: Your doing gud, keep it up, don't ruin it. Fix bugs, add features, insure longetivity. Don't @%!& it up. No pressure.
:P
TL;DR: Your doing good so far, fix typos, remove RNG bosses, and keep it balanced (NOT P2W) and casually fun. Not DarkSouls3D. Down the road, add steam workshop and steam economy, it will do wonders for your game. As for the consumer reading this review, remember: it is in early access. If the devs do not abuse the privilege and properly polish the game, it will be at least a slightly above average mmo. I suggest that if you don't like it now, check in on it again at least once a month. You may be suprised.
Post Script: I wonder how many typos I have? I wonder how many of these issues the devs are obviously already aware of, or have already fixed, that I don't know about? I wonder if a dev will read this?

I bought the Humongous Entertainment Complete Pack during Steam Winter Sales last year when I saw it was compatible with current Operating Systems including Mac and I was absolutely thrilled. At the time this wasn't included in the pack, which made me sad because I had very fond memories of playing this game as a kid. Thinking back on my childhood, it's probably my 3rd favorite HE game, falling short only to SPY Fox in: Dry Cereal and Pajama Sam 2: Thunder and Lightning Aren't so Frightening. When I saw this game had been added to the pack and I had it because I had the pack (or maybe it had just been made Mac compatible, regardless, I saw I could download it) I was absolutely thrilled because I had just been lamenting over not having this game.
While I don't think this would be a particularly interesting game for most adults, there's massive nostalgia value for me and playing it now threw me back to when I played it as a kid. I had a ton of fun and it was like a trip back to my childhood!
I would definitely recommend it if you either A. played it as a child and have fond memories or B. have young children and want games for them. Actually if you have children and can afford it, I'd reccommend buying the entire Humongous Entertainment pack as there's hours and hours of entertainment value in there in pretty simple games originally made for kids to play!
It takes me about 45 minutes now as an adult to get through most Humongous Entertainment games I played for hours as a kid, but as a kid it took me a lot longer, I remember getting very immersed and they had a lot of replay value! I would absolutely recommend this game and virtually any other game from Humongous Entertainment along these lines for anyone with younger kids.
(They're not boring as an adult either, in my opinion, if you want to sit with your kid and help them play or play with them!)
Loved this kid as a game, played it just now for the nostalgia trip.  If/when I have kids, this is going to be one of their first games, no doubt.  :)  Highly recommend for the little ones!

I bought this game a month ago out of slight interest but never installed it to play it. I recently decided to install it to give it a go and I was instantly happy with my purchase.
Hydrophobia: Prophecy is a game that combine combat and platforming in a style of Tomb Raider. The graphics is stunning and the water physics are absolutely sublime; so no matter where you are in the game, you will be blown away by the amazing effort put into the design.
The controls can take a while to get used to and combat/cover can be a little frustrating, but once you get the hang of it, you can easily take out the larger groups of enemies without too much effort.
An interesting feature is the hydrokenises abillities the actually allow you to directly control water inside and outside of combat, which is something i've never seen in a game but it works brilliantly in Prophecy and I would like to see more from this developer and more Hydrophobia. For $3 on sale and $12 otherwise, you CAN'T go wrong.

An excellent concept, executed near perfectly. It's obvious that there was a $10 price tag in mind, but the game does such a good job of immersing you, that you quickly forget. The water physics in this game far exceed anything else on the market, and the company makes full use of the engine by giving you just about every scenario possible. Unfortunately, it's a short game and rather lacking in the story department. I was expecting it to amount to something more spectacular (like seeing the actual exterior of the ship) rather than the same old rooms for six hours, but no. Instead you're left trying to outrun rapidly flooding hallways all while gunning down some rather extreme liberators, as the world's population is far beyond sustainable. Our heroine, Kate, then develops a rather strange, but convenient ability. Then for no apparent reason, she must fight a giant flying robot. A strange way to end it, but overall an entertaining experience definitely worth $10. 8 / 10

Having put just shy of 13 hours at the time of this review, I can see where there might be a change of opinion 6 months down the road, but by that time I'll have gotten my money's worth ten times over. The control scheme could use a little bit of an overhaul, doesn't feel very organic, but with a little adjustment and massive key remapping I was taking down leapords, within 30 minutes. The crafting tree takes some adjustment compared to some other games, but nothing counter-intuitive, once again took about a half hour before I understood the innerworkings. It's a lot more passive than I'd originally thought, although it's not an AFK game (you do need to eat pretty often in game). I've been looking for something that was a little less agressive, something I could play with my 12 year old niece and not feel like one of us were playing something we'd rather not be (too agressive for her, too childish for me). This has all the makings that both of us are looking for, adventure, base building, farming, animals, ships, mining, exploring...etc, without being patronizing about it. Definately worth picking up, even if it's not the most polished game in the world ATM, it provides PLENTY of fun entertaiment for the money.

-Early Release bugs are seriously game breaking, can range from, falling though the map when trying to use a ladder, to host taking falling damage crashing the server. (had a case where i fell though the ground, landed inside a cave, died to the falling damage, crashed the server, and when it was restarted, a empty shell of my character was standing at the spawn-in wearing my gear)

The game started to pick up after introducing a character that is supposed to complete the level non-violently, and this was surprisingly just as fun and much more interesting then the regular, blood and gore combat of the series. All of these innovative, unique missions are scattered with classic hotline miami levels inbetween. So, this review is coming from someone with a racing history which can be seen more as broad than deep; I've played quite a range of different racing game genres, but never really got very far into them. Things as GRID 2 and the old Grand Prix 3 and 4 games are exceptions to that, but let's put those on the side for a minute. Besides those games I've played quite some GRID Autosport, DiRT 3 and Rally (plentifully referenced here), TrackMania, NFSU, Rollcage (quirky, old but loads of fun) and some I don't really remember that well anymore.
I would consider myself a reasonably experienced driver - although most of my driving was done with keyboard, I have to admit - and am playing on a medium-spec laptop. And with medium-spec I mean one that just made it above the requirements to play DiRT 4; it's a 2-year-old Lenovo W541 running an Intel i7-4710MQ CPU (a mobile quadcore running at 2.5GHz, turbos to 3.1) together with an Nvidia Quadro K1100M. As I said, it just made the requirement spec.
Taking all of this into consideration, this review will probably help you if you are on the lower spectrum of compatible hardware yourself.
The atmosphere in this game... I would place it somewhere between DiRT 3 and Rally. It has some of the arcade influences so immensely present in 3, but mixed with some more seriousness and realism from Rally.
Actually, now that I mention Rally - I'm seeing it both as part of the DiRT family and a completely different game. More on that later I guess.
Back to the subject though; the game feels... complete. Cohesive. It feels like you open a package and see all the parts in there, and see that they work really solidly together. Again this is a combination of Rally and 3; the playfulness in the design of 3 has had a transformation which has a small influence of the modernist, simplistic approach implemented in Rally.
Definitely, DiRT 4 has had some lessons from nephew Rally here. Tons of options to tune and tweak the car that I kind of missed in 3 and the self-implemented feature of creating your own team really add to the fun. The main difference with Rally here is that the cars feel... a bit more fake. Or well, arcadey.
If you want to get a full-on sim racing game, I would suggest you pack your bags and move (back) to Rally for this one. I mean, it's fairly realistic, but as much as DiRT 4 tries to get the general public closer to rally racing, DiRT Rally is the game for somewhat more specialistic fun, the more pure rally enthusiast. Its feel in the cars and the scenery is unmatched, as much as the 4 PR team have promised. For what I have found the main DiRT series is about though - getting the public closer to rally racing - it does the job perfectly fine. It feels fluid, quick, and relatively nice to control as well.
Now, here we come to an important point for me. As mentioned above, my machine is not the créme de la créme of gaming computers. I have found the game to run quite smooth, however. I was actually able to livestream the game when running on 720p and the low quality preset. It was laggy here and there but I was prepared for it and actually quite enjoyed it.
If I would really want to compare to Rally here, I would say 4 actually ran a teensy weensy bit better. Understandably; if it wasn't the case... well, I would be ashamed as Codemasters, Rally being a fully in Early Access developed game.
So yeah, in most parts of the stages I got at least 15-20 FPS. Some people will be screaming now, thinking it's not enough, and getting spontaneous headaches, but for me... I don't know. It was playable, felt responsive still, and quite frankly was to live with.
So, in the end? What do I think?
Well, to start with, it doesn't do the game justice to directly compare and judge it based on DiRT Rally. It may share the game series title, but... well, that's where the similarities end. It's a completely different game for a different purpose and although certain promises have been made regarding aesthetics and physics I do get why certain things haven't been implemented.
Having that out the way, for the few hours I've had the honor to take the wheel, I actually felt quite happy with the game. I had some mistakes I managed to save, some championships I won with only slivers of time as margin. It wasn't the same feeling as surviving a slaughterhouse like in Rally - again, different game! - but the essence for me is the fact that Codemasters have managed to capture something unique again, albeit in a different way; the moment of accomplishment, of euphoria, as you cross the line and see you beat your rivals.
So yes, overall, I don't think it's a must-have for everyone who likes racing a bit, especially for the steep price you get charged for the game. If the golden rule of thumb ($1/played hour) were to be true... well, you have to be a bit dedicated to fulfill it. Overall though, it feels solid, put together well and frankly I had a blast playing it.

Artix Entertainment has done a great job with delivering their first 3D game, entirely made with an engine that they aren't accustomed with.  This game was supposed to be made from Flash, but then Flash dropped their 3D support.  These guys had to migrate from Flash to Unity, which is
hard, considering the process of learning the new engine as well as rebuilding the game from scratch.
What saddens me though are the reviews.  They do not understand that this game is still in
, and why some things are meant to be.
For example: This game is supposed to be a game where you can have fun with friends or make friends, without the cost of hardware limitations.  This game only has low graphics because it was made to be played with multiple platforms.
Anyways these are my pros and cons:
✔️ Has an awesome atmosphere similar to Adventure Quest Worlds
✔️ The storyline is a little, but it's pretty great so far in terms of being an Early Access game
✔️ The minimum hardware requirements are barely anything, allowing great performance on any modern device
✔️ Nothing has really bugged out in game; no crashing has occurred(My Experience)
✔️ UI is great for being a game that aims to be compatible with multiple platforms
✔️ The questing and combat system is similar to AQW, which is great
✔️ The amount of bugs in the game is very little for being an Early Access game
⛔️ According to some people, there are quite some bugs, as well as some crashing, so hopefully they can fix those problems
⛔️ Some of the farming quests or side storyline quests get repetitive, so hopefully they could revise on some of the goals in those quests for a much more exciting experience
⛔️ Some items require buying it with real money, but it doesn't really matter to get those items as you can still have fun and progress through the game.
➕ Add more elements in combat
➕ Give more usefulness in items such as gold
➕ Add support for people with greater hardware specifications in the video settings section, such as more post-processing effects, higher resolutions(highest I can go up to is 2048x1536 in a 4:3 aspect ratio), more aspect ratios(such as 21:9 since that is starting to become more popular), etc.
➕ Add some special items that are earned through other games
➕ Perhaps have more immersive maps
➕ Please add that one jumping technique that was kind of like B-Hopping, it made you really fast if you just held jump and ran around!(Just kidding! xD)
It's a great game for being in the early access stages, and I can guarantee it will get better along the way.  Some things might cost a ton of money, but just keep in your mind it will help the developers keep updating the game.  The game's really immersive if you play fullscreen, also just noticed the UI got completely better.  In the meanwhile, you can go play AQW, which is an awesome game as well! :)  AQ3D is a game you should totally be investing time in if you want! :D

First off this game isn't probably going to be for everybody. But as a fellow Adventure Quest/AQW player for around 7 years now, this game really hits home. But before I get all sappy and nostalgic. Let's get to the pros and cons.
TL:DR - Try it out, you might like it after all?
Pros:
- Fantastic open world with plenty of dungeons already.
- Some fun parkour you can do around the world, also helps fighting.
- Interesting cartoony artstyle.
- Fun gameplay, feels grindy at points however.
- Working friending system.
-----
Cons:
- No guilds/clans so far, but that's to be expected with beta.
- Some shader issues I've seen, but nothing that really takes away from gameplay.
- Some dungeons bosses (Such as Mother Hen) has super low drop rates, if any at all.
- Shops are pretty barren at the moment, not much to spend gold on.
- You instantly unlock every ability at level one, right off the bat. Seems kinda weird to me? Might just be for testing though.
-----
Conclusion: Over all I do suggest this game, and I do know it'll get better over time. Even heard there's an upcoming Halloween update which'll be loads of fun for exclusive armor. So go ahead and try it out for yourself! 68 MB download, and can run on a toaster.

I played 140+ hours.
This game isn`t a casual FPS like Battlefield or CoD. Its comparable to Left 4 Dead, but its focusing on melee combat.
It is a coop only team game. Run alone you and your team will die (at least at higher difficulties).
It is not a rewarding game like Battlefield. There is no xp for killing rats. You get XP for succesfully end a level. How you survived the maps is your choice. It does not make a difference at the end.
The loot is randomized by throwing loot dices at the end of the level, which is influencable by collecting special items during most of the maps. Those special items (called tomes and grimoires) use inventory slots, which makes a level more challenging. Decide it by yourself how difficult you want those levels.
Every round is different because of the randomized item , monster and some parts of the map as well.
The "workflow" of the game is:
1. play on easy difficulties to learn the game, maps and ai behaviour
2. get some green/blue loot to be able to win higher difficulties, which gives you a better chance to get better loot
3. increase the difficult
4. have fun by a challenging game
The developer has much space to introduce new content, which they will do! :)

RATS RATS and MORE RATS!!  If you were a fan of L4D or Dynasty Warriors... then this is the game you've been waiting for.
If those two games had a baby.. it would be this.  Imagine the horde/special system from L4D series and the random loot from say Dynasty Warriors 3 boxes on the battlefield.  Then you'd have a vague notion of what you're getting into.
There -is- a loot system but you should not go into this with a loot-minded mentality.  It will only set you up for aggrivation currently.  The loot system is still very much RNG-y and unless you got that magic mojo.. you can expect to be disappointed repeatedly.  However that is a good thing because once you've earned your first "orange" or "red" weapon.. it makes that moment that much more memorable.  The devs have made some good tweaks to the loot system and have some impending updates as well that will smooth things out abit.
All in all, despite early release bugs (most of which have been patched), this has been a fantastic trip down to rat town.

Played 2hrs and was immediately and absolutely hooked. After 10hrs, I cannot recommend this game enough. If you like Warhammer at all, or if you had some fun with L4D, get Vermintide. Hell, even if you didn't, and just like co-op games, get it. Just get it. It's amazing. Granted, there are bugs, and issues, but no game is without its share of those, especially in the first year its released.
Content at this point looks very polished, playing through the same levels again and again does not get old, simply due to the fact that the maps are fairly lengthy, and every time you play it, things are different. Not only do spawns change, but the things that you end up fighting can change too.
Melee combat feels quite natural, takes minimal effort to get used to. Ranged combat is a little more challenging but very rewarding. Survival relies more on positioning and quick thinking, as well as staying together and working as a team, which is paramount to victory.
The loot system keeps me coming back for more, and gives me incentive to continue playing. Others might not like it, I'm sure, but the best weapons in the game aren't *that* much better than some of the weapons I own only 10hrs in, which aren't *that* much better than the tier below it, and so on.
And then there's the characters. Each one has so many lines of dialogue that relate to very specific scenarios, or even subtle interactions with other characters. Each voice actor is perfect for their character.

I've sunk 50+ hours into this game, and I can comfortably reccommend it to fans of Warhammer and Left4Dead.
Positives:
+Great graphics and sound, the world is immersive and well-designed.
+Great level design. The hunt for bonus items to get better loot rolls really shows off some of the intracicies of the world. The Grey Wizard's tower is one of the best levels in any game, period.
+The melee action is frantic and fun. I don't think I've been in a 1st person game that executes melee so well. Dodging, parrying, and striking in a hectic dance of death is really excellent.
+The variety of difficulties make this game easy on newcomers, hard for those who want a challenge.
+The story and campaign are interesting enough. Most of the 'story' will be told ingame through interactions between the five characters.
Negatives:
-The loot system can be somewhat frustrating, but the recent DLC has taken huge steps to make it more predictable and fun. You have to roll dice at the end of each level, modified by bonus items that you've pickd up, in order to obtain better items.
-The community can be iffy sometimes. The Bots won't get you past much, you will need to play with others. It can be a chore to play with folks who aren't communicating with the team.
All in all, I've gotten a lot of enjoyment out of this game. The community is still going strong. If you and a group of friends are looking for a new coop game to play, I would say you should check this one out.

Normally a great Early Access game would be described as "having great potential."  This is true here as well, but it's already a much more complete game than many open world exploration games, and much, much further along than most early access open world exploration games.  It reminds me of Salt, but with much more to do and build, and that game has been in EA for a long time.  For the price, and the fact that it's on sale for only 12 bucks right now, this is one great game for your dollar and it's being developed by one of my favorite developers.  Yes, it has some bugs but it's early access so to complain about bugs at this stage is just silly considering how much you're getting for the price.  There are a lot, I mean a hell of a lot of things you can craft and build.  Some people don't like that it doesn't really give you much direction or tutorial on these things, but you can press F1 in game and get very helpful tips.  I love the fact it doesn't hold your hand and tell you to "Craft 5x of <insert item>."  It just unleashes you and let's you go at it...similar to how Minecraft was a mystery to everyone when it first launched...we just had to figure it out.
The world is HUGE but not infinite...and I'm fine with that.  I think infinitely sized worlds are a novelty that people think they want, but no one ever explores enough of those types of worlds to make it worth it.  So far, I've discovered 7 ylands and each has had it's own character.  I won't spoil anything, but I've found lots of easter egg style things on ylands (and underwater) that makes it feel mystierious...like, "what happened here."
For a pretty cheap game, you're getting:
-huge open world to explore and sail around in
-huge amount of things to craft and build
-multiplayer
-world editor
-some of the best weather and lighting in an open world game
-ships
-tons and tons of clothing, armor, weapons, tools
-a crafting progression that doesn't let you craft the end game stuff quickly at all, which increases the long term interest you'll have in progressing
-easter eggs and points of interest to explore and find, on land, underground, and underwater
-a developer that is established, where you don't have to worry about them abandoning the game once they make money off it
Yes, it has an in game shop for skins, but come on, you don't need any of that stuff because there are a ridiculous amount of clothes and armor in the game.  And what's more, half the stuff in the microtransactions shop is free...that's right, free.
Yes, this game is worth the asking price.

So, this review is coming from someone with a racing history which can be seen more as broad than deep; I've played quite a range of different racing game genres, but never really got very far into them. Things as GRID 2 and the old Grand Prix 3 and 4 games are exceptions to that, but let's put those on the side for a minute. Besides those games I've played quite some GRID Autosport, DiRT 3 and Rally (plentifully referenced here), TrackMania, NFSU, Rollcage (quirky, old but loads of fun) and some I don't really remember that well anymore.
I would consider myself a reasonably experienced driver - although most of my driving was done with keyboard, I have to admit - and am playing on a medium-spec laptop. And with medium-spec I mean one that just made it above the requirements to play DiRT 4; it's a 2-year-old Lenovo W541 running an Intel i7-4710MQ CPU (a mobile quadcore running at 2.5GHz, turbos to 3.1) together with an Nvidia Quadro K1100M. As I said, it just made the requirement spec.
Taking all of this into consideration, this review will probably help you if you are on the lower spectrum of compatible hardware yourself.
The atmosphere in this game... I would place it somewhere between DiRT 3 and Rally. It has some of the arcade influences so immensely present in 3, but mixed with some more seriousness and realism from Rally.
Actually, now that I mention Rally - I'm seeing it both as part of the DiRT family and a completely different game. More on that later I guess.
Back to the subject though; the game feels... complete. Cohesive. It feels like you open a package and see all the parts in there, and see that they work really solidly together. Again this is a combination of Rally and 3; the playfulness in the design of 3 has had a transformation which has a small influence of the modernist, simplistic approach implemented in Rally.
Definitely, DiRT 4 has had some lessons from nephew Rally here. Tons of options to tune and tweak the car that I kind of missed in 3 and the self-implemented feature of creating your own team really add to the fun. The main difference with Rally here is that the cars feel... a bit more fake. Or well, arcadey.
If you want to get a full-on sim racing game, I would suggest you pack your bags and move (back) to Rally for this one. I mean, it's fairly realistic, but as much as DiRT 4 tries to get the general public closer to rally racing, DiRT Rally is the game for somewhat more specialistic fun, the more pure rally enthusiast. Its feel in the cars and the scenery is unmatched, as much as the 4 PR team have promised. For what I have found the main DiRT series is about though - getting the public closer to rally racing - it does the job perfectly fine. It feels fluid, quick, and relatively nice to control as well.
Now, here we come to an important point for me. As mentioned above, my machine is not the créme de la créme of gaming computers. I have found the game to run quite smooth, however. I was actually able to livestream the game when running on 720p and the low quality preset. It was laggy here and there but I was prepared for it and actually quite enjoyed it.
If I would really want to compare to Rally here, I would say 4 actually ran a teensy weensy bit better. Understandably; if it wasn't the case... well, I would be ashamed as Codemasters, Rally being a fully in Early Access developed game.
So yeah, in most parts of the stages I got at least 15-20 FPS. Some people will be screaming now, thinking it's not enough, and getting spontaneous headaches, but for me... I don't know. It was playable, felt responsive still, and quite frankly was to live with.
So, in the end? What do I think?
Well, to start with, it doesn't do the game justice to directly compare and judge it based on DiRT Rally. It may share the game series title, but... well, that's where the similarities end. It's a completely different game for a different purpose and although certain promises have been made regarding aesthetics and physics I do get why certain things haven't been implemented.
Having that out the way, for the few hours I've had the honor to take the wheel, I actually felt quite happy with the game. I had some mistakes I managed to save, some championships I won with only slivers of time as margin. It wasn't the same feeling as surviving a slaughterhouse like in Rally - again, different game! - but the essence for me is the fact that Codemasters have managed to capture something unique again, albeit in a different way; the moment of accomplishment, of euphoria, as you cross the line and see you beat your rivals.
So yes, overall, I don't think it's a must-have for everyone who likes racing a bit, especially for the steep price you get charged for the game. If the golden rule of thumb ($1/played hour) were to be true... well, you have to be a bit dedicated to fulfill it. Overall though, it feels solid, put together well and frankly I had a blast playing it.

I think too many people here are quick to judge. First of all you spend your first 1-2 hours driving modern slow rallye cars (which by the way did not exist in dirt rally), so judging physics based on that is dumb because there is nothing to directly compare. Then you can chose to unlock a modern or group A car in which I have not found too many differences in physics, if anything theyre even more difficult to drive. Way too many people judge the physics based on the cars youre driving at the start, in DiRT Rally you start with the historic cars, 60s, 70s, 80s, cars with little grip, too much power, lots of personality and uniqueness. in Dirt 4 you start off with modern cars who have more grip than power which makes them rather boring to drive. The group A and R4 cars are the ones you unlock second in Dirt 4 which are also available in Dirt Rally where theyre equally boring to drive.
The key difference in physics that i have found is spinning out of control much easier than in Dirt Rally, managing your throttle in corners is far more important.
That out of the way, Dirt 4 is a much more complete and polished game than Dirt Rally, it brings actual personality back to a game like you had in Dirt 2 or the recent F1 2016, you have your own team, your own sponsors, design for your cars similar to GRID 2, you have your own engineering team like in Dirt rally except they have a much deeper impact, they have an actual face! The music inbetween stages is fantastic, the presentation is fantastic, i really like how they managed the used car system with the part conditions, its something very few racing games do due to the difficulty of creating a difference between a used and a new car, codemasters have found a system to make it work which in my opinion it does.
I have dipped a bit into the other game modes like the buggys that came back, its really fun to drive, personally I didnt enjoy hillclimb and rallycross in dirt rally a whole lot, neither did i like the gymkhana and other stuff in Dirt 3, i did love many of the other modes in Dirt 2 like the huge offroad trucks that they would use in Dakar.
I havent yet tried the track editor which would solve the issue of limited content that Dirt rally has. Rally isnt about learning a stage over and over again until you perfect it, that is what racing on a racing track is about, Rally is about exploring the unknown, about rewarding a consistent driving style. Chances are, if you spend hundreds of hours into Dirt Rally, you probably love racing on a racing track just as much, if not even more.
From a technical standpoint I havent encountered any bugs so far, seems well optimized, not quite as good as Dirt rally but I am not running the latest patch yet.
I am driving on the second highest difficulty which is not a challenge quite yet but i wanted to get used to the game before i take the big challenge. Your "career" in Dirt rally basically depended on how far you have upgraded your car yet, without any upgrades it would be nearly impossible to get first, fully upgrade you shouldnt have an issue with that.
As I said in my opening statement, it is a much more complete game than Dirt Rally, it has personality, something many of the current simulators lack.
If you are a purist giving this game a thumbs down because of its "worse physics", im surprised youre wasting your time with Dirt Rally and not play Richard Burns Rally instead because that is the purist Rally game you can find and it is still being updated with mods, youll find endless content by the mod community, youll find WRC content of the past 20 years with all the original tracks, the physics are more realistic than Dirt rally, it also has one of the best driving tutorials along with GTR 2 teaching you the basics but also the more advanced ways to drive a rally car.
Saying the physics of Dirt 4 are dumbed down is like saying Gran turismo 6 has worse physics than Gran turismo 5 which sounds laughable to a hardcore sim racer because theyre still both far less realistic than PC sims. That is what this situation is, if you want a completely realistic experience, what are you doing playing Dirt Rally and not Richard Burns Rally? I bet nobody here has driven a real rally car nor did many here play RBR, so they assume Dirt Rally is close to realism because it simply is difficult but they have no point of comparison which is why this is all so hypocritical.
if PC racing sims didnt exist, Im sure people would also name Forza and GT a close to realism experience.
There is much more to this game youre missing if you are mainly complaining about physics. It has everything that makes a good racing game that Dirt Rally doesnt have and therefore it is a better game

To be honest I am a big fan of Hotline Miami 1 and was very excited for the sequel Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number. When Hotline Miami 2 did come out, I had very mixed feelings about it. Sure you were able to play as multiple characters in the game but it doesn't feel like Hotline Miami, to me at least. Hotline Miami 1 had this very fun gameplay where you had the OP Tony mask that speedrunners would use and the Peter mask which the Assault Chapter significantly easier. But somehow Hotline Miami 2 failed to recreate the same feeling we had when we played Hotline Miami 1. They were shoving the story to out faces and actually having us read instead of slowly piecing together what's actually happening in Hotline Miami 1, it felt like that they were too lazy to make a story in the background so they put the story in the front. It sorta ruined the mystery that Hotline Miami 1 had. There is also a lack of masks in this game. SUre you can now shoot from both sides with SMGs with The Son and Mark and you now have the ability to roll with Cory and The Son, but that doesn't really satisfy me as a fan of the franchise. In the first game there was an abundance of masks, there were also secret masks but in this game there aren't anymore secrets and there is a lack of variety in gameplay. If you compare both The Fans and The Son they are very similar. The Son can have the same ability of Tony where he can 1 hit KO people with one punch, he has Mark's ability where he starts out with dual SMGs and shoot from both sides and he also has Cory's ability to roll, with the only difference is that he starts with a Katana. The Son basically has all of the abilities of the Fan's excluding Alex and Ash's ability for obvious reasons. Alex and Ash are Two people in one character. Also the ending felt lazy. It felt like they had no more ideas and justt wanted to end the story there.
For Fans of the first Hotline Miami this will disappoint you
But for new comers to he series feel free to try this game, it does have its good parts.

Campaign is as stupid as some heroic b-movie. East apparently being totally wasted, this game revolvers around North America versus South America (The Federation). The protagonist is totally silent again and has no personality beyond simply being badass, which allows any player to relate themselves with him. His brother has two voice modes: non-emotional silent   droning (phrase "All this time you've been a Ghost" is the hit) and non-emotional yelling. The sole black Ghost dies first. The Ghosts themselves are described as supernaturally silent warriors, whose tactics involve blowing stuff up and ramming the front gates with their vehicle. The mosquito buzz is FRIGHTENINGLY REALISTIC. The dog is undoubtedly the most charismatic and well-written character. And may gods have mercy on you in case you FORGET RILEY! Also, the campaign mode has no FoV slider, which keeps you stuck in "couch" mode at 65, and zero-tolerance policy for the external FoV changers.
Multiplayer has quite a wide array of customizing your character. It has a free option to make you char female, with a selection of uniforms (no revealing sexy ones, thankfully) and hats/helmets, most of which are acquired through completing the usual grinding challenges, and of course the DLC ones. You can also buy more DLCs to customize your playercard, change the announcer to Snoop Dogg, and morph your overpowered killer dog into an overpowered killer wolf. You can also buy even more DLCs to gain access to exclusive overpowered weapons, and get more map packs. At the first sight, it is the same Call of Duty gameplay with random explosives, one-hit knife kills, one-shot-to-the-body sniper kills, dropshots (spot an enemy, lie down, shoot them in the legs), and SMG dominance. This includes the usual questionable balance decisions: Bizon has 36 rounds instead of 53/64, while Vepr - which isn't even an SMG - has 40 in its 30-round magazine, Beretta has 12 rounds instead of 15, Grach has 10 instead of 18 AND is underpowered, the marksman rifle mags are the worst offenders. Oh, and at this time, only 150-250 players are active, and ONLY in team deathmatch. As a bonus, you can set the FoV to a maximum of 80, because anything higher apparently makes your high-end machine stutter even MORE.
This Call of Duty entry demonstrates that terrible game dev decisions can, in fact, kill the franchise. The biggest bonus in this game? When you remove it, you free up almost 40 GB of space.

Ah, Vermintide.....
Let me clear things beforehand:
I am a Warhammer fan, i play the tabletop and have read a few novels.
Pretty much all Warhammer games that have come out were either really bad or just not my type of game.
These last few years, more Warhammer titles have come out (BloodBowl, Mordheim) and it seems they are improving overall.
Vermintide is absolutely one of them, so lets get on with the review:
For starters, if you liked L4D and L4D2 you wont be disappointed. It is indeed a very close relative to that good old Valve franchise (something like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ brother comes to mind)
In that light, Fatshark has done everything right. The gameplay is tight, the design is polished, ambiance is outstanding, just like L4D.
The entire atmosphere is exactly as in the Warhammer lore, it oozes proper Warhammer feeling and that is awesome. It is gritty, it is unfriendly, raw and dark. Combined with the artwork, graphical design, which is astounding and of high quality it just makes it a pleasure to run around in the areas available.
What bit of lore you can pick up in-game (unfortunately it is not much) is completely coherent with how Warhammer has been unfolding over the last year.
Now for the gameplay, like i said, it is tight. Everything feels right. Sure there are some bugs and glitches. Sure there are some maps that have exploits, sure there are balancing issues between the characters. But who cares? i dont.... Its a co-op game to the bone, where skill and routine trumps everything.
There is a lootsystem which makes it RPG-ish but its very minimal and you shouldnt focus on it. No doubt about it, the upgraded weapons will help you alot and they are absolutely needed in the Nightmare/Cataclysm mode but it will (fortunately) never be a game where items win the game. Even with the crappier weapons, if youre a good player, you can make it. On the hardest modes its all about not getting hit, so thats only skill based, both in movement and in blocking/hitting.
I can underrstand some people that get bored, after having done all maps on easy/normal/hard a few times, you will be doing the same 8-9 maps all the time. It can feel like a grind, especially if you are focussing on getting new items.
To me, i just play it like L4D, its a challenge everytime, especially nightmare and cataclysm.
Despite a few glitches and bugs i really love this game. Matter of fact, i love all about it, even its glitches and bugs.
100% recomendation

It would certainly be easy to write off Vermintide as "Left 4 Dead without guns," but to do so would be a disservice to the game and developers. Yes, Vermintide is iterative of the Left 4 Dead formula: campaign-based, four-player co-op against hordes of individually weak enemies mixed in with special miniboss-style enemies. But Vermintide does more than enough to distinguish itself from Left 4 Dead, and while it certainly isn't better (it lacks in the polish department: there's plenty of glitches, the menus and controls can be somewhat awkward, and the AI isn't as good as L4D, as well as some performance hitches on a machine that exceeds the minimum requirements [Core i7-4720HQ processor, 16 GB RAM, GTX 960M gets me frame dips down to ~40 FPS in thick hordes at medium-high settings]) it definitely stands up as a worthy competitor.
I can't tell you too much about the story as I'm unfamiliar with the Warhammer Fantasy universe, though the game conveys enough information so that newcomers aren't *completely* lost as to the setting and what's going on, and the plot isn't particularly complicated either (the world is ending, there's rat people the place of Left 4 Dead's Infected, and you're battling to save a city from their onslaught). It gets the job done, and it certainly conveys the aesthetic very well: art design is definitely not lacking here.
Gameplay-wise, Vermintide distinguishes itself from its forerunners via several elements, first and foremost being an emphasis on melee combat. The melee system isn't the deepest I've ever seen in a game, but it's not shallow either. I've survived mostly by just knowing when to back off and knowing when to attack, but the game also has blocking, bashing, sidestepping/dashing, and heavy strikes, all of which have their own uses, but are only truly essential on the higher difficulties. There is ranged combat, but true to the setting, it's not the focus. Different characters can equip different weapons including muskets (the muskets work more like sniper rifles though), flame staffs, bows, flintlock pistols, and repeater crossbows and repeating muskets. It's more for distance shooting or taking down special enemies than standard combat. Speaking of the different weapons, the game also has a loot system. Every completed mission grants you a loot drop. I have a few complaints about this -- the loot doesn't quite drop as much as it should especially when factoring in the game's more difficult nature, and not all of the weapons are particularly useful if you choose to focus on one character. Different characters also have somewhat different abilities, mostly due to different weapon sets, unlike in L4D where characters are merely cosmetic.
The game has a good amount of content and by its very nature, plenty of replay value. Not all of the missions are created equal, and some are very obviously more well-designed than others, but with more than ten different missions (which seem to be somewhat longer than the average L4D missions), multiple characters, and the loot system, the game offers a lot. Sadly, there's no versus or survival modes, just the standard co-op campaign, but I have heard that versus mode is planned (and it may have already come out, I haven't played the game in a while due to other games taking my attention for the moment).
Overall, I highly recommend Vermintide specifically as a co-op game, though be warned it is much more difficult than Left 4 Dead, and playing it solo is nearly impossible given the sad state of allied AI. If you're not interested in the basic formula of Left 4 Dead, the game may not be for you, but if you are, then it's definitely worth picking up.

This is a great game.
-Story
The story in this game is surprisingly dark for a sonic game, but that shouldn't stop your from playing it no matter your age. I will admit there are various plotholes within the story. I don't really care though because the story itself it entertaining probably only beat out by the originals. I also love when characters cut each other off in cutscenes! lol The story basically without spoilers is that Eggman wants to take over the planet using a weapon of mass destruction as bait. On his journey he finds his grandfathers greating accomplishment, Shadow the Ultimate Life Form. Shadow shows eggman the Space Colony Arc and how to use the weapon. Rouge then shows up and offers to help them find the chaos emeralds. On the hero side Sonic escapes from the government, he was arrested because he was mistaken for Shadow. After running around ramped for a while he finally gets captured so tails has to free him. Knuckles is searching for the pieces of the master emerald like always. When they catch wind of Eggmans plans They follow him to space to try and stop him. I made all of that very vague so I didn't spoil all that much.
-Graphics
They aren't the best because game is decently old, and they could only do so much when remaking those old models. I personly find the game very nice looking. It's art style really fits the theme of a game about an anamorphic blue hedgehog.
-Gameplay
There are three diffferent gameplay types across the six characters. On the Hero side Sonic: Speed levels, Knuckles: Treasure hunting, and Tails: shoot em ups. On the dark side Shadow(best character N/A): Speed levels, Rouge: Treasure hunting, and Eggman: Shoot em ups. The speed levels are what they sound like, you are racing through the level as fast as possible while trying to rack up points from killing enemies, collecting rings, and most importantly a time bonus. The treasure hunting levels you are searching for the objects, either the master emerald pieces are keys. Even though they are not designed for speed they still go reasonably fast. Finally the shooting stages. I find these fun, the goal is to reach the end of the level while racking up as many points as possible, mostly by hitting as many targets as you can at once. The controls are smooth, the level designs are nice, and each level has 5 different different missions. If you have an A rank on every mission and have all 180 emblems you will unluck a special stage.
-Chao Garden
This is the main reason that I, and many people still play this game. You get your own Tomagachi pets that you can raise how you want to. They have 5 different stats, Swim, Fly, Speed, Power, and Stamina. Which stat you chose to focus on will determine the look of your chao when it evolves (I'll explain that later). YOu upgrade your chaos stats from emerald shards you get from killing enemies, and animals you find throughout the levels. You can also make your chao a Hero, Dark, or Neutral which leads to even more combinations of how your chao can look! Chaos have 2 evolutions. Their first evolution the go into a cacoon and hatch as whatever aligment they are with their focused stat before the evolution. Their second evolution is a gradual thing that happens over time after the first. You choose another stat that will change how your chao looks slightly. This leads to so amny combinations that I honestly have no clue about how many it could be.
You might be asking "why should I even raise these things." They are cute, and you can race them in the chao races. You can also have them involved in karate if you have the DLC. Raising these cute little critters might sound really stupid and lame, but it's actually quite fun I really reccomend it.
Conclusion-
I would easily recommend this game to anybody who likes 3D Sonic games, Platformers, or even just for raising the chao. The only downside of this game for me is that it really hasn't aged well. I personally haven't found any glitches(except for the truck floating over me in the first level like WTF.)
Overall I give this game a 9.5/10, I love this title and I hope you will to!

First things first, I'm an avid fan of the first Hotline Miami game. I love it, adore it, and if It were a real person I'd take it out to dinner and serenade it. This being said, I am not good at it. I have never got an A plus on any round, I have died a hundred times on many levels, and I'm generally frustrating to watch play due to how inept I am.
So, upon stumbling across reviews of the second game when I came to buy it, I was torn. 'Bad level design!' they cried, 'Glitchy AI', 'Bad story/Too confusing' and several other reviews along the same lines that basically said this game was not worth it, that it was bad, frustratingly so. Still, as a glutton for punishment and a curious creature, I bought it.
Even if it was bad, I could appriciate the style and at least attempt it, right?
I'm pleased to say I had no such issues with this game. I didn't once run into glitchy AI, save for one dog that decided to loop in circles for a while. Perhaps he was alerting one of the mobsters to me being hidden just around the corner with a glass bottle in hand. Yes, a couple of times I was shot from off screen, but what people don't seem to realize is that this also happened in the first game. You have to use shift, you have to look ahead sometimes. The story was wonderful, and as someone who doesn't cry often, I choked up like a ♥♥♥♥♥ at the end when that credit music rolled in and those scenes played. How the hell do pixels make you cry? Well, only with brilliant yet subtle storytelling and a killer soundtrack, of course.
I would recommend this game to anyone. If you've been put off by the reviews, please just buy it, play it for yourself. I almost missed out on playing one of my favourite games of all time because I almost listened too.
10/10

If you're mortaring you NEED a spotter and you NEED to work together. On most maps you can go into ANY BUILDING YOU WANT instead of Red Orchsetra 2 in lot of maps you can't go inside any building. Example: Spartovnovka; There are houses EVERYWHERE and you can't go into a single one?

Let me start by reminding everyone that this isn't Dirt Rally 2. I believe Codemasters did an absolutely amazing job revitalizing all the best parts about Dirt and it shows in Dirt 4. There is a simulation mode and a gamer mode, you will never race across handling settings (maybe in a friend event). So I'm not sure why so many people are butthurt over the gamer setting. If anything it brings more players to the game.
PROS:
- You can real-time rally race online now!!! (FANTASTIC BTW!)
- New racetracks, including CUSTOM TRACKS!
- Soundtrack is impressive.
- Rally school and rally challenges really helps you improve your driving skill
- THERE IS NO RUBBER BANDING SYSTEM! If there is I haven't noticed it yet, I play on a higher difficulty and no longer do cars catch up to me just because I have a massive lead. You can either dust your opponents or be dusted.
- Campaign mode is fantastically made. In Dirt Rally it almost felt like a chore because it was from one loading screen to the next, this game breaks up the monotonity.
- Racing team/branding garage
CONS:
- So many people complain about the grippy RWD, I agree. Sometimes you'll come up on a hairpin and can't slide the car like you use to be able to. Even if this doesn't get fixed, it doesn't break the game. It's more of an annoyance if anything.

Why Dirt 4 is not a good game like Dirt Rally:
- Badly optimised game ( Down to 15 FPS in certain areas - just High, not Ultra settings full HD res, single monitor set up) Dirt rally runs 75-120 FPS on the same machine
- Poor Force Feedback (You can't feel the road surface, everything is smooth and feels flat)
- Outdated, PS3-look-a-like graphics Jesus, it's crap
- EGO 2 engine replays (programmed auto-switching cameras, always cuts Nicky Griest's talk, very annoying)
- No detailed Co-driver instructions
- No feelings of Speed
- Stages starts with Gear 1 auto-selected
- Poor looking candy-clothes crowd with annoying looping animations
- Bad looking dust effect
- See-through (invisible) headlight covers
- Car handling is not predictable (You can't feel always really you drives the car)
- No real rally stages exist, 'Your stage' is boring after the first time
- Achievement animations looks total the same as most of mobile racing games
- Several Graphical glitches (flashing up black box when you drive reverse)
This game is defenitely worse than Dirt Rally

Excellent game.  This is how you do game design.  Slick, satisfying stealth entwined with a unique and well done story to add context to everything.  The game slowly adds new elements as you go to keep everything fresh for the 100 levels.  But each level only takes a couple of minutes to complete, making it very hard to put down and giving you that constant "just one more level feeling".
One odd design choice was the fact that there was no punishment for dying at all.  If you die and go back to a checkpoint, your time gets reset too, meaning I wound up completing most missions way under par time on my first attempt (albeit with a few deaths).  Checkpoints are plentiful, and thus the game did fall a bit on the easy side.  There is an option to ramp up the difficulty that removes checkpoints altogether though if you're a true masochist.
100% recommended - go get it now and support this excellent developer - and check out Thomas Was Alone as well.

A clear gameplay recipe: avoid simulated guards' cones of vision, recuperate gems and walk to the extraction point. A handful of useful gadgets, suppressing noise or diverting enemy attention, enable a variety of puzzles and solutions. All of them are put to good use, though the stun gun is quite overpowered and makes any level easy. Hack your way through barriers and mazes, hide behind covers, lure enemies, and expose the evil corporation that has taken over the UK.
Volume proposes a satisfying take on stealth where being seen and chased on purpose is often briefly part of the solution. Its story is surprisingly engaging and smoothly crafted with top quality writing. Adding a narrative could have been entirely optional here but it turns out to give the game most of its charm.
While the AI is overwhelmingly dumb on the surface – guards forget you the moment you're out of sight and react very mechanically to any situation – its highly predictable patterns ensure this game remains securely in the realm of puzzles, not simulation. The gameplay is somewhat reminiscent of a real-time Hitman Go, except less cerebral and more action-packed with the rush of pursuing enemies.
The game yields a satisfying progression curve and proper introduction of new enemies and mechanics. It is lightly challenging and never unfair.
Restarting sections only becomes mildly irritating in later levels while you wait for your gadget to reload. The overhead POV works perfectly for most of the game but makes avoiding lasers unnecessarily difficult.
Between the regular campaign series of 100 levels, near-endless and free online community contributions and the included editor to create your own challenges, there's no shortage of content.
Small levels are completed under a few minutes each. I found it best to play this game in small increments, completing 10 or 15 levels at a time and taking a break.

Vermintide gave me exactly what i expected it to give me. It is a great game for playing an hour or two and then going to do something else. Quests take a felt 15-25 minutes and are nicely balanced. The voice acting is quite nicely done and helps to immerse in the game world at least on the first playthrough.
Like in L4D missions are much easier with a crew that keeps together and uses the classes well. Playing through the campaign on normal took me a combined 6 hours but the loot system keeps me wanting to play and i would like to see some dlc adding more missions and equipment.
The combat mechanics are fun and the game encourages you to use all of your abilities and try different characters.
Enemies work very similarly to l4d, you have your basic fast attackers, assassins, swarms of weak enemies and a big tank enemy. Since those enemies are not brainless zombies though (but indeed pretty awesomely designed intelligent rat creatures destined to bring the apocalypse upon the world) there are some more advanced ctitters with poison grenades, chokehold sticks and miniguns which require teamwork to be defeated.
I did have some connectivity issues which were probably host-dependent since the game has a system which automatically assigns a host. Failing missions over and over due to suddenly losing connection to a host is frustrating and i hope future patches will fix this issue.
Overall i can recommend this game to anyone who enjoys first person hack and slash games and wants a quick rewarding experience with a dark, bloody art style,

Valerie Porter. A 1920s woman who desires to be a star reporter. When she achieves her dream, she gets more than she bargained for. Murder, political scandals, and the mob are just some of the things our intrepid, plucky heroine investigates in her search for her next story.
I'm a fan of search-and-find games like this, so I had to buy it. I wasn't disappointed. The gameplay is excellent, if not very challenging. The objects aren't too hard to find, especially since you can view a silhouette of the object. The ability to recharge your hints through linking items, finding batteries, and a train/trolley ride every level is great, though I rarely needed to use the hints myself. The puzzles throughout the game are not too challenging either.
The graphics are superb. The backgrounds and the items are all detailed and good-sized, so there's no pixel-hunting. These areas are photo-realistic. The characters are more cartoonish, but still very well-drawn. The scenes in between that further the story are even more comic-like, but not in a terrible way.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game. The plot, graphics, and gameplay were excellent. Though not very challenging, it's good if you just want to have fun and enjoy a game without having to struggle. I highly recommend this game to any fan of search-and-find games, anyone who enjoys a good mystery, or anyone who just wants to play a fun, yet simple, game.

I love this game already, and I'm not even done.
One day, I found this game. It looked interesting, so I put it on my wishlist, and bought it 50% off later.
My money was not wasted, I'll tell ya that.
I always have been a fan of tactics. I've played RTSs like Age of Empires and Dawn of War. However, nothing I have played comes close to this game. Y'see, this game means it when it says you make the tactics. The whole thing is controlled by you. The only limitations is how many doors you have to kick. In some missions, you can get multiple deployment zones and entry points and so on... you know what? I think i'll make an example.
One mission takes place in a pleasant little cove beside the ocean. My job is to go in, kill the bad guys, and arrest some dude. The game let me position my team where I wanted. Some came in the front, some in the sides, heck, I was even able to deploy one guy coming in off of the beach. Any door there was into the house, I could take it. That's one of the thing I like; there's not one way of entry. If one way works, try again another way in. Another thing to mention was just the level design in that they were kinda realistic missions. A bank robbery, a drug raid on a house in the middle of nowhere, a hostage situation in an embassy... these were all missions I did. The situation and level design made it feel like this was something that could actually happen.
The next big thing was the character customization of your team. It wasn't just expendable idiot numbers 1-10. It was different people. As well as their loadouts, you could change their picture and names. I soon had a team named after me and some of my friends. Also, they had randomly generated stats. Each person had things they were good at. This person is a great shot, this one can defuse a bomb quick, this one reacts quick... Once again, they weren't just a group of idiots with guns, they were actually different and unique. Then after that, there's 5 different classes you can take, all with special weapons. Stealth (my favorite, as they don't alert every bad guy this side of the equator you're here) take silenced weapons, Assaulters use rifles and SMGs, Shields, well, carry shields, Breachers are shotgunners, and finally, pointmen are cowboys. They all have very different play styles, so this adds in another factor of you asking yourself, "Hmm... what guns should I shoot people with today?"
Now, there are some downsides to this game. First of all, if you don't like tactics, waiting, and thinking, this isn't your game my friend. I know of another game that might be more your pace. It's called Call of Duty. Look it up. Second, this game can sometimes be just INFURIATING. I'm a bit of a perfectionist, so when I do missions, I wanna get all the points, which includes no casualties. That can be very difficult. The odds are often against you. You might have forgot one dude, one corner, one tiny bit of area, and sometimes, that can lead to a mission restart.  Some missions are nigh impossible to do. And then there's everyone's favorite, HOSTAGE SITUATIONS. If one of those guys so much as hears you, they'll shoot a hostage. One hostage dies, and you have to stay completely over. One single innocent down, and it's back to the drawing board. So, this game can be just extremely hard, but I will say this; it feels so rewarding to finally see that "Mission Complete" screen at the end. This is a game that will make you work, but when you get your reward, it is amazing, because you know you earned it.
All in all, I love this game. I haven't played for very long, but I have a lot more to do, including 4 campaigns. That's right, this game has campaigns. I didn't cover everything, but I covered what I think is most important. Now shouldya buy this game, or go waste you money on things like beer, hookers, and collage? Well, I dunno at the full $20, but if there is another sale when it drops to $10, I'd definitely recommend picking it up. It's a fun game and there's a lot of replayability in it. so, kick doors, down tangos, and rage over hostages being executioned because Larry in the back tripped over a twig.
And that concludes that. Now go home and read a book or summtin'.

Mods.
Mods mods mods.
(Don't mind the hours, I played this on another account)
The most appealing thing for me from this game is the insane ease of modding. You can make a gun that fires at 10000 RPM, create a nuclear grenade, have a BULLET weapon fire two shots, or have armor that makes your troops invincible by just changing a line of code in a text file. I'm not exaggerating.
Or maybe not. Maybe you feel like that all Carbines/ARs are completely stuck in Semi-Auto is silly for you and you want to make them fire in bursts or auto. Maybe you feel like a weapon is a bit underpriced or overpowered. Make some quick tweaks why not.
You can also modify any official level in the game. Not only does that give many easy templates to work with and learn the editor without a tutorial, you can have a two dozen enemies in the first map just 'cause.
You can also change parameters like how fast your troopers move, how fast they aim, their FOV, etc. I know some people like testing that kind of stuff in video games.

Some deverlopers say that their game has modding support. There's that and there's this. You don't get this much freedom in most modern games anymore.

There's no other feeling like crawling around in the tall grass as you slowly inch toward that Allied tank eighty yards in front of you carrying nothing more than a STG-44 and a Panzerschreck with only one AT rocket left, praying that you're not unlucky enough to be spotted by the tank commander surveying the surrounding landscape through his binoculars.
This game is filled with these moments, instances where it's kill or be killed and by God it's not going to be you who's dying today, so instead of running and gunning, you think before you act. A vital network of trenches has been overran and it's up to your company to take it back. You fix your bayonet and wait until the man operating the MG starts to lay down suppressing fire, then you're off, sprinting alongside the others on your team onto a field towards a trench wondering if you'll get picked off by a stray bullet; if you'll meet death today. By grace or luck, somehow you make it to the trench line, and when you begin to clear it out you stab a man in the chest when he manages to catch you by surprise, good thing you remembered to fix your bayonet. Now that the location is secure you prepare yourself for the inevitable counter-attack, while someone on the far side of the battle waits for the MG to begin firing as he fixes his bayonet...

Dirt 4 is almost the perfect rally game. Nearly every conceivable flaw you can list that could potentially hinder the experience in a rally racer, Dirt 4 manages to address with an astounding an ingenious simplicity. What’s more, it takes the franchise back to its rally roots, taking cues from Dirt Rally, while also making sure that it’s not nearly as inaccessible as the 2015 game was.
Right as you boot the game, Dirt 4 gives you the option to select between two difficulty modes- Gamer and Simulation. Simulation, as the name suggests, is a difficulty that is catered towards rally simulation veterans, and for those who played and were able to master the mechanics of Dirt Rally, you’ll feel quite at home with this mode. For those who are not that deeply entrenched in the racing simulation genre as some others might be, though, there’s the Gamer mode, which takes the mechanics of the game and tones them down to a great extent.
Gamer mode is a great entry point for those who are looking for an accessible experience and don’t play too many rally simulation games. With plenty of driving assists, much more responsive, slightly arcade-like mechanics, Gamer mode lets you get familiar and eventually comfortable with the game’s systems. When you’re comfortable enough with what the game tries to be, you can finally jump into Simulation mode- not a choice you have to make, by any means, but definitely one that is recommended.

I was introduced to the series by Dirt Rally. For me, this game so far seems to answer everything that I hoped they would change about the DR experience. It has a much deeper career mode, a free roaming mode, proper tutorials, the cars actually have weight now, and the courses are smoother and wider (ie more drivable) than in DR.
Yes, the sim handling is different than in DR, but different doesn't mean that it's worse or less of a simulation that in DR. The cars in Rally had no sense of weight, and so were constantly threating to slide into oblivion or be launched into the sky at any moment. That's exciting, sure, but that doesn't mean that it's some kind of perfect simulation. I've got no doubts at all that D4 is a better simulation than DR.
Now, this game holds your hand more at the begining where DR just kind of threw you into the pool right away. So yes, even in sim mode it's going to be easier at first, particularly for DR veterans. I'm really not worried about it, and I'm sure that this game is going to be challenging enough to be a lot of fun.

However, I believe in this product so much that I have, in the past, bought copies for family members and friends. I bought additional copies for myself on steam so it will always be handy. I think there are people who could probably hate this game, but again it deserves its own genre and it feels completely unique. I recommend playing Warband over the earlier Mount & Blade regular version. Fire & Sword is fun insofar as it offers a more clear storyline a new setting and guns, but again Warband is more enjoyable for most. If you are like me you will have fun, you will get sorely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when captured, and eventually get tired of this game. This is by far one of those "must-have" games.  Strange that I didn't know it until recently, even though it's already been around for a few years.
In short, Mount & Blade is about you as a nobody in a strange land, and there are several routes for you to embark on (with nothing stopping you from completely switching path from time to time).  A few examples are: an outlaw rogue, or a mercenary working for a king, a vassal of a king, or a king yourself (hardest route, though several alternative strategies exist).
The game is, regardless of your choice, a lot about combat.  And this game gets that combat mechanic spot-on right.  Even after a hundred hours, I still find every battle fun and skill-improving, even when fighting a bunch of farmers to a standing army of hundreds, wether is is attacking/defending a castle or a city or just a village.
I had bought this on a sale, but I would also buy it again at full price.  The game is worth the tag.

To sum it up, it's Left For Dead's gameplay in a Warhammer setting with a few twists.
As with Left for Dead you're stuck in a city overrun by an endless horde of monstrosities. (In this case, it's the rat-men known as Skaven)
You and 3 buddies are charged with completing a variety of missions such as collecting supplies and gunpowder for the resistance, clearing paths for smugglers through the sewers or destroying Skaven war machines in their own camp ets.
In each you will be faced by a variety of enemies ranging from tiny, one-hit to kill, slave rat hordes to massive Rat Ogres who can soak up damage like a drunkard soaks up alcohol.
It's enjoyable and can become quite challenging at higher difficulties with more enemies and less pickups. (Even friendly fire is an option.)
There's a decent variety of weapons and classes to try out ensuring there'll always be something to suite your playstyle.
It's not perfect mind you, there's a bug or two that pops up every now and then but they're small enough to ignore or share a giggle at. Otherwise this game is good entertainment at a reasonable price.
Recommended for anyone who enjoys taking on hordes of enemies with a handful of friends but is tired of zombies.

Volume, to put it simply, is a stealth game in the vein of older games like Metal Gear.
*Possible Spoilers*
From a top-down perspective, you control Rob Locksley, an everyday man who decides to rebel against the government that controls his country. Enlisting the help of a malfunctioning AI named Alan, who reluctantly guides you through the game, you plan out several heists using simulations, and stream them to people worldwide, who carry them out in real life.
*End of Potential Spoilers*
The game's controls work fantastically, with only occasional hiccups with quickly snapping to cover, though that tends to be when I have messed up and need to frantically button mash. The game's graphics, while simple, work really well with the setting of the game, and have a certain charm to them. The voice acting is nicely done, and has some good voices attached.
Overall, Volume is a brilliant game, with a great story, good controls, and one of the most satisfying endings I have ever played.
