Zup! is a 2D, block-based physics puzzler where the aim is to manoeuvre a blue block among stacks of other blocks and guide it safely onto a green platform for a certain length of time, which will open a gate and allow you to pass onto the next stage.
Blocks come in different varieties and have different properties - yellows ones are loose and can be knocked around freely, but purple ones are fixed in space, while green ones move in set patterns until touched where they then become locked in place. But it's the red ones that really do most of the work, as these are explosive and will be your main method for moving your target blue block around the stage.
There's obviously a trial and error aspect to the game, but the quick restarts (which are automatic if the blue block falls into oblivion, or manual at any point with the R key if you prefer) make things pretty quick and painless, so you'll never have any trouble with it for too long before making progress.
Everything looks adequate without being spectacular and is more or less what you'd expect for a game of its price. Audio is kinda meh as the ambient music is incredibly low and barely audible while explosions are almost overwhelming in comparison. I think I muted the game by the second or third of its forty-something stages. Speaking of which, there are an additional twenty available as free DLC which will extend the challenge and add maybe ten or fifteen minutes to the original twenty-ish minute experience.
Generally, the puzzles ranged from easy, one-time attempt stages that were largely forgettable, to slightly trickier ones that might require exact timing or have to be done in two or three phases rather than the one-shot deals of the starter levels. I personally found these much more fun and satisfying to figure out and complete and kind of wanted more by the time I'd finished with them.
While there's argument to be made about the value of this game - as I've no doubt there's likely similar free browser games available that'll do the job just as well - whichever way you cut it, it's still fairly cheap and I enjoyed my brief time with it. It's an entirely non-essential distraction that ends just as it's getting started, but I still had fun and found little to complain about.

After playing around ten hours, I can't get my head around the "new" handling characteristics of simulator mode. It felt much more lifelike in DiRT rally. The tarmac tracks in Spain are a slight exception but overall it feels as if there is way too much grip and it's almost impossible to induce a slide. Rear wheel drive cars behave eratically on gravel and have a nasty habit of unexpectedly whipping round, and using the handbrake to induce a slide tends to bring the car to a standstill unrealistically quickly. The rear wheels grip again way too quickly when you do manage to start a slide and the car bogs down on hairpin or acute corners because of this.
The track generator is fantastic. Yes there's
to be repetition of corners. You will occasionally see the same corner twice - maybe even in the same stage - but the idea behind it is that you can't just learn the tracks. The little hidden features in the pacenotes are a welcome addition. I've noticed Nicky Grist hesitate occasionally when reading them which can potentially set you on edge. You may find yourself having gearbox issues partway through a stage, if you've damaged your electrics on a night stage you may find your headlights flicker or stop functioning, or another car may have had an accident and you will see spectators warning you of the hazard ahead. You'll have to see what else the game can throw at you yourself.
You'll notice that there are relevant comments in the news between stages reflecting your performance or the performance of other drivers in the championship, telling you if the weather forecast is likely to change, or even telling you when there's been a rockslide on the tracks in Spain meaning there's debris on the road.
If it wasn't for the (in my opinion) poor handling I would thoroughly recommend this however I'm hopeful that Codemasters will implement some changes in future that will alter handling. I did not enjoy DiRT 3 very much throughout around 30 hours of playtime, but find DiRT 4 is perfect as its successor. If you're looking for DiRT Rally II this
but it's a good new take on rally simulation. An enjoyable game nontheless.

DiRT 4 improved on what was missing in DiRT Rally and what had been in previous DiRT Game.
You can earn money, buy cars, make your own colour scheme, fire&hire crew members, do sponsoring contracts and modify your car performance wise

Crew management is pretty straight foward, there are roles for every part of your Crew, you can fire old crew members and hire new ( better ) ones which can help you in certain aspects, but you have to keep in mind that their contracts expire, so you can't have them forever, and they dont accept too low payments either!
Sponsoring is straight forward too, basically the same system like GRID, absolve specific challenges to get a small bonus.
Car Performance: this is a tricky one
i did not quite understand the whole system yet, but from my understanding it works like this:
You car starts out with parts that are pretty "ok", and cost that much too, you can "upgrade" these parts for cheaper ones which aren't as reliable but are cheaper and faster to repair, more expensive parts survive longer, but are expensive to repiar.
There are also "Upgrades"
You can upgrade pretty much everything, your PR departement, the Lounge for your Crew, Food/Drinks for them, Tools etc. You can upgrade these to make your crew feel better and more comfortable around their work, thus increasing their productivity, but you can also invest in the multiple not-so obvious things such as a slight reduction in parts costs, upgrades for car parts, higher space in your garage etc.

The dreaded topic, the Physics.
The Developers stated that it was an improvement over DiRT Rally, i won't disagree, nor will i agree.
i have never driven a Rally Car before so i cannot say which is more realistic, but what i CAN say is that DiRT 4 Overhauled some aspects of DiRT Rally's Physics.

This is a fantastic game in its own right, but also the best indie game I've ever played. The graphics and sounds are a bit underwhelming, but the gameplay more than makes up for it. I have several hundred hours of play time in.
Rise from a nobody to the king of the entire nation, or support a king and fight for his right to rule- the choice is yours. Build an army. Increase your skills and equipment. Gather hero characters to yourself, skill them up and equip them. Fight your foes in melee or ranged combat, mounted or not (again, all your choice). Siege castles and towns to make them yours, and then hold them against your enemies. Court and marry a lady, if you wish. The game's depth is perhaps a bit less than its breadth, but both are well above average. There are different kingdoms in the game, each with their own flavor, advantages and disadvantages. You have the ability to make choices and decide your own fate- including which kingdoms to ally yourself with, which characters to befriend or make an enemy of. The replay-ability is definitely huge.
The first couple of hours of gameplay can be very challenging, as you strive to keep your army fed and build it up from a ragtag handful of men into a force to be reckoned with. I think many people can get frustrated- I recommend reading tips and tricks from other players to get over the initial hump.
Personally, I think Warband is the best way to play the game- sword and fire messes up the world a bit IMO, and the other alterations such as Napoleonic times and such do the same. There is some very good player-created content available as well. No doubt you too can lose hundreds of hours into this game.

Probably my second favorite co-op survival game, my favorite being killing floor 1. The game plays very simular to left 4 dead, but manages to stand out through several tweaks to the system.
What vermintide does to set itself apart from left for dead:
-The game is more focused on melee combat
-Much superior melee system
-Characters and weapons who playstyles differ from each other, which is done in such a way that there is benefits for creating a well-balanced party but not necessary for success
-Specials that are different, but familiar to left 4 dead's specials
-A loot system, which can be good or bad depending on your viewpoint.
I would also like to note both games do a great job on creating characters with their own set of personalities through commentary and chatter between themselves. What vermintide is weaker than left 4 dead at is that it is somewhat unpolished and buggy which can lead to some very frustrating moments. Vermintide has a decently high skill ceiling and can be difficult, which can either be deterrent or a selling point depending on what you look for in a game.
Overall I feel vermintide is new and better take on the left 4 dead and model and would recommend it to anyone who likes horde survival games like Left 4 Dead.

This is more of a warning than a review, and I believe the devs should be able to fix the issue I have with the game with time. It is Early Access after all.
That said, the game unfortunately runs pretty terribly on my end. Admittedly I do not have the beefiest GPU (GTX 970) or CPU (i5 4690k), but based on the screens I've seen of this game it's kind of bizarre to see my rig struggle with running this game. I've basically been unable to play as a result of really nasty stuttering and massive frame drops.
Anyways, my main issue is that there is no way (to my knowledge) to be able to turn on V-Sync. I only have a 60Hz monitor and the game as it stands likes to run at about 100-120fps on average, so I am forced to render twice the amount of frames as I need which not only leads to some really bad stuttering when the framerate drops, but also puts unnecessary pressure on my GPU and makes it generate more heat for no reason. I have tried every option of forcing V-Sync via my GPU's control panel, but it has had no effect on the framerate whatsoever.
Even if the option was added however, I'm not sure it would help much. Even when I am forced to run beyond my monitor's refresh rate, the game will drop below 40fps sometimes which is only exacerbated when you combine that with the potential drops from 120fps all the way down to 40fps. It feels like it may be a bit unoptimised which is a much more serious problem than the inability to turn on V-Sync. It is these problems I have that as a result make the game feel unplayable for me, and I have not been able to actually review the game for what it actually is (but do intend to if the issues are ironed out).
So yeah, if you are someone who does not play beyond 60fps and doesn't have a high-end GPU, this is just a warning in case you feel you will be met with performance issues when trying to play this game. The game looks cool and appealing, I just can't enjoy it as it stands.

Thomas Was Alone is the previous Mike Bithell game, and it was a cute, minimalist platformer that I enjoyed but would probably never play again. It was fun and all, but it's really a once-and-done kind of experience. Unless you forget the storyline (which forms the bulk of the appeal of the game), there aren't a lot of reasons to keep playing. Volume isn't like Thomas Was Alone much at all. It's better.
Volume is a top-down-ish stealth game. The plot is an anti-authority tale that is irrelevant, because it's not the game's strong suit and it's almost incomprehensible. It's an awful lot like Metal Gear Solid, in that you sneak around and avoid the enemies' vision cones as you make your way through 100 core levels. Each level takes no longer than 5 minutes to play from start to finish, but that's assuming you never fail. You will fail, but the game is extremely generous with checkpoints. The punishment for failure is a matter of seconds lost, not minutes. Each level has a par time. It's almost encouraging speedruns. It took me about 6 hours, 20 minutes from game start to game finish.
The stealth feels rock solid. If you're not in a vision cone or making noise, you are absolutely invisible. Unrealistic in a way, but completely unambiguous. The game has a crisp, clean design with an abstract, minimalist style. Everything is sharp polygons, which is appropriate as the game takes place inside a simulation. There are a half dozen enemies with their own strengths and weaknesses. Each level is almost a puzzle to be solved with your sneakiness and tools. The tools are doled out most of the game, so even late game is introducing new mechanics.
The whole 100 level core game could be considered an extended tutorial as the game comes with tools to build levels yourself right in the game's interface. No need to download sketchy mods or juggle programs; you can browse user-made levels from within the game as well as create your own. The user-made levels also feature a rating system, and there are "staff picks" if you don't trust the judgment of other Volume players.
Where Volume stumbles is in its story and controls. As mentioned earlier, the story is a muddled mess. It's obviously of the "people rising up against The Man" variety, but it's dribbled out across level descriptions, in-game notes, and three cutscenes. It's not great. And the controls, when played with a standard Xbox 360 type controller, are a little weird. The game fully supported the controller, but all of the button prompts were for keyboard + mouse controls, so I had to fumble a little to find the right buttons. Even with the correct buttons located, the controls seemed to eschew the face buttons in favor of the triggers and bumpers. It's a very minor quibble, but still a little jarring in an otherwise extremely well-made game.
I had a hard time putting Volume down. I spent most of a holiday weekend playing it, and it very much invoked a "one more level" feeling in me. It's not a particularly difficult game, but in the more challenging sections, I truly appreciated knowing that it wasn't an unfair game. It's just that I hadn't figured out how to "solve" the particular challenge yet. It's not going to set the world on fire, and it has a couple of minor flaws, but it made me happy for being such a straightforward and enjoyable game. It's well worth your time for a weekend.
I'm sad that I cannot recommend volume, as it should be right up my alley. Unfortunately the stealth is a tad too bare-bones for me and the voice acting grates on my nerves. A shame.

Mystica is plagued by two major problems, in-frequent updates and as a by-product low player population.
So why would I recommand Mystica?
Well for one it is cheap to the point of basically being free (Frankly I would like the price to go up for Mystica so that the Developers actually have some form of income coming in from Mystica.) So the risk of trying Mystica is really only time, and even then you could likely figure out if Mystica is your jam or not quite quickly.
Secondly there is a certain charm to Mystica that is hard to find in other games, it's kind of hard to explain this point really. Just something you have to experience for yourself.
Lastly is the community, granted the online population for this game is often 0 as a result of the extremely in-frequent updates. But when there is people online it's great. Hands down the friendliest MMO community you will find really.
The Developers themselves are extremely friendly as well, it's just unfortunate they don't update the game very often. Which I can understand to a point, as Mystica is a very niche game which is bringing in basically no income for them, so they have to focus their attention on other games that actually make money, Bills need to be paid afterall.
TL;DR - Try Mystica, you have very little to lose even if you don't enjoy it.

What is "Door Kickers"? As you probably already know - it is tactical real-time strategy that puts you in command of a SWAT squad. Of course, this game has some squad based mechanics that are similar to ones of games like XCOM (managing squad, class system, various equipment, leveling up, researching new skills, etc.). However, unlike XCOM, the gameplay here is real-time based which makes it much more engaging. The way orders to units are given can be a bit complicated, but soon you will realize that it's quite simple. Talking about controlling units, you can prepare a plan for them before starting the mission or you can give orders on the go; it's all up to you. The game has a lot of missions and most of them are quite challenging. There is also a random level generator and, if you are creative person, you can use the tool for creating custom levels. All in all, the game is really nice; the only downside is grafics quality - It's not that bad but it could be more deatailed. I would not recommend buying this game for it's full price, but be sure to grab it when it's on sale.
P.S. By the way, this game also has a "replay" feature, that allows you, upon successful completion of the mission, to watch how your SWAT team swiftly secured the building and saved hostages and even save the replay as a videofile.

I played this game in closed alpha/beta, and it hasn't really improved in a meaningful way since launch. I've been supporting this game since it was called "Legends of Lore", a completely different game. I'm even a Legendary Founder, for ♥♥♥♥s sake. The game has grown in a completely different direction than the glimmer of hope I saw in this company and its plans to make an actual mmo.
The combat has been improved immensely from the closed beta, but still needs a tremendous amount of polish. The enemies aren't overly difficult anymore, and rarely require the use of a potion. This is a stark improvent over the closed beta and alpha, where the fights were often one sided and unfair.
This leads me onto my next point, the ui is garbage. The game is made for mobile phones, and that's where it went wrong. If you want a successful game on pc, you have to stop force feeding a terrible ui to the pc userbase. It's bad enough to have to go into a menu during a fight just to heal, but to click through multiple screens to enter my jumbled mess of a inventory is a bad idea.
The graphics are incredibly dated as others have said, but this is because of mobile being a limiting factor as well as their target demographic. Artix Entertainment has always been a children's web browser game company. Their means of making cash, Adobe Flash, is being forced out of the market in favor of html5 for security reasons. They have to reach out to a new group in order to stay profitable, as many of their older games are dead.
It has a nostaligia factor to the many of now teens-20 somethings who played the original Adventure Quest many years ago. This is where it stops, however. The gameplay is mediocre at best, the ui makes the experience terrible on pc and the game feels like a giant cash grab with its crafting system.
It needs a lot of work, and I wouldn't invest in it just yet.

I loved the first Hotline Miami. That game basically showed me the beautiful world of indie games (ok, there was Braid, World of Goo etc). Indie games are very special, because it can contain all the crazy ideas that triple-A games would never do.
Hotline Miami was frenetic, high-speed, aggresive top-down ♥♥♥♥´em up masterpiece with, believe it or not, very interesting and trippy story. And it was frustrating. Oh my gaaawd the frustration. Press "R", you know what I mean. But for me, this masterpiece had one ace in the sleeve. Music. Music was the thing that blasted this game to the sky heights. Music was so memorable, so weird, yet so awesome. Horse Steppin´, that is all I am gonna write.
The second Hotline Miami was one of my most anticipated games of 2015, no kidding. Was it worth waiting? Well, yes.
The gameplay is enhanced by some cool stuff like akimbo shooting, two-in-one characters (Ducks) and lot of other things.
What about the music? The soundtrack is totally amazing. For me even better than in the first Hotline. There is around 50 songs. And every single one is great. I am listening to it every day, at least two or three songs. Yes,  I am addicted :) Psychedelic, trippy, 80s - 90s sound. You will love it. (Carpenter Brut is now my favourite "band").
The story is very, very complex, because often you do not know if it is hallucination or reality. And it is great. I am not saying that I understood the story, but I enjoyed it very much ( like I would enjoy David Lynch movie). Also the story was quite longer than the first one.
Now the bad things. Level design. Level design is, compared to the first one, different. First one was with close corridors, so there were lot of opportunities to make a 10x+ combo. In HM2 you will  spend lot of time covering behind the corners, waiting for the enemies to approach you. It is more stealthy and more frustrating (yes, it is), because since the levels are very open, enemies can spot you from a very long distance and you will end up dead not knowing who shot you (later on you will learn that it was that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the other side of the map). This was basically the only thing that bothered me during my play. I would prefer more closed levels like in the first one.
Besides of this, I enjoyed HM2 a lot and I hope there will be a third one.

Mystica: The Ninth Society is a MMO with a small community at the moment. It seems that this game has a lot of potential and can be really good in the future. The game at the moment has no story, therefore you are just wondering around aimlessly in the overworld killing enemies.
Okay so let's start off with the gameplay of this game. There really isn't much to it, it's a MMO which (at the time of writing this review) has a small community that comes onto the game regulary. The game starts off by having to register, and then pick between 3 classes: Warrior, Wizard or a Villager. Now to me this isn't a very interesting set of classes, the thought of having a villager as a class doesn't sound very appealing against the Warrior and Wizard class. I personally chose the Wizard, because long ranged attacks that the Warrior shouldn't really have. The game starts you off in a small village, there isn't much there at the moment, one of the guys talks about peopel that might try to scam you for you're account (because you have register to play this game) and the other talks about skill points, how to attack and the what each of the stat points help with the characters progression. The tutorial however doesn't seem to tell you how to equip items onto your character. Although it's pretty simple (just double click) it seems that it should at least be mentioned to help the player along. The game to me brought back a nostalgia feel to Zelda, but I soon found that this game doesn't play at all like Zelda. Attacking enemies is very dull, you stand next to the enemie and hold down ctrl to attack the enemie. You take it in turns to attack (I think) and then either you die or the enemie dies. If you die you lose X amount of exp and then get teleported back to the start. If you kill a enemies you get set amount of exp and the possible chance of the enemies dropping a weapon or gold. This sort of fighting mechanic isn't very fun to play, right from the start it sounds like a grind for exp until you can proceed to the next area. Talking about enemies, there is really not much varation of enemies. There doesn't seem to be any mini-bosses or anything other than enemies that are constantly spawning in certain areas of the map. The game requires A LOT OF GRINDING, I wouldn't suggest choosing the wizard. You don't get a spell until you gather enough money (grinding) by killing more enemies (more grinding) and hoping that the enemie drops X amount of gold (Again more grinding). This game just feels like a grind fest, the enemies are unbalanced when it comes to the levels, and some of the areas are too high leveled to be able to kill them. The controls feel clunky, and you are restricted to only squares to walk on, so no walking in the upper left if you get what I mean. The only good thing about thid game that  can think of is that there isn't any microtransactions... yet. I hope that they don't add any that makes you pay for coins or something like that because that will ruin the game completey.
Mystica: The Ninth Society, the art style are 16 bit graphics and are kind of fitting for the type of game this is. The tiles seem to fit in with the 16 bit kind of art style. I seem to remember the sprite that they are using in other games... except recoloured. There is minimum frames to each of the characters and enemies, the battling doesn't even have a animation, just a red cross or whatever you are using as a weapon that is across the enemies you are attacking. I would like to see some walking animations from each of the characters, instead of it looking like it's sliding across the floor.
The game itself isn't worth buying at this moment in time. There is still a lot of work that needs to be done by the developers before I suggest buying this game for £1.59 at this current state. I really want to like this game, but it just feels too grindy, maybe that's just the Wizard set maybe the Warrior set is much easier. I really hope that the developers pull this game up and make it really good.

I’m pretty vulnerable to stylish presentations, enough to help me overlook weaker parts of a title. The clean, ultra-modern look of games like Lumines or EDGE is one I’m particularly fond of, and that’s a space shared by this snappy stealth outing. Volume does a lot right in its look and feel, and luckily doesn’t fall apart in its gameplay either. It might not be revolutionary in its mechanics but the solid quality throughout should be enough to keep anyone heisting through levels.
There’s a lot of story to unpack in Volume so I won’t explain too much, but you should understand enough to get the appeal. You play Locksley, a charming British fellow living under the dystopian rule of Gisborne Industries. He’s hacked his way into a volume, a VR index of real-world locations used to train security in how to keep the valuables of the ruling class away from the grubby hands of the proles. With the help of the volume’s AI custodian Alan, Locksley intends to broadcast himself breaking the security systems wide open so that the people can follow his lead and retake their country from the rich oppressors.
It’s a clever set-up, casting you as a virtual streaming Robin Hood educating the masses in the art of wealth redistribution. Cleverer still are the little bits of dialogue between Locksley and Alan as the human fills in the AI on the events of the past nine years, both for his benefit and for you, the player. The writing here is something special, and further elevated by the very high quality of the voice work. Interactions are charming and flow naturally, giving you plenty of insight into Locksley’s laid-back hacktivist views and Alan’s shift from company algorithm to reluctant anarchist. There are even some worthwhile notes to find, everything from adorable office romances to background on the rise of AI to a tutorial message that realizes its already obsolete.
The story is secondary to the stealing, of course, and Volume gives you plenty to steal and plenty of challenges in stealing it. In each level you have to grab all the gems (VR abstractions of valuables) and reach the exit. This is complicated by patrolling guards whose vision cones need to be avoided by ducking under counters, vanishing into lockers, or using tools to distract. The tools are the most interesting part, numbering nearly a dozen and offering all sorts of ranged or delayed distractions, stuns, or cloaks to get your past particular hazards. One level is full of tiles that make tons of noise, forcing you to pick your way to the other side of it without alerting any guards. At the end you get the Mute which allows you to run silently back through the level and grab everything you missed.
Interesting levels like that are an important part of what makes Volume worth playing. Admittedly the creeping about virtual rooms and hoovering up gems can get repetitive over the game’s 100 levels, so unique layouts or challenges help alleviate that monotony. The different tools are spread wide across the entire range of levels, along with new obstacles like force fields and alarms and guard dogs. You’ll also come across neat gimmick levels like one based on Pac-Man or one where the simulation is glitched out. Later on levels also open up a bit more, offering a choice of tools to tackle them and paths to take.
The stylish graphics and engrossing story do a lot to make the game feel polished, but there remain aspects of the gameplay that detract. The biggest for me is how dim the guards can be once they find you. I don’t mind their small vision cones and I like how predictably you can lead them around with audio distractions, but it’s laughably easy to ditch pursuers in some situations. Guards need several seconds to draw a bead on you, but if you can break their line of sight they’ll only follow to the last place they spotted you. Couple this with the little shimmy you can do around corners and you can simply lose an alerted guard by ducking all the way around a pillar. However, if you get caught out in the open with no corners to juke around, you have no recourse whatsoever.
Volume isn’t a particularly hard game, and it certainly won’t tax your brain the way Thief or Mark of the Ninja will. But as a puzzle game it very much gets the job done, with a layer of panache that makes it worth your time. I can’t guarantee it’ll carry you through all 100 levels, but it’s captured my attention and kept me plugging away at a dozen or so levels a night. I haven’t gotten tired of learning to use new tools or hearing more about the grim cyberpunk fate of future England, even if their guards are kind of stupid. Volume does a lot with solid, if simple, mechanics and offers plenty of style to keep its substance fresh.

The game is interesting to say the very least. It does a decent job at mixing stealth and timing puzzles but feels like it has an identity crisis at moments. Overall it feels very polished and the controls, ui, menus, art, sound, and transitions are all top notch. I don't pay much attention to the story so if its good or not I can't really say.
Each level is pretty linear and are partitioned in a "mini-puzzle" fassion. Each level containing multiple "mini-puzzles" to avoid a bot in some way to collect gems. Collect all the gems to open a waypoint to complete the level. After each of these mini puzzles there is almost always a checkpoint. Checkpoints are so common it ends up in "I can just half♥♥♥♥♥this attempt with no consequence with the hopes it will somehow work". Maybe if they were stretched out a bit more but as is  and the game feels easy even though I know I fail A LOT. Yes it helps doing the same thing over and over but actions lose their consequence and that feeling of "I'm repeating the same♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; is still there only you're doing a shorter task over and over. It's a double edged sword and I don't think the dev really got around it too well. Some levels you run backwards after aquiring a different gadget, disabling alarms, or something else but most of the mini puzzles you complete have no bearing on future events once completed only compounding the feel of linear levels.
The mechanics are varied and introduced slowly; new enemy types, different gadgets, enemy behavior, and environment props. The build up of these new mechanics feels really strechted out and makes the first couple of hours feel a bit slow but I had moments in every other level that kept me playing. Once all of the new enemy types and gadgets are introduced it really varies the gameplay. At the same they are more segregated than I'd like.
There are a few things wrong with the bots.There's a delay before the bots one shot you and if you break line of sight the delay is reset. This way you have a chance to run away. A short range, wider fov, peripheral viewcone would be nice even on pawns as you can easily slip around a corner or stay just out of his fov when you're close to a bot to go unoticed. Also the attempt to "search" is so basic its almost insulting. Go to the last known position of the player/sound, wait 2 seconds and return patroling. Later in the campaign the bots might activate an alarm if they see the player but the bots all go to the exact same location. Also the patrol routes are exact with no variation. All of these feel like decisions to adhere to the puzzle play style but again makes the game feel easy. This is the identity crisis I was talking about.
I feel really conflicted about this game but tried my best to articulate why. It's worth a buy on sale or if you like puzzle and stealth games. If you just like stealth games it might be best to wait for a sale even if the idea of adding puzzle elements sounds interesting because like I said it's a little too much puzzle not enough stealth for me atleast.

I had seen videos of Doorkickers before receiving it in a bundle.  I have played games such as Frozen Synapse and Jagged Alliance 2, and found the tactical genre to be a bit of a mixed bag.  So when I saw videos of Doorkickers, I didn't think much of it.  SInce it came with a bundle of other games I liked, I gave Doorkickers a shot.
And it was far more enjoyable than trailers and gameplay videos could get across.
The joy of Doorckickers is primarily the tactical system.  From movement to breaching to cover and co-ordination, you have to think about them all, and the game lets you control it in a simple and easy to use interface.  The method of control is also flexible: you can plan every move in advance and let the scenario play out, or you can pause at any time to alter the gameplan when things go sideways.  Changes can be made in real-time as well.  The end result of all of this control and flexibility is a deep tactical planning stage followed by a typically short but explosive rush of action.
Each mission stage is a layout of a building, structure, or outdoor location.  Warehouses, beach villas, parking garages, multi-story luxury apartments, and more... with Steam Workshop and a built-in editor, the variety in size, complexity, and tactical options are impressive.  You can play one off missions or dive into multi-mission campaigns where injury and death are long-term inhibiting factors.  A hardcore ironman mode is available to prevent repeated attempts at a mission to save key teammates from injury or death.
Most missions have multiple tactical approaches based on which officers and gear you use.  Some missions are somewhat linear and can be approached methodically, while others usually turn into controlled chaos that you pray doesn't get you killed.  There is an element of RNG to shot accuracy, stopping power, and enemy numbers, but solid tactical choices can be made to deal with it.
The squad you control is manned by officers you can customize in name, callsign, appearance, and gear.  Skill perks are squad training that all officers get the benefit of.  Roles include pointman, assaulter, breacher, stealth, and shield.  Each fills a vital part of the tactics, and they feel useful in their dominant environments.  When the mission changes, you can change up all gear and role assignments.
Weapons range from the ubiquitous handgun, SMGs and carbines, shotguns, and non-lethals.  The variety of weaponry is sufficient, and a slew can be added with the Workshop.  Gear includes various armors, tactical grenades, cameras, and breaching devices.  It's fun to switch up loadouts, but there isn't too much here to overload the player with inventory management.
There are bonuses in each mission to encourage different playstyles.  Lone wolf tasks you with clearing a mission with one officer, which casn be incredibly difficult.  One award is given for playing entirel in realtime with no pauses.  Lastly, an award can be earned for planning an entire breach and clear in advance, hitting play, and succeeding with no pauses or changes to the gameplan.  This last award is the most satisfying of all, and when 5-10 minutes of planning leads to a flawless execution of a 3-4 minute mission... the exhileration is real.  You can also save replays within the game, or export the replay to a video file to share and cherish always.
Bottom line is that this game is a tactical dream that can be played for short bursts or full-auto for hours.  The variety and depth provide a solid amount of content.  Mods extend the life of the game and add all sorts of new weapons, gear, and interface alternatives.
If your satisfaction is partly predicated on price, I would wager $10 to be wholly worthwhile.  That's 50% off the standard price, which might be steep for most.  Luckily, the game has been around a while and sales on this title are frequent.
So gear up and get tactical!  It's time to sweep this hot spot like an efficient wave of justice.

Other than that minor detail, it's a great game that had me hooked when I was younger and even to this day. Heck, I've played it on steam for a VERY long time. The three different stories is probably my favorite part of the game along with the chao and whatnot.

The small, meticulously crafted maps are replaced with giant map after giant map. Any attempt at melee combat is incredibly tedious and annoying, and the extremely broken and as-of-yet unpatched AI for all enemy types ensures either an annoying experience or an unfair death every two or three restarts.
If they finished the game before release, I might recommend it.The game has great sound design and amazing visuals, and on its own is a great game. But the core mechanics and the systems that support them, which were perfect in HM1 are so unpolished, and so underutilized by the map design that it almost feels like they forgot what was most important to the game. It's a damned shame that this game has to stand far beneath the shadow of the first.

Expectations upon indie developers with a single major hit are perhaps the Damocles that keeps many of these creators stuck within their own strengths and genres to reiterate their past successes rather than branch away to different ventures.
It would be quite the accomplishment for Mike Bithell if Volume happened to handle being both an indirect successor to Thomas Was Alone in terms of gameplay and story depth from the 2-D introspective platformer about context into a simplified Metal Gear Solid game about its lack of context. Unfortunately, the execution falls short of handling both changes, which undermines the narrative praise from TWA and the gameplay potential within Volume.
As someone who appreciates the arcady-stealth approach from early Metal Gear Solid titles as well as the playful sandbox stealth games that followed MGS3, Volume manages to scratch that itch of the playfulness of disbelief and puzzle-like manipulation of the original titles that hasn’t been seen by MGS for a long time. Some people may dismiss this derivative nature to the VR package of MGS1, but Volume goes to show that just because a game has obvious source material there is still merit in the imitation. Even the minimalistic design inspired by the VR Missions feels distinct for Volume as the attention to detail of gameplay and style learned from Thomas Was Alone sets it within a game of its own right.
It would be easy to claim Mr. Bithell chose to focus solely on refining the gameplay without regard to the narrative touches that made TWA so beloved by many people. However, it’s the emphasis on gameplay that tells the half of the story by what makes Volume a sequel in its own special way aside from a subtle reference about the “seven architects.”
The real beauty behind Volume as a “successor” to TWA is how both the gameplay and narrative accommodate the transition from 2D to 3D with all the small touches of characterization found within Volume’s usage of shape, design and color. Whereas with TWA these small details and narration cemented strong personalities that gave faceless shapes distinct traits, Volume utilizes these details to inform the player about the level-design of the simulation, the real-world effects of each level and the growth of the main characters, Locksley and Alan. The one-hundred levels tell more about the plot than all the text-logs and prompts of every mission screen as the layouts are an idealized window of Locksley’s view of his battle and Alan’s adaptations to the level's design are his clarifications into the real-world. Despite how disjointed the narrative is with its overall exposition, especially with the antagonists not given enough presence, this is the caliber of quality that puts these games’ minimalistic design into a league of its own.

Having praised the small touches that tells so much about the game’s world and narrative, the actual plot behind Volume is far weaker because of how jarring the game’s events are to the real-world consequences it wants you to believe has happened. As much as the gameplay wants to work in tandem with the storytelling, it will constantly break any sense of disbelief from the simplest of unresolved questions to an option within the menu.
The set-up for Volume is you are playing an allegorical Robin Hood figure in the near-future where AIs have evolved to a point of competing with human labor as the resulting conflict has developed a dystopian England under a corporate entity that has monopolized the democratic process by merging the corrupt corporate interests with national security. Although we never really see the effects of this dystopian society on the AIs that emerged from TWA, it’s implied from the guards that they are as bound of their potential as the masses enslaved by their poverty. As intriguing of an idea for a retold classic, the process by which Locksley goes about to redistribute the wealth undermines the seriousness of this plot as he live-streams his simulated heists to steal abstract riches for the masses to do the dirty-work for him.
Sudden tone-shifts aside, the problem becomes worse when combined with the gameplay. As previously mentioned, one option allows you to set check-points rather than do a full-restart on capture, which doesn’t sound bad until you realize you can abuse those check-points to make progress just before you get caught. Furthermore, there are tons of gameplay elements that takes away all sense of realism such as enemies’ cone vision shortcomings and lacking peripheral vision, the unreal usage of gimmicks in each level like shadows, and the usage of sci-fi cyberworld gadgets. Even if you could ignore all these conflicts as “It’s a game” the amount of time given for the story that plays its events out as well as the fact that a public stream is not being countered by Big Brother is beyond believable.
To describe the matter more succinctly, many games nowadays have used the fourth-wall to immerse the player with the consequences they make whereas Volume is the Deadpool of video-games where it is so immersed in breaking the fourth-wall it’s hard to take anything seriously.

As for gameplay, however, how does Volume hold up? The basic gameplay is a polished version of arcade-stealth controls that annoying lacks a run button but offers a whistle button to compensate for your limited speed with various gadgets, environmental effects and superb level-design. No level or gadget feels wasted in exploring the game to its fullest potential amidst its many constraints that will bother avid fans of Metal Gear Solid titles.
Perhaps this was done to not overwhelm the player with so many tools to use for every level, but the biggest problem with Volume’s gameplay is the one-item limitation for gadgets. The game plays so close to MGS and mimics its VR-aesthetic; however, it fails to capitalize on the levels of interactivity that helps mitigate the linearity of these games with open-ended tools of chaos. Even if this limitation was to keep the game from becoming too complicated or exploitative with abilities like cloaking, the game already requires you to pick-up gadgets in every level and there is a resource-meter to prevent spam abuse. (This resource meter is also an annoying anchor to gameplay as you have to wait for a full recharge every time you respawn, regardless if it’s ready for use.) Another form of anchoring the player is the usage of banter within levels that can last up to 90 seconds without interruptions when caught and the blaring usage of chase-music that baffles me how the alert-phase for a MGS-inspired game could get it so wrong with how abrupt it is and its lack of pace. (Even the name Volume feels misplaced in a game that has no sound mechanics.)
When it comes to the issues of Volume, it’s not one single matter that breaks the appeal of the game but the many small oversights and blunders that keeps a good game from being great.

As unlikely as the possibility of there being a direct sequel to Volume—especially if you consider how much each game has deviated in this “series” as well as the fact how the one-hundred levels explored the limitations to let the built-in editor and community explore whatever was left—I am excited to see what Mr. Bithell has in mind as there were a lot of lessons gained from Volume and a lot more left to be learned. The only thing I can hope is that any future limitations have more confidence behind them and seek to push the potential of whatever grand idea is in store.

My First Play on Launch Day in early Access Video & REVIEW:
PROS:
1) Awesome little sandbox online game where you can do whatever you desire!
2) Lots of different locations, dungeons, mobs, npcs, shops, and fun to be had!
3) A bank box to store your extra loot and gold and keep it safe
4) You can chat with other players online either privately, locally, or globally.
5) The game offers PvP once you reach level 10 (and the other player is level 10+)
6) This game will run on almost any old computer
7) The best part.. NO MICROTRANSACTIONS!
CONS:
1) Graphics are VERY dated and VERY simple 2D sprites
2) It's still rough and doesn't have key customization (for example i would love a key to auto target the nearest mob or player and couldn't find such a key)
3) Sometimes the attack Function keys you can set don't seem to respond when you hit them and they attack/spell is available you have have plenty of spirit to use it.. requires multiple presses sometimes, sort of annoying
4) Players can steal your mobs even at level 1 and also steal your loot if they move over your loot drop before you do
5) Because PvP is allowed, players can murder you once you reach level 10 and this might be a negative for some players.  I haven't reached level 10 yet, so I don't know if there is a penalty or karma system or if the victim of a pk murder drops loot or gold.  ..Will update once I find out.
Still, a very solid game for the price and knowing there is no micro-transactions is very comforting.  This game scored an impressive 78% on my scoring system in my livestream video above.  Highly recommended for RPG fans who can accept very simple 2D sprite graphics.   Easily worth it's asking price!

This game is brilliant.
Pros:
-The price point is extremely accessible
-There are no microtransactions
-The gameplay is very simplistic and somewhat laid back in a good way. There is a classic charm to just earning loot and new types of spells, leveling, choosing your stats, and exploring new areas with friends in typical classic rpg fashion with no bull.
-On that last note, this is an absolute must for co-op, collaborating and discovering the fun with others is half the game in my opinion, and this is entirely possible to do since the game is so accessible and cheap, plus this allows for way more strategies in a fight if you are using different classes.

I had seen videos of Doorkickers before receiving it in a bundle.  I have played games such as Frozen Synapse and Jagged Alliance 2, and found the tactical genre to be a bit of a mixed bag.  So when I saw videos of Doorkickers, I didn't think much of it.  SInce it came with a bundle of other games I liked, I gave Doorkickers a shot.
And it was far more enjoyable than trailers and gameplay videos could get across.
The joy of Doorckickers is primarily the tactical system.  From movement to breaching to cover and co-ordination, you have to think about them all, and the game lets you control it in a simple and easy to use interface.  The method of control is also flexible: you can plan every move in advance and let the scenario play out, or you can pause at any time to alter the gameplan when things go sideways.  Changes can be made in real-time as well.  The end result of all of this control and flexibility is a deep tactical planning stage followed by a typically short but explosive rush of action.
Each mission stage is a layout of a building, structure, or outdoor location.  Warehouses, beach villas, parking garages, multi-story luxury apartments, and more... with Steam Workshop and a built-in editor, the variety in size, complexity, and tactical options are impressive.  You can play one off missions or dive into multi-mission campaigns where injury and death are long-term inhibiting factors.  A hardcore ironman mode is available to prevent repeated attempts at a mission to save key teammates from injury or death.
Most missions have multiple tactical approaches based on which officers and gear you use.  Some missions are somewhat linear and can be approached methodically, while others usually turn into controlled chaos that you pray doesn't get you killed.  There is an element of RNG to shot accuracy, stopping power, and enemy numbers, but solid tactical choices can be made to deal with it.
The squad you control is manned by officers you can customize in name, callsign, appearance, and gear.  Skill perks are squad training that all officers get the benefit of.  Roles include pointman, assaulter, breacher, stealth, and shield.  Each fills a vital part of the tactics, and they feel useful in their dominant environments.  When the mission changes, you can change up all gear and role assignments.
Weapons range from the ubiquitous handgun, SMGs and carbines, shotguns, and non-lethals.  The variety of weaponry is sufficient, and a slew can be added with the Workshop.  Gear includes various armors, tactical grenades, cameras, and breaching devices.  It's fun to switch up loadouts, but there isn't too much here to overload the player with inventory management.
There are bonuses in each mission to encourage different playstyles.  Lone wolf tasks you with clearing a mission with one officer, which casn be incredibly difficult.  One award is given for playing entirel in realtime with no pauses.  Lastly, an award can be earned for planning an entire breach and clear in advance, hitting play, and succeeding with no pauses or changes to the gameplan.  This last award is the most satisfying of all, and when 5-10 minutes of planning leads to a flawless execution of a 3-4 minute mission... the exhileration is real.  You can also save replays within the game, or export the replay to a video file to share and cherish always.
Bottom line is that this game is a tactical dream that can be played for short bursts or full-auto for hours.  The variety and depth provide a solid amount of content.  Mods extend the life of the game and add all sorts of new weapons, gear, and interface alternatives.
If your satisfaction is partly predicated on price, I would wager $10 to be wholly worthwhile.  That's 50% off the standard price, which might be steep for most.  Luckily, the game has been around a while and sales on this title are frequent.
So gear up and get tactical!  It's time to sweep this hot spot like an efficient wave of justice.

I'm not a big gamer - in fact, I hardly have any experience with videogames at all (just the occasional PC games for me!) - but I really enjoyed this game. It's fairly quick - I was able to finish in about 5 hours. There's also not a whole lot of background story because you just jump right in, and I was perfectly happy with that. The puzzles ranged from very easy and intuitive to those requiring a little more creative thinking and time. There was at least one or two really challenging puzzles per level which was great. This is really meant as a relaxing, casual game that doesn't have a whole lot of depth to it. So, I can understand why some people may not like it. I don't think they are as "brutally difficult" as other users have described, but they will be challenging enough for those who are unfamiliar with gaming clues/norms/hints (i.e. the kinds of things you would "know" to look for only if you have gamed regularly in the past).
I didn't have issues with unresponsive controls, but I was playing this on my laptop.
The art was great - simple, colorful, imaginative. I found myself smiling at some of the very cute and quirky drawing styles. I sometimes get overwhelmed if there is too much going on visually in a game, so I can appreciate a graphics style where it is both visually appealing and well-balanced. I liked the change of pace (and scenery!) for the underwater levels, although I was also very happy when I was done with them. I think the biggest issue people may have is the learning curve with timing; however, I'm used to playing PC flash games and maybe I've just learned to accept it. It wasn't so frustrating that I ever quit the game, and it's not keeping me from wanting to replay it!
I would strongly recommend it for anyone who is just starting out getting into gaming or for kids - I would not recommend this for anyone who is looking for something with complexity or depth, whether in story line, puzzles, or otherwise.
Full disclosure: I bought this game for $1 and was really pleased with the amount of entertainment I got from it. I'd probably pay $5 at most if I had to repurchase it again. I don't think it's worth more than that.

I received Mimpi as a gift for the holidays, and while it has its charms, I feel that these charms are offset by a few very significant flaws.
Firstly, the charms. The game is super cute (like, have you SEEN that dog?!) and the music and general theme is totally funky and surreal. It's really neat, and definitely adds to the experience. Mimpi looks really great walking, jumping, and peeing around; just seeing it brought a smile to my face. Mimpi also has a hint system, which is great for someone like me, since I'm rather terrible at puzzle games.
Now, the flaws. Mimpi's control is... very loose. Extremely loose, in fact. I died many times making what I thought were sure-fire easy jumps because of this. It's funny at first, but it gets frustrating fast, especially after you manage to get through a difficult sequence only to die because of a minor gameplay hiccup. Mimpi's UI is also very unhelpful. Everything is unlabeled, so you have to really do some trial-and-error to figure out what buttons do what. This is a minor flaw, but one that I really feel like should have been fixed before the game came out (I really can't remember the last time I played a game that didn't have any buttons at all labeled). The puzzles themselves can also be rather repetitive and uninspiring; I saw many of the same types of puzzles being reused, as if they were just filler or something like that. It's a shame, since the puzzles are rather charming at first, but they get old rather quickly once you realize it's mostly all you're going to see.
Overall, I think that if you're willing to look past Mimpi's very loose controls and repetitive puzzles, then you might enjoy playing it. However, I'm not too sure if the charms of the game - which aren't really at all gameplay-related - make it worth it. In my experience, I tried liking the game a lot, and I really enjoyed the dog and the art, but, ultimately, I ended up disliking the game due to its gameplay. It's just not very fun. :/

To be enirely honest, I went into this with very low expectations. This was mostly due to my prior experiences with Super Duper Flying Genocide 2017, another recent title that markets itself in a similar fashion. "Short, Simple, Earn loads of achievements". And I'd be lying if I said this game is perfect, but I have to give praise where praise is due. This game really surprised me!
The very first distinction I'd like to make between this and Super Duper Flying Genocide 2017 is that unlike that dissappointment, I would actually consider this a game and a rather enjoyable and intuitive one at that! It is clear that Zup! goes for the same demographic; achievement hunters, completionists, whatever you want to call them. I consider myself part of that group, so I felt inclined to give this game a try despite my rather low expectations. Very much like the building blocks that you interact with in Zup! my expectations were blown away! This is definitely a puzzle game first and foremost, and an achievement treasure second.
Your objective is to bring the blue square onto the green tiles through the use of explosions. The red squares are explosive and clicking them will make them blow up, knocking any yellow and blue squares away in the process. It really is as simple as that. But just because the mechanics are simple it doesn't necessarely mean that the game itself is easy, in fact I'd say far from it.
The levels start out easy enough, and for the first few levels it feels like this might have actually been a bad choice after all, just another cash grab copy paste job with loads of achievements attached, but then you reach level 10 and things start to get interesting. As you progress through the game each level becomes more and more challenging and you need to both think of the right solution and make use of your reflexes and predictions to launch the blue square with the right trajectory and force to get it where it needs to be.
Soon I had forgotten about my prior pessimism and was instead joyfully exploring in how many ways I could try to knock the yellow block-towers down and with what sort of speed I could send the blue square flying in order to solve the puzzle in front of me. The simple yet addictive nature of the game had caught me entirely off guard and I was getting more and more intrigued and hopeful for the next challenge the game would provide me with...
And then it ended. Just like that.
If anything, that would be my only real gripe with the title, it is extremely short. I beat the whole thing with 100% achivements in only a couple of minutes, and I wish it would go on for a bit longer as I was actually having quite a bit of fun with it. But to be fair the game has a very low price point and the tags do describe it as "short" so I should have been expecting it to end rather quickly.
All that said, I hope you understand my thoughts about this game but in case I was too lengthy in my description of it and the enjoyment it gave me let me try to sum it up in a few short words:
This is a short but fun and intuitive physics puzzle game. I had a lot of fun with it and the achievements are a bonus rather than the main focus. I recommend this highly if you want some quick fun, and I suggest you pick up the Zup-Zup! Bundle which hosts all three games for a very affordable price. I have not yet played the other two titles, but if they are anywhere as good as this then I cannot recommend it enough.
Enjoy!

From my initial 3 hours of playing, I can say this game brings a lot of interesting ideas to the table for this franchise, especially the team management aspects of the career mode. The presentation and UI of the game is slick, while not being too flashy like the previous numbered entries of the series. Rally-cross is overall improved from Dirt Rally, and Landrush is a very fun palette cleanser.
However, the sim handling is an overall downgrade from Dirt Rally, even when taking the improved weight and aero into consideration. I don't follow the mantra that less grip = more realistic, but the rally cars in this game simply have TOO MUCH grip on gravel. The cars simply refuse to kick their tail out, even the RWD cars.
About the content of the game, while it's technically true that you can have a near infinite amount of stages, they are extremely bland in comparison with the hand-crafted stages of Dirt Rally, and with the limited amount of preset chunks that make up the stages, they end up feeling MORE repetitive. You will often see the exact same corner with the exact same scenery surrounding it multiple times in the SAME stage. As for the circuit racing disciplines, more than half of the RX tracks are carried over from Dirt Rally, and Landrush only features 3 locations which are all very similar to one another.
This game has a lot of potential, but unless Codemasters patches the handling and adds more locations to maintain variety, you might want to stick with Dirt Rally for now.

It's extremely difficult, if not impossible to accurately describe Deios II // DEIDIA. It looks busy at times, yet the gameplay is very zen. It has an 80s/early 90s design aesthetic, yet it's unmistakably modern, in no small part due to its abstract and mysterious cyberpunk-occultish setting, top-notch graphics and audio work, and the total confusion you experience every second you're playing it.
Although the game is certainly confusing, it's not particularly difficult. Obstacles include puzzles where you spam jump, move a ball or turn knobs, and gates which you unlock using currency (DeityCoin) that you find in the world or gain from the incremental mini-game. You can try cheesing your way through obstacles with the game corrupter, but it by no means gives you a significant advantage, as you have limited control over the effects, remaining airborne for 2 seconds respawns you, and you can't move if you're stuck in something.
+ Super interesting lore
+ Fantastic art style
+ Incredible sound design
~ Really floaty horizontal controls, although this is somewhat offset by the game corrupter
- A bit on the short side
- Incremental game seems to be more of a novelty than anything else (although maybe BARCHboi is trying to make a statement?)
- Going into fullscreen (which really improves the immersion imo) messes up the cursor and opening the console to do so takes a screenshot since it's bound to F12
Buy it if you want to feel like the apes in 2001: A Space Odyssey when they first saw the monolith.

Much like the original DEIOS (which I could never finished because of those damned boss fights), Deiois II // Deidia can described as such: A mystery that I cannot solve.
Perhaps the meaning behind the game is to invoke that sense of mystery, that sense of that there is a secret hidden deep within this game that you are supposed to find. Maybe that secret exists only within yourself.
Maybe I'm just stupid.
I've finished the game, or at least as close as "finding the end screen," allows it and while I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys experimental indie games, there are a couple of things that might turn people off. I think most can get past the cryptic elements of the story and just take the game as a whole work but there is one thing that cannot be overstated: the controls.
BARCHboi, I love your music. I love your aesthetic designs. I bought Deios and ended up buying the USB of this game AND a copy on Steam (because I honestly thought that I was missing files, you sneaky dev.) The general wonder of Deios, DeityNet, and DEIDIA keeps me coming back for more but my man, these controls actually *hurt* my wrist. They are floaty and imprecise, and the wall jumping can sometimes just come down to mashing. You've built it into the game well enough but when it gets to the point where I have to strain my wrists in order to get through some parts, it ain't working.
Regardless of that, BARCHboi has created something utterly unique. Depending on how much you spoil yourself you might not stay very long but just the work that went into the visuals is something else. The music isn't anything to scoff at either, this guy makes bangin' tunes. I hope to see more of his work coming on Steam.

Only recently started playing this game but I am definitely enjoying it! Trying to survive with friends and escaping maps is my favourite part :)

so, up front this game tries to do what L4D does, only realistically. depending on the difficulty, you can have
A: plenty of supplies/minimal zombies
or
B: you get two bullets per player and only headshots can kill the massive endless hoarde of zombies.
the inventory system does help to promote teamwork as you can only carry 4 items at a time. this includes healthkits, keys, flashlight, and weapons. sharing is caring in this game because you will run out of ammo. the accuracy of most weapons is a bit..touchy, but overall a headshot is a guarenteed kill. just be careful because every hit from a zombie has a chance of infection (server preference) and once a player zombie spawns, the difficulty cap starts to kick in.
because of the accuracy issues of the weapons + the sometimes laggy servers, player zombies have the run of the field and most other players will give up just to restart the round.
maps are usually a form of escape mode or "hostage rescue" where the players work to get from point A to point B with certain map variations (randomly generated objectives or closed off paths which force going a different way.) as much as one would thing this would help with the repetitive nature of the game....it doesn't. you'll still be doing the same thing over and over, but in a different path. the game is probably the most terrifying when played solo, but it's also the most difficult if you don't know what you're doing or where to go.
speaking of navigation, all you get is a phone giving you a general location to move to and a waypoint marker that has a hot or cold proximity counter. the instructions aren't always clear so get ready to be lost and confused for your first playthrough. objectives and instructions are given through a sort of text message system by one of the player characters (or just texting yourself solo) while realistic, it can be distracting to try and read your phone while being attacked.
there is a multiplayer versus mode as well, which is a deathmatch scenario with zombies thrown in for fun, but those servers are hardly ever populated.
overall it's an ambitious title that tries too hard to be realistic. you'll enjoy it for about a week unless you're a true co op zombie fan.

Any attempt at melee combat is incredibly tedious and annoying, and the extremely broken and as-of-yet unpatched AI for all enemy types ensures either an annoying experience or an unfair death every two or three restarts.
If they finished the game before release, I might recommend it.The game has great sound design and amazing visuals, and on its own is a great game. But the core mechanics and the systems that support them, which were perfect in HM1 are so unpolished, and so underutilized by the map design that it almost feels like they forgot what was most important to the game. It's a damned shame that this game has to stand far beneath the shadow of the first.

Volume is a great top down stealth game. And that comes from a person that doesn't enjoy playing stealth games, and hates most stealth sections in every game as I've hated bioshock's dlc and beyond good & evil for having them.
The story aspect of this game is pretty insignificant, I didn't get very intrigued by it. It has some collectibles laying on the ground, which interfere with the gameplay a bit, as well as talking sections during the level, which I didn't really like as I've tried to focus on them and just ended up standing in the middle of the level waiting for those sequences to finish.
The graphics are very neat. Pretty minimalistic artstyle showing the simulation's surroundings works very well with a stealth game, removes everything unnecessary and makes things very clear.
The gameplay mechanics were very appealing to me, they were also kept pretty simple but required figuring out the enemies as well as the gadgets. Those gadgets start appering after completing the first few levels, but are added throughout almost the entire game. They make the game really interesting and fun, as you need to figure them out, as well as apply them to get past various kinds of enemies, which all act somewhat differently.
The soundtrack was pretty nice, but I don't remember any of the tracks well, except the chase sequence music, both because I was caught a lot and it was really good and made me feel like a part of something really intense.
Overall, this game was a very good experience for me, and even though I didn't really enjoy the story, I've decided to go as far as collecting all the notes and 100% the game. Amazing stealth top down game, would recommend to any stealth game fans, and even people who don't enjoy them, same as me to at least give it a try.

This is, yet again, the same company trying new perspectives on their games. The same people that brought you AQW, DF, and the original AdventureQuest. This isn't a 2D Flash game anymore. This is their FIRST 3D UNITY GAME! I'd say they have a uniquely good start on it. I'm not too fond of some of the character design right now, but the maps look gorgeous. Sometimes, I just like to sit in Greenguard all day enjoying the view from a high/far away distance than return back to my recommended level map.
Granted, this game just went into open beta, and like most, if not all their games, will contain massive amounts of bugs. However, the devs usually work very well at being responsive to those bugs... even if they have to tell a funny story to describe it. xD
Gameplay wise, compared to AQW, it's much more improved, especially Mage. In AQW, Mage usually beats enemies with a stick (or whatever weapon you had) and use some spells. BORING! In AQ3D, you use a magic missile for an auto attack, dealing the same damage pretty much like the other classes, but it's actually ranged, which is what Mage is SUPPOSED to feel. It also has a charged skill in which you need to plan on your timing to stay alive to cast a fireball for massive damage. Anyway, what is the gameplay? It pretty much is like AQW, like I said, using 4 skills, plus your auto attack, in real time combat with your friends to take down a group of monsters and a boss. However, unlike AQW, it is not enhancement based, where you can apply enhancements to your gear, but instead, and Dragonfable players like me may recognize this more, it is stat based, where each item has their own stats that are better than the other, but sacrifice some other stat power instead. It makes you strategize more on what you want to focus on for yourself to survive a swing and a beating from monsters rather than making it simple that any casual can just join in and get off. This also makes PvP more diverse, when it comes out.
Another improvement is the chat system. In AQW, if you accidentally attempted to swear, it either doesn't send through and tells you a crazy swear word that you never typed at all (Seriously, I typed in a class and I got some Spanish word I never heard of!), some of it censors through with ****'s and makes it a bit confusing to read, or you get a temporary mute for like 5-10 minutes, maybe worse, if you intentionally cursed. In AQ3D, they take it down a notch and fixed a bit of those mistakes by replacing swear words with the usual &!#% vocabulary. That doesn't mean they probably won't ban you if you try to find a loophole though. It is Rated T, so I don't know what they're going to do about their chat system rules exactly.
One thing I do want to talk about is the UI. I'm not so sure about the in-game menu. I mean, I don't hate it, but for some reason, I don't like it either. Of course, not everything is final yet, but still. It's basically 2 buttons, one leads to your potion use and the other to a list of everything else. It just feels... different. Maybe I do like it because it's actually a legit pause menu kind of deal, but if you ask me, keep the combat UI from the alpha test, make it a little bigger, move the potions button to match it, and maybe move the UI menu to the bottom right. The combat buttons are a little... large, and strangely shaped as if it was your hand. Interesting design, but like a lot of MMORPGs I played (Or anything skill based like that.) just feel normal being at the bottom that are a bit more normal. Maybe have it as an option to switch between UI's? I doubt that could happen.
Lastly, I'm going to close this. This game has so much potential for AE. They are adding in new elements, whether they're useful or not (yet still looks really neat!), about every week when they can and they are rewarding the players that are testing the game, depending on your phase that you joined. Obviously, like I said, this game is NOT a full game, and it will contain bugs. People that are making small reviews saying it sucks are clearly not reading it's in Early Access for players to play a game BEFORE it's stable (or mostly stable). I really recommend this game. 10/10 for its decent state.

Reboot sequel to the original Adventure Quest from 2002. I played the original Adventure Quest for about a year and a half with periodic breaks back in 2004, the writing and gameplay were fantastic. It was one of the lesser known browser RPGs out there, however it held it's ground very well and had continuous bi-weekly updates for nearly 6 years.
The development team have always pushed out content updates based off of community feedback, something not a lot of games can do nowadays. Now, they are going a step further with true cross-platform support, the first MMORPG of it's kind! It may be primarily developed for mobile, the steam version still feels like a PC MMO. The amount of dedication the Artix Entertainment Team have kept with their titles has been astounding.
I have never been that big of an MMO genre guy, but this sequel really hit some nostalgia points for me. Happy to be a part of the testing phases of Adventure Quest 3D. I wish the team at Artix Entertainment the best of luck with the success of this game!

I've been playing Artix Entertainment games since 2005, this is their next newest title aimed at the older market. The game at it's core is well enough but it needs much more work and many things need to be redesigned or the game will fail. I can't currently recommend it for anyone, honestly the game should still be in late Alpha not open Beta.
The combat system leaves much to be desired as it was aimed at the mobile market, which is fine, but there's no depth to it.
The leveling curve is brutal, as one zone ends the next begins you'll find yourself two or more levels under the next zone.
The way to gain item currently is through crafting, crafting involves a lot of grinding for materials followed by a long wait time to get said items,
Zones are laid our poorly, with very little variety in quests or monster types. You can stand right at the entrance of a zone and complete 90% of the quests which mostly involve grinding.
The game is already accepting money for classes, items, and speeding up crafting. None of which should be included until a game goes live.
The AE team is already focusing on adding more content and limited time events while the game needs much more work before it's even ready to hit live.
Right now, I can only suggest playing AQ3D for testing purposes and to caution players about spending money until the team has gotten around to improving the games basic core.
