Every so often there's that one game that you see on TV that looks really interesting when advertised, and looks like it could be very fulfilling that first game for me was Sonic the Hedgehog 2006.  Firstly I was 6/7 years old at the time, everything looks different then second off, Sonic was the character that solidified my interest in games so I wouldn't hesitate to get if I could, I did and was not disappointed.  I'll explain that elsewhere.  Due to being young I never saw SA2 advertised but games within its era made references to it I only understood years later, so you can imagine how  felt when I got this and realised that it is some of the best sonic team have to offer.
Sure, it was easy to lose momentum in areas and having to wait to activate the spindash took getting used to but once you got the full set of powers you were almost unstoppable.  I know thta people would like another game like this but it's often better to leave things where they are.  Yuji Naka's not there anymore and neither are Yoshihisa Hashimoto or a lot of the development team, that vision's gone.  It's not impossible since Sonic Lost World PC has shown SEGA are doing their best to listen to fans but a lot of things are better left alone.
Bottom line, Story's great, multiplayer is good every now and then,  the character's are fleshed out enough and the gameplay is simple enough to warrant replayability.  I know many people find the original cast's voice acting cringeworthy but hey, it's better than mainstream series e.g COD, Tomb Raider, Battlefield and the rest where cusses are warranted every few minutes.  Definitely worth a buy if you haven't played the originals.

Do you like Tetris? Cool. Do you like fast-paced platforming? Cool. Have you tried them both at the same time? No? Try this game out!
I got this in a bundle, and (as is usual with any bundle game I haven't heard of) was not expecting much of anything. I mostly buy these bundles in search of a diamond in the rough, something I get a lot of playtime out of for around a dollar. While this game isn't anything incredible in particular, it IS quite a bit of fun.
You play a small person with a gun, and you must clear the level of all the blocks. The way to do this is to match colors of blocks, and shoot the group until it disappears. When the entire map is clear of blocks, you win the level and progress. There are different powerups and items, and you unlock new characters if you do well on the level.
The main thing I look for in bundle games are games that I feel compelled to keep installed. This is one of those games. I can see myself coming back to this every now and then for a twist on Tetris with some fast-paced platforming.

I bought this game for its interesting premise: what if you were trapped in a Tetris-style puzzle/arcade game, and had to survive the falling blocks?  I think I came into it with reasonable expectations, but Super Puzzle Platformer Deluxe falls short for me.
The gameplay is simple, fast-paced, and controls well once I got used to it.  However there were no instructions or tutorial provided.  I start a game, and I have to guess how to move, how to interact with the blocks, and even what the objective is.  I go to the options to see the controller map, and there isn't one.  You go to controls and you're already changing them, one by one.  I have no idea what the default keys are now.  Plus, the text is hard to read - always inexcusable, 8-bit or not.  My first impression could've been much better with just a little more effort on these points.
If you're in the mood for a cheap indie 8-bit platformer built around a few simple mechanics, I'd look at other offerings - VVVVVV, for one.

Volume is a top down stealth game where the emphasis lies on manipulating the guards' movements, rather than waiting for the right time to strike (for the most part).  The gameplay is at it's best when you're fluidly navigating around the map between multiple guards, distracting them and ducking into cover to get to your objectives.  Sadly, only a quarter of the levels pull this off well, and the game suffers from some poor decisions later on; certain aspects, such as shadows and veil, simply seem to take more from the gameplay than they add.  Ultimately, however, the stealth is satisfying, and the majority of the puzzlelike levels are fun to beat.  My biggest gripe would be the low difficulty.  The majority of the 100 levels are too easy, taking under five minutes each to beat.
The game itself has a gorgeous art style and soundtrack, with a surprisingly decent story.  I experienced only a single bug, and that was that the game first initialized with a very low resolution, in windowed mode, meaning I had difficulty navigating the menus to up the settings.  After that however, the game played perfectly.
If you want a distilled stealth experience I would definitely recommend Volume.

Volume is very remniscient of Metal Gear Solid 1+2 VR Missions becasue of its top-down perspective and very explicit vision cones and consistent guard behaviour. Because of this explicitness, and its generous checkpoint system, it allows the player the courage to make some bold plays. Even in the first few missions (that thankfully omit or make optional the more obvious tutorialization) there are some edge of seat sneaking moments.
One thing that this game could do a lot better is narrative content pacing. Remember in the old days of GTA III where you'd drive during a conversation, and then wait just outside the destination checkpoint because they weren't done talking yet? That happens to a pretty insane degree in Volume.
It's awkward being in a timed first mission (that normally takes 10 seconds) waiting for a 90 second conversation to finish. It's awkward when a few levels in, they introduce a fairly complicated gadget at the same time as revealing the first major plot twist. I actually didn't catch everything the first time through. I attempted to re-do the level after completing it, just to sit in spawn and re-listen to the (geniunely interesting) cyberpunk politi-military dystopia backstory unfold, but it seems on retries they squelch the conversation. Great for speedrunners, not so great for a distracted audience.
Other than that, I'm having a lot of fun, 20% into the story. The gadgets are cool and somewhat unique, the introduction of mechanics has been at a perfect pace, and the story seems to have a few remaining tricks up its sleeve.
Definitely check it out if you're a sneaky sneaky boy.

Its called "Dirt 4" and not "Dirt Rally 2". The numbered Dirt games were always designed for accessibility, and 4 is no different. Funnily enough, it does get pretty close to Dirt Rally's driving if you turn all the assists down in simulation mode, so I'm not even sure what all the crying is about. Besides -- DR had way too little grip, especially on tarmac, which is now correct in DR4. So it's not a "step back in every way", thats for sure. For those who aren't obsessed with the idea of 100% simulation, the good news is that DR4 is a great rally game. I'm a bit sad to see the diversity in the disciplines just kinda disappear, but I suppose I'd rather have this over gymkhana. The added progression and team building to the career mode is a welcome change, and the track generator works fairly well. Graphically the game isn't staggering, but it does run extremely well even on lower spec PC's in exchange.
Overall a solid package.

So far, the game is really fun and I'm finding the initial experience of the physics quite good, but I feel a bit let down on the side of performance and graphical quality. I understand that you have to make sacrifices for stuff like procedurally generated tracks, but it shouldn't be nearly this bad in Landrush and Rallycross.
So, somewhat positive so far. The team management is deeper than I expected and I'm liking the more structured career mode.

"Like DiRT Rally but better" in terms of handling doesn't seem to be true on dirt.
With all assists off on a steering wheel/shifter/pedal setup, it still feels like there's several assists on to keep you from oversteering half the time. Like everyone else is saying, the tarmac physics seem to be a good bit better than DiRT Rally's, but the gravel/dirt, the name of the game, feel behind. AND THE CO DRIVER IS TERRIBLE.
Aside from that, I'm really liking the career mode and the stage generation changes the entire game. You can't practice a few dozen stages and then beat the times of anyone who hasn't practiced in multiplayer (which this game actually has, unlike DiRT Rally). DiRT 4 doesn't rely on track knowledge, but pure rally skills. You have no idea what the track is going to look like four corners into the future, or even if you'll be able to see the track without fog creeping in or your lights malfunctioning. Your co-driver is everything, which leads me into the next big issue:
Co-driver call timing. I've had the "open hairpin left" call only come up as I was passing the apex of the hairpin turn, way past the point of no return. Without playing the same track twice (usually), there's no way of knowing and accounting for this aside from making all of your calls earlier which can throw everything else off. The calls also come at random enough intervals so you don't know if that left 2 is 100 meters away or 10, which is infuriating to say the least. It's not a huge issue in multiplayer since everyone hears it late, but in single player, it definitely can be. This should be a simple fix, but it's a problem for now.
The steering radius is finally fixed, something DiRT Rally could never do. If a specific car's wheel will only turn 540 degrees, your steering wheel will only turn 540 degrees. If it's 360, yours soft locks at 360. This was incredibly annoying in DiRT Rally but they finally fixed it here.
I have to say it's a great game overall, at least this early into its release. You start to get used to some of the reused track segments, and I'm not sure how well this will age, but it's nothing gamebreaking yet. DiRT 4 seems to have the truest rally experience you can get, with the risks to not upgrading parts of your car, having your team miscalculate repair times, dynamic weather, instrument/part failures depending on damage and part quality, having each course be new to you, weighing winning vs appeasing your sponsors, etc.
They definitely have the foundation to improve upon, like adding more than a few team decal options, including some more 'fun' gamemodes like cat and mouse from DiRT 3 (since they're catering to that audience), fixing the dirt physics and overall physics for the historic rally cars, and one thing I'd love to see - rally with an actual person as your co-driver.

TLDR: Fun first couple of hours, got ruined for me at Level 3.
The beginning of the game was quite fun, the graphics are decent (even though not nearly as nice as the sceenshots up there) The Infanterycombat was done nicely, but a little samey... In Games like Battlefield 1942, from the first second of the game you could chose from 4 Countries 4 Classes with all the Gadgets, you could drive tanks, fly Airplanes, even command submarines. In this game you start with a rifle and some granades. Thats it. And it will be for about ~3 hours. At this point, you will have also gotten a SMG and a Jeep-like-car. For one of the Factions. Everything must be unlocked.
However Matchmaking was nice, meaning I as a new player was mostly playing with other new players, and the community was also helpful in a sense, that the guy who already had a jeep would actually wait till the jeep is full until driving to the front, so noone had to walk. This is also necessary because the game doesnt feature front-spawn, squad-spawn or anything. Its always from the back to the front.
Somewhat dissapointing was the lack of levels: Until Level 3 there are only 3 Levels. After level 3, some more (3?4?) were added. Theser were not "skirmish" but were assault. (For Battlefield players: not conquest but domination)
When I hit level 3 with one of my Characters (you start with 3 - one of each faction) the game changed drastically - for the worse. The reason for this is, that after level 3, matchmaking seems to believe that you are now a diehard-professional and throws you into games with all other players. Now in a game like, lets say battlefield, the skill-difference that would be given in a case like that is reduced, because if you get for example the Tank, you might win against that better player that only got the jeep, Airplane beats tank and so on. Skill surely matters, but you can have fun (and some feeling of accomplishment at the end of a round) in a group with way better players.
In this game, this problem is actually enhanced, since every player has his own gear/vehicles, meaning as a new player level 3 you can have (if you specialized in tanks) a Panzer 1 or equivalent in uselessness. If now you as an inexperienced player with a panzer 1 are thrown into battle with highly experienced players driving Panzer IV (Tiger) or equivalents, then its just not fair game. If you picked infantry, you will find yourself at level 3 with your regular rifle and a weak SMG. The experienced, better players, however, have sniperrifles, stronger rifles, stronger SMGs and so on. Because this isnt unfair enough yet, they will also have their guns modified with all sorts of enhancements, making them even better. The game is not fair and as a (nonpaying!) new player you're mostly there for the enjoyment of the highrank players so they can boost their stats a little.
The "grind" (leveling up and unlocking new things) goes horribly slow. I played 5 hours so far (and was pretty good before level 3) and am still only that level. To unlock everything you need to get to level 18 i think (or 20?) with that character. But then you only have 1 (!) character with that level, meaning now you have for example a "German Tankdriver", who can literally not do anything but drive a tank, he cant even USE rifles! Not to mention the other factions. For each faction you will need ~4 Characters to cover most of the game! (one Tankdriver one Pilot one Sniper one Frontline Soldier) Also: The Leveladvancement slows down drastically meaning I spent more time playing my level 3 guy than I spent on level 1+2 together. If this keeps going like that, going from level 10-11 will already take Weeks!
THE BIGGEST FLAW:
You will have to grind for hundreds of hours for decent gear. OR you might just buy it, because EVERYTHING can be bought instantly, and since, lets say that tiger tank, is not "cosmetic" this game is DEFINATLY Fee to Pay/Pay to win, whatever.... If you've seen my Hotline Miami review you'll know that it's one of my favorite games. When I heard that the 2nd one was confirmed, I tried my hardest not to get my hopes up too high. The first one was so good that it'd be near impossible to live up to... or so I thought. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number blew me away. At first I thought it might be the fact that I might've just been expecting it to be good, but then I found myself clearing rooms with a pistol while a guitar riff started going off in the background and dismissed the the notion almost instantly.
Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number took all of the great aspects of the first installment such as the intense, fast gameplay, the action-movie grade music, and the pleasant graphics, then put all of those on steroids. The story wraps up nicely, answering most questions the first game asked, introducing a bunch of new interesting characters. Unfortunately since it does this, the game had to compromise the freedom to choose whichever mask you want on whatever mission you wanted to use it on, instead only allowing certain masks to be used on specific missions.
I definitely recommend this game to anybody and everybody that enjoyed the first game.

Sonic Adventure 2 does NOT deserve all the praise it gets, yes the Sonic and Shadow stages are fun for the MOST part. But the rest is just not fun. The mech stages don't control very well, and untill you get the hover power up for both Eggman and Tails, you will suffer many, many deaths, and even after you do you will still fail with all the cheap enemy placements and cheap shots, there were many times where I reached a platform, but got hit by an enemy which would cost me a life, and it doesn't only happen in the mech stages either. The early treasure hunting stages can be fun when you have a pattern to find then Master Emerald shards or keys, but it still can only be enjoyed at random, but both Knuckles and Rouge control very well.
The camera is TERRIBLE, I have died multiple times because of it, and why can't I freely control the camera? You can only move the camera to the left and right, but if you move or jump the camera snaps back to where it was in the first place, plus if you're playing a mech stage you can only move the camera when standing still! Why isn't the camera always behind the character? Some times the camera is in an akward possition and 1. it can feel very disorienting and 2. it SOME TIMES changes the control, but not always, once again feeling disorientig, if they just left the camera behind the charater it would have been much better.
Ok, now the stages: for the most part they aren't (that) bad or maybe just too much trial and error (Which many people criticize Lost World for but almost every Sonic game does it, especialy the classic games) like the grinding stages Sky Rail and Final Rush (There are other stages that do this FYI), but there are a few that are terrible like Mad Space and Crazy Gadget these two stages play with gravity. Mad Space controls change every time when you go on the under/up side of an asteroid, and to put it briefly the controls shouldn't change at all. As for Crazy Gadget, the fault is in the camera once again. If they just left the camera behind Sonic it would of been fine.
The story has so many plot holes that it's not even funny and the voice acting is awful (thus the reason why I leave it on the Japanese dub), So why do I still recomend it? Well like i said the Sonic and Shadow stages are almost all fun (looking at you Crazy Gadget), the sound track is fenomenal and you might just fall in love with the Chao Garden. So despite every thing bad about this game, I still like it, and recomend every Sonic fan to at least try it.

How I would like to describe this game is: Imagine Minecraft and Ark Survival Evolved had a baby together. Let me explain.
While Minecraft simplified everything to a whole bunch of cubes with low res textures, Ark Survival Evolved tried to be really close to reality using advanced world designing and nice looking textures trying to mimic real world. Ylands stands in middle. The graphics are obviously more advanced than Minecraft but remains a bunch of polygons. They are not as refined as Ark's graphics but a bunch more sophisticated than Minecraft.
In Minecraft, you should hit stuff with your hands and/or tools. In Ark, you can gather few small objects on ground and make tools to gather bigger objects (rocks, trees, etc). Ylands is closer to Ark. You actually don't end up breaking stuff with your hands. You gather few things interacting with objects on ground and have to make tool for heavier duties. I didnt play Ark in a long time but my guess would be that the gathering system is just more advanced and more complete in Ark than the one of Ylands. But the general idea is the same. And I prefer this over Minecraft smashing-all-you-can blocks gathering mechanic by far.
At this point, I'm not sure exactly how deep Ylands is and will be in term of survival. It seems more advanced than Minecraft as you need to eat to not die from hunger but I have no idea if you have to avoid storms and stuff like this to avoid dying from cold or something. In Ark, you have to manage almost everything from hunger to thirst without forgetting to keep you warm enough during cold nights but also cooling you enough during hot days. Ylands doesnt seem to be as sophisticated as Ark and honestly, I would like to see a bit more survival aspects in Ylands without necessarily becoming as crazy as Ark is. It would make the game better.
Everyone whines about the shop and I dont see why. The shop is costmetic only. Don't buy if you don't feel like it. When I bought, what mattered to me was: Can this game worths anything for the 8$ I'm paying? Is it working well? Is it full of bugs. crash? Answer is: NO! Game works flawlessly so far. No bug, no crash.. I'm not saying there are NO BUGS at all. I'm saying this game is more than playable and way better than most EA games. You are not buying crap that is not working. This game is working well. Maybe they could add a bit more content it's true (and they plan to) but, you still pay for a working game. You can survive, gather, build.... it's working work in progress. Not a huge mess of bug and crap. If the only reason people leave negative review is the store then it's just sad. Review the game for what it is. And ignore the store. Overwatch is paid game with a store. Destiny 2 is a paid game with a store. Are people complaining about it? NO! Why? Because it's COSMETIC crap. Who cares!
Honestly, this game could be/should be a simplified version of Ark.. while Ark require, in my opionion, way too much investment in term of time played, Ylands seems way easier. Maybe a bit too easier. Making it a bit more hard would be nice but without becoming as crazy management as Ark can be. But it doesnt deserve negative review. It's working and the price is pretty low and the ingame shop can be easily ignored completely without missing any content of the game.

I feel that this is a very good game. I like the game concept and pacing of the missions. The missions are interesting but short enough. The game mechanics are not difficult to learn, but level design and the equipment customization ability allows one to try multiple approaches to complete a mission. With good planning of equipment and paths, the team can complete the actual mission in very short time.
There are some things that can be improved. For example, the UI makes it difficult to pick individual team members when they stand very closely together. Path creation UI can also be improved, e.g. to allow easy modification of an early segment without having to redo the rest of the path. The variety of weapons also don't seem to matter so much -- for example, many of rifle choices for assaulter class don't seem to offer distinct advantage compared to e.g. P90 or SAR-18 option. Lastly, it's better if some action options are added, e.g. ability for a team member to look around and clear the room before moving. At the moment, there's only option to look at one direction, confirm that it's clear, move slightly, look at another direction, confirm that it's clear, and so on. Another ability that will come in handy is the ability to synchronize team member to only move after a flashbang (without using go codes), the ability to specify alternate action (e.g. when the door that is supposed to be breached is already opened by someone else), and ability to combine actions on one item during planning (e.g. unlock the door, then throw a flashbang through it).
Having said that, those issues are minor, and I still highly recommend this game.

Larks and frivolity await those who try to enter the big top at the circus. Dare the ringmaster use those animals after that scandal? Will the clown's facepaint reflect the innermost thoughts of a damaged and troubled mind? Will the lion eat a child?
All these questions are very good but when we get to the nub of the issue, they are irrelevant.
Darkest Hour: Europe '44-'45 is a reality tv show starring Vanilla Ice. This show aims to recreate the horrors of the western european theatre of war via partying on the Jersey Shore. With ensemble cast members such as Joe Scificiccicio, Emily "Cut-throat" Furzenschieldfelmacher and Kyle Scudding the whole affair seems somewhat "in terrible taste". The recreation of the battle for Iwo Jima is not only rather inaccurate (There were NO Japanese Cavalry divisions that consisted of Samurai riding Panda bears) the makers also seem to have forgotten that this battle did not actually take place in Europe, a little known fact.
How can I recommend something like this when "Big Jack's Circus", the local performing act, is struggling to keep the business ticking over? With a ringmaster who is going bald, a potent metaphor for him losing grip of life in general, leading a cast of performers who'd rather not be there with the zooalogical equivalent of a septic tank kept in the back for the animal sections of the performance one must wonder: How can we enjoy life around us when so few others enjoy it with us?
What can one reviewer do in the tide of content that flows upon him? Is it possible for him to keep up with every single game without having to cut corners whether in terms of his product or his very own thoughts.... his very own mind?
The worst bit of this is that it doesn't support controllers so jog on Vanilla Ice, we'll be watching some other circus.
Or will we?

REVIEW UPDATE FOR 8.0 (Nov 11th 2017)
Here I am in 2017 writing an update to my review - the amount of work the authors of this mod put into making the game even better astonishes me. The new 8.0 update fixes in-game VOIP so you can communicate with those on your team nearby you in addition to using a new squad-radio. The new squad system improves gameplay and teamwork dynamically - it's very project-reality esque. A new squad-command system allows squad leaders to direct their squads fire or movement. Squad leaders can also give defend and attack orders on the objective map for their squad to see as well as pointing out enemy tanks, infantry movement or enemy defences for the entire team. Squads can now move supplies using logistic trucks in order to construct Platoon HQs, Sandbag Defenses, and even lay down forward static AT guns.
On the battlefield, squads will often find themselves skirmishing other entire squads - using flanking manuevers and utilizing defences, rallypoints and support weapons to overcome the enemy force and take the objective.
This mod is worth buying the base game (Red Orchestra: Ostfront) several, several times over. You can pick this game up for cheap, especially during a Steam sale. Buy it, install it, play it and enjoy it because this hidden gem of a game never fails to satisfy my WW2 realism hunger.

You're a little block-shaped guy trapped in a Tetris pit and given the Polar Star from Cave Story. Your mission is to achieve a high score and survive for as long as possible against colored blocks and hazards constantly falling on you. You can clear blocks by shooting at them, and any adjacent same-colored blocks will also be damaged by your shots. Destroyed blocks drop little triangles (also from Cave Story) which will level up your gun. Getting crushed by a block will level down your gun, but most hazards (including the spikes at the bottom) will outright kill you and end your run, so you’ll have to be careful.
The main gameplay takes place in eight endless levels, each of which has its own set of hazards. Through continued play, you can unlock the different levels, as well as different characters, and about thirty “survival” challenges each of which will require you to dodge a preset pattern of hazards falling on you. I found everything in this game highly addicting and satisfying to defeat. The instant death traps were indeed frustrating, but they made the eventual success that much sweeter.
My favorite part of the game had to be the soundtrack. Unlike most retro-inspired chiptunes which sound like the NES, this game’s music is beautifully molded after the Sega Genesis (or perhaps old AdLib midis, if you prefer). There wasn’t a bad track in the whole game, and they all got me pumped to try again just one more time.
The game’s about 10-20 hours long depending on your skill level and your desired goal of completion. Getting the very last few achievements requires beating some sadistic levels which require you to survive for thirty seconds against a terrible onslaught of hazards. They are difficult, but manageable with some persistence. My only real gripe with this game was that the fourth level (Cookin Cave) seemed to be the hardest and most frustrating with some instant-death hazards which seem to come out of nowhere, but it’s doable once you notice the patterns in the level. Overall, the game’s length was about perfect and it didn’t overstay its welcome.
I recommend it to all achievement hunters, and anyone who likes the looks of the trailer. I think I’ll be having fond memories of this game for quite a while, at least until I can get the awesome music out of my head.

This is a third-person stealth puzzler with stylized graphics. The game takes place in cyberspace, with the character 'Rob Locksley' (a not-Robin Hood) taking stealth action against a totalitarian regime that has taken over UK. There is a 80s-90s retro feel to this, the plot bringing to mind a punk mentality and comic books like V for Vendetta. The main gameplay influence of course would be Metal Gear Solid, but Volume is surely a game that stands on its own feet.
There are a 100 levels to the game, with each one taking about 10 minutes to complete (I am currently at 27 %). Gameplay feels crisp, fresh and fast. While the visual look is stylized and minimal, there are still a decent amount of items and environment features that can be used.

This is a game that you 'almost' could find as a free Flash game somewhere out there, but the graphics and execution of this one far surpass what you would find. For sure not everybody will like this particular combination of over-the-top plot, minimalist stealth and fast puzzles, but I for sure am enjoying this.

An adequate but unexceptional top-down stealth game. You play Rob Loxley, a punnishly named spoiled rich kid who has found a Volume and is using it to FIGHT THE POWER of the government by starting up a video stream of him going through simulated environments and stealing from various places owned by Gisborne and his allies, a man who has conquered England via a coup and has a totalitarian regime which eliminates anyone who dares to defy him.
All in all, this is a pretty minimalist game; the levels aren’t too large, generally things you can beat in 5 minutes or less. There are 100 of them, and in total the game takes about six and a half hours to beat – or seven and a half to get all the achievements.
As the game is entirely composed of simulated environments, the game gets away with very simplistic graphics – but the levels do end up looking pretty samey after a while. There is some variation, but it is very minor, and ultimately there isn’t that much to look at here.
The upside is that the very clean graphics make it very clear exactly what is going on – everything in the game is very clearly marked, including vision zones of enemies, shadows you can hide in, places you can duck behind vs walls which totally block line of sight, hidey-holes you can hide in, ect.
Your goal in each level is to collect a number of floaty diamonds, representing… a wide variety of things. They use the same thing in every level, missing out on the opportunity for different mission objectives.
Instead, all of the variation comes in the form of the hazards you face in the levels. New hazards are introduced on a regular basis, and while there aren’t very many enemy types, the game still manages to mix things up with a variety of environmental hazards to contend with or things which can help you hide. There are also a variety of devices, ranging from a couple variants on enemy stunners, a cloaking device, a disguise which won’t hide you from dogs but will trick other enemies, footpads which prevent you from setting off noisy pressure plates and also allow you to run faster, and a couple of ranged noisemakers.
All in all, the levels present fairly reasonable challenges, and the game doesn’t feel overlong or overstay its welcome. That being said, there isn’t that much variation in the end, and the earlier portions of the game at times felt a bit samey and tedious as a result.
The story of the game is passable, but only about once every five to ten levels do you get any sort of voiceover conversation – it is fairly minimal in that regard after the early game, which is rather disappointing, especially as you approach the end of the game. There are a few greater things which are hinted at, but unfortunately a lot of these plot points – such as the “king” Gisborne claims to work for – don’t really end up going anywhere in the end. There are some vaguely interesting hints in some text clues hidden around the level, but they, too, ultimately don’t feel like they have much payoff in the end, and while the game has a cute twist ending, I saw it coming by the end and it ultimately leaves the story hanging as an obvious sequel hook. One of the biggest problems is that the protagonist is the least interesting character in the game; both Gisborne and Alan (the AI who runs the titular Volume you’re using to do your simulated heists) are more interesting characters, and ultimately there wasn’t much of an emotional payoff.
Ultimately, this is really the problem with the game as a whole – it is competent enough, but it is not EXCEPTIONAL in any way. It is basically a bunch of reasonably enjoyable top-down stealth puzzles, but in no way does the game really excel. It is just kind of average all the way through.
If you’re in the market for a top-down stealth game, this is about as good as The Marvelous Miss Take, with a much higher level of predictability (everything in this game is 100% predictable) but less style and variation than that game has. This has a slight edge over that game, which is perhaps too long for what it is, and is easier to just pick up and play, but while this game may be less frustrating, it has less variation, too.
In the end, I can’t say I regret my time with this game, but it is pretty run-of-the-mill.

Hotline Miami 2 is not the classic Devolver title you know and love like it's predecesor. Gameplay wise the game takes about 3 steps in the wrong direction. The levels to each stage are usually huge with enemies sniping you far beyond the reach of your Shift Sight ability. The levels were more horde mode super meat boy style than ever before meaning that absolute perfection was needed and an excact strategy had to be employed each time without any room for expirmentation. This is mainly done by gimmicks as you are shoehorned into them at each stage for a unique playstyle, which is often not complimentary but in fact detrimental to the map and likely by design to♥♥♥♥♥♥down your neck. This means you will either be meleeing basically everything silently or pot shott'n every corner.
Consider this example: In the 24th scene "Take Over" you by this time have three playstyles to choose from. Start with a Katana, Have Lethal Punches but no Guns or start with Dual SMG's that must be used before discard. Two rooms on the first level both have un-melee-able enemies, meaning you must bullet hose them till death meaning the first non-gimmick playstyle is out, since you can't effective get a shotgun or rifle. Dual SMG's work then, but then you come to a un-shootable Swordsman who ducks past bullets, meaning you'd have to use 100% of your only advantage on the first floor just to deal with a single enemy. The only reliable way to go at the start is lethal punches and even that is hard as balls. Fast forward to the second floor where every room is basically glass with a ♥♥♥♥ ton of dogs that will charge out of sight and youre in for a tough time, but that's the only way to play and if you don't like it tough luck. That's nearly every experience in HLM2.
Enemies can snipe you at distant range, quickscope turn, may not see you directly standing in a doorway but caught a glimpse of the air you breathed back in 1985 and charge out to kill you. Sometimes pathing will get screwed up on certian special enemies and they will go in a circle killing any chance of your victory. Doors sometimes don't knock down enemies or prevent you from hurting them. Technically the game's poor execution and/or bugs buffed every advantage to the AI's favor with it never working for you.
The Story is pointless. Undeniably pointless. It's also poorly told, out of order, and usually meaningless. The originally did a good job of telling you a story without too much talk, it did this through suggestion, with the Bikers side story being a huge turn/reveal for the truth of the games events.
Hotline Miami 2 is like some bad spin off. All the characters are loosely connected to the event of the first, but if you didn't read the wiki or write down every date and compare it to the originals timeline then ♥♥♥♥ me if you are supposed to know that. Jake the Snake's extent of "epic" story is now you know where a dead body in HL1 came from. Whoopidy doo. Your also expected to know that Jacket is in the game because there is a character whose blonde and shows up 3 times or something. He never speaks and gives no indication of who he is because he is never seen in his Letterman, and his hair appear's to be a slightly different style and shade. But this is of course what passes for good story telling these days; needing to read an online comic or check a wiki. The Story is Objectily pointless because nothing you do matters in the end. All the characters die, either when you play them once, or at the end when the Developer just decided "♥♥♥♥ it" and decided to have them all nuked for relatively no reason related to anything imparticular. It just happens because of other events in the universe. Not only does this make all the characters actions pointless, but so to was Jackets. Nothing mattered.
The only good thing about this game is the rad soundtrack. Youtube it first, see if you like it, and if so, pick it up seperately. If Hotline Miami 1 was the Alien/Aliens of a generation, than Hotline Miami 2 was the Aliens 3 and Aliens Ressurection. It drags the orginal so far down that you almost wish the creators would come out and declare it non-canon.I cannot reccomend this game to fans of HL1. For me it gets a 6/10, and that's being pretty generous.

Dirt Rally on steroids.
The best feature, of course, is track generator which promises endless fun (and proper rally experience as you aren't getting a chance to memorize the road in the real world), but I obviously don't know yet how in-depth and diverse procedural generation is.
Another nice addition is simultaneous competitive multiplayer rally mode with matchmaking and rankings.
The game can be even more hardcore that its predecessor if you want (I do): then you have to stop manually after the finish, manually control windshield wipers and lights; car damages more during racing and in crashes. There's finally an option to disable restarts, even between events in championship. And when it's foggy you can close your eyes as well, you won't need them.
Now, to the most controversial topic. It's hard to judge physics model until you put hundreds of hours into the game but as far as I can say it's even better, for example, Group B Peugeot 205 is even more wild, while 90s Lancer Evo is capable of long controllable slides. Many cars easily spin out when you touch the roadside now. It's still playable with a gamepad though. I think some elitists are forgetting that difficult =/= realistic. Remember timeless masterpiece Richard Burns Rally? It had pretty easy and forgiving handling, but it was still a great rally sim.
Anyway, I'm having great fun with Dirt 4.

Heroes and Generals is a great game and one of my personal favorates. Currently I can safely say that this is one of the best World War 2 games released. The game includes many different, and amazing, features; such as the different playable nations the American forces, the german forces, and the recently added Soviet Union forces. In each of these different nations there are hundreds of weapons, tools, uniforms and classes. For instance, when you begin the game you start out as a basic soldier, but with some easy and quick games you can soon become a veteran, unlocking and allowing you to use the many different weapons and classes in the nation that you play as. There are five different classes other than the soldier including; the tank driver, pilot, paratrooper, recon, and general. You unlock these many different classes by ranking up your infantryman, once you reach a certain level or rank you can unlock the different classes. For an example the Tank driver is unlocked at rank three. However for the weapons you must unlock them by leveling up certain skills like the rifle or smg assault, but some weapons can still be unlocked through basic ranking. To earn vehicles you will have to rank up in a certain class, so to earn higher teir tanks you would need to level up your ank driver. Although, you must remember that all the weapons and vehicles are specific to the forces you are playing as, and once you choose a class you cannot switch unless you rebuy that class. But do not fret because you can easily just buy another Save slot or entirely new soldier to rank up once more. And aside from the nitty gritty details, the combat and battles that you will face are extroardinarily fun and are definitely worth your hard work in leveling up. All in all, I would personally play this game even if it were twenty dollars, but seeing that it's free and hearing this review there is absolutely no reason why you couldn't get this game. In fact there is only one reason why you wouldn't, and that's if your computer sucks but if you're even looking for a game right now, chances are you have a reasonable computer. So get out there and buy this game.
P.S. Everything in this is historically accurate, making it not only a great game for FPS lovers, but also one for the casual history junkie.

I got this game as a birthday present from a distant friend. He knew my passion for strategy and planning.
It is hard to add to the many other positive reviews. On the plus side, this game is well-thought, simple, and yet it allows for various degrees of sophistication. In particular, I like the opportunity to try different gaming styles (planner, aggressive, solo, non-lethal, etc.). This adds to a high degree of replayability, with achievements that will satisfy all the min-maxers around the globe. Another praiseworthy feature is the possibilty to download further content, both official and user-generated.
On the aesthetic side, scenarios are pleasing to the eye and graphics are detailed without overworking the engine (as it is expected in such 2D map games).
I didn't really like the star system, becaue it rewards timekeepers over perfectionists. Moreover, it makes it very easy to access powerful gear very early in the game, but apparently that's also true for real life: some of the most effective guns in the world are not the most expensive, and have been around for ages. Random mission generator is a bit boring, though, and this game's strength are the campaign and official missions, each of them with their own peculiarity (storming the embassy, freeing a cruise ship, boarding a plane, etc.). In my version of the game I miss a "shuffle" button for randomly generated maps: this means I have to enter and exit the menu to generate new keys and new scenarios. Finally, although background audio effects are interesting at first, they become repetitive quite soon.
Overall, my judgement is more than positive, because the pros clearly outweight the few cons of the game. My congratulations to all developers, artist, and producers for such a neat product. Also, a big thank you to Texisthelex for having sent me this gift.

I had issues with the first game, enough to put it into the "not recommended" category, but was still able to put up with it enough to play the puzzles. The same cannot be said of the second game, which is readily apparent as being far inferior in quality. If a good game were equivalent to Ghostbusters, the first game was Batman Forever -- not good, but with enough redeeming values to be enjoyed. Puzzler World 2, however, is more on the level of Manos: The Hands of Fate; on several levels it doesn't just fall short of its goals, it fails to even be recognizable as making a worthwhile attempt.
The issues of the first game not only remain, they are exacerbated. The "picture quiz" game, which has absolutely no business being in a puzzle publication on account of not being a puzzle (memorizing isn't problem solving), remains, as does the kindergarten-level Silhouette. Codeword, one of the more creative and intelligent games of the original, is removed. Hangman is still set at a level that is too easy for anybody who can read at a first grade level. The maximum number of wrong guesses one should be able to get in Hangman is 6, a quarter of the alphabet. PW2 allows eleven wrong guesses. Another irritation from the first game, that being crossword answers that have multiple viable spellings not being accepted (and not being blocked because it doesn't completely interlink the way a proper crossword should) also continues here... along with some clues just being wrong, at least by American definitions. ("Mooch" does not mean "skulk"; it means "freeload".)
Still, issues of the puzzles' difficulty levels would be minor complaints on their own. What sinks this from a C average all the way to an uncontested F is the interface. There are numerous design changes in this version that are just baffling. The "hint token" prize boxes of the first game -- mildly annoying on their own -- are replaced by a "Wheel of Fortune" spinner, complete with requirement that you spin it with sufficient speed (remember, this is a puzzle game, not a skill game). The Fitword puzzle now requires that the words be manually dragged into their places rather than typed. The "Sum Up" puzzle has the answers floating around aimlessly for no reason other than to make it harder to see what you're trying to click on; the actual problem solving isn't made any more difficult, it's just the physical aspect that's made irritating. The crossword puzzles skip over filled in letters while you're typing -- so for example, if you already have the "N" in from another word, you can't type "ORANGE", you have to type "ORAGE". Worst of all, the Link-A-Pix puzzles, the most fun game from the original, are rendered completely unplayable by a decision to require the user to scroll around the screen instead of showing the full puzzle.
As if these bad design decisions weren't enough, the game is also severely buggy. There's visible lag in response times, items don't always line up the way they should (the word search lines are often off-center), and worst of all, a lot of it just doesn't work. Scrolling in Challenge Mode can't be done with the mouse, but only with the keyboard. The scrolling in Master Mode and the Trophy Room don't even work with that. There are arrows there, but you can't click on them, you can't spin the mouse wheel, and you can't use the arrow keys. You're told there's stuff to scroll to, but you can't scroll to it. And to top it all off, there doesn't appear to be a "QUIT" button for the program. I had to use Task Manager to shut this piece of crap down. I won't be starting it up again.

A puzzle/stealth game, made by the same guy that made Thomas Was Alone.
The gameplay is solid, it combine puzzles with stealth and does it in a way that's fun and exciting.
The story in this game, while rather minimal, is told through notes and excellent voice acting.
The soundtrack is superb and changes depending on whether you are hidden on not.
What I really like about this game is that during the levels, various characters talk to eachother and create a human element, that most puzzle/stealth games miss.
It has 100 'core' (story) levels and a virtually endless amount of community levels, and you can still create your own.
The story lasts about 6 hours and while that may seem a little steep for the price of (currently) $20, it is well worth it.
Buy it if you love puzzle/stealth games.
A must-buy when on sale.

Mount and Blade Warband is a game that surprised me. It might not look like a game you'd get hooked on for hours on end, but after playing it for awhile, you'll suddenly find yourself getting distracted in ways similar to a game of Civilization, always going for an hour or two longer than expected because a war was going so well, or a kingdom is SO CLOSE to defeat and you wanna make sure they are finished off before you call it a night. Funny, I thought the same thing about Civilization too... And that game also had a habit of sucking me in for a few more turns.
For those wondering, this is kinda a Sandbox Action RPG, where you have the freedom to do almost anything and be whatever you want to be. Want to be a noble knight, serving his king with honor and loyalty? A barbaric horde who leaves a path of fire and blood everywhere you go? Maybe even become a famous fighter across the world, fighting for the entertainment of the crowds and making tons of money in the process. Or, you know, a humble adventurer for hire. Your choice.
It is this freedom that really gives you a lot of bang for your buck, ensuring a massive amount of replay value in the basic game itself alone. The modding community, however, is there if you get tired of swinging the same old sword after a dozen different playthroughs. You'd be surprised how refreshing the same old game could get with an era change.
Really, when it comes to positives, It would be a little too much to discuss all in one page.. So rather, I'd might as well point out a few things that aren't all that great about the game.
For one, the early game for beginners is quite harsh, even on default settings, so noobies should be prepared to get their butts kicked for awhile until they get used to the combat mechanic and understand the game better.
The Ai is nothing to write home about as well. It isn't bad, but it still has its faults.
There are also some balancing issues as well, which can lead to players abusing the system to make nearly unbeatable armies.. But for the most part this takes a lot of work to aquire in the first place, but still worth informing about.
Also, don't get me started on multiplayer... While it can be fun sometimes, most of the time it is frustrating, with an awful gold system where each kill earns you money to buy armor and weapons. This might not seem bad at first until you realize that every time you die, you lose money, and thus the items you bought as well, meaning if you were doing well at first and had some bad luck, well... Goodbye to your heavy armor. There are no assists either, so expect some kill stealing to take place and your hard earned kills to be rewarded to another. Also one hit deaths... Fun..
To be honest, though.. It was kinda hard to think up some legit downsides to this game, and I played it nearly 1000 hours too, so I seen all sorts of crazy things, but for the most part... I rather enjoyed the game. Despite what flaws it may have [some I didn't bother to mention due to their lack of importance], this is a really great game with lots of replay value. If you enjoy action RPGs that let you play your way instead of following a set path, this game is worth buying.

Addicting. That's the one word I would use to describe this game. It's a simple platformer in which you shoot colorful blocks that fall from the sky while avoiding anything that tries to kill you, of which there will be many and increasing in number as the game progresses. Earn as many points as you can and top the high score while bouncing along to upbeat chiptune music. It's kinda like... Tetris on drugs? Except you can't control where the blocks fall and you're actually trapped *inside* the box. I honestly didn't think I'd find controlling a little block of cheese to be this fun until I took a shot at it (no pun intended). I was flat out addicted to this thing for weeks. Don't play it if you have a deadline or a ton of homework to do....

An action platformer set in a stage for a block puzzle game, where you must destroy blocks and hazards in order to gain points, but not so much so that you no longer have a floor to stand on. You destroy blocks with a gun, and they drop little shard things that you use to level up in order to increase how fast you break blocks and how many points you gain.
The real fun of the game comes from the fact that like other block puzzle games, blocks of the same color combine (there are three color varieties) and must be chipped at in order to be destroyed (the health of a stack is the sum of each individual block), and large stacks of them give huge payouts in shards and points, but preserving and growing a stack until you decide it's too dangerous for it grow any larger (the higher and more cluttered the floor is, the harder it is to dodge hazards) is a balancing act of increasing difficulty and patience. Various trap blocks fall, and you must destroy adjacents blocks or stacks to dispose of the hazards. The tight controls and the enticing risk-reward tactics make this game surprisingly fun even for an infrequent fan of platformer games.

TL;DR
Addicting crafting game with fun exploration, survival elements, freedom galore!  However multiplayer is challenged by connectivity issues more often than not: ultra-bummer because the multiplayer is a great deal of fun!
PROS
-Great single-player experience
-Excellent multiplayer experience
-Creativity welcome and rewarding
-Doesn't feel repetative
-Immersive lighting, sound effects, weather, music, and artwork.
-Harvesting/Planting/Hunting/Fishing/Digging/Building/Sailing/Taming/Riding/Driving things is/are/were/fun Blah
-Exploration fun timez
-You don't NEED to set up a dedicated server in order to play with friends.
CONS
-Poor base character customization choices (For now)
-Connectivity issues can make it difficult to play with friends. (Ought to be top priority)
-There seems to be an in-game store in the works for the games eventual full release...  I am just always weary of these.  If it's just for cosmetics and done in a way similar to say... ESO?  I'd be ok with it.  But if there are micro-transactions in order to be able to craft certain items and stuff that interrupts gameplay, I think it would ruin my immersion/emmersion?  And I'd be done playing.
MY RANT
This game is amazing!  And has the potential to be even more amazing!
SIDE NOTE:  I, for one, am super excited for Sea of Thieves. Within that excitement I've been searching for games that will hold me over... I thought I'd give this one a shot.  IT TOTALLY DOES!  Playing exploration mode, building up to a point where you get to travel the seas comfortably; it's addicting.
I do have one issue with this game so far, however, and it's a large one:
Connectivity issues while trying to play with friends online.  The system is there, it works!  You can host a game that friends can join, up to 8, and so long as the host stays online, people can enjoy the world together.
However, some of my friends have had to try logging in to my game multiple times, getting failures, sometimes taking up to 30 minutes to successfully connect.  Usually, if they can complete the connection we'll be able to play for hours and be fine; it's just not very dependable yet.  BUT!  Saving works well.
As a single-player experience:
Excellent for a chill/creative/curios mood.
The universe is immersive!!  The music is wonderful, even slightly chuckle-worthy while crafting; if this had large-population dedicated servers this would totally be my online home.  There are so many features I still haven't even mentioned...
The pricepoint right now is more than reasonable, give it a shot.

In the search for the ideal top-down tactical shooter, I've tried Hotline Miami (too twitchy), Forzen Synapse (too random), Monaco (close, but too gimmicky), and recent XCOMs (on the abstract side). None of them quite scratch the itch created by Julian Gollop games. Until Door Kickers.
The heart of the game is a series of buildings your SWAT team must clear of bad guys. Sometimes there's another objective such rescuing hostages or collecting evidence before the suspects can destroy it. These require various tactics and give the game flavor. But the core remains moving from one room to the next shooting people who are trying to shoot you.
Every character possesses some level of agency. Enemies (AKA, tangos) respond to sounds and other cues in reasonable ways. For instance, they might turn to face the door your pointman is forcing. Alternatively, they might decide to shoot the hostages or destroy the evidence. Your operators might ignore orders in order to respond to immediate threats. In fact, you don't order them to fire at all; you tell them where to go and they just take care of business.
As a result, you can set up a plan at the start of a level and let the game play itself. I know that sounds boring, but it really isn't. Plans involve dozens of little decisions, such as how to breach a door, where to toss a flashbang, when to turn to check a hallway and so on. You can charge though most levels with a lone shooter (there are achievements for it) or carefully coordinate a full team with go signals. If your plan works, the payoff is a minute or two of perfectly choreographed violence.
Truthfully, however, perfect planning doesn't happen the first time around. More often I need to adjust because I failed check a blind spot or I blundered into shotgun crossfire. Plans can be redrawn on the fly or you can pause the action to give yourself time to think. Immediately after completion of a level, I find myself restarting it so that I can fine tune the plan.
There is an overarching game of unlocking tactics, roles and armament. Faster times unlock up to three stars for buying new guns, body armor and equipment. Officers earn experience points which open up new roles (assaulter, breacher, stealth and shield) and tactics. Missions can technically be played in any order, but the effect of the leveling system is to gate off more difficult levels. Skipping missions or forgetting to upgrade increases the challenge quickly.
On the other hand, once you have a stronger team, it's rewarding to go back to earlier levels and get an improved result. In addition, campaigns are unlocked once your squad levels up to a certain point. However, don't think of campaigns as stories since they are just missions strung together to force you to pay the consequences for deaths and injuries. I'd complain campaigns are too shallow if I weren't excited to play new maps.
Not that there's any lack of maps. In addition to 84 single missions and 6 campaigns, there are user-created missions for download and a map generator. These mean you will never need to play the same mission over again, but they also highlight the skill of official level designers. Levels designed by other users are wildly inconstant in challenge and quality. The generated levels can be anywhere from boring to near impossible depending on which settings you use and how the random number generator rolls.
In the final analysis, Door Kickers provides copious amounts of tactical decision making with simple controls and plenty of chrome.

Greatest Sonic adventure to date? Not exactly.
Sonic Adventure 2 is by no means a bad game, if anything, its a pretty solid game with a lot of fun to be had throughout.
However, Sonic Adventure 2 feels very much akin to that of a good 'direct to video sequel' rather than a full fledged follow up to the original Sonic Adventure game.
Levels have been stripped down, and it is very rare, especially in Sonic's sections for levels to branch out into multiple pathways and as a result levels are extremely linear. Despite the lack of pathways, levels still manage to be fun, however on repeated playthroughs they become repetitive and boring due to the lack of variation. Sonic also seems to control much stiffer this time around, and the slower spindash removes a lot of opportunities for playing around as well as sequence breaking.
Knuckle's treasure hunting stages have also been stripped down; being able to only find one emerald piece at a time is a cheap way of having the levels play out longer, and the mech stages are slow, stiff and do not feels like Sonic at all; and are a huge step back from Gamma's stage from the first Adventure.
The story is much more involved however, whilst not amazing; it is fun and perilous. Characters are colourful and there are a ton of memorable moments throughout and the darker tone is balanced nicely.
The chao garden is of course a highly regarded element, and I have to agree. It is so easy to lose yourself in this vast virtual pet mini game. There are many types of chao, each with their own personalities and talents. Mini games for them to partake in. Levelling them up and strengthening them to your own liking. It is well structured and well thought out, and the multiple gardens are relaxing and it is a fun way to wind down after playing the main story.
Whilst not the best game in the world, Sonic Adventure 2 is definitely a fun platform game; even if somewhat basic and stripped down from the game that came before it.

Pros:
-Different take on a zombie killer is a breath of fresh air.
-Players' ability to be common zombies is definitely another breath of fresh air.
-Workshop support, and by extension, modability.
-To make up for the difficulty of hosting games over the Internet (details below), it does have rather decent single-player gameplay.
Cons:
-Seems to need a powerful computer and graphics subsystem to play, i.e. something more powerful than even L4D2 needs.
-No lobby to gather friends or other players in.
-Woefully lacking network support that other Source games have makes it really difficult to host games over the Internet.  Needs either Hamachi, NeoRouter, Evolve, Tunngle, or router/firewall portforwarding/port unblocking wizardry to work at all, let alone well.
-No Linux dedicated server.  Most dedicated server establishments are built on Linux owing to the expense of getting a Windows license, not to mention the fact that the best place for a Windows system is behind a heavily-fortified firewall.
-In light of the above, the price on a game this modern might scare off others.  Were this in GoldSrc, I'd give it a pass.  Not this time.
A mixed bag, but the best time to pick up this game is when it has a very steep discount applied to it, i.e. during seasonal and "special event" sales.  Until these deficiencies are addressed, my thumb goes down.

The sound of the zombies bashing on your door, or the unexpected "call" from another player as they get attacked from a zombie leads you to panick. And shooting a gun? You might want to re-think that, because just like in The Walking Dead, the zombies are attracted to sound and they quickly swarm. This game truely highlights the tag-line "Fight the Dead. Fear the Living".
But hey, don't worry, if you die...you get a second chance. You come back as one of the zombies and you can control the hoard and bring them straight to you're friends front doors...literally!

Normally I wouldn't post a review after only 73 minutes of gameplay, but there have been so many negative reviews posted with as little time I figure I'd give my early impressions.
For me, impressions are very good. My rig is Intel i7 4770K 3.5GHz, 16GB RAM, GTX 780 3GB, Win7 64bit Home Premium, 480GB SSD main drive. I'm running graphics at High, one step down from Ultra and everything looks great at 1920x1200 and I'm getting a steady 60 fps in rallying. I'm using an X360 controller, just as I did in DiRT Rally and it works fine. The driving physics are easier than they were in DiRT Rally, which is fine with me as I seemed to crash out a lot in DR. Also I'm running in Gamer mode, rather than Simulation, since I don't have a wheel and I'm old.
My X360 controller was recognised automatically, so no problems there. In fact the only tweak I had to make was to enable VSync.
In Gamer Mode the tutorial gave me a rating of Champion, one down from Fearless, which surprising since I was rather inept at Dirt Rally. However, even on Gamer Mode the game is no pushover. Folks complaining about the lack of realism might want to check their assist settings, these are enabled by default to some degree unless you are running Fearless difficutly.
I ran a couple of event rallies and also tonight's Community Event, which is a Throwback Thurday with a Mini on compacted snow on an eight segment, 8.27 mile stage. I managed a 9:33 which I imagine isn't very fast, but I managed to keep it upright and off the snowbanks, well, except for a couple of times.
So far, and I've only got 73 minutes in it, I'm happy. It is early days but so far I have no issue with what I've seen. No crashes or lockups, everything easy to find in the menus, lots of options to tweak the game as you prefer and although I've only put in a few minutes with the Your Stage stage generator it seems to work as promised.

I don't usually write reviews, but this game is so much fun and I can't wait to see where it's going, so I thought I'd share a bit of my gameplay.
I started out learning how to craft different things and one evening by my campfire, a wolf walked up, only to run away. I figured, either this game is super realistic and wolves are in fact afraid of fire (which I'm pretty sure I've heard of in other places, before), or that all creatures are cowards, such as the boars and rabbits. The day after, I proved my first theory right, because I was slain mid-day by a wolf as it wasn't afraid of me when I neared it without the presence of a fire in some form. Then I created a copy of my dead character and received a testament of the past one and thought 'hm, pretty cool feature'. I ended up staying on the same, first Yland for quite a while, building up a tiny cottage with no idea if building doors was implemented yet, it took ages to say the least. Eventually, I thought.. I'm-a build a boat, then saw how many resources I'd need that I had no idea how to craft yet. That's when I found the recipe for the raft. I built it, drifted off and hoped I'd find another Yland, and if not, hopefully I'd get back to the previous one before dark. It took me a while, but eventually I saw kelp floating slightly in the sea, followed by more terrain and eventually, an island. And oh boy, a shark swimming right beneath my raft! When I landed on the island, the weather was harsh and wintery. I didn't survive many days before I was slain by a puma. But my next character, a third copy of my first, still lives. I started trying digging for resources for the first time, and ended up building my own cave. It felt like home, a home I didn't have to build from logs that took me ages and ages of sleeping outside. I dug more and more rooms in my cave and now I have a load of old-fashioned 'technology' such as different ways to melt things down and my own blacksmith workstation. But now I feel like I need to find a bigger cave soon, because further expansions are gonna be tricky. Oh, unless I build them deeper down! Hah, great idea. I'm sure that will turn out good and not hit me back at all.
Anyway, love this game, please keep updating it and adding more features 'cause I do not wanna tire of it. Also, the green-eyed wolf in a huge cave I found? Terrifying, it made me run out immediately after I shot it dead with crossbow bolts (it took many, many bolts), easily because it was scared and started running into the wall without getting anywhere.

Greatest Sonic adventure to date? Not exactly.
Sonic Adventure 2 is by no means a bad game, if anything, its a pretty solid game with a lot of fun to be had throughout.
However, Sonic Adventure 2 feels very much akin to that of a good 'direct to video sequel' rather than a full fledged follow up to the original Sonic Adventure game.
Levels have been stripped down, and it is very rare, especially in Sonic's sections for levels to branch out into multiple pathways and as a result levels are extremely linear. Despite the lack of pathways, levels still manage to be fun, however on repeated playthroughs they become repetitive and boring due to the lack of variation. Sonic also seems to control much stiffer this time around, and the slower spindash removes a lot of opportunities for playing around as well as sequence breaking.
Knuckle's treasure hunting stages have also been stripped down; being able to only find one emerald piece at a time is a cheap way of having the levels play out longer, and the mech stages are slow, stiff and do not feels like Sonic at all; and are a huge step back from Gamma's stage from the first Adventure.
The story is much more involved however, whilst not amazing; it is fun and perilous. Characters are colourful and there are a ton of memorable moments throughout and the darker tone is balanced nicely.
The chao garden is of course a highly regarded element, and I have to agree. It is so easy to lose yourself in this vast virtual pet mini game. There are many types of chao, each with their own personalities and talents. Mini games for them to partake in. Levelling them up and strengthening them to your own liking. It is well structured and well thought out, and the multiple gardens are relaxing and it is a fun way to wind down after playing the main story.
Whilst not the best game in the world, Sonic Adventure 2 is definitely a fun platform game; even if somewhat basic and stripped down from the game that came before it.

When I saw Sonic Adventure 2 was available in the Steam Store, I got pretty excited. It'd been a while since I played the game and recently viewed walkthroughs made me nostalgic for it, but I didn't expect the amount of trouble this gave me.
It feels like they didn't even try to port this game correctly. Having it in full screen mode crashes it. Having the Steam HUD activated crashes it because the game was not re-formatted for it. It took me 3 days of searching the internet to find fixes for my problems since I bought the game already, and spent too much time trying to get myself past the Story Mode screen to quit.
After way too much time, I got it to wory, and haven't had any problems since aside from the controller support. If you have a USB xBox 360 controller, you shouldn't have too much of an issue. However the only working USB controller I have is my Ps4 controller. I needed to install InputMapper to use it and trust me, you're gonna want to use a controller for this game. The Keyboard controlls for this game are...not...good.
Aside from those issues, once I got it to work, I've been enjoying it ever since. There's a whole bunch of Mods to choose from and it makes the game more entertaining for those that aren't satisfied with mere nostalgia. There's even mods that make raising Chao much less of a grind.
TL;DR If you want this game to play it immediately, you're probably better off finding your old Gamecube and getting Sonic Adventure 2 Battle. If you don't mind working for it and dealing with frustration after frustration until it FINALLY behaves, then go right ahead and get this game on Steam.

What is volume ?
Well I can tell you what it isn't : a stealth game. It's a puzzle game using stealth element and setting to tell a story.
And it's good. Why ?
The visuals, athough very simple are easy to read, the controls are responsive enough that you only get caught because of your own mistakes, and the voice actors do a decent enough job that you can actually see the characters as characters and not only pawns on a board.
Besides, any puzzle game that is well made enough to have a story is worthy of one's time.
But it sucks. Why ?
It's sold as a stealth game. Which it isn't. And after a few missions, it gets repetitive. You don't have enough possilibities to get to the ending. Most levels only have one way to get through them. And the problem isn't that you won't be able to enjoy a second playtrhrough, it's possible that you won't even enjoy the first one. And if (like me) you are not hooked enough by the story, you won't finish it.
The game shows all it has to offer on first half-dozen missions. If you like it, great ! Else, well too bad, the other missions will feel bland.

Except it turned out that Volume isn't really "that" type of a puzzle game either.
In Volume the goal is not to complete the level. The goal is to complete the level as fast as possible. This means that from a puzzle-point-of-view the game is *really* easy I and I get no satisfaction restarting a level again, and again, and agains just to steal one more second from the time.
I'm sure that the game is a good game to those who like this kind of games but for the fans of stealth or puzzle games, it's a grave disappointment.

A very co-op intensive game that never lets up in terms of action and combat. It is most enjoyable when played with friends while communicating on voice chat.
Vermintide has a heavy emphasis on melee combat with ranged weapons being more reserved for sniping and situational combat scenarios. So be prepared to hack and slash your way through hordes of rat monsters most of the time.
The gameplay mechanics are very well-balanced and have been refined to play smoothly. There are a number of quirks regarding the range of the special rats, notably the Packmaster, but I suspect these issues will be fixed over time by the game developers.
Overall, difficulty-wise, when I first started Vermintide, I thought that the hardest difficulty level: Cataclysm was undoable. However, once I fully understood the game's combat mechanics, rhythm and tactics & strategies, I realised that this game simply requires combat skill, timing, positional awareness and a good communicative team to complete it on any given map and difficulty setting.
Now, having completed the game and cleared everything, I await to see what new content Vermintide will receive with its upcoming patches and DLCs.

This game is often described as left4dead but with rats. I don't think that does it justice. Vermintide plays more like a cross between Payday 2 and Skyrim.
I say Skyrim because melee combat is a mechanical focus and is executed so that it's easy to pick up and hard to master. Payday 2 is a mention for me because of the team challenge factor Vermintide features. Careful communication and teamplay is absolutely necessary in the higher difficulties and even on normal-hard when picking up Grimlores.
Vermintide has left me wanting more of everything it provides: haunting and intruiging level design, fun and interesting characters, a diverse range of special enemies and quirky AI. Having said that, the game isn't at all lacking in content or replayability and is worth its full price as is.

Vermintide is a great game with a hardcore Left 4 Dead feel set in a well known fantasy universe under distress (which is a super cool & unique combination, might I add). It's really great considering games like this have been missing lately. A fun reward system is included after a fun team-focused experience with optional objectives to change how your run will go down. A good and interesting variety of weapons and maps are in the game, but there is for sure room for more. The only larger downside apart from that is that it is missing some fatures that I felt would have been great at launch (more character customization being one of them) but a lot of what else I felt was missing is being adressed in free major updates (such as realism mode, endless mode, ect.) which is awesome, and should be rolled out semi-frequently. Definitely a must-have if you enjoyed Left 4 Dead and are a fan of fantasy settings!

So, I feel like this should be obvious. But it's worth noting:
This isn't Dirt Rally 2.
Even though I started the game immediately in sim mode with all the assists off, It felt very strange coming directly from Rally. It didn't take too long to pick up the nuances of the relationship between traction and weight transfer, but I noticed immediately that the cars are VERY twitchy, which can become an issue if you're expecting to set up for a flick, and end up in someone's yard. That element alone is a tough thing to 'feel' for and seems to be inconsistent. Speaking of feeling: the force feedback was very fun and really helped feel connected to the surface.
As far as the difficulty of stages, this procedural approach to stage creation is really exciting and keeps me on my toes. This was very refreshing since I had just started to learn every turn, surface change, and pointy rock of death present in DiRT Rally. I found myself sweating on a few segments that had a pucker factor I haven't felt since my first rallies in DiRT Rally. Only gripe here is that a Poways 'hairpin' has a circumference that you could fit a football field in. Not very hair... pinny.
The cockpit view feels very strange, as if the native position is 5-6" too high (at its lowest setting). I DID get used to it because I had to, but it's still an odd placement that doesn't really support people like myself who prefer a lower seat position.
It's very clear that they applied a good bit of what was learned in DiRT Rally to DiRT 4, coming from DiRT 3 (yikes).
Graphics are... Eh. The dynamic range and depth seen in DiRT Rally is completely absent. Everything feels very washed out, and the textures extremely muddy (no pun intended). I had to double check to make sure I was on Ultra settings...
I'm still amped as hell to be playing this, though, despite my complaints. I'm just keeping my eyes peeled on the appropriate forums for mods. I think with some solid tweaks, this could be a daily go-to long after the career is maxed out.

Don't listen to the wannabe purists that assume that less grip = more realistic. Matter of fact the tarmac physics system is loads better than Dirt Rally. The only part of the graphics that have been downgraded is track detail; the cars look and particle effects and crowd look as great as ever. Campaign and multiplayer have been greatly improved with a whole "build your own team" subsystem that really adds a lot of depth to something to what was once barebones. I don't really care for the rallycross or landrush modes, but I don't feel like anything has been taken away from the regular rally experience. Complain all you want about the lack of handplaced detail within each stage but I'd rather have different rally stages every time then memorize the same 6 stages per location that I could do in my sleep ala Dirt Rally. Force feedback has also been improved in my opinion. UI is great, sounds is great as always, and the licensed soundtrack is much improved over the ultra generic 4 tracks that made up the entire soundtrack of the last game. My only real grevience with the game is the lack of 2017 WRC cars, but including them would've been impossible without the WRC license. To add on to that now your girlfriend or other friends can play the game with the arcade handling and not get frustrated by crashing into a wall every 5 seconds. The more people who can enjoy rally, the better.
