Genre - Games Workshop co-op squad based survival/action
I am an ex-Warhammer minatures geek until I got less time and friends to play it with, or you coudl say I got a girlfriend ;-)
There are a load of Games Workshop games flooding the market and some are clearly better than others. Made by fans and not just for profit. This game definately falls into the latter category.
The game plays like a Fantasy version of Left for Dead. For instance instead of the Tank you get the Rat Ogre, instead of pills a health potion etc. This is obviously more focussed on melee combat though due to the setting. It seems to work really well with Skaven (Rat Men for the uninitiated) replacing the infected.
It is obviously better with friends and the different rarity of items that drop after each level completion make the game have a high replay value. You also have difficulty settings for more of an organised team challenge. I wouldn't recommend a party of noobs on hard or higher.
It manages to stay true to the universe but still be a very accessible game. There is also definately potential to add more at a later date.

Ginger: Beyond the Crystal is a 3D platformer which reminds me of games like Crash Bandicoot. Does it hop away to success or falls into its own abyss? Let’s find out:
Ginger: Beyond the Crystal puts you in the shoes of Ginger, a blue coloured creature who is supposed to save the entirety of the land by purifying various crystals. The story that the narrator tells you in the start of the game makes you feel like you’re watching a movie made completely for younger people in mind. It is fairly generic and nothing to write home about. There is a decent tutorial system in place that makes you comfortable with the game’s environment and how the main character is controlled. What should be a simple concept soon turns frustrating as the amount of bugs and glitches keep you from enjoying the game.
Ginger constantly falls through the game world and glitches through enemies bodies when in combat. On top of that, there are constant crashes and freezes and a huge amount of lagging which makes it a really frustrating. Ginger himself is very finicky and is terrible to control. Combine that with awful camera and the combat sections become very hard even though the enemies die fairly quickly.
The game contains 3 major hubs which are connected to each other. Whenever you travel from one world to another, there is a huge loading time which takes around 2 minutes every time. That is a really long loading time for a game like this. Your main objective is to spend the crystals you collect in the path and free the villagers who desperately need your help. Contrary to popular game NPCs, the villagers are not happy when you free them. They need to be more spoilt by making them new buildings and keeping them happy.
Along the way you will be fighting various enemies which are really dumb. Unless you’re playing really bad or the game is lagging or glitching, the enemies die very easily. The combat system itself is very basic with a punch and a dash button available to fight your opponents. There is little to do for customization too.
The main meat of the game is platforming and the game does that really well. The puzzles though not difficult require some thinking and the level design is good. Ginger: Beyond the Crystal does little to invent but whatever it does, it does it really well.  The three hub worlds are nicely done enough that you would want to explore them, at least in the start. If you manage to look past the glitches, the constant crashes, huge amount of lagging and really long loading times, there is some good gameplay hidden in Ginger: Beyond the Crystal.
I have mixed feelings for Ginger: Beyond the Crystal’s visuals. There are times when I absolutely loved the way the game looked, but for each one of those moments there came a moment where I realized that it was very bland. There are some brilliant character designs and then there are those which are as generic as it gets.
Ginger himself looks a mixed version of Kid Buu and well, blue colour. The UI is pretty simple and is easy to get used to.  Ginger: Beyond the Crystal’s features a world that is colourful and vibrant but there are times where there is nothing interesting going on the screen. Overall, the visuals Ginger: Beyond the Crystal are a mixed bag which has its highlights but is also really bland at times.
Sound design is a field where Ginger: Beyond the Crystal excels. The music is soft and easy going on the ears. It also captures the imagination of the player and sucks him in. It has the kind of soundtrack which a child would really like, a target audience for this sort of game. The voice acting is minimal and fairly good. There were a few audio bugs here and there but overall the music of Ginger: Beyond the Crystal is excellent.
Ginger: Beyond the Crystal has a huge amount of potential. It has some excellent platforming sections and has a stellar soundtrack. But the number of bugs and glitches really hold it from being great. The combat is really bad and could’ve been avoided by the game developers. It seems to be just forced down the game’s throat.
The visual direction has its highlights and the story is all right for younger audience. But you will really need to look past the huge amount of loading times, lagging and bugs to enjoy this one. The game needs to be patched before it can be absolutely recommended for anyone.

I want to start off quoting one of my favorite scenes from Willy Wonka and The Chocolate Factory, in the scene they come up to a wall covered in flavored wallpaper. (Btw, genius idea if not slightly gross.)
The scene starts with Wonka saying, "The strawberries taste like strawberries, the snozzberries taste like snozzberries."
Then comes this vile little troll of a child who responds, "Snozzberries, who ever heard of a snozzberry?"
Gene Wilder replies with one of the most epic lines. A line that stuck with me for my entire life. He grabs her by the face and responds, "We are the music makers and we are the dreamers of dreams." The intensity of the look in his eyes and the way it completely silences her is utterly amazing.
Okay, so you didn't come here for Movie Quote Fun Time with Jorge, so why I am bringing this up? Also what does this have to do with Ginger?
Well, the answer is simple. Instead of being amazed and awe in wonder at this joyous creation, the child immediately found fault and responded in incredulity. Quite literally not being to look past her nose.
Gamers tend to do the same thing. Making games is far from easy and it comes with hard work, hundreds of hours of dedication and most of all, risk. Which is why I am utterly baffled that no one is talking about Ginger: Beyond the Crystal.
In a world obsessed with Mario's, Yooka Laylees, Conkers, Bandicoots, and apes playing bongos, Ginger comes in with a unique style, plenty of fun ideas, and all the 3d platforming one could want. Capturing the magic of the aforementioned titles is no small feat but from the moment I loaded up Ginger, I was blown away by the level design, exciting/fun aesthetics, and how approachable it all was. Don't get me wrong, Ginger is not a perfect game and has its fair share of issues, we will cover that in a bit but the good far out weighs the bad.
The premise is rather simple, big blue crystal macguffin needs you to restore it after mysterious evil breaks it into pieces. The world goes into chaos, people disappear, towns are destroyed and its up to you to fix it all. and save the world.
The story itself is simple, really its just a means to get the fun going and explain why game mechanics are in place, such as town reconstruction. While more attention to the story would've been nice, its not super high on the list of priorities when it comes to 3d platformers. It's not like Mario ever questioned his existence or why Peach doesn't stop getting kidnapped.
There is quite a bit to unpack when it comes to Ginger, so we will start with the graphics. The reason I wanna start here is that I feel like this might be the most polarizing issue when it comes to Ginger.
Ginger is a gorgeous game, it has all the polish and pedigree of a triple A title, despite the fact it came from a developer you've never heard anything about. Every area and level does something different and is constantly changing things up. One level is a hedge maze, one level is a circus fair, one level has you racing to collect honey, its constantly shifting its design, themes, and clever use of mechanics. The three different towns you save, all have a unique aesthetic as well and come with their own unique enemies.
The polarizing issue lies in the fact that the game has some graphical optimization issues. I had to spend a good forty five minutes playing with the settings, then loading up the game to get it going to a clean 60FPS.(Another gripe being you can't access graphics from in the game) I had a fellow reviewer suffer the same issues with a better rig. Keep in mind though that with thousands of graphic cards out there, your experience is going to vary. Shadows seem to be very demanding on the GPU for some reason and just slow it down massively. There is no way to change view distance, which is also a slight problem. The good news is that the developer is still actively patching the game so these issues can be resolved.
Gameplay itself is exactly what you would expect from this genre, but does have a couple of tricks up its sleeve. Gameplay is broken up into two sections; town reconstruction, and the actual levels themselves.
The more of the town you reconstruct, the more levels you can access, its simple but it works. You reconstruct towns by gathering supplies, building homes, and using gems(game coins) to restore villagers. Town reconstruction takes place in three hub cities, and to be honest I was afraid it was going to be something just tacked on and pointless. On the contrary. It really does a good job of breaking up the pace of going from level to level. It encourages exploration, using different abilities(more on this soon), and even giving you more activities and side quests to do. You can also purchase collectable items for your villagers to wear that make for some humorous moments. I have very little issue with the town reconstruction aspects,  but just wish there was more to play with as far as buildings and benefits goes.
Levels themselves are also a simple "get from a A to B" type of scenario, but the in-between part is completely different every time. One level may need you to repair a space-stations generators, another ride a mine cart while dodging Indiana Jones like traps. It's always different and it's the one aspect I enjoyed the most about Ginger, It never got dull or repetitive. There is a wonderful sense of play here that the developers captured very well and it should be commended. Ginger is genuinely fun for the sake of being fun. There is a alternate difficulty mode for those seeking a more traditional platform style game, where if you run out of health you start over the entire level. Otherwise if you die in the normal mode there isn't any real consequence most of the time. I would say that Ginger does fall on the easy side of things, but I am very familiar with platformers. That being said there are also challenge levels. These are purely about landing jumps perfectly and not falling. These are where you're going to rage, I know I did.
The last two levels have a bit of a difficulty spike that is worth mentioning. I am not a huge fan of instant death scenarios, but lets just say I had my fair share. The last challenge level is nearly impossible as it completely removes jumping from your control. I raged. I raged so much.
Another thing I loved about Ginger was the way our blue friend gained new powers. Every couple of levels you would rescue someone who gave you a new outfit. These outfits aside from being adorably designed, also give you powers, such as breathing fire, bat flight, huge bombs, and shooting stars Buzz Lightyear style. As more unlock, it gives the game greater replay as former levels had previously inaccessible areas, somewhat in the same vein as Lego games. Some outfits are one trick ponies but the game does try to make good use of its outfits, as often as possible.
When it comes to combat and controls, Ginger has its wrinkles. You can attack enemies with a variety of punching, slamming attacks, and the good ol' jump on their heads trick. Some outfits also add abilities to combat as well but the combat itself feels like it needed to be a bit more refined. Using my dragons breath on enemies should've been awesome but came off a little bit flat. Also pretty much every enemy can be defeated by the jumping slam attack. Using another attack is almost downright pointless, unless you are trying to get somewhere fast. While combat isn't a huge part of the game, I would've liked to seen more integration from the outfits into combat. The developer did recently put out a patch(Nov 15th) that did make certain actions far smoother and continues to improve on the games combat.

This game has potential, but I gotta say.. I do agree with most of the reviews so far (the ones on a variety of game-related websites at least) its glitchy, buggy, and has a lot of untapped potential.
Unlike some, I did not go in expecting the quality or gameplay given to us by Nintendo in the past (Mario 64/galaxy) but I did expect something rather more solid than the state this game is currently in.
I fell through ceilings and floors a few times, my girlfriend found a way to jump out of the first level, when changing the graphic settings a few times trees lose their texture occasionally, conversation skips that not work, hitting an enemy that miraculously hits you the same moment, stomping onto enemies not working, stomping on tree-stumps that need to be almost exactly dead center else they wont work, and not to mention the horrendous minecart controls (protip if you are stuck, right analogue stick, up>down>up>down REALLY fast)
And a god forsaken amount of fetch & kill quests.
Oh, and I almost forgot to mention the more than occasional weird choice of sentences and words, sometimes it makes me wonder if the dev's haven't practiced their English lately, other times the chosen words don't feel well placed.
(a static font going "great" after finishing a level feels cold instead of warm and joyous)
And yes, you got that right.. I am currently only two hours in and this is already taking its toll on the rather cute, mild, kiddy gameplay non/semi-hardcore gamers might like. (i.e. my girlfriend)
The art (read: environments) are rather nice, the flowers, plants, rocks, houses, it all looks stylized and well made.
Caves look like caves, mines look like mines, forests look like forests, and the village looks like a mess only a mother would love, but in a good way.
"I am sure he'll clean up nicely in puberty"
The characters could use some more "character" to feel more alive but nothing really annoying.
The enemies feel like simple AI though.. Their animations are short and simple and lack the toonesque feel you'd expect from games like these, especially when occasionally the animations of NPC's do shine (like the big rat in the Mine when you try to walk past him)
The gameplay is simple, you can jump, double jump.. But it sadly doesn't feel all that solid.. The last second jump when walking towards ledges often results in falling to your doom, and more than often everything is spaced apart in such a way that its either a hit or miss situation, especially with the bad camera angles the game tries to auto-force on you over and over.
As I said though, the game has potential and I really think if the dev's fix all the bugs and glitches.. This could be quite a kiddy-version ala Mario 64.
I am sad though that they didn't take it a little further, made the movement of Ginger more smooth, added some wall jumping/ledge grabbing, made costume changing faster, and overall gave it some more polish.
Would I recommend the game though?
Yes, but I'd wait for a discount or hope the devs iron out all the hitches and glitches.

I was optimistic for this game but wasn't sure enough about it at the usual price, so grabbed it when it was on sale. I feel like I went on a date with a hot teenager: Lots of potential, but it's not ready yet.
I like Minecraft. I like ARPGs. I like colonial space age sci-fi. This game has aspects of all that, but it all fizzles out. The main problem is that it runs so slowly, my laptop can't keep up even on the lowest graphics settings. As you can see in the screenshots, this game isn't exactly pristine when it comes to graphics, so the low performance is either poor game design, or it's just not feasible to make a voxel game look any more detailed than Minecraft or Trove.
EDIT: The game actually has a similar problem to Dragon's Dogma, in that it runs very poorly even on low quality settings, but runs decently if played in a small enough window. Still though, you shouldn't have to do that in either of these games.
It's also very poor at tutorializing the player, even with the tutorial level. It takes a couple minutes to complete assuming you aren't playing through a full second control lag, it doesn't tell you the gamepad equivalents, which are not what you'd expect, and it doesn't even tell you how to use bows, guns, vehicles, anything like that. I'm also uncertain why there isn't just a blank survival mode, only "Story" and "Adventure" which both have quests and NPCs that distract from the experience a bit.
The controls are awful. It basically doesn't work on gamepad despite having native support for it, and even on keyboard controls, there are far too many keybinds to memorize for it to be fun, and it's quite tedious to try and rebind when you run into things like not being able to rebind something the Shift because it doesn't register as a single button press. Calling on some fair comparisons again, Minecraft, Trove, Skyrim and most MMOs have controls that are so much more intuitive despite encompassing basically the same - or even more - actions that need to be perfomed.
I sort of want to keep this in my library, considering I have worse games that I failed to apply a refund for, but I would recommend leaving this one alone until it gets a sequel, reboot, spiritual successor, or major, MAJOR update. As is, this game is an amateur mess that needs serious reworking.
EDIT: Oh come on! Steam refunds only apply if you've played less than two hours? I probably spent half that time in the character creator and another quarter just trying to get it to run smooth enough to be playable! That refund policy is a little tight, is all.
Now if only this was a good game.

The first thing I tell people when I am bragging to them about this game, is how no matter what kind of gaming you like, it is in Planet Explorers, even if just a little. Like FPS? It has that. Like farming/crafting/resource managment? It has those too. How about hunting, cooking, exploring, mining, or building? Yep, totally. This sandbox world of free-roaming play is just the thing to get your buddies into playing a game style that they would otherwise not enjoy. PE has a story mode, creative mode, online multiplayer mode and even designing your own in-game objects, in detail, all to a beautiful ambient soundtrack. It really does have it all. It also has glitches and errors, but those are highly mitigated by the fact that the autosave does it's thing every minute or so, making it super-easy to not lose too much progress if a glitch does happen, even if you have forgotten to save in a while.

This is a fun game, with a lot to do, but it is not complete. It is full of bugs, performs extremely poorly (980ti, i5-7600K, 32gb RAM: 1080p <40fps), the movement is jerky and janky, going into first person causes a vibration effect... I came back to this with my friend the other day and the list of bugs goes on.
Before I get into the problems, Planet Explorers does lots of things you can't really do in many other games, at least all in one application:
- Voxel-based world, so you can dig out the ground and tunnel to your heart's content.
- Build very easily, with a very detailed system that can allows you to make some really interesting structures. This combined with the ability to dig gives you a ton of creative freedom.
- The world is cartoony, but very pretty.
- The music is fantastic! The sound and atmosphere in general is terrific, though it wanders away sometimes, see in bug list below.
- You can create your own custom weapons and vehicles with a very detailed crafting system, where even the types of materials you use have their own properties. So you could, say, make an airship out of marble but it'll be incredibly heavy. So cool! You can also download many of these off of the workshop. That's terrific.
- Fun co-op story content. It's hard to get a good story-based co-op experience that fits this sort of game-structure, these days. You can get a lot of open-world cooperative titles, but you won't necessarily be getting a story.
- Lots of voice-acting though... It's mostly laughable in terms of performances. However, I kind of like it, along with the cartoonish style I find it charming. Really, though, it's not great.
- Make a world-spanning train system customized the way you like (wow).
- Create a colony with a crazy amount of choice in how you'll do it: on top of a mountain, in the sides of a giant cliff where you've carved homes into the side of the cliff's face, underground, on platforms over the ocean...
- The glider pack and jet pack are genuinely very fun to use.
- Can tame and ride various animals (though I have yet to try this).
However... Wow. Bugs. I'm not sure you can say this is out of Early Access, and they're already onto another title.

- Gerdy floats around 20 feet in the air above her bed.
- The movement is very janky, with weird vibrations.

- I'm running a i5 7600k, 32gb ddr4, geforce 980ti. PE runs like garbage. Though it runs perfectly at first, it will drop to a steady 40fps at 1080p and mostly-high settings. I've turned down a lot of options and.... it's still janky as heck.
- When I shut down PE - my PE server keeps on running. This would be fine if I could actually access it, but it's just sitting there in the background doing it's thing and I have to end-task it. That's super, super lame.
- If I host a server, go into it, and then exit back to the lobby it won't let me re-join my own game for several minutes. It just tells me that game's already running. I then have to search for my own server and join it, it won't let me otherwise.
- If I then go and close said server, there's no visual indication I've done so. I click "close"... but nothing on the screen changes so I wind up checking if it actually did it or not. You couldn't even be bothered to tie a sound effect to pressing the close button?
- When I exit PE it thinks it's still running. Have to shut it down in the BG or restart Steam! If I try to get back in it says it's already running.
- When you turn down the volume, but flick your mouse over menu options, it "forgets" your volume settings on those activation sounds. "clickclickCCCCLLLLLLIIIIIICCCCCCCKK" SUPER ♥♥♥♥ING LOUD. Ear-hurting loud. I'm using the volume controls so I can hear my buddy over Discord, so this is an awful problem.

- You sleep with your eyes open. Couldn't get us to close our eyes?
- Campfire's scale appears to be too large, even in terms of texture.
- When you make armor it goes into the equipment tab not your armor tab!!!
- Grammar: in Carter's inventory, you can buy "the poisonous blood". First of all, none of your other items have "the" in the title. Secondly, all the others have capital first letters.
- Want to swap items on hotbar? They just overwrite. Seems small, but this is a simple thing to do.

This thing is FUN.
It's not your everyday 'shoot the enemies' or 'match the colors', it's an amazing combination of both those things.
While you play, blocks slowly fill the screen. You're equipped with a gun, and your job is to shoot these blocks down in colored sets, such that you still have room for moving around, yet you don't open a hole into the spikes below.
During your careful shoot-a-thon, the game occasionally changes things up. For example, you might suddenly see spike blocks or cannons falling down into the arena - additional hazards to avoid. These hazards change with the level 'theme' you select.
The fun part of this game is that it's so simple, yet complex when you think about it. If you just shoot everything you see, blocks that match colors will open wide holes you'll have to jump into at some point. So, you need to have an ability to plan for at least short-term, on the fly.

On the sixth, I bought this game on a whim. I played it until two in the morning, and while I figured some things out, I knew effectively nothing.
On the seventh, I started a new world with my new knowledge, and built a large ship. I sailed for hours, and found some other Ylands and gathered a lot of their resources.
Today, I figured out that I can expand my ship. I now have a floating many-masted base that I have sailed around for almost the entire day today. I have nearly frozen to death, swam to the bottom of what I thought was a bottomless ocean, explored airplane crashes, underwater greenhouses, and a lot of other things.
This game reminds me a lot of Minecraft circa 2009. It's new, it's vivid, and the exploration is exciting. Even if I can sail west for three hours and see nothing but water, the things that I can discover are interesting and keep me going in that direction. I haven't tried the other gamemodes that are currently available, and I haven't even constructed the Foundry or an alchemy table yet.
Ylands is a game that has got more depth to it than I expected in my first four hours. I originally thought that this would be a lot like Stranded Deep, or one of those other "Oh, you're on an island in the ocean, build a house for funsies and explore the surroundings", but instead what we've got is a weird and quirky survival game that is filled with some sort of weird electricity, the ability to build cars, some strange floating items, and we're only in very early access.
!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!
That's insane! I'm excited to find more islands and to see what comes out of the gamemodes. I'd love to see some kind of skill system RPG thing come out of it, as well as larger land masses. I think I'm also going to build a second large ship and see if I can link them together and sail them using one helm. I'm not sure how long that's going to take, but I do know I'm going to enjoy it.

Stealing from the rich and giving to the poor is an old concept all of us are familiar with. Volume provides a futuristic re-telling of the classic Robin Hood story wrapped up in a tightly designed stealth puzzle package. Players take on the role of Rob Locksley on a journey through one hundred self-contained and relatively short levels mostly to steal information and valuables from the head of a huge and powerful corporation that effectively rules over England.
Volume utilizes an isometric camera. However, when hugging a wall, it shifts to a top-down view so you can get a clearer overview. One of the first things you’ll notice about the game is its clean and simple visual aesthetic. As you go through the game, almost each level features a different color palette. Levels usually consist of only two or three main colors, but they are expertly used to create a striking visual style. Not only is the art style visually pleasing, but it directly facilitates clarity of design. It’s extremely important for stealth games to be instantly clear about everything that is going on, so that the player can effectively plan and react in any given moment. Volume achieves this in an almost effortless way, but it is, in fact, the result of intelligent design.
Volume is actually a simulation within a simulation. As the game starts, Rob hacks and reprograms a hostile artificial intelligence that works for Gisborne, the aforementioned head of Gisborne Industries. The artificial intelligence, Alan, then proceeds to allow Rob access to key locations of the corporation. The story tackles some interesting themes such as the dangers of completely unregulated capitalism, internet celebrities, the fear surrounding artificial intelligence and the ethics of dealing with them. Unfortunately, the problem is that the story isn’t particularly well told. There were some inspired lines that grabbed my attention, but for the most part, it’s rather dull. There are optional texts you can find in each level which provide some backstory, but those are boring for the most part as well. It’s a shame that the story falls flat because the themes it covers are genuinely intriguing.
What really makes Volume shine is the design. Levels are pretty much designed as puzzles and it’s up to you to figure out how to finish them without getting yourself killed. Rob cannot kill any of the enemies in the game, he can only hide or otherwise evade them. He has a variety of tools at his disposal to achieve this. The most basic ability, which will actually remain useful throughout the entire game, is getting the attention of guards by whistling in their proximity. For example, hiding behind a wall and whistling will cause the guards to either move from their spot or break their patrolling pattern in order to investigate the noise. You can use that moment and navigate the space they were guarding. Rob can also use the environment and hide in lockers or jump over certain walls. Later on, the game introduces shadows which effectively make Rob completely invisible in certain spots.
However, the most interesting way to deal with guards is using various gadgets that you will find in each level. Some gadgets will enable you to distract guards by creating noise or place a shiny item that grabs their attention for a while. Others will allow you to stun guards for a precious few seconds, trick them by wearing a disguise or even turning invisible in the later levels. There’s a healthy amount of gadgets to use and each level is designed around using a single or several gadgets.
There’s a nice variety of enemies as well. The most basic ones have a standard cone of sight and will just shoot you in the face with their assault rifles. On the other hand, snipers have narrow and long sight range, but they shoot slower. Knights are fearsome and fast melee enemies with a huge line of sight and they’ll hunt you down and hack you up in a heartbeat. Turrets are stationary, but have an exceptionally fast rate of fire. Dogs won’t directly attack you, but they’ll alert nearby guards of your presence. Also, considering they mostly rely on their ability to sniff you out, they can’t be tricked by disguises. All of these elements provide a lot of variety and help to keep the game fresh from start to finish. But the best thing about Volume is how it masterfully pulls off the synergy between these components and creates a coherent whole.
Volume skillfully straddles the line between being challenging and accessible. You will never get stuck on a level without having a clue as to what you’re supposed to be doing. You also won’t feel as if you’re just going through the motions. The difficulty is just right which makes the pacing almost perfect. I also have to single out the sound design and soundtrack both of which fit the game perfectly and help to create a compelling atmosphere. Your completion time of each level will be uploaded online and you’ll be able to see how you stack up against all players and your friends. Apart from the story mode, Volume also features a robust, easy-to-use level editor. Players can upload their levels and download other people’s levels very easily, it’s all just a couple of button presses away. The problem I had with this is that I simply didn’t crave for more. I felt as if I’ve seen everything and simply had no desire to play more levels. It doesn’t really feel like the type of game that could facilitate hours upon hours of gameplay without running out of steam. But for those players who want more, this could be a potentially great way to get more value out of the game.
Volume is a really good stealth puzzle game featuring incredibly balanced design and pacing with a genuinely strong presentation. It just lacks that certain something that would elevate it into truly great territory. Maybe a compelling story or perhaps bolder design would push it into the realm of absolute excellence, I’m not sure. However, the one thing I’m positive about is that Volume is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for a well-designed stealth puzzle game.

Further more, Volume has a built in community level editor. You can create and share your own levels with the world, effectively giving the game endless replayability.
The cherry on the cake is an interesting Robin Hood story in a future dystopian England, even if it is prehaps not center piece to the experience.
For these reasons, the closest comparison to another game I'd have is to Little Big Planet: simple, charming, effective and (post end-game), community driven.
Recommended to anyone who is interested in a barebones yet elegant stealth game.

Short Version:
A simple but fantastic top down shooter that refines much of the potential present within the original Hotline Miami!
Long Version:
Hotline Miami 2 is generally an improvement over the original in all the ways that would matter to me. The pixel art is more detailed and colourful than before, which was something I didn't consider possible, and there has even been the inclusion of more physics based objects in the background (rotating clothes racks in a department store) which just add to the "flavour" of each level. Levels are also noticeably larger and enemies farther apart but this has been offset with a more forgiving window of opportunity for pulling of combos; to the owners of the original HLM I'd say that the new combo window is more similar in duration to what you had with the Zack (frog) mask.
On the one hand this somewhat slows down the pace of combat especially since some enemies may not be in your immediate line of sight, BUT with sufficient practice it is absolutely possible to anticipate and eliminate these targets (use the shift key and learn to abuse lock-on my friends). There are still levels where you can just tear through a small army of opponents without too much effort as in HLM of course, but these are definitely in the minority. More problematic however is the loss of significant amounts of progress in those levels that are larger especially if you have been creeping along cautiously. That being said I never once felt that I was cheated with respect to any of my deaths, as I have come to accept (as should anyone who wants to enjoy this type of game) that this will require a trial and error approach.
HLM2 also makes some significiant changes to HLMs gameplay and story telling mechanics. You now play several different characters belonging to various in-universe factions. The "fans" are probably the most enjoyable faction as they consist of various masked vigilantes with unique gameplay altering benefits. For example Alex and Ash (swans) are controlled at once, with Alex wielding a chainsaw controlled by the LMB and Ash using a gun fired with the RMB; movement of Alex is controlled by WASD and Ash follows (ideally though this is somewhat bugged when going through certain doors).
Other interesting additions include a pacifistic reporter who can complete levels without killing a single enemy and a soldier who is restricted to one (ranged) weapon of his choice and a knife; you are permitted to replenish ammo for that ranged weapon however. Each of these characters and their respective changes are thrust upon you as you progress requiring that you re-evaluate your existing strategies and ensuring you are never too comfortable with any particular playstyle. However the game ALWAYS presents you with some degree of choice, whether it's what type of weapon the soldier wields, what "fan mask" you decide to use, or whether the reporter truly plays as a pacifist.
Also of note, is that the changing characters bring various prespectives to events occuring both before and after the events of HLM1. Since the game has a great deal more flexibility in settings this time around (you do still visit Russian Mafiya dens but also jungles in Hawaii), HLM2 does a good job of never feeling like an expansion for HLM BUT at the same time the story is a lot more (intentionally) disjointed than before. Expect to get lost if you are not following along carefully with the dialogue of which there is a LOT this time.
I've probably gone on long enough at this point so I'll conclude with the statement that HLM2 as it is isn't always the perfect execution of the ideas of the previous game and there are some annoying bugs (especially with enemy AI and the AI that controls Ash's movement) but the game is all in all a solid experience. One I would recommend to fans of HLM that are looking for something more challenging and more varied (in terms of gamplay and storytellling) than what HLM had to offer. Individuals who have never played HLM1 should try that game first (as it is cheaper and should give an idea of what to expect) and those who did not enjoy it ought to proceed with caution.
Note: I got this game on sale during Summer Sale 2015 (-33%) so my perception of value vs expense will obviously be different from those who purchased HLM2 at full price. Also this game has an as of now un-released level editor planned for a future update which I will certainly discuss in a later revision of this "review".

I got this game in early September 2013, when it was in early access. I liked it as it was then (and it was well worth the rather cheap price at that point), and it has only improved. I see that it won best tactics game of 2014, and this makes me feel a little pride, knowing that I have supported it from the beginning :)
Your team is pretty customizable. You can rename each trooper, select from a number of different portraits, choose each trooper's class, and also customize their equipment and weapon loadout. There are several different campaigns to undertake, each with different focuses, enemies, and situations. There's also a bunch of individual missions you can try.
For extras, there is a mission generator, map editor, and you have access to the workshop. You can download maps, etc from the workshop which is always nice.
The gameplay is characterized by pausing and unpausing (or, not). You can pause, and while paused click and drag each trooper's path through the level, designating actions to do once they reach a door (like flashbanging it and clearing), which way to scan when they reach a certain point, and so forth. You can map out as much or as little at a time as you want. There is a bonus if you successfully run through the level fully mapping it out in the beginning, and not interfering. There's also a bonus for completing the level with just 1 trooper. Hopefully this makes sense.
The selection of equipment and tools, combined with classes, can make for plenty of replay value. You could run 1 level many different ways depending on which troopers you use, what equipment they have, and how they enter a building, room, or area. For instance you might run the level very differently if you have one or two stealth troopers on the mission, than if you have a pointman with a pistol, assaulter with a rifle, or breacher with a shotgun.
I certainly recommend this game.

First of all, I bought this game when it was just beginning, the controls were weird and you had no limit to how many barrels to put on your self made guns. Over time, I saw this game grow from the small little game it was to a slightly more fleshed out and immersive game. I will be commenting on multiple aspescts of this game, including controls, graphics, and overall story telling.
First of all, controls. The tutorial will give you a decent education on how to move yourself, and it is fairly smooth. The UI in this game is very good once you learn how to use it, and I have not experienced a glitch with any of the tools or weapons concerning controls or response times. Secondly, the graphics. For 2017, these graphics are decent and sometimes supurb concerning the grass, trees, and sometimes ships and characters. However, the texture of the ground and materials aren't all that good, and I can see why. The main reason for this lack in texture for the ground is that this is a voxel, sandbox game, were the world will be procedurally generated when you take from it. Detailing the texture of the voxel ground would be a very pricey process for your computer and this small development studio.
And Finally, the story-telling. I cannot comment on the whole story because I have not finished the game yet, but from what I have seen, it is not as good as it can be. The voice acting is amazing for some characters, and some sound like they were recorded on a laptop. Your task is to click on red blocks that explode in order to direct a single blue block to its place on a green surface. While this may sound easy, the game’s explosive tendencies oftentimes cause the blue block to overshoot its target. Figuring out which red block to explode so that your blue block will travel the necessary distance is a matter of trial and error.
There are also yellow blocks, which typically block off your green landing pad, but they are flung out of the way when you detonate a red block.
Later on, the game introduces two different coloured blocks—purple and green—which add a bit of variety to the core gameplay. Both add a timing element, so that you can’t just click blindly to proceed.
There are 44 levels in total. The first 20 or so fly by, but the later handful will actually challenge you. Meanwhile, you’ll be unlocking achievements by the dozen.
.Bottom Line.
is a n ideal game for achievement hunters: it costs less than a buck and will net you 118 shiny new achievements in around half an hour. Outside of that it’s a genuinely enjoyable, though very short, puzzle game with tranquil background music and a solid physics engine.

Zup! is a physics-based puzzle where the objective in each level is to get the blue block on to the green zone. The only points of interaction are clicking on the red explosive blocks
so not much time is needed to figure out the solution.
The game is amusing for its large number of achievements (118) that are unlocked for trivial actions; for example, starting a level grants an achievement, while clearing it gives another. This can be an incentive for achievement hunters looking to boost their achievement count and game completion rate, and the designs (letters, numbers and basic punctuation) are useful for decorating profiles while keeping a homogenoeus theme.
Gameplay, however, is minimal; some coloured blocks are introduced in the later levels with new mechanics, but they do not affect the level much, and the objective remains the same. The game can also be completed in under 30 minutes which may be a deterrent for those looking to maximise their gaming dollars, but at least the low price means it is accessible to almost anyone.
Ultimately, (a big) part of the value lies in the achievements, so if that is what you are looking for, pick this game up, set aside a few minutes and enjoy some demolitions along the way.

Some issues :
* Fall damage can invoke insta-death?  Why.. this is a platfomer!   I have it set to hard mode, but still.. what a lame mechanic.  A small fall should be a small amount of damage and a huge fall should be half health (just copy SM64 here!)
* The first enemies you face will lock on to you in a single frame when you attack them.  It looks like someone was making their first game with their animation.
* All the enemies I faced, it's NEVER obvious who is going to win the fight when you dash at an enemy and the ground pound is a little too slow so it induces some randomness.  Contrast this with the enmeies in Mario 64 where you can always formulate a way to attack the enemy with the outcome entirely on you.
* Dialog skipping isn't available until animations fully play out, but it will pop up an annoying message to skip the entire scene if you try to forward the dialog before the animation plays
* Checkpoints aren't actually checkpoints but health restores.  Again this could be because I'm playing on hardmode, but change the text.  I actually died of fall damage 90% through a level and instead of going back to the checkpoint, the level reset.  I don't care about losing when it's my fault, but I was playing more risky because I had JUST gotten a checkpoint.
* Draw distance culling is very poorly implemented.  I was getting > 60 frames when looking at the average scene but because the scenes are so richly at some parts, I was getting ~30 frames.  I ultimately had to turn my graphics way down because the spikes weren't worth it
I WISH this were an early access game and not a multiplatform release--then it might show more restraint with these issues because there's no guarantee they will fix these problems.  I HOPE they fix the above issues because the music, art, and worlds are pretty interesting.  The cutscenes were fantastic (especially the introduction).  With some critical updates, this could easily be an 8-9/10 game

Have you been looking for a cartoon 3D platform that is reminiscent of 1990s and early 2000s platformers? Ginger: Beyond the Crystals may be the game you have been looking for.
Basically Ginger: Beyond the Crystal is what you come to expect out of a 3D platformer. You jump, you fight enemies, and you solve some easy puzzles. While that might not sound that original, Ginger: Beyond the Crystal is a fun platformer. Basically if you like 3D cartoon platformers you should really enjoy Ginger: Beyond the Crystal.
Probably the best part of the game is the game's level design. The game has fifteen main levels along with 15 bonus levels. While all of the main levels basically use the same mechanics, the game does such a good job creating unique ways to use the mechanics to make a fun platformer.
As far as difficulty I would say that the game is easy enough for children to play and yet is not so easy that adults will be bored. If you play a lot of platformers you probably won't die a lot but it is challenging enough that it is still satisfying.
Regarding the length I would say that the game is probably around four to ten hours long. If you just do the bare minimum to beat the game I would guess that the game would take four to six hours. If you want to 100% the game I would guess that it would take closer to ten hours.
If you don't really like cartoon platformers or really want a challenge, Ginger: Beyond the Crystal is probably not going to be for you. If you are looking for a platformer reminiscent of 1990s and early 2000s platformers though I don't think you could go wrong with Ginger: Beyond the Crystal.

-At the time of writing this review, ive completed 75% of the game-
Volume is Mike Bithell's second game (the first one being 'Thomas was alone'), and it is incredibly good.
Storywise, the game is a futuristic retelling of the Robin Hood legend, in which Robin 'Rob' Locksley is not stealing from the rich and giving to the poor, but is instead streaming a simulation on how to do just that, without using violence. The people of England can then copy his moves and take back what they deserve by themselves.
Gameplay wise, it is a stealth game. Well to be precise, its a semi-minimalistic isometric hardcore non-lethal stealth game. The gameplay includes sneaking around (obviously), along with using all kinds of gadgets to distract guards and get from point A to B. Because Locksley does not intend to kill/maim guards, he did not bring any weapons. He cannot fight. if this is a problem for you, you will not enjoy this game. The objective is to collect all the gems (which represent valuables) in a level, and then continue to the exit. There are also walls that can be jumped over, closets/floorboards that can be hidden in/under, taps & toilets that can be activated, etc.
I really enjoyed each level, but they can feel slightly repetitive. Take breaks in between whille playing this. Playing it in one sitting is not advised.
The guards' AI is not perfect, and as a result, it is fairly easy to make them lose sight of you (provided there are lots of corners in your immediate vacinity). There are also a few minor bugs that still need to be ironed out (nothing gamebreaking though).
The voice acting and music are very well done. The music fits well with the game, and is frankly quite beautiful. The voice of the main antagonist (voiced by Andy Serkis) sounds really good too.
All in all, i personally really enjoy Volume, and i think Mike Bithell has definitely proven that he is not a 'one hit wonder'. The game is not perfect, but if you are a fan of hardcore stealth games, you will definitely enjoy this!

The Good:
- Combat is simple yet satisfying
- Graphics are excellent, immersive, and smooth
- Sound is equally excellent and immesive.
The Bad:
- Loot system is high risk, low reward
- Replaying the same dungeons can become dull
- Voiceover / character comments can become repetative
Adding a loot system to a game like this (Left for Dead sytle) is a brillant idea, poorly executed.  So poor in fact, that I don't even want to play anymore.
Imagine playing a carnival game over and over, hours upon hours, until you get it perfect.  Success!  And what is your reward for all your hard work?  Instead of the carnival attendant reaching up and grabbing the oversized teddybear, he grabs some dice and says "If I roll a 6, you win the teddybear". But he rolls a 1.  Too bad... and hands you a sticker with a rainbow on it.
I suppose if i won enough rainbow stickers that I could fasion it into an oversized.. something.. but again, I wanted the bear.  Nope, Too bad. Play again.  And again, and again. Maybe next time. Still no teddybear?  Or next time.  Or next.  Or never.
It actually IS too bad, because a loot system is supposed to reward players, not punish them, which is exactly how it feels. "Congratulations on beating the game on hard (or nightmare): here's the same reward you would have gotten if you had failed on easy."
Long term, I would not recommend this game until the loot system is changed to allow players to choose their own reward, or be given a reward more appropiate for their class and/or difficulty level, or done in such a way that doesn't randomly punish you for your success.

I have been a comic book fan for much of my life. Even when they weren’t super popular among my group of friends growing up I was a fan. With the resurgence of super hero movies over the past decade or so my social circle has occasionally relied upon my knowledge and input in regards to the back stories and the histories of the franchises that have hit the silver screen. It’s been a nice change. Unfortunately, there hasn’t been very many comic book style games that have been of a very high quality released. The best that I can remember are the Freedom Force games. Thankfully, ComixPlay have brought the genre back to life with the superb ComixPlay #1: The Endless Incident.
The great thing about the game is that it actually is in the form of a comic book. It has 124 pages and makes for an enjoyable read. The action sequences that are typical of a comic book are transformed into turn-based combat bouts not too dissimilar to those featured in the likes of Final Fantasy and many other games. These combat sequences are not as easy as you may think. You need to survive a number of waves before you successfully complete a battle. It’s certainly a case of one complete battle feeling like a war. Thankfully if you find yourself unable to advance you can skip them and continue reading the comic and return to them later.
There are a number of different characters within the game and this has both advantages and disadvantages. The advantages is that it creates a significant amount of variety within the gameplay with different tactics able to be employed throughout the game. Of course, you may find that some of the available tactical advantages are stronger than others but much of that will be determined by your own strengths and weaknesses as a player. One of the disadvantages in my opinion is that by introducing so many different characters the story feels a little disjointed and cluttered when compared to other comics.
Although I quite appreciated the comic artwork involved I did have a problem with the soundtrack. I think that its just too bland and it doesn’t really add anything of a positive value to the game. If you can follow a comic book and listen to a podcast or a television show simultaneously then this is the perfect game for it. Voice acting may have been a nice touch but an admittedly unnecessary one.
The game takes advantage of Steam in regards to achievements and trading cards. At $6.99 (15% discount until tomorrow morning) you’re looking at about the standard price of a comic book. If you’re a fan of comics then you should pick this game up as there is no reason why you wouldn’t enjoy it.

The turn based battles do require some strategic thinking. As there is no progression per level the interactions between different heroes abilities and the way they effect the villians become the focus. If your a fan of superhero team comics that concept in and of itself is a tried and true one. Recently other games like Sentinels of the Universe (digital and desktop) and Marvel Legendary have allowed fans a chance to interact and dictate the various battle royales of the mighty warriors from . This game takes that concept and blends it together well with a comic book itself. Introducting the players/readers to characters via the battle system is as far as I know a unique concept and I really enjoyed playing through this.
If your a fan of comic books and/or choose your own adventure games this game is definetly worth taking a long look at this title.

I got this game in early September 2013, when it was in early access. I liked it as it was then (and it was well worth the rather cheap price at that point), and it has only improved. I see that it won best tactics game of 2014, and this makes me feel a little pride, knowing that I have supported it from the beginning :)
Your team is pretty customizable. You can rename each trooper, select from a number of different portraits, choose each trooper's class, and also customize their equipment and weapon loadout. There are several different campaigns to undertake, each with different focuses, enemies, and situations. There's also a bunch of individual missions you can try.
For extras, there is a mission generator, map editor, and you have access to the workshop. You can download maps, etc from the workshop which is always nice.
The gameplay is characterized by pausing and unpausing (or, not). You can pause, and while paused click and drag each trooper's path through the level, designating actions to do once they reach a door (like flashbanging it and clearing), which way to scan when they reach a certain point, and so forth. You can map out as much or as little at a time as you want. There is a bonus if you successfully run through the level fully mapping it out in the beginning, and not interfering. There's also a bonus for completing the level with just 1 trooper. Hopefully this makes sense.
The selection of equipment and tools, combined with classes, can make for plenty of replay value. You could run 1 level many different ways depending on which troopers you use, what equipment they have, and how they enter a building, room, or area. For instance you might run the level very differently if you have one or two stealth troopers on the mission, than if you have a pointman with a pistol, assaulter with a rifle, or breacher with a shotgun.
I certainly recommend this game.

I rarely write reviews, but this great little game needs more publicity, and the devs deserve the credit.
In Freeholder, you play as several escaped slaves who need to survive in the wilderness while also developing enough resources to pay off the greedy Roman bureacrat who shows up annually to harrass you with demands for money and wheat. You'll need to carefully balance feeding yourselves, gathering firewood and medicine, planting/tending/harvesting your fields, expanding your territory, building up your village, crafting trade goods, and interacting with nearby towns. There's loads to do and the choice of what to prioritize feels exciting, since success can be very lucrative, while failure can be devastating. It can be tempting to pursue a long-term goal, like the construction of a new building, while neglecting short-term needs (such as firewood), so there's a good amount of strategy involved.
The classes all have good variety and there seems to be quite a lot of ways to make money. The only mandated task is farming enough wheat to appease the census-taker, though it may be possible to simply buy it on the market if you earn enough. My first few attempts have focused on agriculture, hunting, and leather trading, which was a very satisfying way to play. You can also be an artisan, a thief/spy, a warrior, or even a priest(ess). I haven't gotten to all of these play styles yet, so I can't say whether they're all equally viable. But I'm looking forward to finding out.
The game's difficulty is, in my opinion, just right. It's quite difficult to meet the census-taker's yearly demands, but it's rare to have your entire game undone by a single stroke of bad luck. There's a lot of complexity, but you won't spend hours and hours debating your next move. Your success or failure will come from the cumulative weight of your decisions, rather than a single choice made at a crucial point of time.
The only negative about this game that I can see is that the pace of updates is very slow. It seems like the devs are struggling to balance Freeholder with their other committments. I very much hope they'll be able to continue to add new features and work towards a full release, but even if they don't, Freeholder is already more than worth the 10 euros they're asking for. I'm completely hooked.

Freeholder's a fantastic gem in the making. Visually unappealing, but loads of highly challenging survival and rogue-like fun in a really unique genre mix you have almost certainly never seen before. It's a novel idea, done with a lot of attention to detail and already tons of fun, if you are into this kind of gameplay. You're managing very scarce manpower in a huge playing field of possibilities to survive in a rough Roman environment with starvation, seasons, criminals, wild animals, a mean Roman ruler and lots more being your constant challenges. There's exploration, magic, combat, crafting, trading, diplomacy, quests and so on and so forth. And everything requires you to evaluate how many of your monthly resources you can invest in pursuing any of these activities or whether you have to spend everything on mere survival.
Your villa is a hex-based map managed similarly to some 4X games, but on a very narrow scale in terms of resources to divide between activities. You and your two friends, all former slaves, each have two or three points to spend on these activities and some even require you to spend two points at once, meaning you usually have 7-9 points to spend on gathering food, preparing firewood for the winter, gathering secondary resources to build structures and craft tools to make life easier otherwise and potentially free up points for other tasks, hauling trade goods to the market, helping out other settlements on the city map by driving away criminals or fulfilling other special deeds, gathering reagents to sell or make potions / high quality food from etc. pp. all the while being subject to random events such as droughts, making everything even so much worse to handle.
The list of possibilities is sheer endless and you are constantly forced to look for perfect efficiency putting your very limited manpower to good use. If this almost claustrophobic atmosphere in gameplay and the huge variety in things you can specialize your playthrough in sparks your interest, give FreeHolder a fair go.
It's far from perfect, has plenty more work to do and as mentioned above looks like garbage, but this can eventually become one of the best games on the entire platform in terms of game design.

TL;DR
Overall - 9.5/10
Graphics - 10/10 Fell in love with the original, and nothing has changed.
Gameplay - 9/10 Some elements appear to be part of the floor, but are actually things you can get stuck against
Soundtrack - 10/10 Only adds to the feel of going on killing sprees, the synths and deep beat make you feel as if you're tripping the entire time
Story - 8/10 While confusing at first and seemingly fragmented everything comes to a conclusion at the end. Could be bumped up to a 9/10 due to the slight changes in story if playing on hard mode after completing the first run.
Level Design - 8/10 For the most part exceptional, though in some sections it is nearly impossible to clear the entire floor in one combo due to distances between enemies.
Probably a perfect sequel to the original Hotline Miami. The game flicks between flashbacks and present day for multiple characters. With different characters and different time periods the challenges change, in some cases only having access to a single gun chosen at the beginning of the level and an army knife, where you must look for the very rare ammo dumps if you do run out of bullets. In other cases you cannot use guns at all.
The new fan (mask) system adds a refreshing spin on the old system from the original game. Each character only having access to a few different fans, and these give only slight differences in abilities. Gone are the days of cycling through the tens of different fans trying to decide which would best suit your playing style or be most effective for that specific level. All fans are effective in each level in their different ways.
The story, while confusing at first does tie up all the loose ends upon completion of the first run. Even going so far as to explain the history behind the original Miami Killer and other seemingly minor characters in the original game. I would highly reccomend immediately starting a replay on hard mode after completing the first playthrough, as there are some small differences at the beginning of the hard mode story.
The gameplay is as good as ever, with only slight issues where elements that appeared to be part of the floor actually end up getting you stuck and killed. Upon switching to hard mode the levels actually flip, with the same layout but this time from a different perspective. While this seems as if it wouldn't change much, it does make the levels harder, changing sight lines of enemies and the way that you approach that 20X combo. In hard mode guns you pick up will have extremely reduced ammo, with shotguns only holding 3 rounds instead of the regular 6. (This is the only one I remember, as I don't usually pick up any other type of gun) Enemies in hard mode seem to have almost supersonic hearing and hawkeye vision, forcing you to react much more quickly and plan everything on the fly.
An incredible soundtrack accompanies the game. I downloaded the soundtrack weeks before the game was released, and enjoyed it extremely. Back to the roots of the original Hotline Miami, the synths and deep beats keep you on the edge of your seat while mowing down enemies one after the other.
Not much can be said about the graphics, pixely as they are I fell in love with the art style of the original Hotline Miami, and no changes were made for this one, making me one happy guy. *cough* Binding of Isaac Rebirth *cough*
The only real issue I had with the entire game was that one floor of the apartment where the stairs were set up in the most awkward configuration. Who hired that architect? No wonder there was a serial killer in that complex, if I had to go through that every day I'd probably be on the lookout for someone too.

You have to come in to Volume with the correct expectations to appreciate it. This isn’t a tightly told story like Thomas Was Alone. It’s more of a stealth arcade game, in the vein of the Metal Gear Solid VR missions.
Compared to Metal Gear Solid, Volume is simplified. You can’t crawl or hide in narrow spaces, there are no melee attacks, and your inventory is reset between levels. In any situation there’s usually only one way to progress, in a way that feels rigid. Because of your limited abilities, the challenges never feel particularly interesting. The solutions are immediately obvious, and it’s just a matter of brute force trial and error to get past. AI and checkpoints are easily exploitable in a way that feels like a deliberate design choice, as a workaround for you not having anything to do if you’re discovered. All this leads to levels feeling disposable. Once you’ve finished them once, there’s not much more you can do with them. It’s only slightly more complex than Thomas Was Alone in that sense. Compared to something like Thief, it’s more Trackmania than Gran Turismo. Every level is a one-off, instead of something you’ll be coming back to over and over to explore alternative solutions. I came in expecting this, so I was fine with it. But if you’re a hardcore stealth fan it might not be enough. Like Trackmania, Volume has a level editor, and there are already tons of new maps out there. I haven’t looked at them, but it wouldn’t surprise me if the game comes alive through them in a way that the campaign mode doesn’t.
The story was the greatest disappointment for me, mostly because of how underwritten it feels. There’s 100 levels in the campaign, and you go several levels at a time without seeing the ghost of the story. Levels are purportedly based on machines you’re hacking, where the dirty laundry of corrupt government officials and heads of corporations are shown to the world. But during levels this isn’t evident at all. I was hoping for something like Tron 2.0, where the visual design of the levels reflected the kinds of systems you were inside, with emails exposing the internal workings of the system. But Volume isn’t like that. This isn’t a grand story arc that unfolds over the 100 levels. Instead it’s a story for a game 1/5 this size, with the majority of the levels being there because it’d be poor value for money if it was any smaller. You do read emails and documents, but they seem to have no connection whatsoever to what’s going on. This is a complete waste, because this story needed more. It has loads of characters, but with most only existing as portraits in the main menu.
The music does a better job of capturing the theme of the story than the writing. Much like the Ys games, it felt at times like I was playing it more to enjoy the music than anything else, with the story only becoming more nonsensical the further I got into it. Most character development happens off screen, and the stakes are so poorly telegraphed I had no idea what was going on when the end came. At one point the connection between the game and story breaks down completely, making it clear no effort was made to make the parts gel. It’s inelegant, and because of how thin it is, Volume ends up being both blunt and vague.
So the story is disappointing. But if you approach it with this in mind, that it’s primarily about stealth puzzle challenges, then it’s still reasonably fun. Thanks to the music it felt like a nice place to be. With every level taking 2-5 minutes to finish, it was easy to just keep playing, even if the next map probably wouldn’t add anything to the story. It’s not bad, but I am disappointed.

Full review at:
But to sum up?
Ultimately I think Volume would have been better off if it could have been happy as a tiny little action-puzzle game along the lines of Mike Bithel’s previous venture Thomas Was Alone but with better presentation and a robust level editor. Instead it tries to tack on a poorly conceived story and some questionable voice talent to make for a game twice as expensive as it needs to be and half as interesting as you would expect for the cost.

I kinda want to like it more than I actually do. It's not terrible. It just feels kind of slight. The game takes a long while to really get to interesting puzzles, I want to say at around the 25 percent mark at earliest, and even those aren't much to write home about. From about 50 percent on it's a fairly good game overall, but it feels less like a stealth game and more like a puzzle game. You've only ever got one gadget at a time and there's only I want to say 5 levels where there's actual choice in gadgets so solving most puzzles tends to be pretty linear. That's not to say there's no creativity. The game has checkpoints and "shadow" systems are blatantly exploitable and instead of ignoring that actually has some fairly cool puzzles designed around knowing players will cheese those sort of mechanics.
There's a story but it's pretty bare bones. It's Robin Hood in VR. There are only a few characters, including a villain voiced by Andy Serkis, but for the most part there's not a ton of story. The narrator from Thomas was Alone returns to voice an AI, and some youtuber voices the lead character and is kind of terrible. It flits in and out, and it ends on kind of an anticlimax.
There's a level editor and you can easily share levels and download others. There's leaderboards for every level But I don't think the game's core gameplay is interesting enough to see me back to it.
It's a good game, but I'd wait for a sale.

I'll admit that I bought this game solely because I am such a huge fan of Thomas Was Alone. I mean, I don't even like stealth sections in games, let alone entire games about stealth.
However, what I found was that although I don't like stealth games, I love puzzle games, which is what I found this game to be. The gameplay is simply phenomenal, and the stealth puzzles are all extremely intuitive. I found that I could easily solve most puzzles on my first try about halfway through the game because I started getting into the game's rythm of which way guards are most likely to turn and the best way to use items to get guards to look the other way for long enough to get the thing.
When it did turn into a stealth game, I got my♥♥♥♥♥kicked. I'm looking at you lasers.
The plot was very good, and it's the type of game where you have to piece together a lot of information from the clues the game gives you to get a greater understanding of the world. And I was so very pleased near the beginning to discover that this universe is the same one that Thomas Was Alone takes place in.
I did some trouble with the menu though. Going in for the first time I found the opening menu a bit un-intuitive. It didn't seem to like the Xbox controller I was using, and some of the menus were clearly meant to only be used with a mouse. The first instance that springs to mind is when scrolling through the list of the 100 main-story missions. This takes 5 seconds with a mouse, 5 minutes pressing down on the controller. Also when you unlock character customization, it's impossible to select a color with the controller (Bright Green Ninja Thief of course). But honestly when the worst thing about your game is the menu then that's something to celebrate.
The gameplay is varied and extremely fun with new items to help you sneak around showing up every 15-20 levels and new enemies/obstacles that are immune to those items showing up at about the same rate. The backgrounds and sets are all absolutely gorgeous. The difficulty can spike at times (f'ing lasers) which caused me to breeze through a batch of levels before bashing my head against the wall on one level for as long as I spent on the easy ones combined. And the game itself is incredibly addicting.
I'd highly recommend this game for anyone and everyone. Some mechanical aspects of it could probably use a good spit-shine which may be done in updates, but the core game is still a gem. I'm really looking forward to what Mike Bithell gives us next!

The game is entertaining and has many great features, but it has many bugs including the following:
1. Sometimes the keyboard/mouse will not move you correctly after loading; disabling controller settings can help this however these settings are on by default and it may be a recurring problem if you are not diligent about checking them.
2. There is no way to tell if you are going to spawn as a zombie when joining random games, so if you're interested in cooperative play to meet objectives, you need to arrange your match ahead of time for any guarantees.
3. Every time I have completed a map, the game sits on the final score screen and I am forced to exit the game which results in my not having any of my achievements recorded on my steam profile.  Annoying to not be able to track your progress.
4. Between my kids and I (three computers), whenever we try to play together on LAN, if one of the games crashes it crashes the game for all three of us.  The two who do not crash get a "Game Paused" message and it never recovers, and the person who crashed (if it was not the host) is unable to rejoin the game.  We have not yet been able to complete a mission together on LAN due to this.  This may actually be two problems; either an actual game crash, or a short break in our wifi which I believe is the cause for the "Game Pause" message, however both have the same result of being unable to finish a level.
If these issues can be resolved then I would recommend this game.

Hello Im Skill Incarnate and Welcome to My Games Review Series.
My reviews cover indie games that i have bought, had gifted to me and have been provided by developers for review.
All of my Games Reviews are rated out of 10 and are judged on four factors
1: Gameplay: How much fun is this game to play. How original is the ideas and concepts in the game. Does the gameplay flow well
2: Graphics: Here i judge a games graphics on their fit for the game. As these are indie games i will not be judging how good the graphics are compared to triple A titles, rather i review how well the graphics suit the feel of the game.
3: Playability: How much value will you get in terms of game length. Does the game entice the player to go back and finish it again after completion.
4: Value for money: Is the game priced correctly for length and quality of the experience.
In This Episode I am reviewing the Survival/RogueLike Game Freeholder.
This is an interesting and unique game with a Fusion of a Survival/Roguelike/Turn Based Strategy Game
Review Score: 7/10 Recommended for fans of strategy games like Civilization.
Please Note: Game was provided free of charge by the Developer
================================================
Freeholder Game Review

Freeholder on Steam
================================================
-Survival on the Frontier of Ancient Rome.
You must avoid starvation and frostbite while working under the thumb of a corrupt census taker, and turn the tables on him.
-A Unique Blend of Genres.
From farmsim to survival, role-playing to strategy, FreeHolder presents a compelling and revitalizing blend of classic game genres.
-Detailed Character Evolution.
With seven classes and over thirty skills (with many more of each planned), you can be everything from a master sculptor to a hardened warrior to an efficient rancher.
-Roguelike, not Roguelite.
Challenging and highly replayable, like games should be. Over a dozen procedurally generated factors gives you a new experience each game.
-Original Retro Soundtrack by Blue Mage.
Drawn from a lifetime of obsessive involvement with video game music, the soundtrack for FreeHolder has been crafted to evoke memories of the classic console era.
The Story of FreeHolder -
You and two comrades are escaped slaves who while fleeing Roman territory, stumble across a recently-raided farm, and although almost everything of value has been taken a small amount of wheat, a few tools and a couple silver denari might allow you to eke out a stealthy existence on the fringe of Roman lands. Unfortunately, you agree to run the farm together just as the Roman census-taker is knocking on the small home's door.
Only slightly terrified of being found out, you are unable to convince the Roman that you are anything other than escaped slaves. However, this particular census taker is, 'flexible' and offers the fugitives a deal: if they run the farm and produce enough wheat to fulfill the wheat quota demanded by Rome, and toss a bribe on top for himself, they can go on running the farm instead of being sent back to face their master. With no other options, and no way out, you and your compatriots agree hastily.
This state of affairs does not have to last, however. A slave you may have been but you can choose to resist the Romans by stealth, subterfuge, or brute force, and by allying with the northern tribes. Or you can purchase freedom for yourself and your friends and buy your way into Roman high society. With ten different classes from agronomist to ranger, engineer, rancher, witch, and gladiator, with multiple different upgrade paths and special actions, you can play exactly the way you want to.

Awesome game, simple graphics, 2D, and yet very fun. It's a tactical strategy game where you customize your own squad, names, callsigns, loadouts, and roles (like shield, stealth, assaulter, breacher and pointman) and assign them to missions, and there are a ton of missions, premade missions, campaigns, community-made missions, mission generator and mission editor as well. Different objectives like hostages, bomb defusals, pure hostile killing, etc, The design of the plan system is very nice and well-made, you can plan out tactics and pause at any time of the game. You can make a whole plan from the start of the mission, or you can play a more real-time playstyle where your plan is improvised as the operation goes, or a combination of both.
If you are interested in conducting anti-terrorist/crime operations(e.g. SWAT) and is not too picky with the graphics, you should definitely give this a try.  It's got the Rainbow Six/SWAT atmosphere but the gameplay style of XCOM converted to real-time.
