First off, let me say that I FREAKING LOVE THIS GAME!
TL;DR - BUY THIS GAME. PLAY SINGLE PLAYER UNTIL YOU CAN MANUAL BLOCK. DOWNLOAD C-RPG MOD. START SMASHING FACES ONLINE.
This is THE epitome of a medieval simulator. You start as a peasant, hire a few men, work your way up the political ladder, and eventually gain land and kingship. The multiplayer is almost like a whole new game aside from the story. There are tons of mods to choose from that keep the game fresh after you think you've finally grown tired of the game.
Among the greatest mods ever made are C-RPG(online persistent characters) and Battle Time(play your single player battles with friends). The creator of C-RPG is even making a standalone game called Melee Battlegrounds, which can be found on Kickstarter.
The game exemplifies the "easy to learn, difficult to master" gameplay. Sure, you can just swing your sword at enemies until they die, but can you properly parry an attack from your left, follow up with your own thrust, then swing from the right, only to cancel into another parry all while dodging arrows and ordering an army of home-grown soldiers? With enough practice, this will become second nature as you tear through hordes of mercenaries, adrennaline pumping through your veins, and blood staining your armor.
After spending 200 hours in the first Mount & Blade, then 300 more in its sequel, I can safely say that M&B is one of the most underrated franchises in gaming history. And with mac and linux support now available, there's no reason not to get it.

I had some odd crashing issues the first time I started it, not sure if this was my computer having some odd hiccups or not but the bugs was gone the next day.
But the game itself got a nice atmosphere too it, with decent sound even if it overlayed strangely at times. As if not layered properly. The platforming worked but was at time spretty annoying. I also found the story to be a bit odd, not rushed or anything but you get dropped into something that feels like you missed out on the first half an hour to an hour of the game. No background, no information beside your gang being forced to leave their hide out and you get left alone.
From there on it escalates into your average zombie survival, side scrolling game where you get through Seattle to find your family and your travelling companions. The main guy is a ruff gruff ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but he works for the role. The story of our  ruff gruff ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is not the best in the world but it works out well enough and keeps you playing to see what will happen. It is only 4 hours so you will breeze through it. I found the first half better than the second but the second had more story and character interaction but also more annoying platformin, Especially in the sewers. The main character also has odd dreams which gives a bit of a odd touch to the game. Some parts feel like there is a higher power out there which is just growing stronger from all the talk from gruff ruff guy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about layers of hell, shadows and ghostly apparations.
It got a bit repeative in the end but since it is only  hours it do not overstays it's welcome. It could make for a sequel or other games in this version of the zombie apocalypse. But I think we won't see more games. I wish I could give this game something inbetween yes and no but there is non. It is decent enough on most levels and the short play time makes it a decent fit for a short game a sunday afternoon or a boring weekend. Bleak and atmospheric.
Without a doubt the best thing going for this game is it's atmosphere. I personally loved the art design. The hopelessness and dread of the world really ooze from both the environment and the great soundtrack, which fits the game well. The zombies are a genuine threat and you need to make sure you don't get surrounded by them. There are also a few exiting chase sequences. The world feels as fleshed out as it can be in a side scrolling platformer and the various collectibles are a nice touch.
The game is short and you will beat it in around 5-6 hours. This is not a huge negative because it never outsays it's welcome. The story is engaging enough but fairly typical and straightforward for a post-apocalyptic zombie game with a twist that many will see coming. However, due to the aformentioned short length of the game this is not an big issue. The protaganist Randall is believable and voice acted well if a little two-dimensional. However I was on board and invested with him on his perilous journey. I myself am a fan of hardened, grisly and damaged characters.
My only main issue with the game is that I found the platforming frustrating at times such as Randall not grabing onto the ledge that I wanted him to or finding it difficult to grab hold of/jump to platforms within easy reach. Situations like this caused a number of deaths and became annoying. However, It is only at certain areas that these sort of issues are a big problem and it does not detract from the game as a whole.
Overall a fun and atmospheric little game. I can easily recomend and during a sale I would say that you should definitely pick this up if you are a fan of platformers and atmospheric games.

Review for Volume from Bithell Games
__________________________
Quick Overview:
Visuals: Sharp, but minimalistic. It is cleverly done, creating solid aesthetic. The vibration animations are very neat. I love how sound interacts with the environment.
Sound: Also strong. The soundtrack is spot on, with great music for sneaking around corners, and incredibly jarring "YOU DONE GOOFED" music that makes me jump everytime. Sound effects are also nicely done, especially in how they tie in with the rest of the game. The voice acting varies from strong to excellent. Serkis does a tremendous job, and the Jim Sterling cameo is delightful. Some of Loxley's quips seem oddly dissonant with his demeanor during the main conversations he has. Alan is spot on.
Story: The world is steeped in fascinating lore. It is a shame that I only got to see ghosts of it. The story is drop fed to you occasionally, on certain levels. This creates pacing issues, with large stretches of levels without a story pulling you along. Very interesting, but the pacing complicates matters.
Gameplay: Arguably the game's strongest attribute. It nails stealth by keeping things straight forward and simple. It layers on logical complexity as time goes on, always abiding by its own rules, which are very clear. This makes any mistake your fault. As it is a stealth game, this is a big bonus. It also makes me want to swear very loudly. Stealth is not a genre I find particularly engaging, but this game's solid framework, and fairness made it far more engaging.
In Depth Discussion:
Volume is the sort of game that perplexes me. Story is often what draws me into a game, with a good tale making me very willing to overlook a lot of janky gameplay. Volume gives me the opposite problem. The story isn't bad, just not delivered efficiently. The way it gets interrupted by gameplay, often making the story feel like the sideshow, is a little jarring. As great as the voice acting is, it just kind of gets in the way of what makes the game great, its super solid stealth mechanics.
Which is really a shame. This is not to say that I think there shouldn't be a story, quite the opposite. The story is practically absent for huge stretches of the game, letting it slip from the mind. Then when it comes back, it is a little jarring. If it were more consistently present, even in the form of short conversations at the beginning of each level, It would likely feel more even. I would love for Loxley to actually talk to some of the stream watchers, because it is the world around Loxley that is more interesting. Loxley is causing waves in the world around him, but all we get is the occasional message from Alan letting us know that it is happening. As much as I appreciate having things left to the imagination, I feel that this is a sorely missed opportunity. Also, these near blank slates of people that we are helping get robbed could really have used some development, as characters. The world is so interesting, I really wish that it interacted with Loxley more, rather than us essentially putting on a play and hoping that the viewers catch the moral and run with it.
However, I still maintain that Volume is a good game, with "game" being more operative in the literal sense. There are clearly defined rules, with clearly defined implementations, with clearly defined goals. It is so prestinely smooth that I want to punch whoever designed those lasers. Because I hate them. And every error is my fault, not the games. I broke its rules, I got the consequences. But, screw those lasers. Volume's gameplay is so cleverly streamlined that there are few faults I can find in it. The only one that really jumps out at me is the cooldowns on your powers after you respawn. Loxley has tools that he can use, but each has a cooldown. When Loxley gets murderated, he respawns with his tool on cooldown, meaning you have to wait a bit before you can get going again. Which isn't a huge issue all of the time, but there are sections where you will die frequently, with that time stacking into annoyance. Not a huge issue, but a qualm that will likely irritate some more than others. Other than that, the gameplay tricked me into enjoying a stealth game, which is one heck of a con. It has a very "one more level" vibe going on. I happily worked my way through the game, having a blast, often getting blasted by guards (screw lasers).
For those looking for a mechanically masterful stealth experience, look no further. For those looking for a mechanically masterful stealth experience with a masterfully told story, I have some major caveats. The story is interesting, but its method of deliverly is poorly executed. It is as if someone is drip feeding me chocolate mousse with an eye dropper. It is still delicious, but it takes forever to get there, making it far less enjoyable. As I mentioned at the beginning, I am used to letting mechanically flimsy games get off nicely if their story whisps me away. Volume has convinced me that the opposite is also true, with its truly engaging gameplay willing to deal with its famine level rationing of story nibblets. Also, the team seems very intent to continue supporting the game regularly, so some of my qualms (likely not the story ones) may get addressed. I would like to thank the people at Bithell Games for putting all their wonderful effort into this game, rage inducing lasers or not (screw lasers).

I wrote a more in-depth review here
, but here's a short summary. There are definitely some neat ideas floating about (running a stream LP on how to steal from locations is rather novel, and it's a pretty gorgeous game), but the checkpointing encourages you to finish levels in a clumsy fashion instead of properly sneaking, and even when you DO play it "properly," the abysmal guard AI and sluggish movement combine to make it a miserable time. Even the story falls flat: the person who voices Locksley isn't great, especially next to Andy Serkis, the plot is delivered haphazardly, and just when it starts to get promising, it ends.
I was really looking forward to this one, but it falters in nearly every regard. You'd be better off playing The Marvellous Miss Take or Mark of the Ninja, if you're looking for a great indie stealth game.

This is a slightly different take on the 'match colored gems' genre. Blocks will fall out of the sky, randomly, and it's your job, as a playable character, to destroy these blocks with your gun. If you shoot a block, all the other blocks connected it will also be destroyed. As long as they're the same color. Destroyed blocks will give you stars and earning enough of these stars will level up your character allowing him to shoot much faster and also to get hit should a block fall on him. Your level equals the number of times you can get hit, except if you fall onto the spikes or a weaponized block hits you. So, a level 3 character allows you to get hit 3 times. It's a challenging game, but you'll learn how to play it in a matter of minutes. 'Easy to learn, hard to master' has been never more appropriate.
Collecitng enough stars will unlock new outfits that give you more abilites, like a double jump or a jetpack, making the game slightly easier.
The retro graphics are charming and the music is pretty good, but gets a bit repetitive after a few games.
There are also challenges to be unlocked, but instead of relying on skills, they actually rely on memory. They can be frustrating, but fun, since they only last 30 seconds.

Credit where it's due, Sr Pelo was the way I discovered this game exists.
How many of us have imposed self-made challenges on ourselves to old platformers we know by heart? Those silly, pointless rules that nevertheless made an otherwise mundane segment into something much more challenging, leading us to question our own decision making and/or skills?
Skeleton Boomerang is that, personified. In the ultimate case of "Why am I making this so hard", the boomerang juggling for points changes what would otherwise be standard platforming fare into a combination of physics manipulation, reflexes, and luck for your score. It was smart of the game to tie your upgrades into your accumulated score in order to encourage this, and it creates its own replay value in two ways when you return somewhere both to bump towards and upgrade but also for your own standards. It'll also be the reason you fail to take down an enemy before taking damage, leading you to at some point to go "Why juggle when I can just throw it at them straight?" But that's okay, you'll silence that corner of your mind over time.
The art style is lovely with Hunter having charming little animations (and for your many, bony foes), and the music is so catchy it's one of the factors that got my attention to buy the game. I do think a few levels tend to drag on to the longer side than what's necessary (mainly because you only get a mid-level checkpoint in each), but that wasn't enough of a factor to make me look at this negatively.
Oh, and I hope you like a combination of bone puns and facts. "Bonunaga's Ambition" as a level name made me die in the best, possible way.

FreeHolder is an indie game that released in it's alpha stage on 5th July 2016. The game itself combines strategy, RPG, rogue like, and survival elements all into a single game. Don't be fooled by the games graphics, this game is very complex and is a fairly in-depth game.
FreeHolder is a great styled game, that combines a lot of genres that I really enjoy in games into one game of itself. Playing this game for the first time was quite a experience, I was really unsure what to do and what was going on in general. So to start off, the game itself has no known tutorial as of creating this review. Now this can be seen as understandable as the game has so many mechanics and is so in-depth that it would literally take ages to add a tutorial into the game itself. But, then there is the other point that the game is so in-depth that you have to look up how things work because of the games complexity. Although the game has no tutorial, it does have a fair amount of tips to help you through the game, but even then I still found myself looking up certain things because I was unsure how some of the mechanics work.
The game has a lot of replay ability and play styles that you will be able to choose to suit your needs. When you first start playing the game there are several characters that you can choose from, all of them having their own strengths and abilities. This gives the game a lot of different play styles and replay value as each character is different from others. As well as several different characters, there are also a few different abilities with each character that you choose, having their own buff that will help you in some way in the game.
The main point of the game is to survive as long as you can, now there is a lot of ways that you can lose in this game. You will get a game over when all of your characters die, and as the game has so many mechanics that are all so in-depth you may die more than you would expect. First off, there are different seasons in the game that will, obviously, affect the weather. This will affect a few mechanics in the game, the first and the most important is the soil of the farms that you use for your main source of food. Depending on the season will depend on what 'type' of soil the farm area is, this effects the crops that you plant in order to get food and might speed up or slow down the process of how long it will take for the food to harvest fully. The next thing to worry about is the weather itself, if it is winter then you are going to need fire wood in order to survive the night or you might get frostbite on your characters.
The game has a rather compelling thinking process that may take you a hour or so to decide what you have to do. As each character has a certain amount of actions points that you can spend each turn, you may find yourself trying to way the pros and cons over what to do with a single action point. This really shows that the game itself is really in-depth and has a lot to do in the game.
With the game having rogue-like elements implemented into the game, it keeps the game challenging but at the same time it keeps the game fun. The problem with most of the rogue-like games on steam is that you might get angry at the game because you lost. But this game has the right sort of rogue-like elements to keep the game fun and not getting you to rage at the game.
The games graphics are something that I feel could do with a bit of polishing up. I do like the graphic style that the developer went with, and I understand that the developers focus is more for the core mechanics of the game but I still feel the need to point out that it needs a bit more work.
Although the game is very fun and addicting, I can't help but feel like the game is overpriced even at this early Alpha stage. For a game that costs £6.99 I would expect this to be at least a nearly finished product, I just don't feel like the game has that much to offer for the amount it's asking at the moment. I understand that there is a lot of mechanics in the game, but this is just my own personal preference.
The music of the game is just amazing, its soundtrack is obviously 8-bit styled and really compels me to play the game more just to listen to the soundtrack more. The soundtrack is original and is really well done by the developers, defiantly one of the strong points about this game.
+ Lots of play styles to suit the way you play
+ High replay value
+ In-depth gameplay
+ Lots of customisation
+ Great original music and sound
= The game has no tutorial, only a coupe of tips. I am willing to forgive this as the game is fairly in-depth and has complex mechanics.
- Game seems to be overpriced, even at this early Alpha stage of the game and that the game has quite a lot of mechanics. But I myself feel like it is slightly overpriced, but then again that's just my own opinion.
- The graphics are something that need to be improved on in my opinion. I like the style of the graphics, but I feel like it really needs a polish and some work on.
I feel like this game has a lot of potential, it is a very in-depth game that has a high replay value, great mechanics and just so much content. Although, I personally think that the game (at this time of making the review) is overpriced at this early Alpha stage but that's just my own opinion. The graphics could do with a polish up and the soundtrack is just amazing. I would defiantly recommend this game if you enjoy turn-based RPG with survival and rogue-like elements.

FreeHolder is fun and continues to fill with more content on every update. If your a fan of games like Civilation, this has a gameplay style similiar with a story-driven RPG Final Fantasy meets Harvest Moon feel.

FreeHolder has the elements to become one of the most addictive and replayable games of all time. Really. It combines tile-based procedural regeneration, in-depth RPG character development, wonderful sound effects and music (the music is astoundingly good!), and meta-strategy that I haven't seen since the famous roguelike, Dungeon Crawl. The fact that every click of the mouse has significant consequences is highly compelling. I often found myself mulling over how to spend one or two action points for a particular character and in what order to spend them! Every new game gives a different experience; combine that with switching your main character's class at the start of a new game and the possibilities and play styles truly seem infinite. Never been hooked on a game in its earliest stage of development!
This is a thinking-man's game! This point is supported by the fact that the friggin' soundtrack is basically 8-bit Bach (i.e., all highly complex counterpoint). It's an original soundtrack I could only compare to the likes of Hotline Miami! Bravo, Devs!
Also, it feels fantastic to have a game that is as challenging as this one. Most games get boring on account of being too easy or the characters becoming too powerful. The roguelike aspect of the game really keeps things feeling fresh, yet I don't find myself pounding my desk in anger!
Let's talk about the price point. $9.99 is a modest price to pay for the amount of work it appears these devs have put in. On top of that, the profit from sales will go directly back into the game. It's a number that I feel is fair, even though at first glance might seem high for an early Alpha. However, think about what you spend on alcohol? It's one freakin' beer. A beer gives you 10 minutes of enjoyment. The evident timelessness of this game's look combined with its gameplay means endless enjoyment. Far more worth $9.99 than a pithy beer (no disrespect to beer, of course).
To sum up, FreeHolder seamlessly integrates the best aspects of a number of my favorite games:
- the enjoyment of working the land I got from Harvest Moon back in the day
- the Final Fantasy style battles and music to pump you up
- the randomness and challenge that comes with roguelikes such as Dungeon Crawl
- in-depth game play and a surpisingly simple yet compelling story-line that drives your efforts
- the crafting and customizability of Minecraft
Another intriguing fact is that the devs are super involved in the community. It really feels like "the people's game" so far. Looking forward to further interaction with the devs.
Can't wait to see FreeHolder develop into a mighty independent title! The sky's the limit with this one.

I came into this on recommendations from my brother and some close friends. They told me 'It's a lot like Left 4 Dead, but instead of guns you stove lads loafs in with maces, axes, swords, staves and hammers...and then maybe shoot them afterwards.' (Or something to that effect. :p )
So first, the good.
+ The four player co-op vs horde that made Left 4 Dead such a breakaway hit is as tried, true and tested here as it was all those glorious years ago.
+ There are 5 characters to choose from, each of whom play a little differently from each other out of the box. There's a little something for everyone here, with a fast attacking, rapid firing yet somehow sniperiffic Elf, a hard hitting, hard shooting but slow moving Dwarf, an armoured wall of steel in the Sergeant, a rapid gunning Demon Hunter and most difficult but useful of all a pyromaniacal Bright Wizard (Basically a human flamethrower.)
+ Each class can be customised with several different weapons of each type, ensuring that you can always find a way to work with any of the classes.
+ The level design is very, very good. In much the same way as Left 4 Dead allowed plenty of routes through a level as well as plenty of hidey-holes for Special Infected, Vermintide keeps this tradition alive and well.
+ Warhammer authenticity is absolutely spot-on. Weapons look and feel like they should, character design is on-point, backdrops are exactly as you imagine they'd be in Warhammer Fantasy.
+ Skaven are the perfect enemy for this first game. There are plenty of enemy types that can offer any level of challenge you're looking for.
+ The best Warhammer Action game since Fire Warrior in terms of fun.
+ No Microtransactions. I bought this game at a great price brand new and have access to all of the content, which in 2015 is a rare and admirable decision. It would have been easy to take a low-road approach to cosmetic items, weapons and maps in this game, but Fatshark instead took the decision to actually sell us a videogame! (A very good one at that!)
RESPECT!
Now for the stuff I'm not so sold on...
- AI partners are very, very stupid. They oftentimes will not pick up items, even when signposted by the player to do so, they regularly ignore your plight when you're hooked or stabbed, they often stand right in the gas cloud and they are generally useless in a fight. (Though an AI Elf will rip up with a bow.)
- No Checkpointing. If your party wipes, it's game over and back to the lobby. No continues, no going back to the midway point. I feel this is a negative because there are times when the AI throws everything but the kitchen sink at you and no matter how well you play, sometimes you're getting the dreaded Hook, Assassin, Gas, Horde and Ogre attack at once that is just insurmountable in this game without a cohesive team with the best of loot. Some gamers will like this, but not all of us have the kind of free time available when we're working full time to constantly retry levels over and over with little reward or ability to progress. I'm not asking for the game to 'be casual' but I am suggesting that it could have taken a leaf out of the L4D playbook just one more time.
- Enemy balance is slightly off. Hook Rats move far too quickly while dragging a player character, especially in light of how slow the player moves with a grain sack or barrell. Assassins can't be blocked, even if you're rocking a shield. Stormvermin on the harder modes seem to shrug off headshots and do insane one-hit damage. Rat Ogres are far, far tougher than tanks in L4D and in alot of these maps, there are environmental traps like water and ledges that the Ogre can knock you off in a single hit and with the limited range of the dodge, it's extremely difficult to evade or even conduct combat with the Ogre effectively without some real problems. Some minor tweaks would improve game flow.
- Movement glitches. Multiple times, I found myself getting stuck immobile on stairs and staircases and in a game where mobility is as important as it is in this one, that's something that really needs to not happen. At times, it's like running into an invisible wall.
- Randomisation of the loot. I've been playing this game for 18+ hours so-far and I've got to say, the amount of times I roll the dice and the dice turn up all blank has been slightly alarming. Dice rolls can often be a difficult mechanic to nail down but curently it feels like there might be something janked about the RNG, because even with special dice from an incredible run, I have extremely rarely got above three successes.
- No cameos from other types of creatures in this game. We get to a crypt that has an eerie green glow and there's no undead? In Warhammer? That's a little odd. I can understand, this is the first game and what they've put outthere so-far is excellent, but I think that could have been pretty cool. Just a nitpick, not a huge thing at all.
- It's a little too similar to Left 4 Dead. I love L4D, it's a phenomenal game that gave me the best multiplayer experiences I'd had since Resident Evil Outbreak 2 (My favourite ever online game) so it's a great template to use, however I feel that there's just a little too much of that and not quite enough to set this game apart. Again, I'm nitpicking, because in all honesty, you're giving me more of a good thing here.
And finally, the ugly.
- - Always Online. If the connection to Steam drops, say for an unexpected outage, your game won't continue offline, it will simply reset. Last night, I lost three games to connection issues on the server side, which is potentially three loot items and upwards of three XP levels...that's a hell of a blow through no fault of my own. More importantly, it's a hell of a waste of my ever dwindling free-time!
- - The loot system in this game is completely random and will only pay out to a player on a successful completion...This leads on nicely to the next point;
- - Level-based matchmaking system has bred elitism into this community. Unfortunately, some groups of players will look at your level when you join a game in progress and turn their nose up at the help. With the AI being as poor in utility as it is, it absolutely baffles me why some groups will throw you out of the party when you've used the 'matchmaking' service in good faith. At over level 15, I find myself when I solo queue for some Hard Mode games, I'm kicked from the group after helping them through a particularly tough fight because 'You're too low scrubnoob.'
While I can understand the frustration that can be caused by new players jumping immediately into the hardest modes, as this game is longer and longer released, you're going to find that new players will become ostracised and frustrated by this kind of ingrained elitism. Alot of this problem isn't necessarily the community themselves, but more to do with the design decision on how loot is distributed. If a player goes through a 40 minute + slog through a level, only to die right at the end and get absolutely nothing for it with no checkpointing or continuing mid-game, (Unlike L4D) of course they're going to be *slightly* precious about maximising their chances of winning, matchmaking be damned.
Overall, Vermintide is a very good game that offers up some good co-operative gameplay, fun challenges and all at an impressive pricepoint. For the money, it's well worth giving this a go, especially if you enjoyed Left 4 Dead or other co-op games. I'm very impressed with what FatShark have given us here and this game is only going to get better as it's further patched and updated. I hear they've got a content patch coming adding tonnes of new gear and such this coming December and that at this point is exciting.
My faith in Sigmar is strong.

tl;dr - Very overrated 2.5D platformer. Lousy control response; part of that "die and retry" flood of shadowy atmosphere marketplace games that hit after Limbo's success.
Long version - I really like the 2.5D style; the game reminds me of Shadow Complex in that regard, and I'm a big fan of that "retro concept but modern style" format that these games have. That's about as far as I can go praising it, though. The story is generic and the main character's motivation for moving forward ends up being a pretty big cop-out. But the real problem here is the "die and retry" system combined with the horrible controls. Yes, they suck. THEY SUCK.
The problem is the "real life" responses. The main character staggers when sharply changing direction, his jumps are erratic, the run+roll function isn't available in the first second of his full run animation, the run+jump function isn't available in this first second of run animation either, etc.,. So, yes, it makes for a very ragged and harrowing experience when being chased through areas with endless zombies, but more often than not, it just creates a world of frustration.
There's a particular scene in the game where you have to jump across a water pit (the character cannot swim, and therefor jumping into any water higher than your waist is an automatic death) and escape through a collapsing building. The problem is that the controls, being as horrible as they are, offered me no clue as to what I was doing wrong and resulted in at least 10-15 obnoxious deaths. The reason being: after the jump, you have to run through falling debris and then wall jump to a platform, then jump to another platform and race out. Simple enough. But the first time I ran through, the guy died on the last pipe that falls just before the wall jump. I tried again, hopefully faster, but the pipe falls and kills him. So I figured "okay, I'm supposed to roll." So I jump across the water, run, roll, get under the pipe and end up face-to-face with the wall. But he can't walljump from a straight vertical jump. So I had to dash backward, lunge at the wall and... by that time, he's dead from more falling debris. So now I'm thinking I have to roll earlier and immediately transition into the wall jump. But after the water jump, his run animation starts in, and for that first second, the roll isn't available - he ends up crouching and dying. To make matters worse, I tried this one other time and without rolling, I was able to get to the wall jump. So I'm completely confused on what to do. (As near as I could figure, you actually have to jump early, barely cross the water so that your run can hit 1.1 second and you can roll ahead of the final pipe and hit the wall jump correctly. That's a lot of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t just for "realistic" controls)
I also want to mention at certain times (not all, in fairness), it can be really difficult to determine what platform you can stand on and what one you can't; conveniently this shows up in places with death traps/pits.
There's some issues with collision detection and zombies as well, but it takes a back seat to this control mess.
Overall, this thing is way overrated. The aggregate should be mixed at best: I've played worse games, but I've played far better (marketplace) games. The game is also short as♥♥♥♥♥♥ The 4.3 hours logged includes a couple restarts wherein I didn't save the game on a cloud server and the whole thing went with the uninstall process. The actual playthrough of the game for me is 1.3 hours. That's just not worth it at $15.
Pass on this. I know it has very positive reviews, but it's simply not worth the price or annoyance. Though I will say realizing I was watching the ending cutscene was a joy.

I can only recommend this tentatively and ONLY with some of the better mods, because that's the only way I can enjoy it in spite of its many, many, many, many, MANY problems.
As for the good, the open sandbox nature of the game is enjoyable whether you want to be a jumped-up bandit, a self- made king, a mercenary, or the leader of a small band of heroes. The management of your party is generally good and leading an army into battle is something few games can really deliver on the way warband does.
As for the bad, oooooo boy. Let's make a list.
First, the hit detection in this game is literally the worst I've ever seen. The sheer number of times I've watched my lance or axe pass through someone's torso without any impact is staggering, and it's like that for plenty of other weapons whether you're on foot or on horseback, melee or ranged. One of the most frustrating things in the game is when you ride at an enemy horseman and swing for his head with a sword and watch it sail over his horse's head, only to see a little damage log in the corner say "delivered X damage to horse". This, of course, if usually followed by the horse's owner smashing your face in.
Second, the game's speed bonuses and penalties on damage are garbage. If this is using some kind of physics engine to make the calculations, it is truly an awful one. It's usually less of a problem on foot because it's less finickythen, but I have had plenty of times when I suffer a speed PENALTY to damage even though I'm running or riding at an enemy at top speed when I hit them, and I've sometimes even had speed bonuses to my damage even though my target and I are standing stock still.
Third, the interface can be immensely frustrating. Want to check your inventory while resting in town? ♥♥♥♥ NO. You have to exit the town menu entirely to even interact with ANY of your own menu options -- including to level up your party members or check your food supplies. This also happens when you are inside a castle being besieged or (even more frustrating) when you are the one doing the besieging. In the latter case, this means that you actually have to ABANDON THE SIEGE to open your party or inventory menu.
Fourth, this game explains NOTHING to you. The tutorial is solely how to manage your character in battle, and nothing else is ever explained. Where can you find jobs? How do you give your soldiers orders? How do you perform raids or establish yourself as a lord? You better know someone who knows how to do all of that already or you'll probably have to check the wiki. For that matter, many of the numbers you see are never given any context. What does a reach of 110 even mean? What is a speed rating of 99, and how much slower is a 90?the game will also fail to notify you of important things, like NPCs being unhappy with how things are going. I just recently lost my best engineer character because he was apparently unhappy with some of my other companions. I only know this because I loaded an earlier save after he left and specifically asked him how he felt, because the game never thought to bring this to my attention. I don't even know WHY he's unhappy with my companions, he just IS despite the fact that I've never been shown anything indicating a reason.
Fifth, in battle this game is immensely fond of what I call "because ♥♥♥♥ you" moments. Have the settings set so that you only take 1/2 damage from enemies? Watch as a mid-level enemy swordsman takes out half your health with a single swing in spite of the fact that you are wearing some of the best armor in the game. Think that you can take out that rider you just dehorsed before he can stand up? Tough♥♥♥♥♥♥ since he's going to block you despite being incapable of doing so because it will interrupt his standing up animation to do his block, magically snapping him into a standing position. Want to hit that one guy in the back while he blocks your ally's attacks to his front? Nope, he can somehow block behind himself with a shield that is in front of him. Why? Because ♥♥♥♥ you, that's why.
Sixth is the weaponry. There are a TON of weapons, but way too many are just awful, so you'll end up just picking whatever is the most powerful weapon in its category. There are also all kinds of weapon possibilities that are inexplicably left out or that just leave you scratching your head. Why are there no axes that can be wielded in either one hand or both? Why is a longaxe primarily considered a polearm when that's not how they were used and it means that it will be used to thrust at enemies by default whenever you use it on horseback? What the hell is a warblade? It's not a real weapon, I can tell you that much -- it only exists in one or two tapestries depicting medieval warfare. Why does a morningstar deal piercing damage, when they only had those spikes in reality because they helped direct the force of the blow that that it wouldn't bounce off armor?
Seventh, collision. Ooooh boy, collision. For this one the devs especially deserve a smack upside the head. In battle, AI controlled characters can swing through one another to hit their enemies. You, the player, cannot. This means that you will find yourself unable to hit the enemy in tightly-packed quarters while they have no trouble planting their pointiest sticks somewhere between your lungs and colon. Even worse, AI units can phase a significant portion of their model (i'd say roughly half, give or take a bit more) into one another, and if ONE of them is blocking your attack you will bounce off and do no damage to ANY of them. I cannot count the number of times I've been forced to backpedal to avoid being surrounded only for my enemies to form a human centipede/conga line where a few of them will block in different directions just before I swing while others swing at me. The result is that I literally CANNOT hit them no matter what I do and they will beat the crap out of me.

Aside from the gameplay itself, the music is enjoyable, and fits very well for the cartoon-y atmosphere. It's the same case for the SFX, with a heavy use of xylophones to truly give off the cartoon skeleton vibe. My only real gripe with the game is that I can't seem to find out what I'm supposed to be doing with the Bone Chips (I guess in a sense they're like coins if it were a Mario game, but there's no stored lives, so they seem kind of useless).
Overall, the smaller components of this game stack up to make a much more fun experience, and I reccomend that if you were to play this game that you actively sought out all of the collectible items. Please, try it!

A brief summary of Ylands,
So far I have put quite a few hours in Ylands and am still being pleasantly surpised and entertained on a regular basis. This is a very casual survival game (for the most part, although I have been killed) that seems to focus on a deep crafting system and exploration. I payed 12 bucks for this game and its been one of the best steam purchases I have made in a while. I dont normally write reviews but with all the nonsense from people who dont even play the game on the discussion forums I figured it would be worth it to add my support here.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics despite the low poly style. The lighting and the water are two particularly nice things.
-Casusal gameplay. I find the game relaxing when I want it to be, but with an option to get yourself into trouble when you choose.
-Immersive and interesting crafting system. Most things I encounter make sense with how they are made and if you know anything about its real life counterpart you might be able to conjure a guess on how to make it.
-EXPLORATION. Its a simple concept that in my opinion is executed very well. Loot and points of interest are done in creative and interactive ways. The biomes are nice and varied. I dont even know how many their are because aside from an occasional crafting reference I refuse to use the internet to learn too much about the world because walking, riding, and sailing around really is that interesting.
-Great and flexible building system. You can free place anything anywhere. You can customize your boats, rafts and ships (although your limited until you get to the ship and large ship platforms)
-Probalby a lot more but I dont want to type all morning.
Cons:
-Cant browse forums for tips and experiences without an idiot complaining about DayZ
-A few movement glitches, most I have noticed with ladders, got myself stuck on top of a mast the other day.
-Combat, especially swinging swords and hammers seems a bit wonky.
Other thoughts;
If a developer sees this, I hope they are working on some sort of rating system for weapons and armor or atleast some sort of stat viewing option to know how thermally insulated you are and things like that. I got my moneys worth out of this game the first couple hours and will undoubtedly put a couple hundred into it before its all said and done. I for one didnt even realize there was a ylands store to spend money in so that has had no impact on my opinion of the game. This is not a hardcore PVP game so even if the items for sale were "Pay to Win" there wouldnt be much point. My understanding is thats its all skins and furniture stuffs, but like I said, been too busy playing and enjoying the game to even  look.

I've played through the first half of the game twice now. It's a very endearing game that gives you exactly what it said it would. Yes, the concept is simple. Yes, the enemies ignore you when they should be able to see you, but it's the way the game was designed. It is a puzzle game with a focus on stealth and misdirection to enact acts of theft and espionage.
Once ou realize the story that is going on you find that the graphics, the 'logic', and pretty much all of it make sense. It've very cohesive even from aesthetic right down to the characters. The interactions with Alan and Locksley are priceless.. and Gisborne is delightful. No really he is. Humour is spot on.
The story and backstory unfold nicely as you move through the game. Sure, the official gameplay might be a bit short, taking a few hours to get through the first half of the game.. there's 100 level by the way... but the game's replay value is utterly extended by one simple feature.. level creation tools. The tools provided look to be practically what the developer would use himself. They are a bit clunky, especially if you are not a level editor like me, but they provide you with pretty much whatever you'd want.
These levels are also made available for other players to test their might, and the devs will pick from among the best for Staff Picks.
All in all.. this game is amazingly wonderful. It can be frustrating.. it can be super easy.. it can even get a bit repetitive at times, but not once have I not had fun while doing it.
Only complaint.. the Locksley/Alan banter is only for the first time through a level until you complete said level. So sad. Love those parts. They are the best.

When you load up Volume, you are met with the text, "We are very proud of this game." I bring this up because Volume is very, very much somthing to be proud of.
Firstly, the game is beautiful. the textures are not terribly detailed, but they are done so in a stylistic manner. The game has terrific visual effects, the most notable being the "exploding triangle thing".
Story wise, Volume carries one of the most mind blowing things for me in recent history. While this may have been a result of myself going into Volume with certain expectations, I do not want to spoil it for those who have done the same. All I will say on the matter is: "Ryan 192nc9s"
Gameplay wise, Volume follows the ideal indie game approach, as Mr. Bithell is prone to do, that being "do one thing, but do it very very well." The whole game is of the 'soft stealth' variety, in which being seen is not always a death sentence, but only if you get seen intentionally. While unfortunately, many of the gadgets are just variations on the same noisemaker, this game does promote their small differences strongly, as you cannot kill in this game. all of the gadgets are there to distract your foes, not remove them from action. You must therefore apply the small differences in the gadgets in incresingly clever ways if you want to make par time, or even complete the level in the first place.
In conclusion, Volume is a very good game made by a very good team. I bought Volume on Mr. Bithell's reputation alone, and I am glad that I did so. The levels often force you to think outside the box, and all together this game is so addicting that I had to forcefully rip myself off of the next level button just to write this review.
Oh, and did I mention that the soundtrack is made (once again) by David Housden? The soundtrack alone is worth 20 bucks.

Ignore the time Steam says I have played. I have played about 14 hours of the game overall, most of it done offline while I was traveling.

Pros
-Simple controls that anyone can pick up.
-Can be played with one hand.
-Game mechanics may be simple, but allow for extremely complex strategies to be played out.
-Versetile level editor.
-Lots of content in the game, hundreds of standalone missions ranging in difficulty, as well as a handful of campaigns lasting 1 to 2 hours each.

-Scenario Variety
-Perfect game to play on a laptop if you have a mouse.

-Pause and play allows you to assess the situation on an action by action basis, giving the player time to think and plan.
-Good soundtrack.
-Playing with your own music/podcast in the background takes nothing away from the game.
Cons
-Enviroments can get repetitive. (The level design is varried, I'm talking about the way they look)
-Controls don't work well when trying to play in real time.
-Some of the bigger levels can get tedious, especially if you are stuck looking for the last enemy, hostage, bomb, etc.
-How fast your guys react to getting shot at is random at times.
-Steath is underdeveloped.
Conclusion
This is the most fun I have had in an RTS ever. This is coming from someone who doesn't really like RTS games. I decided to give this game a shot, mainly because I am a fan of squad based Tactical FPS's (Swat 4 and Arma 3 being my favorites) and this game shared the same concepts. Overall, the game is accessible, but still has the complexity to please seasoned RTS verterans.
Recommended to: Players who are looking for an accessible game that has a challenging tactical experience that does not rely on clunky UI or twitch shooting.

The first thing I noticed was the camera smoothing, or camera inertia as this game calls it. For those that don't know, camera smoothing gives the player's "camera" artificial weight, when you move it starts out a bit slow, then takes a tiny bit to stop, instead of halting on the spot like any other video game or actual eyes. This feature might be prefered for some people, but for me it feels terrible. Good thing they added in a setting to turn it off, except that setting does nothing, even if you click "apply" before closing the menu.
Speaking of menus, this game has the worst menu interface I have ever used. it is so unneccesarily complicated and difficult to navigate that I can't do the first objective it gives you. That might be just a user error though (probably not).
The world and alien life look worse and are less creative than 60s sci-fi. The land alien life includes: goofy rock throwing monkey, stegosaurus but smaller, Tree but instead of branches and leaves it's green tubes, and giant plant stargate. The ocean alien life includes: moldy cloth with eyes, a normal fish and an angry fish but two lower jaws and dreads on it's tail.
The early game combat is also horrendous, every thing has a lot of health so it takes forever to kill anything, and when you attack with a melee weapon your character lunges forward so you are constantly readjusting where you're aiming at, which wouldbe tolerable without the camera inertia.

I came into this on recommendations from my brother and some close friends. They told me 'It's a lot like Left 4 Dead, but instead of guns you stove lads loafs in with maces, axes, swords, staves and hammers...and then maybe shoot them afterwards.' (Or something to that effect. :p )
So first, the good.
+ The four player co-op vs horde that made Left 4 Dead such a breakaway hit is as tried, true and tested here as it was all those glorious years ago.
+ There are 5 characters to choose from, each of whom play a little differently from each other out of the box. There's a little something for everyone here, with a fast attacking, rapid firing yet somehow sniperiffic Elf, a hard hitting, hard shooting but slow moving Dwarf, an armoured wall of steel in the Sergeant, a rapid gunning Demon Hunter and most difficult but useful of all a pyromaniacal Bright Wizard (Basically a human flamethrower.)
+ Each class can be customised with several different weapons of each type, ensuring that you can always find a way to work with any of the classes.
+ The level design is very, very good. In much the same way as Left 4 Dead allowed plenty of routes through a level as well as plenty of hidey-holes for Special Infected, Vermintide keeps this tradition alive and well.
+ Warhammer authenticity is absolutely spot-on. Weapons look and feel like they should, character design is on-point, backdrops are exactly as you imagine they'd be in Warhammer Fantasy.
+ Skaven are the perfect enemy for this first game. There are plenty of enemy types that can offer any level of challenge you're looking for.
+ The best Warhammer Action game since Fire Warrior in terms of fun.
+ No Microtransactions. I bought this game at a great price brand new and have access to all of the content, which in 2015 is a rare and admirable decision. It would have been easy to take a low-road approach to cosmetic items, weapons and maps in this game, but Fatshark instead took the decision to actually sell us a videogame! (A very good one at that!)
RESPECT!
Now for the stuff I'm not so sold on...
- AI partners are very, very stupid. They oftentimes will not pick up items, even when signposted by the player to do so, they regularly ignore your plight when you're hooked or stabbed, they often stand right in the gas cloud and they are generally useless in a fight. (Though an AI Elf will rip up with a bow.)
- No Checkpointing. If your party wipes, it's game over and back to the lobby. No continues, no going back to the midway point. I feel this is a negative because there are times when the AI throws everything but the kitchen sink at you and no matter how well you play, sometimes you're getting the dreaded Hook, Assassin, Gas, Horde and Ogre attack at once that is just insurmountable in this game without a cohesive team with the best of loot. Some gamers will like this, but not all of us have the kind of free time available when we're working full time to constantly retry levels over and over with little reward or ability to progress. I'm not asking for the game to 'be casual' but I am suggesting that it could have taken a leaf out of the L4D playbook just one more time.
- Enemy balance is slightly off. Hook Rats move far too quickly while dragging a player character, especially in light of how slow the player moves with a grain sack or barrell. Assassins can't be blocked, even if you're rocking a shield. Stormvermin on the harder modes seem to shrug off headshots and do insane one-hit damage. Rat Ogres are far, far tougher than tanks in L4D and in alot of these maps, there are environmental traps like water and ledges that the Ogre can knock you off in a single hit and with the limited range of the dodge, it's extremely difficult to evade or even conduct combat with the Ogre effectively without some real problems. Some minor tweaks would improve game flow.
- Movement glitches. Multiple times, I found myself getting stuck immobile on stairs and staircases and in a game where mobility is as important as it is in this one, that's something that really needs to not happen. At times, it's like running into an invisible wall.
- Randomisation of the loot. I've been playing this game for 18+ hours so-far and I've got to say, the amount of times I roll the dice and the dice turn up all blank has been slightly alarming. Dice rolls can often be a difficult mechanic to nail down but curently it feels like there might be something janked about the RNG, because even with special dice from an incredible run, I have extremely rarely got above three successes.
- No cameos from other types of creatures in this game. We get to a crypt that has an eerie green glow and there's no undead? In Warhammer? That's a little odd. I can understand, this is the first game and what they've put outthere so-far is excellent, but I think that could have been pretty cool. Just a nitpick, not a huge thing at all.
- It's a little too similar to Left 4 Dead. I love L4D, it's a phenomenal game that gave me the best multiplayer experiences I'd had since Resident Evil Outbreak 2 (My favourite ever online game) so it's a great template to use, however I feel that there's just a little too much of that and not quite enough to set this game apart. Again, I'm nitpicking, because in all honesty, you're giving me more of a good thing here.
And finally, the ugly.
- - Always Online. If the connection to Steam drops, say for an unexpected outage, your game won't continue offline, it will simply reset. Last night, I lost three games to connection issues on the server side, which is potentially three loot items and upwards of three XP levels...that's a hell of a blow through no fault of my own. More importantly, it's a hell of a waste of my ever dwindling free-time!
- - The loot system in this game is completely random and will only pay out to a player on a successful completion...This leads on nicely to the next point;
- - Level-based matchmaking system has bred elitism into this community. Unfortunately, some groups of players will look at your level when you join a game in progress and turn their nose up at the help. With the AI being as poor in utility as it is, it absolutely baffles me why some groups will throw you out of the party when you've used the 'matchmaking' service in good faith. At over level 15, I find myself when I solo queue for some Hard Mode games, I'm kicked from the group after helping them through a particularly tough fight because 'You're too low scrubnoob.'
While I can understand the frustration that can be caused by new players jumping immediately into the hardest modes, as this game is longer and longer released, you're going to find that new players will become ostracised and frustrated by this kind of ingrained elitism. Alot of this problem isn't necessarily the community themselves, but more to do with the design decision on how loot is distributed. If a player goes through a 40 minute + slog through a level, only to die right at the end and get absolutely nothing for it with no checkpointing or continuing mid-game, (Unlike L4D) of course they're going to be *slightly* precious about maximising their chances of winning, matchmaking be damned.
Overall, Vermintide is a very good game that offers up some good co-operative gameplay, fun challenges and all at an impressive pricepoint. For the money, it's well worth giving this a go, especially if you enjoyed Left 4 Dead or other co-op games. I'm very impressed with what FatShark have given us here and this game is only going to get better as it's further patched and updated. I hear they've got a content patch coming adding tonnes of new gear and such this coming December and that at this point is exciting.
My faith in Sigmar is strong.

Deadlight is a 2d Action Platformer developed by Tequila Works and released in 2012. Deadlight is definitely worth a play through, there are a few puzzles I've been hung up on, but it's mostly a 6-7 hour experience.
The protagonist for Deadlight is Randall Wayne, I don't think they ever mention his last name, typically he goes by Randy. I call him Gravel-McScratchy-voice.
As per usual for this genre of game, the Zombies outbreak has happened and everyone's been effected by the infection either directly or indirectly. For some bizarre reason they insist on calling zombies "shadows". Randy is trying to track down his friends and family.
Without spoiling the ending, I wasn't that impressed or pleased with the conclusion or the twist, but it was worth a play through.
Deadlight is played in that cool-stylized 2d gameplay in a 3d modeled world. and the story is told in fancy still-image-layer-animated-flash movies. So in the style department they're batting darn-near-perfect.
However the movement controls are a bit more clunky then I'd like... especially where chain-linked fences are concerned. You move around with WASD in 2d space, so mostly A and D, sometimes pressing control to duck or roll after a jump, aiming and firing with the mouse.
clearly the game was designed for controllers in mind, but the keyboard and mouse controls transitioned very well.
In conclusion I enjoyed the time I spent playing Deadlight, I have no intention to complete "Ironman" mode, known as "nightmare mode" in this game. Chain Linked fences are the devil, the momentum gets kinda wonky at certain platforming bits.
For further illustration feel free to check out my Unscripted thoughts video. Thanks for reading!

The controls are okay when it comes to the platforming aspects. The platforming is where this game shines...if you can say it shines at all. Even during some platforming areas I was struggling with controls. The game wouldn't let me roll when using mouse and keyboard. I was forced to switch to a controller.
Combat on the other hand is a complete fight with the controls. Especially when it comes to melee. When zombies in the background they are unattackable but when they are transitioning from background to the characters plane it seems as if they can attack you.
The games pacing left me with a desiree to see the world. I think the pacing is meant to emulate the constant of life and death hordes, but I really wanted to just stand and look at an area for a moment to enjoy the art and the environment. There was no time for that in most areas. You are basically moving from one puzzle or combat encounter to another.
I found myself enjoying the game early on but became frustrated with controls and iffy combat scenarios later in the game. In the end I felt like I was forcing myself to finish.
Worth a play for $5 or less.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a medieval RPG that takes place on an epic scale. The closest thing to finishing the game is taking over the world known as Calradia, for yourself or a faction of your choosing. The idea of the game is basically, raise a company of troops, take as many places for yourself and make lots of cash, and it's lots of fun.
You start the main game by picking your backstory/background, depeding on your choices you will begin with different items, cash, skills and attributes. After this you get a screen where it shows your skills and attributes, and gives you some points to improve these, this is also where you name your charcater. Next you will be presented with a character customisation screen where you will pick how you look. You are then dumped in an alley and left to fend of a robber. Afterwards, (whether successful or not) you will find yourself talking to a merchant of the city, and he will offer you a simple starter quest to get you started.
After this you are released the world, you can hunt bandits, join a kingdom (or maybe start your own), and grab quests from the various importqant people around the land. It is not a good idea to do this alone however and you are expected to hire some troops and keep them well fed and payed in return for them helping you not be a prison ♥♥♥♥♥ the whole game.
Now thats what you do in the game and how they do it is good too. You basically have an overworld map where you wil lead yourself and your party into groups of people and locations where you will be presented with menues and a chance to walk around. The field battles are good and the seiges are... well quite messy but can still be fun! The controls go along the lines of easy to learn hard to master, and there are tutorials for combat and such.
Anyways i haven't gone into great depth but i have given you enough information to make your mind up about the game, and if not theres a demo of it to try. If you enjoy this game you will also find a great modding community that will expand the games life tenfold. I most definatly reccomend this and hope you enjoy this as much as or even more than i have.

Mount and Blade is a fantastic game that combines attributes of Sandbox, light RPG, and real time strategy to a seemless medieval world.
What I like about warband is there are various different activities in the fictious world of Caldaria, from figthing bandits, to playing politics, trade, arena fighting, or even starting your own rouge nation from the ground up.
I also really like how the combat works, because you can control which direction your character attacks and with weapons you have to match attack directions with block directions to make the most out of melee combat. Ranged combat also has some interesting features where it takes into account your movement and projectile drop off when taking shots. That light RPG aspect comes into play also as your character gets stronger, faster, and more precise as you develop his skills, making him either into a lethal warrior, an agile bowman, or a cunning tactician. Which gives the game a lot of flexibilty as to how you go about it.
The world is a true sandbox in that it doesn't require you to do anything or go certain ways, but gives you all the tools to make things happen your way but also have the world adapt to your actions in a way that forces you to continually change your tactics when approaching situations.
I myself have sunk hundreads of hours into this game and have reccomended it to everyone I know on steam. I would even go as far as to say that this is one of my favorite games of all time. This is definitely a must own game, and if your not aware of it and like hack/slash gameplay with character skill progression give it a shot.

Not only am I a fan of medieval themes in games, I'm also a fan of strategizing and thinky games. And Mount and Blade: Warband fits right in, from it's management of one's army, to the strategic combat out on the battlefield. It also features RPG elements like a customizable personal character with his or her stats and skills, the skill system is very elaborate and involved with all the different skills with their own unique purposes, encouraging the player to think carefully about what they want to put their points into when they level up. My favorite part about this game being the combat, of course, striking down enemies is ever so satisfying, and it's also most gratifying to loot an enemy after sending your men to mow them down. The factor of appeasement being added onto when it is executed after using a plan or good tactic that works, and learning what strategies are effective. My only major complaint is how frustrating Mount & Blade games can be at times. I had a hard time playing this game.  It's not due to the game's difficulty, but part of it is the programming.  Twice the game crashed, loading screen froze three times in a row that prompted me to restart my computer, frame rate drops, idiotic AI that stop in front of you and you can't go around them, and enemy AI that focus all their fire on you and can hit you while only a portion of your body is exposed from 50 yards away while your partner AI is 25 yards away and firing at them as they stand in the open and can't hit them.
What's worse, the campaign is boring and predictable.  There's not real engaging characters and those that might become interesting, like Astronaut Mosley, are killed off in just a few minutes.  Having a portion of the campaign in Space would have made things interesting.  Not just a run and gun, but trying to figure out things in a 3D and weightless enviroment while watching the world below descend into chaos, listening to the radio chatter as frantic people either encourage you or explain what's happening around them.  That would have been a good injection of fun, but instead we have a linear run-and-gun campaign with a few different gadgets attached.  I mean, after so many games in this franchise, we still can't even take enemy prisoners.  No.  We just have to kill everyone!  That gets dull for me.
I know how the game ends, I know who Rourke is and how it all ties together even though I only have a few hours playing it and I know what happens at the end.  It's just boring in terms of writing, style, and the programming is flawed.

Remember turning to meet your nasal assassin, only to see half a cafeteria of barely-pubescent corpses strewn about the tables? One last child stood amongst the carnage and held the herald of your salvation in his hands. The cold barrel of his father's gun met your lips as his hand trembled incessantly... your first kiss. You thought it'd be more romantic.
The least important of these questions is whether or not he decided to pull the trigger. The only question that remains after the police tape goes up is: why? Why, when so much of life was ahead of us all, would he decide to close the curtain so soon?
Sonic Adventure 2 is a comprehensive study in the stimuli that cause these tragedies. What must a child have witnessed to decide that candy and gameboys were no longer in his taste, but that blood would make a fitting substitute? The awful level design of this game leave the mind feeling trapped. Like a cornerned animal, its option to flee has been rescinded and its only recourse is to lash out at anything and everything that stands in a direct line between their current position, and the glowing red exit sign. The exit sign that was once a part of the scenery now becomes a glowing beacon of salvation that's never seemed so distant.
And what of the incessant sound effects: the beeping, the horrendous voice acting, the awful music that's "good" because it's "ironically bad?" Well... if you need to know more about that, just ask the sinners in the deepest circle of Hell whose ears were shattered by the bloodcurdling screams of their family.
The chao garden's pretty cool though.

I've already spent a lot of time in this game since release, and plan to spend much more.  And the thing is---I've done this all mostly solo, I can't wait to get more into the multiplayer with friends (Once I convince a few this game is pretty awesome).  In the time I've built myself a pretty decent ship, scouted for hours on said ship, got good and lost, before finding an island on my way back home and going there to explore.
Found a bunch of new and different things on that biome before returning home, and also started a house on the beach-side, with a keep overlooking everything down below.
The building in this game is fun---not always the easiest, but sure as heck miles beyond most survival games.  The fact I can make my own ships/cars and homes while also exploring is fantastic.
Exploration is great.  You can live on the sea and travel around what feels endlessly, going from shore to shore to see what you can find.
Items in this game are persistant---you can use them to decorate, but they can get kinda clutter-y.  However, oddly, it hasn't affected my frame-rate at all, it usually runs at a consistant 60+ on the ultra settings---so it's actually pretty friendly to my PC.
Everyone is complaining about the Microtransactions, but I haven't even bothered with them---because there's one huge factor to them that I love.  They aren't intrusive, they stay out of my way, and only exist if I want them to really.  It's all cosmetic crap and a handful of furniture that doesn't look at all alluring to me when I have other options that seem much better.
Only downside really for me is that the multiplayer is -super- wonky right now.  Been trying to play it with my girlfriend steadily but it either lags out terribly for us or she can't connect in the end, which isn't the greatest of experiences.  Hopefully that gets fixed and also hopefully more than ten people can join a server at a time in the future.  Would be neat to get a good sized RP server going at some point, as there is a lot of potential here for such things.
So, do I recommend it?  Yeah.  It's cheap, it provides a lot of fun, and the additional monetization isn't even noticable unless you seek it out.  My way to do that kinda stuff all around.

For those of you expecting there to be guns and grenades...not the game for you. Those of you who love stealth with tools to distract and counter guards (no killing) then this is the game for you.
It is a really interesting game to play, where even in the later stages of the 100 core levels you are introduced to new techniques which can be combined with others to make you a master of stealth and distraction. The game is a modern twist on the classic tale of Robin Hood with a heavy influence of the VR training missions from the older Metal Gear Solid games. Visually it is quite astounding to see. Most of the games design is based around the shape of a tittle (diamond shape with sharp edges). The colour scheme throughout the 100 core levels reflect not only the story but also the environment that is being simulated.
Voice acting goes along way in this game. Some people dislike it, others like it. I for one enjoy hearing the dialogue to help draw me into the world created by the visuals, gameplay and ambient sounds. For those of you wondering if you didn't know it already the voice actors are Charlie McDonnell, Danny Wallace and Andy Serkis.
In terms of gameplay the core story based levels you play through come in a set of 100. On top of this are the Staff Picks in which you can also play. The main thing I like about the custom content for this game is that every single platform has the level editor made available to them. This not only means that you can create levels on every platform, it also means that every other platform can play the ones you design. Such as PC players can play levels designed by the folks on console and vice versa.
Overall the game has drawed me in and made me feel like I was Locksley, dodging and sneaking past guards to deactivate alarms, collect gems and laughing whilst I confuse the hell out of other guards. I've followed the development of the game since Mike announced it and I am purely astounded by just how well the game has turned out to be.
For those of you who enjoy a stealth game that gets progressively harder (as well as making your own level of hardness) then I would highly recommend this game to you.

If you enjoyed the more puzzly pattern/position based sections of the Metal Gear Solid games, odds are you'll enjoy this one. I know I did. The levels are short, well designed and not too taxing, so I was never stuck on the same problem for too long. New mechanics and enemies are introduced at regular intervals to keep things interesting, and I enjoyed figuring out new ways of fooling the guards. The graphics are simple, but clean and reasonably stylish, and serve the concept well. The controls work well (I played with a gamepad), and though I did encounter a few bugs, none of them were game-breaking or detracted from the experience in a major way.
Gameplay-wise, the biggest problems are by design: A checkpoint/restore system that resets your enemies' positions but not your own accomplishments is easily exploited, and some challenges can be overcome by simply running through them and hiding afterwards. It felt like I blundered through them instead of solving them, and the game didn't punish me for it or give me compelling enough reason to go back and try to solve them properly.
The story and setting are OK, pretty standard "rising up against the totalitarian regime" fare, but since the playfield is so abstracted, it felt like I was being served the story in parallel to the gameplay rather than actually playing it out, and this left me feeling a little detached and not fully invested in it.
There were some sound issues. While the sounds of the guards and the environment were good, the character voiceovers lacked cohesion in terms of recording space and audio quality, enough so that it became a real issue for me. One character in particular sounded like it was recorded in a vat of wool, which may or may not have been intentional, but it threw me off regardless. A few dialog bugs were present as well, such as some levels playing a random line instead of their opening dialog, but I'm sure these will be dealt with promptly.
Overall, I enjoyed my time in the Volume. 6-8 hours is a good length for this type of game, and though plenty of games offer more content for the same price, it still feels like decent value, especially considering the tons of user-created levels that are forthcoming thanks to the included level editor. I liked Mike's first game, I liked this one, and I'm excited to see what he comes up with in the future.

Welcome to Insurgency, with the realism of Red Orchestra or Arma 2, but with a little bit faster pace to it. You're thrown directly into the battlefields of Afghanistan or Iraq, including real-life locations like Fallujah. The gameplay at first glance can really overwhelm a new player. Although the level of combat is actually on a small scale, it really can show what real combat is like. The pop and whizz of bullets passing around you and the blur as dust is kicked in your face.
Now, I'll admit it, this game is NOT for people that don't like working as a team. If your a COD kiddie, or something along those lines where you don't care about your team and just want some cheap kills, this game won't work for you. If you're interested in teamwork, realism, and some legit skills and kills. This game is the right thing. Get some friends and work as a team, the players that do this always fare better than the ones that go lone wolf.
Camping is an actual part of the game. Your machinegunners and/or snipers are best used when left back, allowing them to properly use their long range and supportive roles. Your grenadiers, rifleman and other assaultive forces are what moves up and takes the OBJ.
I'll admit, it has it's flaws. Teamkilling can be a real issue as very few servers have proper admins to ban people. ANd finding a good community may be really tough at first. But once you find the right group, you should be fine.

I REALLY wanted to like this game more than I did. The premise and 2.5D gameplay is interesting, but so many things mar the game's potential. FYI, I vaguely discuss the ending below, but avoid any specific story spoilers.
-The controls are janky and always feel like they are working against you, at least with an Xbox controller. You'll jump to where you want to jump about 50% of the time, and this alone is frankly fatal for a game that has a major platforming focus with tight timing. Maybe the game is better with keyboard, but I honestly don't care for the game enough to try it.
-The visuals are gorgeous, but ultimately hamper gameplay. Too much visual clutter, and there is frequent difficulty in telling foreground from background (with lethal consequences for your character.)
-Many would-be awesome setpiece moments (chase scences, collapsing buildings, a booby-trapped sewer) are hamstrung by stupidly tight timing and poorly telegraphed hazards. Combine this with the poor controls and visual clutter, and instead of being highlights of the game, these moments are instead infuriating and unenjoyable.
-The voice acting is noticeably amateur. Even the protagonist's admittedly wonderful, gravelly voice is spoiled by poor inflection and emotion. Also, I SWEAR the protagonist's in-game sound effects (shouts, yells, grunts, etc.) are from a different voice actor than his narration voice actor, which really kills the immersion as well.
-The music is pretty generic. Nothing awful, nothing to write home about.
-This is very subjective, but I felt that the ending was a terrible, terrible cliche. By the time I reached the end of the game, the story was the only thing keeping me going, and they just completely botched it at the end. ALSO. the protagonist makes a choice at the very end that seems contradictory to the lesson about life he has supposedly come to learn throughout his ordeal.
Overall, the game just really feels like it was lacking polish and proper playtesting, and I sadly cannot recommend purchasing it.
