So, I just finished this lovely game.
It goes by the name of Volume.
Back when I first heard about it, I knew I had to have it.
It's essentially a cyberpunk re-imagining of Robin Hood mixed with VR Missions from Metal Gear Solid.
If that's not enough to make you rush and pick it up I don't know what else to say.
But let me start at the beginning, that's where all the good stories start I hear. If you're lazy and want to know if it's good that's down at the bottom, somewhere. (Yes, it's good.) (it's  at the bottom too)
In this game you start simply enough with a few things you can do such as crouch against walls and walk around and explore. Then there is information that is gathered which sheds some light on the world, and provides a nice way to introduce backstory without a ton of exposition that people will hit escape on. The world is there, the world is substantial. I was invested in this world, not because I've lived it, but due to the excellent writing and narrative it provided.
The writing was humourous, light-hearted and entertaining where it was needed and serious enough to drive this story of corruption and power.
After the first few missions you start obtaining items that can be picked up and used, but only one at a time so plan accordingly. These vary through each map, so you're never feeling completely comfortable or stuck with an  item.
When I sat down with this game, I told myself that I would play it for a couple hours and then I would do a work in progress review. Four hours later I hit the halfway mark, and I kept going. Seventy-five percent I said, and I'll do my review. Which brings us to now, Eight hours after I first clicked play. The game is complete, for now.
I am sad, only because I can't experience this again for the first time. But at the same time, I'm so excited, because now I have to look forward to the community levels making my own, going back through and beating my own time as well as fighting for a place on the leaderboards.
The soundtrack was hauntingly well done, filling every crevice in the game with a sense of wonder, and dread that that one frickin AI was going to just turn around and spot me and put an end to my shenanigans. Said shenanigans include throwing whistles through the air, turning invisible, dodging electric traps and lasers. It's like I'm a young James Bond, if only his bestie was a robot AI that kind of enjoyed sarcasm.
When I first set out in the game I had issues with it. I didn't like the voice actor for the main character, he sounded bored. But, as the game went on he grew on me. He wasn't bored, he was just alive, reacting normally how someone might react. There was no need for overhyped dialogue. It fit perfectly.
Sometimes the AI seemed a bit random in it's movements. Where one time I would do something and it would work and then die/get caught before the next checkpoint and do the exact same thing and it would fail. But, with patience I was able to get through those parts by finding a new creative way to push on through.
Sometimes the controls don't respond normally, and sometimes when you're in stealth or cover the AI enemies will bump into you and push you out and you get spotted.
Two of the bigger complaints I have is that sometimes the color choices for the level make it very hard to see where the AI is looking when patrolling, but that was rare, and that the enemies can walk through each other, but they're a brick wall to you.
Do those things take away from the game? Not one damn bit.
This will be sitting on "my shelf" of games that I talk about for a long time. Up there with The Metal Gear Solid series and Gunpoint.
If it's not obvious and you find yourself asking "should I buy this game?"
The answer is a resounding 'Yes', Mike Bithell as managed to take a game genre that was lacking and gave it exactly what it needed.
A voice.

Volume combines an eclectic cast of voice actors with poor delivery and poor characterisation. Charlie McDonnell plays his character well, but the character is "twee British person who streams a video game", and those lines manage to be both cringeworthy and repetitive. The world-building is severly hampered by it's rigid adherence to a "retro" aesthetic, with all evidence of a future Britain controlled by a dictator being limited to 3 line paragraphs before each mission and the mission spaces themselves are completely utilitarian "house", "office" or "museum" spaces. There is no further variation in level style, but you wouldn't notice because those 3 spaces look almost identical anyway.
The stealth mechanics are expected to be innovative but instead boil down to "the noisemakers" that stealth games have employed for years and various flavours of invisibility/disguises. Unlike other stealth games though, those noisemakers are on an obnoxiously long cooldown which you must wait for after every death, adding another 15 seconds to the respawn time. In desperation, you may find yourself running at enemies, chrouching intermittently around non-descript blocks to temporarily break line of sight to avoid instant death before leaping at a checkpoint that will reset the guards' positions while moving yours further. This is the most fun the game gets, but the results are inconsistent and the fact that the developer has announced that he wants to remove this feature indicates that is not intentional. Volume also features much slower movement than other excellent action/stealth games available on Steam at the moment, which will leave you sitting on the edge of your seat not because the action is tense but because "Rob Locksley" refuses to stop crouching for any situation and move a little faster when he has a gun trained on him.
The Robin Hood imagery is not just unsubtle, it's spotlighted multiple times. In fact, the game has a habit of highlighting it's own flaws, with a cameo starring Jim Sterling being particularly galling as he completely demolishes the game's plot with his characteristic flourishes. The game awkwardly acknowledges this and then continues on, doing little to rectify its issues. There's been a lot of talk about the game's humour, and not the good kind. It makes jabs at today's streaming culture but doesn't follow it up with a message, and it briefly flirts with the meta-humour found in Thomas Was Alone, but that tragically fails when the game is no longer examining the nature of platformers, as in Thomas Was Alone, but instead turning inwards on it's own mistakes. These issues are compounded by the inclusion of 100 levels, as the talent has to be spread thin among endless identical corridors. I stopped playing at around 50% and the game had already outstayed it's welcome by about 2 hours. I knew it was around 50% because the game proudly tells you how far you've progressed. If the game was enjoyable, then it would feel like an unwelcome harbinger of when the experience will be over. The game is not enjoyable.
If you are looking for a stealth game featuring comedic elements, I would reccomend Gunpoint.
If you are looking for leaderboards in a stealth setting, I would reccomend Monaco.
If you are looking for a stealth game set in the near-future featuring mega-corporations, I would reccomend Invisible Inc.
If you are looking for meta-humour (humour about the game itself), I'd reccomend Bithell's own Thomas Was Alone.
If you are looking for geometric people shooting at you, I would reccomend the upcoming SUPERHOT.
If you are looking for British People, Charlie McDonnell vlogs on Youtube at charlieissocoollike.
The above games are all much cheaper than Bithell's offering and are all made by independent studios with smaller budgets than Volume's. Maybe one day we can get an update to Volume, offering faster movement for abilities be usuable immediately after spawning as well as lowering their cooldown and to balance that smarter AI that can't be ignored by briefly touching a wall. Then this game might be able to compete with some of the stealth antics offered above, even if other aspects pail in comparison. Maybe Bithell could call it Volume II.

Comparisons with Metal Gear Solid always were inevitable considering the top-down/isometric stealth gameplay and simplistic blocky geometry. Indeed, reading the 'Making Of' e-book, the developer takes some time relating in depth his collating of stealth games like Metal Gear and Hitman for inspiration. There's even a humourous anecdote of a meeting between hin and Kojima-san. The e-book, it turns out, is a must-read for all aspiring game developers.
Volume itself takes the gameplay of games like Metal Gear, Hitman, Splinter Cell et al, and distills it into its purest form. But its when the soundtrack kicks in, with its 3-note motif, more than a passing nod to the Tomb Raider theme, that it hits you: above all else, Volume is not just a stealth game, its a fan-made homage to all those games of the 80's & 90's, Tomb Raider included.
Games whose gameplay preceeded 'realism' and, using Tomb Raider as an example, were just a series of conceptual puzzles strung together in a narrative. Volume then is a genuine harkback to those 'golden-days' of gaming.
So, avoid guards (and their triangular lines-of-sight), collect orbs to create an exit and use some genuinely fun gadgets. Gaming has suddenly become fun again.

Volume is a stealth game where the main objective is to sneak your way through the levels, navigating around guards using different means such as whistling, hiding, throwing a distraction grenade type thing etc. Ultimately, the goal of the entire level is to collect all of the cones and reach the exit. There are 100 levels of the main story which will take you around 10hrs to complete. Every few levels a new element is added to the game which will change the way you play out the next few levels while some narrative/story telling goes on.
Firstly, I want to talk about positives. The games option menu is good. It's perfect and what you should expect from a game like this. Different sliders for volume, AA, shadow settings, resolution and fs/windowed. All keys are remappable (for keyboard). I also really like the art style. It's really unique, colourful and visually appealing.
Unfortunately, there are a lot of negatives for me. (Please remember this is my personal opinion so please keep that in mind and be respectful).
Ok first the voice acting. The voice acting of the robot (Alan) is well done. I believe it's the same voice that narrated TWA. But then your characters voice (Locksley/Rob) is a bit meh to be honest. As soon as he says a few lines it completely breaks the immersion of the game for me.
Secondly, I would like to talk about the AI. The AI seem to suffer from a very serious case of short sightedness. Their entire view is about 2m in length and spews out in a cone shape. This means you can literally stand 2.1m in length away from them and bingo! They can't even see you! Or you can stand right by the side of them (clearly being in their peripheral vision) but they won't know any different! Ok, I really like the fact that if you do get in the view cone, the enemies begin to chase you down. A really nice element. This is where you can try to run away from them and avoid being in their sights for too long otherwise you fail the level. The AI on this is a bit so so. At one point a guard was right on my tail and I reached a dead end. So, I decided to go up against the only wall in the dead end room and yeap the AI couldn't for the life of him work out where I had gone! It's like I vanished!
I'm also just going to add a little section here. It's a "Stealth game" but to be honest, it's pretty linear. Everything is kinda layed out for you and there only really seems to be one way of doing particular sections. For me, this is one of the most important aspects of a stealth game. Having the freedom to choose exactly how I progress through the level, but unfortunately that seems to be missing from this game.
Finally, coming from the creator of TWA (which had an excellent story) I was a little disappointed with this. I couldn't seem to get to grips with the story of the game and the notes dotted throughout the levels didn’t really seem to add much to the story. The whole story felt a bit disjointed.
Worth £15? Well, to be fair you get quite a lot of content for £15 so I think that is well justified. You also have online, and a level editor which is an excellent addition to this game. But for me, it doesn't quite do it. It needs more depth. I want the freedom to approach levels how I want to, play the way I want to.
(Again, please bear in mind that this is my opinion, and all I ask is to be respectful towards it. Because hey, not everyone is going to like the same games) :)

Greatly inspired by Metal Gear Solid and Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty, especially the accompanying VR missions for those games, the game takes the best from its influence and simplifies it in a fun, challenging and pick-up-and-play way. Simplification here is not bad, at all, nor does it imply a lack of content or depth in the game. It is from actual appreciation of its inspiration that the game manages to deliver some good stealth puzzle action. I have always wanted an expansion to the MGS’s VR missions, and Volume fulfills that gap.
This isn’t to say that Volume is just a direct replica. It has its own feel, own way of playing and its own experience. But it can’t be overlooked that it serves to revitalize a stealth genre that is honestly not looked into more. First, “Not the Robots”, and now “Volume” are bringing back stealth puzzle games, and I love it.
From my short play of the game, the controls feel responsive and intuitive. I did come across some weird audio glitches where characters say lines out of nowhere, without context, that they have said before. I’m not sure if this is intentional or a glitch that can later be fixed, but it did distract me a few times.
Visuals are great, again, the MGS VR inspiration is very apparent, but the “volumetric” approach to how the maps look is striking, To put it simply, I really like it.
I would say, play this game. It’s really fun so far, and I have a feeling ii will be the more I play. I will update once I have finished the game.

I want to take you back to a simpler time in your life. Remember when you were in middle school sitting at the lunch table, and you were wolfing down your peanut butter and jelly sandwich as quickly as you can to maximize your time at recess? Remember smelling a faint note of rat♥♥♥♥♥♥wafting in from the corner like a fart-filled Hindenburg, waiting to immolate your sinuses? Remember turning to meet your nasal assassin, only to see half a cafeteria of barely-pubescent corpses strewn about the tables? One last child stood amongst the carnage and held the herald of your salvation in his hands. The cold barrel of his father's gun met your lips as his hand trembled incessantly... your first kiss. You thought it'd be more romantic.
The least important of these questions is whether or not he decided to pull the trigger. The only question that remains after the police tape goes up is: why? Why, when so much of life was ahead of us all, would he decide to close the curtain so soon?
Sonic Adventure 2 is a comprehensive study in the stimuli that cause these tragedies. What must a child have witnessed to decide that candy and gameboys were no longer in his taste, but that blood would make a fitting substitute? Mount & Blade: Warband is a medieval RPG that takes place on an epic scale. The closest thing to finishing the game is taking over the world known as Calradia, for yourself or a faction of your choosing. The idea of the game is basically, raise a company of troops, take as many places for yourself and make lots of cash, and it's lots of fun.
You start the main game by picking your backstory/background, depeding on your choices you will begin with different items, cash, skills and attributes. After this you get a screen where it shows your skills and attributes, and gives you some points to improve these, this is also where you name your charcater. Next you will be presented with a character customisation screen where you will pick how you look. You are then dumped in an alley and left to fend of a robber. Afterwards, (whether successful or not) you will find yourself talking to a merchant of the city, and he will offer you a simple starter quest to get you started.
After this you are released the world, you can hunt bandits, join a kingdom (or maybe start your own), and grab quests from the various importqant people around the land. It is not a good idea to do this alone however and you are expected to hire some troops and keep them well fed and payed in return for them helping you not be a prison ♥♥♥♥♥ the whole game.
Now thats what you do in the game and how they do it is good too. You basically have an overworld map where you wil lead yourself and your party into groups of people and locations where you will be presented with menues and a chance to walk around. The field battles are good and the seiges are... well quite messy but can still be fun! The controls go along the lines of easy to learn hard to master, and there are tutorials for combat and such.
Anyways i haven't gone into great depth but i have given you enough information to make your mind up about the game, and if not theres a demo of it to try. If you enjoy this game you will also find a great modding community that will expand the games life tenfold. I most definatly reccomend this and hope you enjoy this as much as or even more than i have.

Mount and Blade is a fantastic game that combines attributes of Sandbox, light RPG, and real time strategy to a seemless medieval world.
What I like about warband is there are various different activities in the fictious world of Caldaria, from figthing bandits, to playing politics, trade, arena fighting, or even starting your own rouge nation from the ground up.
I also really like how the combat works, because you can control which direction your character attacks and with weapons you have to match attack directions with block directions to make the most out of melee combat. Ranged combat also has some interesting features where it takes into account your movement and projectile drop off when taking shots. That light RPG aspect comes into play also as your character gets stronger, faster, and more precise as you develop his skills, making him either into a lethal warrior, an agile bowman, or a cunning tactician. Which gives the game a lot of flexibilty as to how you go about it.
The world is a true sandbox in that it doesn't require you to do anything or go certain ways, but gives you all the tools to make things happen your way but also have the world adapt to your actions in a way that forces you to continually change your tactics when approaching situations.
I myself have sunk hundreads of hours into this game and have reccomended it to everyone I know on steam. I would even go as far as to say that this is one of my favorite games of all time. This is definitely a must own game, and if your not aware of it and like hack/slash gameplay with character skill progression give it a shot.

Not only am I a fan of medieval themes in games, I'm also a fan of strategizing and thinky games. The factor of appeasement being added onto when it is executed after using a plan or good tactic that works, and learning what strategies are effective. My only major complaint is how frustrating Mount & Blade games can be at times. Like when, in spite of your path finding skill being well leveled and having a good horse, your party travels so slow that even on-foot partys of outlaws can outspeed you, which is just absolutely stupid. Regardless, this game still holds up in it's appeal to me.

It is really hard to just give this a thumbs up or thumbs down. Visually it gets a big thumbs up and the enviroments have a great level of detail, so much so that in numerous scenarios it seemed like you could step right into the backdrop. The story could go either way, it is fairly standard for the genre and so it fit the game, and wasn't anything overly creative, but used some techniques to keep you invested. The problems start when it comes to what felt like QTEs. The character movement is fine at first, and suits you well for the first couple checkpoints. Then they start adding in more keys and those keys don't always do what they should. After one particularly frustrating scenario I stayed where I was and tried the same button combo twenty times. Thirteen times it did what it should, seven it didn't, and I couldn't tell the difference in what I was doing. The zombie interaction is really awful, and seemingly completely random. Shooting a pistol takes more time than a full swing of your axe. Sometimes they will be as large as every other zombie, but not actually be in the foreground and you can't interact with them unless they are there. Still, it is manageable, as you aren't really meant to always fight the zombies. The run scenes, where you have to do everything perfect are the biggest problem with the game when coupled with the wonky controls. They aren't difficult, it just requires you to die at least once in some scenarios just to tell what is actually happening, and then hoping your character's actions register the way you wanted them to. There is one instance where a warehouse roof is falling. I died the first couple times trying to run past it, so I spent another five minutes dying and messing around with it, only to figure out you really do have to just run past it but aparently whether or not you make it is arbitrary. Still, the reason I gave it a thumbs up is that I love the look and feel of it so much, I feel they need to be credited for that. The price tag shouldn't be more than ten bucks though with all the issues, and it really only gets a 5/10. The art style just gave it that fraction of a point earn the thumbs up. Actually, I would also say it might be worth playing for some people, just to hear the voice-acting on the soldiers...

Spoiler Filled Review:
The combat and movement feels cluhnky, final mission you get shot but your health doesn't deplete it just ends the scene. Game feels more like a proof of concept than an actual game. Timing of events and planned actions sometimes feels really wacky causing much frustration as you have to repeat the mission or look up guides online to figure out how to move on. On the final mission when you climb through the window after shooting the guards who say, "hands up". When you fall instead of jump from the window, you glitch out and teleport to the other side of the window which you just crawled through, and can't get back in. Meaning you have to commit suicide just to reset the checkpoint and try again. A lot of the game feels more like a proof of concept with the glitches, weird timed events, collectibles that have no meaning to the story, etc. It's got good graphics for it's time, a great story premise that could've been much longer, but the combat and movement really hold this game back. For instance if you're at the top of a wall and climb over, and click "right" or D on the keyboard to move to the right, you climb back over the wall on the left. Which makes no sense because in other sequences of climbing/map movement, you hold right and click shift to jump to the right. The story telling through the comic cut scenes was really enjoyable, but when you change the audio settings in-game, it doesn't change the settings for the cutscenes so you lose hearing because of it, or the audio randomly stops and you're lucky you have subtitles on cause you don't have any clue what the cutscenes are saying. Another thing, is if you accidentally click the keyboard while a cutscene is going, it skips and heads directly to the next mission. Most games have a popup that says, "Are you sure you'd like to skip this cutscene?" and you can cancel or accept. This game doesn't, forcing you to go back to the main menu, scene selection, select the current scene you're on and rewatch it without touching anything because the devs didn't forsee this as an issue. Which it is.
Like I said, this game could be so much better, but unfortunately it just feels lackluster and like a proof of concept instead of a final product. Really disappointing considering all the positive reviews this thing has. I expect a more polished game honestly.

Dennaton Games has delivered another great gaming experience that combines nostalgic elements  from the late 80's and early 90's with fast-paced and gritty gameplay. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number (HM2) features gameplay that is virtually identical to it's predecessor, but revamped with larger stages, more enemies, and a deeper plot.  The game deviates from the perspective of a nameless anti-hero, and instead features a narrative from multiple characters that eradicate foes from a 2D top-down perspective.
If you played the first Hotline Miami, you will have no trouble adapting to its sequel. HM2's controls are virtually identical, with the exception of a new aiming feature that allows players to 'lock' onto enemies from a distance. This is helpful at times but just often feels too awkward and clumsy to use. Each stage is now also much larger and swarmed with enemies. This makes for longer kill combos and more epic engagements, but can also be frustrating when enemies with ranged weapons one-hit you from off screen now. This will happen frequently and annoy you especially after you have just completed a difficult sequence. I felt that HM2 lacked the free-flow run and smash combat mechanics of its predecessor, and instead felt like a camp-fest.
As mentioned earlier, HM2 introduces several new playable characters from different factions. When starting  most missions, player have the option to pick a weapon set or perk, similar to the first game. There are a few characters who do not have the ability to spawn with weapons or perks, and must start the game with their bare fists.  Each character has different perks that dictate how they must play through levels. An interesting character, Evan, cannot pickup lethal weapons, can only wield baseball bats and pipes to  knock out foes. Ash and Alex, a tandem of masked vigilantes, can play simultaneously while wielding a handgun and chainsaw.  Another character  'Beard' does not possess masks, but can instead choose a firearm before stages.
HM2 graphics are also pretty much similar to the original game. Each level is unique while some featured cool visual effects, like falling rain, mist, rolling tides, or even strobing disco lights. The game's soundtrack is  beyond awesome, and features synthwave songs by Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, MOON, Scattle and many more. It is a major selling point to this game and can also be purchased separately. It creates a great immersion factor and really helps players feel like they are playing a game made in the 90s.
So lastly we have the plot and themes.  The first Hotline Miami did not really have a significant plot, unless the player collected a series of secret objectives. Even then, the plot was intentionally left shrouded and left open for interpretation. I always felt this was executed perfectly and would made the original game stand out amongst other contemporary peers.  HM2 has eight story arcs that all interweave to provide an intriguing and surprisingly deep plot.  While the game's motif is still kill anything that moves, we are now provided why everything must die a horrible, horrible death. I really enjoyed HM2's story that touched on theme's like patriotism, post-traumatic stress disorder, and vigilantism.
All in all, I was greatly impressed with Hotline Miami 2 as a sequel. Even though  its gameplay  and graphics are largely similar to its predecessor, the game still has plenty of action that will keep you coming back for more. Hotline 2 also features a level editor, which is nice but a bit limited to use. There are more ways to dispatch your enemies and new allies to help you along your path.  Aside from a lack of multiplayer and a few design errors, Hotline Miami 2 is a great release for gamers looking for a retro 2D action game.

As it stands in 2016,  Far Cry 3 is the peak of the series. Progressing through the game feels like it means something, as you and your character go from avoiding fights to seeking them out, the experience of which is enhanced by the game's smooth gameplay and a variety of options. The story of the game itself is a double-edged sword. On one hand, the story is just ok, enough to go along with the game and the missions themselves are trash. But the characters, dialogue, and tone are so much more fun because the writers embrace the fact that Far Cry 3 is a game, and play with it.
The only true negative to Far Cry 3 is the problem of hindsight. When it came out and I played in 2012, it was an impeccable and unique experience. Today, it carries many of the problems the term "Ubisoft Game" implies before it truly became a problem. However, those problems are far less prevelant in Far Cry 3 and it's still an incredible fun experience to pour dozens of hours into.

ZUP! is a physics-based puzzler that, while incredibly short, is oddly satisfying as well. Your task is to remove any and all obstacles that prevent the blue block in each stage to rest securely on the green platform below. Doing so will award you access to the next level. The game sounds simple enough and it is relatively so, even throughout the 40+ levels it has to play through. While that may seem like a significant amount of levels to keep you busy, you’ll find yourself breezing through them quickly.
The charm that encapsulates ZUP!, in my opinion, is that it isn’t frustrating. Sure, the difficulty could be increased dramatically to better challenge the participant, but I didn’t mind as I sat down and exploded blocks across the screen; I found something this simple to just be, well, fun, regardless if I completed the level or really progressed at all. The handful of levels I kept failing miserably at still had me smiling, even after watching myself fail again and again.
It is important to say, however, that ZUP! is painfully short, despite boasting well over 100 achievements. The main issue I had with ZUP! is that by the time I became fully engaged in it, the game was over. I prefer a meticulous approach to games, scouring every inch and trying everything I can. However, with just a mere 23 minutes of gameplay I was done; I had completed everything there was to do. I felt cheated, teased with a marvelous, yet simplistic idea. Even now, I feel as if I’m floundering as to say anything else about the game. There’s just not much substance to it.
On a final note, as mentioned earlier, ZUP! does come with practical and useful achievements for those looking to dress up their Steam profile. While this shouldn’t be a positive to the game itself, I suppose one could consider it a consolation prize in the end.
All in All

This game is 4 people who work together to get to the end of a map, usually doing small events during the map that involves holding out an attack by a horde of enemies, or transporting sacks of grain/barrels to key locations, all while being attacked by hordes of enemies. On top of the normal enemies who are mostly just fodder, there are special types of enemies, much like in Left 4 Dead, that require teamwork to kill.
The maps are very linear, with small areas to explore for various loot that can spawn in set locations. There's a total of 13 maps varying in length and difficulty. The different maps help to keep things fresh, but there's just one problem. You most likely wont be playing most of these maps at all.
The progression system is what fights against the different maps, because only some maps are long enough to contain special items that you can pick up during the mission, to improve your loot drops at the end of a mission. This bonus to your loot is so significant, that it feels completely useless to play any other map than one where you can get all the bonus loot items.
Additionally, some maps are just easier than others, but they all drop the same loot. You can see this on the matchmaking time, people are mainly just playing the same map over and over, because there's no reason to ever go to another map.
If you love getting loot, then you will most likely end up in the same situation as me. Clearing the same map over and over, so that's definitely something to keep in mind. I personally still like doing that one map, because of the special enemies that spawn randomly, every run is never completely the same, and even though there's effectively only a very small number of maps, the different classes add spice to the game.
There's 5 classes: A bright wizard, who can shoot fireballs or beams of fire and other fire related destruction, depending on what weapon she uses. Then there's an elven archer with a variety of bows and fast melee weapons. A Witch Hunter, who can dual wield pistols. An Imperial Guardsman, who can choose to be a tank, or use a slow firing but strong gun. Last a dwarf, who can also be a tank, with interesting gun choices too.
All the classes have a few different ranged and melee weapons to use, that change up the gameplay. You have limited ammunition, so you will have to use a mix of melee and ranged combat, which is a lot of fun.
The loot that drops at the end of a game has 4 different types of quality. White, green, blue and orange. Each step up in quality gives the weapon one extra random trait, that you need to unlock by salvaging other weapons . That ends up being a lot of random. You get a random weapon type, for a somewhat random class (higher chance for current class), with random quality with random traits. The chance of getting that one weapon type with the traits you want, is really low. The randomness and different quality gives you incentive to try out another class after you've found that cool orange weapon for him, but it can also be really frustrating to keep getting items for a class that you do not want to play.
It should be mentioned that the AI bots are horrible. If a player disconnects, or you're having problems finding people through the matchmaker, you gotta think twice before going on as only 3 people. Playing solo with 3 bots is basically impossible, so if you're not keen on playing with other people, then this game is not for you.
Conclusion
The game has decent map variety, if you're okay with getting severely worse loot drops. If you aren't okay with that, the game makes up for it with great class diversity and randomly spawned special enemies. A fun game to enjoy with a few friends =)

Addictive and fun indie stealth game with great soundtrack and awesome voiceovers by Andy Serkis. You are playing as a thief in a distant future, and you're stealing gems from rich and corrupt people. Isometric view helps you to plan your steps and react quickly to what is happening.
You have some simple tools that help you on your quest - you can throw sound decoys to distract your enemies or put 'oddities' on walls to keep them occupied and indifferent to sound. You can use the environment to your advantage as well - stick to low walls to avoid being seen, use doors to hide or sound traps to break enemy movement patterns and get out of tricky situations. Be aware that you cannot kill anybody and that it makes the game even more interesting and fun.
Graphics are interesting and intriguing as well, yet simple enough to allow the game to run smooth even on older PC's. Controls are convenient and intuitive - it's fun to play both on keyboard + mouse and gamepad. With 100 levels and level editor, Volume will keep you occupied for hours. It's definitely worth its price so don't hesitate and grab it - you won't regret it!

Volume is Metal Gear Solid burned down to it's very core, keeping it simple with classic stealth game tropes but not losing the fun in the process. I have been looking forward to playing Volume for a long time, as I am a big fan of it's creator Mike Bithell, who also created Thomas Was Alone.
Instead of taking place in large areas with different rooms, Volume is set in multiple small levels. Each one has a different colour scheme and layout, so you don't have to worry about getting bored quickly. The game has a very minimalistic (cheap, hehe) design, similar to Thomas Was Alone, but in a 3D enviroment. All in all, Volume is a beautiful game. However, I must note that a lack of a death animation or even sound effect means that death has almost zero impact. The fact that all items aren't already loaded when you pick them up or respawn means that you sometimes also have to wait around for them to hurry up so you can use them.
It is also oozing with charm, with spot-on voice acting featuring not only multiple YouTubers such as Charlie McDonnell, Jim Sterling and Dan Bull, but also Andy Serkis, from Lord of the Rings and Planet of the Apes fame. The dialogue is brilliantly written, with humour often tucked in. There is also plenty of backstory to read while wondering through the levels, which adds a nice layer of mystery to the game's plot.
For the speedrunners out there, leaderboards for the time it takes to complete a level are placed to add a layer of challenge to the already rather difficult game. I wouldn't advise rushing through it though: take your time to marvel at the visuals, laugh at the dialogue and read through the creative backstorys.
Everything about Volume reeks of Mike Bithell, from the design to the wonderful music, composed by Thomas Was Alone composer David Housden. If you liked Thomas Was Alone or the Metal Gear Solid series, you will adore Volume.
EDIT: Unfortunately, some negative stuff, but just tiny nit-picks in the general scheme of things. You should be warned that I have found a rather glaring issue with the checkpoint system, which almost feels like cheating. It involves plassing through a checkpoint to save your progress while being chased by a guard. The guards sometimesalso don't do what they're supposed to do when using an item called the "gimmick", which is supposed to distract the guard by making them look at a certain place and note respond to sound. On numerous occassions, however, the guards have moved to where the sound came from, even though the visions cone stayed focus, and on others they have straight up ignored the gimmick when they hear a sound. The not-so-smooth transition between the standard stealth music track and the "seen" track is rather irritating after a while, and Charlie McDonnell's portrayal of the main protagonist can get a little I-don't-really-care-anymore. I wish I didn't have to say negative things about Volume, I really do.

As a fan of Thomas Was Alone I was excited to see what this game would hold. Seeing returning voice cast along with what seemed like a neat little story concept, an interesting art style and so forth, this had the hallmarks to be another indie darling of a game.
How wrong I was to be truthful.
First I have to say the voice acting, especially on the main character is awful. It's nearly jarring. The computer isn't nearly as bad but the line delivery seems to lack a certain punch to it. The performance feels phoned in which is disappointing. There is a wealth of text based snippets on the floors, these in some cases are quite funny, and I can't help but feel we've been done a disservice by not having them also voice acted.
It is impossible not to compare the writing and acting to that of TWA, and if you compare the first few levels in each game there is a vast vast difference in terms of things to pull you in. Volume simply has nothing to compel you, the early levels are literally a tutorial with very little story direction or real concept of anything other than learn this thing. You are given literally no context at all during the opening segments to why you are doing anything other than a computer told you so, and not in the Portal kind of way. In the drab, this is the game kind of way.
The gameplay itself is typical isometric stealth gameplay. That's it. Obviously it has this level editor and so on, but there is nothing more to it. The absence of story or any driving factors early on means there was very little reason for me to continue playing past the 15 minutes or so that I was actually playing. The game touts "100 levels" But the first level is literally walking to the exit and the ones that followed were equally simplistic with next to no dialogue. 100 levels is only a real number if each level is significant content, the first 5 at least were nothing but saying "look! stealth game!"
The art style as well, when actually playing does not feel like it adds to the experience. For such a minimalistic experience it actually feels overly busy and complex. details such as toilets to flush on the walls etc... aren't particulalry clear features to pick out until you stand next to them and get the text box in some cases.
It might sound like I'm being overly scathing for having played so little, but this is the age of the steam refund system and the significance of first impressions of a game has never been more apparant with so many games on the market. I am simply not compelled to delve any further because I have not been given any reason for anything I was doing.
A final irksome point is the random phrases spouted by the main character when collecting gems. Some of the phrases harken to elements of the story to do with gaining popularity and noteriety, however none of that has been discussed in the game thus far, yet he is spouting the phrases none-the-less. This dispels all immersion that could have existed.
I'm sorry mister Bithell but I donot think this game is worth £15, to me it has a much less compelling opening than TWA, the voice acting and writing is poorly done on all levels and there is simply nothing here to suggest it is anything but a generic stealth game. I'm sure I could be wrong, but I don't see a reason to delve further. Putting in my refund request now.
--Additional--
On reflection I believe I should add a few things here for clarity and fairness. At it's core it's a stealth game that works and that much is true, but it's not a stealth game that is worth £15. You can see where your money goes on this one, and it's pretty much on the graphics and voice actors which seems very silly when they are probably the least engaging parts of the game. People who like this game will like it for the stealth and the level editor, but those wanting more substance will be left confused and bored.

Knight & Damsel takes a unique spin on couch co-op and makes it... less than friendly. In this very inspired game of "tug-of-war," you and a friend compete to clear as many rooms as possible in order to save the other person. While playing, your actions directly affect what is happening on the other player's screen. Knock a plant from your view? It drops down and overgrows on your opponent's screen. Boot a cannon out of your way? It will fly to the top of the screen and shoot a cannonball to knock your savior from their path.
The idea behind having both players trying to rescue each other is both endearing, and works really well with this game. The game screens are split up nicely, giving each player and adequate view of what is happening both on their own screen, and their opponent's screen. Coupled with the absolutely breathtaking visuals, and this game is worth getting the support of the developers to build more!
My absolute only gripe about this game is how short it is! My girlfriend and I completed the cooperative part of this game in just under 15 minutes, and due to the limited environments and props, the replay value is small. I'd love to see the developer revisit this game and expand on what could be a game that is picked up any time you have a get together. $10 might be a bit too steep for how short the game is, but if you catch it on sale, I would definitely recommend it.

This game is a massive mixed bag. The standard deviation on it’s good and bad qualities are huge, and honestly makes me so ambivalent about the game that it is impossible for me to give any kind of recommendation.
This game was made as a console style RPG so it’s understandable that it’s keyboard controls are terrible. But since there is no warning on the steam page ‘strongly recommending a controller’ I have to assume that using the keyboard is a recommended way to play the game. As such I can say that the controls for the keyboard were strained, unnatural, and gave me grief. Given that both the overworld and battle phases punish you for slow reaction times or hitting the wrong buttons it is frustrating I was handicapped by poor controls. Eventually I got used to it but it was jarring and even 20 hours in I was still getting frustrated by them.
The overworld platforming segments work and are interesting but are also put down by clunky keyboard controls and the tedium of ferrying all the party members around separately. You have to beat each overworld level by moving each of the three characters (who each platform a slightly different way) from point A to point B, fighting enemies and collecting treasure along the way. The tedious part is having to, after having beaten everything in the level, to have to individually ferry each party member to the exit. If the assist characters can just teleport to the next area why can’t the other two main characters? This is exacerbated if you aren’t used to platforming with said character and miss jumps, fall into pits, or bump into enemies you wanted to run by. It’s just a waste of time. Trine handled this very well (Or at least Trine 2) where all 3 characters ethereally occupy the same space and you can freely switch between them at will.
The puzzle solving was pretty much trivial, ‘move character A with the particular skill B to point C and press the D button’, which just involved even more ferrying and tedium, (with one notable exception at the end of the game.)
The story/lore/characters were engaging and personally had me invested in them, however they eventually fell flat with weird plot twists, confusing reactions, and an endgame that just made me say ‘So what’s the point?’ and ‘Well, what did you expect to happen?!’ The story line didn’t build to a climax like it should, it started out slow, keeping going slow, then climaxed suddenly and ended. It was so abrupt and made me feel like nothing I had done up to this point was related or of consequence. I expected one more chapter and was caught off-guard when it ended. So many of the characters didn’t behave like I expected them to, like Tox for example who claims to be Rik’s loving brother but is most definitely the top contender for the ‘Worst Brother of the Year’ award after (Medium Story Spoiler)

The combat itself is not terrible and is unique to any RPG I’ve ever played (which isn’t saying too much.), however the battle felt more like crowd control than attacks and counters. They literally throw dozens of enemies at you and I eventually found that area damage was key, not trying to exploit elemental resistances, not targeting particular enemies first, just area damage. It made me wish for a good boss fight so I could sink my teeth into a static foe I had to actually examine and strategize against. But that leads me to the next section, difficulty.
This game doesn’t keep a consistent difficulty well. I played on ‘light’ mode, which is the middle difficulty, and blew through the first 3/4ths of the game with my only deaths being to utter carelessness when a weak party member was caught on their own. Towards the end they actually started stepping up the enemy encounters and it was nice to have to treat them like a threat. That is what I expected on Medium difficulty. HOWEVER. The last 3 boss fights were the most grueling thing in the game and were magnitudes harder than anything before. The first 2 bosses were fine but the final 3 wiped the floor with me and each eventually had me so frustrated that I had to stop playing to come back and beat them later. I felt that the first 2 of the last 3 were disproportionately hard but I still beat them and didn’t feel it was utterly unfair, sure they had 1-hit party KOs but you just needed to learn to block them. The last boss however was utter baloney with adds that protect the boss and fully respawn after each turn. It wasn’t like the others where I had to use elemental weaknesses against them and had to keep a stable proportion of area and single target attacks, it was just baloney. This was the only fight in the game I took the easy way out and fought on a lower difficulty. That’s right! I went through the entire campaign on easy mode and I STILL had to beat the final boss on a lower difficulty. It’s just not right.
And while we’re at it can I just say that the game insults you if you play on anything BUT the highest difficulty! That’s right! After evertying, an emotional ending, the game has a character that comes in at the end and taunts you saying you don’t deserve the end-game content because you’re playing on easy mode! Screw you! You can keep it!

As the developers like to put it, Knight & Damsel is an uncooperative game. Knight & Damsel is essentially a competitive puzzle game. Both of the players (two players required) are trying to be the player that ends up rescuing the other player. To do this players push, climb or destroy the obstacles in their way. Some of the hazards can also be moved onto the path of the other player in order to slow them down.
I had fun with Knight & Damsel. The gameplay is interesting if you have another person to play the game with. The game is easy to pick up so it could work for people that don't play a lot of games. The hazards do tend to create a runaway winner problem though since one hazard leads into another hazard and so on. While fun Knight & Damsel is the type of game that is best in short doses instead of long playthroughs. I think it would work best in 15-30 minute sessions.
Knight & Damsel is also really charming.
If you don't like these type of puzzle games or don't have anyone to play the game with, I don't think you will enjoy Kinght & Damsel. If you like the theme, have someone else to play with, and the gameplay looks interesting I think you will enjoy Knight & Damsel.

So, the thing to keep in mind is, throughout all of this review where I'm grading The Tenth Line as if it were a AAA Squaresoft release, it's not. It's the product of one very small, very indie team. That alone makes it worth the purchase. If the first official game for Sungazer software can go toe-to-toe with major jrpg releases, it's a studio worth supporting. Or, at bare minimum, watching.
A little bit of background on Sungazer, by the way. I said 'first official game', and what I meant by that was that the studio head, Deltree, has three full, published, freeware games already under his belt. They're all feature length jrpgs, they all take creative (and different) approaches to their gameplay, and they all flesh out some backstory (or frontstory, since the continuity is a bit out of sequence) for this title.
If you'd like to find them (and I sincerely recommend you do, since they're really good), navigate over to
and look for The Reconstruction, I Miss The Sunrise, and The Drop. Again, freeware, and they don't look at all like the average rpgmaker offerings. If you're still reading, seriously, open a browser tab and key whichever one of those titles looks the most interesting into a google search.
You're back? Good. On with the review.
The Tenth Line has problems.
It has problems in such a way that it's easier to talk about what it does wrong than what it does right. To be clear, it does a *lot* right. Its graphics are lovely, its music is pleasant, and it ventures out of comfortable, familiar design-territory to try and tackle new mechanics and systems.
Unfortunately, it's that last decision that causes it to fall on its face a lot. None of Tenth Line's issues are game-ruining. In fact, they're all very minor, but they add up to a mounting wave of frustrations.
Let me show you a few of them:
-The game is *very* dialog heavy. Most of the dialog feels kind of ho hum. It's not bad or badly written, but it's Final Fantasy dialog. It doesn't compel me to care. Unfortunately, towns are FULL of NPCs who have these long, detailed, back-and-forth conversations with each of your three characters. This makes each town you visit into a kind of hell of words, which you must valiantly wade into in hopes of maybe uncovering a quest.
-Character advancement is done three ways. There's a Final Fantasy X grid where you lay down items to unlock stats, there's a training system where you can burn items to upgrade your weapon up to a certain limit, and then there's quests that increase that weapon limit. Unfortunately, those quests are 90% of the time either find a hidden chest, solve a hidden puzzle, or find all the chests in the level. Which means that in order for your characters to keep pace with the monsters, you have to find 100% of everything in each dungeon. This isn't an exageration. Falling behind by two weapon levels turns all your attacks into garbage, and fights are graded based on how quickly you finish them. How well you do in fights determines what kinds of items you get, which in turn determines how much you can upgrade your stats.
-That would all be merely bad, but there are only a few times in the game when you can backtrack, and you can never backtrack all the way. This means you can get permanently locked out of being able to keep up with the monsters by consequence of not having found all the treasure chests in the game. wtf.
-Level navigation is done as a 2D platformer. This isn't objectively bad, but you control all three characters individually. Which means you have to pilot each of them through the level, and if one of them gets into a fight far enough away from the rest of the group, they end up by themselves in combat for a couple of turns. Which usually means they get killed. Which wouldn't be the worst thing, but being killed kicks them (or sometimes, for no clear reason, your whole party) back to the level entrance. Which means you have to make a long slog back to where you were and attempt the fight again. In the early game, this isn't as bad, but by late game just getting from screen to screen feels sisyphean.
-The story is broadly pretty interesting, but loses me on the specifics. The characters are basically 100% their best selves, forgiving each other for really serious things at the drop of a hat. There's fantasy racism, but instead of digging into how complex and self-perpetuating those kind of beliefs can be, multiple NPCs say things like "now that I've met a kobold, clearly they must all be okay". The actual conclusion to the story is pretty good, and has some genuine narrative tension, but then the game moves into the post-game and the fourth wall is snapped clean in half when everyone starts talking about how they're in a game and nothing matters any more. That's not a spoiler. The characters straight-up tell you that they've stopped being canon.
So, where does this leave us?
I think the path to good design involves a lot of experiments like the Tenth Line. I think it's definitely not a bad first game for a studio. I think Sungazer is a studio worth supporting, and I think if you're deep into the jrpg (or rpgmaker) scene, there's a lot here that you'll genuinely enjoy.
However, for all its polish, I think Tenth Line is still just a diamond in the rough. Deltree's other games are a lot more satisfying and, if you specifically want a 2D sidescroller RPG, you might be better served by picking up something like The Spirit Engine 2, which is this but without the frustration. It's also free.
Judging solely based on content, The Tenth Line is a reasonable buy at $20. However, if any of the above nitpicks made you clench your jaws in frustration, I'd suggest waiting until it's around $10.
Incidentally, Sungazer does have another game coming out soon, and that one ditches the Tenth Line formula entirely, so that may be worth looking into as well.

[Disclaimer]  I played this game on Lighter Mode.  Some other reviewers note that the full mode is punishing and complicated (but rewarding), and this is true, but my review is going to deal with the middle difficulty, Lighter Mode.
First and most importantly, the game has an excellent story, well-told through an older-school aesthetic.  It's not quite retro, but it's not modern either, and it oozes enough charm that I felt the graphics were an asset as opposed to a drawback.  There's some sidequesting, and a semi-extraneous yet fun card game, but largely it's a linear romp that stays tightly focused.
On Lighter difficulty, the combat mechanics are pared down so that the focus is on how you improve the character via the game's stat/skill board, and how you utilize the character's attacks in battle.  Harder difficulties add more things you have to do to optimize your character before battle, and add some more complexity to the order of abilities you use on 2 of the 3 characters.  Even on the 'lighter difficulty', the game is not trivial.  The first couple of chapters anyone can get through with ease, but at that point if you aren't keeping up with the character's leveling up or figuring out how to mix building SP with chaining attacks you can still die, and the bosses will provide a decent challenge.
The core mechanic of combat is that hitting enemies builds a momentum bar that recharges each character's mana (SP) at the end of turn.  More hits = more SP, and slaying an enemy yields considerably more than just hitting it.  Additionally, on the opponent turn, there's timed blocking/dodging that can earn you additional SP as well as lower the damage you take.  You then use the SP to select attacks that will hit various positions on the enemy's 3x4 grid.
On most normal encounters, there are more enemies than fit on the 3x4 grid, and they trickle in over several turns and as you kill the ones currently there.  Bosses tend to have neverending trickling reinforcements to allow you to build up momentum on chumps to help you use the big skills on the boss themselves.  It's a satisfying system, and works well.  The UI can be a little sluggish at times, but nothing particularly irksome.
Between combats you're playing a platforming game where you switch between the three characters to manuever places and get treasures.  I found this a little more tiresome mostly because the later levels involved jumps where when you screw up you have to walk one or more of the characters the long way around to get back where you were.  On the platforming maps are the random enemies, which don't respawn unless you leave the dungeon entirely.  No grinding is required, you can simply kill everything once as you go through and be perfectly suited to handling all the bosses.
I heartily recommend this game to any J-style RPG fans, try it on the Full Experience and if it seems too micromanagement for you fall back to Lighter and you'll still have quite the fine time.  If you don't like platforming at all, that might be a turnoff, but unless you truly hate platforming I'd still give this game a solid thumbs up.

Initially, I was mostly drawn to this game because I really enjoyed the creators previous freeware games (The Reconstruction, I Miss The Sunrise, and The Drop <- All highly recommended, by the by). So there's that.
When I got the game, I was immediately drawn into into the story and the characters. As I went on, I found it a refreshing twist to something that I would see as a sort of silly, cliché story plot in something else. What really made the game stand-out to me were the characters. They were wonderfully written, and I was extremely attached to them by the endgame, and they sent me through this roller coaster of emotions that I don't really feel for a lot of other games. Not everything is as it seems within the game, and I think that's my favourite part of it all.
The combat system in the game was interesting, though I will say that I didn't really get "the feel" of it until quite late into the game, honestly. It's a little hard to wrap your head around at times, but all-in-all, it was a pretty interesting way to present battles. Although I will say it got a little formulaic at the end, using the best moves when you can, and stalling until you could, but it's not a major gripe with me, because I tend to experience that with almost EVERY RPG I play. Despite that, I still did try to experiment.
The powering/leveling-up system in this game was unique in its way. I've never been real good at item management, but I had to catch on real fast if I wanted to utilise their powers to their fullest. And so I did, and then my players got really powerful, really fast.
Quad Pro Quo is really fun in its own right, and I kind of just kept playing games of it to play it.
The platforming of the game was simple, but could be a little more than awkward at times, at least for me, anyway. But otherwise it was perfectly okay! It was mostly just trying to figure out whether I'm going to be able to pass through it or not, and if not, can I get through it without bonking my head and falling into the pit and having to slowly walk back to where I was (looking at YOU Tox).
Otherwise, I highly recommend this game. I had pretty high expectations for it, and it did not fail to deliver. There were a few problems and a few frustrations along the way (a couple of things could be really vague at times), but otherwise it's really well-made and well-polished game!

After 190 hours i can truthfully say that this game has its ups and downs, but whether it is a good game or not mostly depends on the gap between the kind of game people excpect it to be and the kind of game it realy is. Through my personal experience with the game i have not faced any game breaking bugs and i have enjoyed the story mode & the adventure mode in single player. In an attempt to help others decide if this is a game for them or not i have come up with the following questions:
1. Do you like an open world with outdated but aestheticaly pleasing graphics?
2. Do you like a sand box experience where you can craft what you design (with in game editor)?
3. Do you like the option of playing on a random generated planet (with some key aspects of your choise)?
4. Do you like the concept of building and managing a colony (ranging from building design to colonist equipment)?
5. Do you like the option of finding 'dungeon loot' that other players designed?
If your answer is 'YES' to ALL of the above and you have 15 Euro to spare then try this game out (or try the demo version or wait for an offer period and try it then).

I first played this game when it released and loved it, then quit it for a long while to play other games.  I more recently returned to it and am still in love with it, so here's a more full review.
GRAPHICS/WORLD
Graphics and textures are pretty good but you'll likely want to turn down your graphics settings if you are having trouble with stutter or fps.  You'll want to do this for this game because you will want as little lag as possible when playing on higher difficulties as one hit from a rat can hurt bad.  Overall, the game is beautiful on higher settings with a dark, sinister look to many maps.  This is best exemplified in some of the Dracenfels DLC maps.  The maps have secret loot for you to find that can increase your loot roll chances at the end of the round.  It's a risk/reward system.  If you find and carry these items to the end of the round, you are making the round harder, but the payoff is better.  Your choice.
This game manages to help you understand more about the lore just through the banter between characters during adventures than most games do through direct narration.  You can also find lore pages throughout the world to understand more about the Vermintide world.
CONTROLS/ANIMATIONS
If this portion of the game were bad, it wouldn't be fun to play at all.  Fortunately, the combat controls are very good and responsive.  It feels meaty and viceral when slaying rats.  The game balances out your abilty to slay with rats coming at you from all directions.  But, good players learn to dodge and move constantly, always checking their flanks and rear.  Learn to dodge, stun block, and push at the right times and you will slay like a master.  The only time where controls aren't good is if you are playing with a host that has a bad internet connection.  In this case you will get lag and probably suffer the entire round.  I recommend just letting your teammates know you are getting bad lag and need to leave, they will understand.  Find a new match with a better host.  This isn't a frequent occurance, but it will likely happen once every couple hours of playing.
DIFFICULTY
The game is very easy on lower settings.  You aren't really playing the game until you get to NIghtmare or Cataclysm modes.  These modes only unlock when you beat a map on the previous setting.  Also, you need to play through much of the story to unlock the maps, so don't think that because you only see a few maps at the beginning that there isn't more.  There are many more maps, and even more with DLC's.  It's not until you play Cataclysm that you see the real team game shine.  It takes resource management, skill, and good decision-making to make it through.  It's really satisfying to complete a Cata mission with a random team that chose to work together.
LOOT
Along with the enjoyable team combat, the loot is likely why you will keep playing, always trying to get better loot with better traits on the weapons.  The game allows you to reroll new traits on weapons, "craft" new weapons, or break weapons down for shards that you can use to make new ones or unlock traits.  My only complaint here is I wish there were more variation to the weapon skins.
COMMUNITY
The community for this game is great.  Sure, every game has a jerk out there waiting to scold you on every mistake you make.  But, with this game, because each player relies on the others to make it through alive, you will find most players, even high level players, are willing to offer advice.  Pleae listen to them and feel free to ask questions.  The Reddit subforum for this game is also really helpful and active.
CONCLUSION
Buy this game if you love combat, teamwork, and a skill curve that gets more challenging and rewarding.
11/23/17 update:  With the purchase of Vermintide 2, you get the final DLC for Vermintide 1, Death on the Reik, for free.  That is a developer treating it's fan base with respect.  This game has always gotten better, and Fatshark deserves your money.

Warhammer: End Times - Vermintide is a fun game. I recommend it.
Why I liked it:
The game is heavy with atmosphere and character. The story is easy to follow and grasp without heavy exposition and lots of work trying to uncover it. Its all around in the game and is baked into things like the weapons, and the enemies, and objectives.
The Co-Op hordeshooter genre is really tapped into in this game, you'll be working to adjust your strategy to both your partners, to the creatures you need to defeat in each level, and the items you are able to scavenge.
Each of the characters feel unique in their own ways. They are not identical, so you will probably find a favorite.
What I didn't Like:
The game doesn't do a particularly good job of exposing all the nuances and rules. This is cool for some people, and discovering something "new" is always fun, but you'll spend some time experimenting and every iteration of a game that is basically a Co-Op campaign will begin to push you closer to that point where you've had enough.
The enemies are sometimes choppy, and able to hit you beyond the range you'd expect. This can be frustrating as the game fails to communicate with you clearly. This really takes away from the feeling of being skilled as you try to weave and dodge attacks and land blows. It's not choppy enough to really force you to put the game down, but I find myself looking to my USB controller often. "Do I want to trade aiming for movement?" is not a fun question to find yourself asking.
Wrap-Up:  Vermintide is a new game, similar to the Left 4 Dead formula, and is worth what they are charging for it. This game is big for Warhammer fans, and Co-Op shooter fans. When looked at critically; it has its weaknesses, but it does a good job of flexing its strengths.

Dennaton Games has delivered another great gaming experience that combines nostalgic elements  from the late 80's and early 90's with fast-paced and gritty gameplay. Hotline Miami 2: Wrong Number (HM2) features gameplay that is virtually identical to it's predecessor, but revamped with larger stages, more enemies, and a deeper plot.  The game deviates from the perspective of a nameless anti-hero, and instead features a narrative from multiple characters that eradicate foes from a 2D top-down perspective.
If you played the first Hotline Miami, you will have no trouble adapting to its sequel. HM2's controls are virtually identical, with the exception of a new aiming feature that allows players to 'lock' onto enemies from a distance. This is helpful at times but just often feels too awkward and clumsy to use. Each stage is now also much larger and swarmed with enemies. This makes for longer kill combos and more epic engagements, but can also be frustrating when enemies with ranged weapons one-hit you from off screen now. This will happen frequently and annoy you especially after you have just completed a difficult sequence. I felt that HM2 lacked the free-flow run and smash combat mechanics of its predecessor, and instead felt like a camp-fest.
As mentioned earlier, HM2 introduces several new playable characters from different factions. When starting  most missions, player have the option to pick a weapon set or perk, similar to the first game. There are a few characters who do not have the ability to spawn with weapons or perks, and must start the game with their bare fists.  Each character has different perks that dictate how they must play through levels. An interesting character, Evan, cannot pickup lethal weapons, can only wield baseball bats and pipes to  knock out foes. Ash and Alex, a tandem of masked vigilantes, can play simultaneously while wielding a handgun and chainsaw.  Another character  'Beard' does not possess masks, but can instead choose a firearm before stages.
HM2 graphics are also pretty much similar to the original game. Each level is unique while some featured cool visual effects, like falling rain, mist, rolling tides, or even strobing disco lights. The game's soundtrack is  beyond awesome, and features synthwave songs by Perturbator, Carpenter Brut, MOON, Scattle and many more. It is a major selling point to this game and can also be purchased separately. It creates a great immersion factor and really helps players feel like they are playing a game made in the 90s.
So lastly we have the plot and themes.  The first Hotline Miami did not really have a significant plot, unless the player collected a series of secret objectives. Even then, the plot was intentionally left shrouded and left open for interpretation. I always felt this was executed perfectly and would made the original game stand out amongst other contemporary peers.  HM2 has eight story arcs that all interweave to provide an intriguing and surprisingly deep plot.  While the game's motif is still kill anything that moves, we are now provided why everything must die a horrible, horrible death. I really enjoyed HM2's story that touched on theme's like patriotism, post-traumatic stress disorder, and vigilantism.
All in all, I was greatly impressed with Hotline Miami 2 as a sequel. Even though  its gameplay  and graphics are largely similar to its predecessor, the game still has plenty of action that will keep you coming back for more. Hotline 2 also features a level editor, which is nice but a bit limited to use. There are more ways to dispatch your enemies and new allies to help you along your path.  Aside from a lack of multiplayer and a few design errors, Hotline Miami 2 is a great release for gamers looking for a retro 2D action game.

There's a little less replayability in the levels because many of them lack masks, but the levels are more tightly designed than Hotline Miami's. The gameplay is fast and satisfying, the music is loud and chaotic, and the visual are polished to mirror shine. If you liked Hotline Miami, you'll like this. If you haven't played Hotline Miami play it first, not only is it cheaper but you'll need to have played it to understand what the game's strory is about.

Basic:
At its core its a good rpg with a good plot and fun characters
Though it's biggest issue is that it tends to overcomplicate things somewhat with its level up and training mechanics, and these can require a bit too much micromanaging in some parts; though on lower dificulties the attention necessary for those greatly diminishes
It also has a really addicting and rather fun card minigame similar to FF9's own card game minigame
combat:
It takes some practice to get used to how combat works, in particular the defences, but you eventually get there and it can be rather satisfying to get everything working well.
It is based on button presses (depending on the attack chosen) timing and knowing when to attack or rest; as well as what types of defences to use
Defences also based on button presses, where normally you have to watch the attacks and which characters they are going to hit and time the button presses right, with each of the 3 characters having diferent styles of defence
each of the 3 also has a super defence that is a direct counter to an enemy attack type, ranging from blocking all physical close ranged attacks, all physical ranged, and all magic; each with its own side bonuses to it (such as the physical block healing allies with every blocked attack) and timing to be triggered for maximun effect
Dungeons/levels
On bigger gameplay sessions these can be rather annoying and time consuming; though I found that, if played in smaller bursts, they are not as bad.
they are heavy on a sort of puzzle element, where you work to bring all 3 characters to the end of the dungeon, finding all treasures and possible sidequests along the way, each of the characters having a diferent ability to use, and diferent capabilites of movement (for example: one of them moves rather slowly, and cannot clear distances with his jump; but they jump much higher than other party members and have a longer ranged in their battle-starting attack)
enemies are present in the map, you can attack them, either for a surprise attack (if they are not aware of you) or an normal battle (they are aware but have not attacked you first); being attacked first will have you be ambushed
in adition to that, you must mind the distances between each character; as the farther away they are from each other the longer it takes for them to join the battle, with them joining instantly if close enough (though not in the case of an ambush)
Mechanics
As mentioned above, mechanics in this game can be somewhat overly complicated; as you have not only a linsence board style leveling up system (which is the simpler one, and easier to manage) and a more complicated training system that varies from character to character
all leveling up and training is item based; you get bulks of items from enemies, buying them via the menu or treasure chests
the regular leveling up is simpler, you place items in tiles to gain certain stats and work your way towards unlocking skills (matching item types with the right tiles gets you bonuses)
Training is... rather more complicated, as it is limited in between battles/events; it is required to strenghten your weapons (while you do obtain weapon level ups during the main game, those just increase the max you can train your weapon up, and will have NO effect unless you first train the character up)
while weapong strenghtening IS permanent, other things are not (such as bonus damage, and one character's defence duration)
In adition to that, the training option can be used to alter each individual character's personal mechanic, with some preparation definetely necessary to face certain thougher fights (or to solve some puzzles in the dungeons)
Final note:
It is definetely a good game and well worth a purchase
one just has to pace their time with the game, as bigger sessions can and will likely lead to some frustration
in addition to that the world and story are interesting; and the game feature post ending content and even as new game plus
