I cannot highly recommend this game enough.
Are you a fan of satisfying and viceral melee combat?
Do you like the L4D objective and special infected style?
Do you like having different classes/character/loot which radically change your gameplay style?
If you answered yes to any of these, I would recommend getting this game. At the price point of 30 dollars, it is a steal. On normal, the entire game will take you 4-6 hours to simply complete all the levels available on first go. However, due to the loot, and the increased difficulty of hard/nightmare/cataclysm, and of the hidden tome/grimoires on each level to find, you will want to come back and play more. Even 70 hours in im still finding new areas I haven't noticed on prior playthroughs.
The combat itself is incredibly satisfying. Every weapon acts differently, and the grusome decapitation and dismemberment of rat men will never get old. The special skaven make it so that sticking together is a necessity, and yet still incredibly challenging. Add in the fact of the random spawns, and each playthrough of the same map will always turn out differently, and sometimes really crank up the difficulty when a skaven patrol rounds the corner at the worst possible time.
Also count in the fact that the developer has announced a massive free DLC pack for new weapons/features december 3rd, this is worth your time to purchase and have a great time.
The game is brought down to the fact of numerous bugs (although quite small, only few times have I noticed game/match ending bugs, maybe 3 times), but only by a small amount. Also, a bit of lackluster netcode makes it incredibly annoying when the host leaves, forcing the entire mission to restart from the beginning. When playing with friends however, this is never a problem.
Overall, if your a fan of the warhammer universe, 9/10. If your not a fan, 8/10.
A very solid and engaging game, which cruel RNG loot system will make you come crawling back for more, brought down only by the fact of small bugs littering the game like so much skaven filth.

After having pumped 200+ hours into the game I think I should write a review to support the game, so here I go.
Mount & Blade Warband, released in 2010, a kind-of sequel to the original Mount & Blade, is a First/Third Person Action RPG/RTS set in a medieval open world. You set your own goal - live a life as a mercenary, become a Lord of one of the kingdoms, join a claimant to a throne in his battle to take, as he/she thinks, his/her rightful place as king, or go against all of the kingdoms and create your own.
You start the game completely on your own in one of the capital cities of your liking where you happen to get your first quest. You then recruit soldiers for your troop and either be a good samaritan who takes care of the bandits and helps villages, or be the feared vandal by raiding caravans and villages.
Now, putting together your troop and controlling it in battle is where the RTS part comes in.
All your soldiers can be put in groups (similar to ordinary RTS control groups which you select with the 0-9 keys) to always only select those soldiers you want, giving you a lot of control over them. In battles you can give them all sorts of commands you could think of, including, but not limited to, telling them to use only certain weapons that they possess.
Another special thing about this game is the very skill-based combat system.
The melee combat system is based on attacking from four directions and being able to block them - of course by blocking in the direction the swing comes from. This can be really tough sometimes when there's a lot of stuff going on or if your opponent has a rather fast weapon.
You can set up how you want to swing and block independently. Do you want it to work by going into the corresponding direction? Or only by mouse movement?
In singleplayer, for beginners, you can even enable automatic blocking. This will result in you only having to press the block button when a swing comes in, of course you still have to know when to block and when to swing. This setting does not apply to multiplayer though, there it is up to the server wether there's automatic blocking or not - but most likely you'll only be seeing automatic blocking in player vs bot games (there are special modules that are based on fending off enemy waves with other players).
The multiplayer mode is something that first came with Warband, and I think it's pretty solid for an indie game (except for some minor things, but later onto that).
It supports up to 250 players and several modes, including Deathmatch, Team Deathmatch, Capture the Flag, Last man standing Deathmatch and of course castle siege, similar to sieging a castle in singleplayer.
Apart from all that great stuff the game also has an amazing mod support. Search
for Mount & Blade mods (for both the original game and Warband) and you'll understand what I mean.
As many pros as this game has, it also has a few cons.
A big problem in multiplayer, similar to other games (like Chivalry, for example), are the trolls.
There are a lot of times when you have a lot of fun and fight a bunch of great battles, and then there's the trolls' prime time.
At that time, things are going to get messy. You randomly get hit, shot and kicked by a teammate just to annoy you and then that person just runs along as if nothing happened. When you try to take revenge, they will turn things around and make you look like the vermin, causing everyone to go at you. Classy trolls.
That's about the negatives I could think of and it isn't really the games' fault.
To round this review of, I'll give a short summary:
Pros:
-solid melee combat system
-troop management
-good graphics (remember that this was and still is an indie game - I think the graphics are absolutely fine despite what others have said. Besides, the graphics in M&BII have been improved by a lot.)
-great multiplayer with a high number of players supported and several gamemodes
-mod support
-always challenging
Cons:
-engine limitations
So I come to the conclusion that I can clearly recommend this title to others. Also keep an eye out for the upcoming sequel!

=Review as of August 22, 2017=
If you asked me to define it in a single phrase, "Broad but shallow", is how I'd describe the gameplay of Planet Explorers. It's a game with an enormous amount of content, yet that content all turns out, disappointingly, to be only surface deep. That said, the game remains fun and interesting to play... especially with friends.
Planet Explorers is a survive-collect-fight-build style RPG, where you play a stranded astronaut who must struggle to survive after crashlanding on a strange alien planet. The game follows the usual trope of slowly building up a base while fending off local wildlife, mining and exploring the area. Players will slowly build their way from wooden axes and shovels to drills, energy weapons, ships and flying AI companions. During this time, they will also build and improve their own colony and fill it with NPCs whom they will recruit from settlements all across the planet.
-Things I liked-
+The game is very pretty to look at and leads to a lot of "Ooooh" moments
+Fast travel system makes exploring a little less onerous
+The replicator (crafting) system is very neat and easy to use. I think it's extremely well done
+Creating a colony feels like making your own town, and you easily become invested in making it perfect and managing your colonists
+Large variety of interesting creatures and plants to discover and murder
+Money is handled really well and you never end up being super rich and wondering what to do with it all until you've completed every other aspect of the game possible
+You can design your own vehicles, aircraft, boats, guns, weapons, armour, drones, turrets etc
+Story is very engaging in story mode and well-paced
+You don't CONSTANTLY have to eat and drink; something that most survival games seem to implement
-Things that need improving-
- Adventure mode progression is terrible and all over the place. This sometimes leads to hours of grinding just to get that next tiny thing needed to unlock more technology
- Tech tiers make no sense: You possess a replicator capable of building anything and yet it gives you shovels to dig with and swords to fight with. Shouldn't it produce laser mining tools or something?
- Everything is shallow. That is to say, every single system in the game exists almost like a placeholder for more content. For example, towns will provide a bunch of fetch quests but will ignore you forever afterward once you complete them. Dungeons are fun at first but become a very samey grind very quickly and lack variety. Vehicles are fun but reserved only for players with huge amounts of resources, by which point you might as well build a battlecruiser instead of a car. Colonies are exciting to build but ultimately possess no depth as to how they are run. You assign colonists to work, and they basically reduce timers or provide resources every so often. Diplomacy doesn't exist, even though they tell you that you can make peace with the locals. You can't place your own fast travel points. The map has like 5 biomes which constantly repeat. There are only a handful of character weapon archetypes (sword, spear, dagger, gun, laser gun) and all weapons are just those with varying levels of damage. Monorails are end-game tech but why build a train when you can literally teleport to any town you've visited? Towns also have very little variety and mostly consist of a premade template which repeats over and over.
- For some reason after you send a chat message you have to press enter twice or it thinks you're still typing which almost always leads to getting into issues later
All in all the game is a lot of fun to play with friends, but lacks the depth needed to really hook players for the long run. Perhaps with time it will gain this depth, but for now, expect to play it once and put it down.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

In a cold and oppressive futuristic world ruled by material and technology. Intellectuality, individualism, and expression are outlawed in favor of physical gain, and strange mechanical overlords exert control over the minds of humans who dare to think on their own terms. From the two-person development team behind RymdResa, Morgondag have perfected their beautiful simplicity into a fine art;
imprint-x is a puzzle game with an incredibly unique premise. Like the traditional metal puzzles of Japan, mechanical simplicity is utilized to create a formula of exploration with endless possibilities. Various mechanically sealed cubes must be activated through a series of cryptic buttons and eventually with well placed timing. Through a bit of hand-eye coordination, muscle memory, and sometimes sheer trial-and-error it's up to the player to discover the trick to activating and opening each progressively intricate contraption.
Opening these mysterious and alien cubes is an act of peculiar curiosity. Seeing button shapes, lights, and indentations that beckon your touch but give no indication of their purpose. Not until that curiosity takes over, and every possibility poked and prodded at that things become clear, and in turn very satisfying to execute.
As this sense of personal exploration goes on the boxes slowly unfold with each series of correct presses. With each flap unfolded and each tab extended more and more strange and unexplained contraptions appear, and fold back into themselves as the final correct combinations are attempted for a satisfying completion.
The surreal and celestial setting around you pulses with cosmic color and sound. The ambient soundtrack builds in complexity alongside the puzzle-boxes you unravel, and the inter-galactic lightshow dances in tandem with the beat. Hard puzzles that soon require precise timing are now even more pulse-driving and difficult to focus on as this chaotic ballet of sound and visuals assault  your senses.
imprint-x is one head trip of a game. It's more of an experience than a game, I suppose, like some kind of cosmic Christmas morning gift unwrapping ceremony with freaky extra-terrestrial relatives. Each box is stranger and more perplexing than the last, and each beckoning button more satisfying to push with each success. Superbly trippy, ultra addictive, and a serious pleasure to look at and listen to.

This is an incredibly addictive strategy game whereby you command a team of SWAT officers in raids on various compounds.  This game boasts a fairly hefty list of single missions, and a number of multi-layered campaigns.  The briefings are simple, with no overblown storyline - just the basic facts of how many Tangos, and what your objectives are.  How you go about assaulting the compounds is essentially up to you.
The player generally gets to command a team of 2-8 officers that, as you progress grow in skill.  The more you play, the more unlocks become available, allowing even more playing styles through different classes (Pointman, Assaulter, Breacher, Stealth, and Shield).
Insertion points are fixed, but there are generally some options as to where your team will start from, and who you include on the assault.
The game provides an interesting playing experience with it being almost turn-based - but not.  The player has the ability to pause the game and command their officers in where to move, where to look, and basic actions.  This can be done in real time, but more success is had by trusting in your officers AI.  At any point, if you feel your orders aren't working, you can freeze time and change your commands, allowing you to command (somewhat) on the fly.
I picked this game up on sale earlier today and have spent around 6 hours playing - so the value for money is high.
This is a great game for short stints - allowing you to log in and make an attempt or two at a difficult target, without too much commitment out of your day.  Or, you can just spend hours grinding your way through the various levels.
The game is very much like chess, where you need to think a few moves ahead.
Basic knowledge of MOUT/urban warfare can help, but trial and error can eventually be as effective.  Just remember to check those corners!
The AI Tangos are quality, with numerous classes to go up against.  Just don't be upset if a hostage taker decides to kill their comodoty before they turn the gun on you.
The UI isn't perfect and I still fumble with issuing breaching commands on a 'go command', but remember the 7 P's and you'll do alright:  'Proper Planning and Preparation Prevents♥♥♥♥♥♥Poor Performance'.

For 2012, Zombies was the it genre. Infestation, Black Ops 2, the peak of numerous multiplayer zombie games like Killing Floor, L4D, etc. So Deadlight came along with its fresh new platformer spin on the golden genre. The game should be lauded for its mediocre story, collectables that would be worth interacting with if the protagonist was more interesting and original platformer level designs. In fact, the level design and background environments are the strongest assets to the game.
But while the game lives through its strong visuals, it dies by its controls and clunky player movement. A pivotal aspect of the game is climbing, and the registration of where to stand in order to climb is painfully off. To add insult to injury, instructions are often ambiguous or unclear in how to advanced through flawed sections of levels towards the middle of the game. You will find yourself dying over and over in areas that demand frame-perfect jumps or rolls that are uncharacteristic of the genre. Solutions will come down to muscle memory over anything else. Because this is paired with a foolish layout of controls, sluggish environmental registration with your character and combinations that are bound to leave you with carpal tunnel, you’ll end up dying enough in an unforgiving zone just to ask yourself what you’re doing it all for.
I’m hopeful that the gameplay elements will be tweaked in the subsequent sequel, and Tequila Works will be able to give us the mechanics that are on par with their high concept story and striking world.

I don't recommend the game, not because it's "bad", but because it's mediocre. There's nothing really special about this game to recommend it to anyone. I got it on sale, and it's given me about 20 hours of moderate fun, so I'd say I'm satisfied. Don't pay any more than $5 for this.
Pros:
- It's fun to shoot zombies
- The Sig Sauer is really fun
- The flashlight looks great
- Boarding up a house and then shooting zombies through doors is really cool
- Big levels
Cons:
- Zombies are only really affected by headshots. Contagion prides itself on being more realistic, but a .45 ACP to the chest will slow anything down - as it is, anything other than a headshot is wasted ammunition.
- Guns sound bland, except for the Sig Sauer. I really wish game developers would take field trips to gun ranges to hear what guns actually sound like, rather than just relying on movies.
- Too much bullet spread. If guns were as inaccurate as they are in this game, nobody would use them. I pointed a rifle at a wall about 20 meters away, didn't move the mouse, and fired five times, waiting enough time in between each shot for the rifle to settle down again. I checked the wall and there were five different bulletholes. At 20 meters, you should be able to put a round in the same place all day long.
- It isn't cognitively demanding at all. If you try to take it slow and be smart, you'll be disappointed, as every encounter ends up being a non-stop headshot fest.
Overall, I think they could've done better. It feels like it's in Early Access, or something that might have once appeared on XBox Live Arcade. Underwhelming stuff.

(edit: However, rewards for these do not scale well with the increasing difficulty of the missions)
Cons:
-Camera can be buggy and snaps around when levels get too fast
-Not a lot of upgrades/later upgrades take a lot of grinding
-Past level 8, levels get impossible. Random generation + the speed of the levels means impossible obstacles are sometimes created or are being created too quickly to react to (you have to just predict what type of jump you'll need before the obstacle is even on screen)
Edit:
So I finally completed all achievements, you can see how long it took. Not really worth it, but this was mostly a background game while I listened to podcasts. There are 10 levels. It is possible to beat all ten. There is nothing special for doing so, and multipliers don't increase past this point.

it's a simple 2D side scrolling runner game where you have 2 buttons: jump and slide. It was originally a game designed for mobile devices, and later ported to PC version.
You play as Emma Jones. She's a firefighter and your mission is to guide her along frenzied levels in flames and save the largest possible number of kittens. With this, you'll collect money and points that can later be used to purchase power-ups. Maybe a little cute concept game but nothing more.
The camera is quite bad (it jerks around like nobody's business and doesn't show the important upcoming stuff). The menus are too poor, meaning you'll spend a lot of time waiting in them.
The gameplay is so bland. It's just a runner game without nothing new to offer. It's just always the same scenery, and an horrible uninspired grind. With ten levels to overcome, the diversity of adventure will not much beyond what appears at first, especially with the visual scenarios.
Graphically it's clearly based on
fashion that seems to have been, but the style doesn't encourage. At the same time it's a freaking jumping game - the problem isn't the speed of the game, the problem is that it isn't involving skill, it's involving impossibility and unpredictability. You have to jump to pass the flames, and if you jump, you stub yourself into the logs behind, you can't reach the ground to slide under it, so the level can't be completed. Add to this, a huge repetitive game.
could have been successful if it had been more ambitious but the limitations of converting a mobile game to a home console format quickly become all too obvious. While there's some fun to be had in short, quick sessions,
doesn't take long until it becomes too repetitive and its overall components are clearly weak to what is expected from a platform game. There are so many better runners games and free. I can't recommend this.

Doorkickers feels a little bit like Rainbow Six 3, without the FPS part.
You manage a squad of 2+ (depending on the mission) officers who have to clear a building, secure evidence or rescue hostages.
Before starting the actual mission, you are to forge a plan of how to tackle the situation.
You can give orders to each officer individually so that in the end they work together to clear the building as quickly and safely as possible.
You may also give each officer different weapons, or a completely different class.
Need a shielder? No problem.
Or rather a breacher? You got it.
A stealther? Sure.
If you are not satisfied with certain aspects of the game, the modding community is doing their job for sure.
From different/new weapons or armours, to completely new classes and obviously loads of user made maps.
The cartoonish graphics are definitely no throw off. You will be way too focused on your tactics trying to keep your officers alive than to check out the beautiful flower pots in the bathroom.
Just don't go thinking "Easy peasy". You will have your squad killed easier than one would think. A proper planning phase is half a victory.

The underlying mechanics of this game are solid and the more "realistic" approach is certainly appreciated as it actually does require you to make some tactical considerations, however the game undermines itself in a pretty severe way. And that is the maps themselves. They are still designed around more arcade style shooters, and so what you often find happening is that there is never a defensible point, and no choke points to have any sort of firefight. Inevitably every public match will end up becoming a sort of free for all death match where players sprint around the levels hoping to get the drop on an unsuspecting opponent. The most fun I have had with this mod was when it was more popular and people where running counterstrike source maps in it. Those maps actually had good design philosphy and worked especially well with the shooting mechanics in this game. As insurgency stands now though, I cannot recommend it. It is an oddity, the parts that work, work really well, but it is unfortunate that the developers never bothered to create functional maps. If they had I suspect the community would have stuck around.

This game is all about taking ideas that were out there already, cleaning them up, and making money on them. Not a bad idea, give the good ideas, but poor execution that is out there. And BI should be able to do a good job: they are the people who did the Arma series, afterall. However, this "EA" was release too early, and is simply buggy, unfinished, poorly documented, with problematic features. In short, it's hard to play through a whole game without something going fatally wrong. Additionally, the community is completely toxic, as you would expect, with most of them coming over from Rust. Don't bother playing this on the public servers; the lag, community, and experience are all horrible. Instead of focussing on getting a working product, it would appear that the concern is whether or not the cash store works. That's right, a cash store in an EA title.
Can it be enjoyable? Yes, but it's really more of a demo than a game. Ask for technical support, or ask for a tutorial, and BI will literally blow you off, tell you it's on the website or included as a Codex (which has the technical depth of instructions for using toothpicks), or simply not answer, or tell you it's in the works (which amounts to the same thing).
True, it's cheap. I got my copy for $12. And frankly, as of this moment, that's about all the game will ever be worth. But it's early still, and there's a lot that needs to be done. Let's hope this game gets completed, unlike several other BI titles I could mention (*cough cough* DayZ).
Stay away from it for a while until they start getting things worked out - that's my advice.

Despite what negative things you might hear, this game is actually extremely enjoyable. Playing Left for Dead as a kid kind of let me feel nothing in regards to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ loot, because there was no loot in Left for Dead. Why are you mentioning Left for Dead, you might ask? Well, this game borrows many concepts from L4D, (in fact, you can argue that Vermintide is basically modelled after L4D) such as the enemy mobs equating to those zombie mobs in L4D.
That said, if you are unfamiliar with the Warhammer setting, it is quite easy to say that there is only war everywhere and everything wants to kill you (on a less extreme than Warhammer 40,000). The enemy of the game, the Skaven, are humanoid rat people who are overruning the city of Ubersreik. The description of the game by the developers offers a pretty solid explanation of what's going on.
Vermintide revolves around you and three other companions (from a total of 5 to choose from, the Dwarf Ranger (melee/ranged combatant), the Imperial Soldier (same), the Witch Hunter (primarily ranged/mixed), the Elven Ranger (same), and the Bright Wizard (primarily ranged/magic). Completing a series of objectives to accomplish a mission, you and your party must venture through the rat-infested city to do so. It is quite fun, although replayability might not be a strong suit. With this said, bear in mind there are minor bugs and some kinks that the devs haven't worked out yet. If you can look past these, I'd say you'd love this game.

Left 4 Dead style co-op gameplay with "Skaven" (rat people) instead of zombies, set in the wonderfully brought to life, Warhammer Fantasy Universe. Only minor bugs, very challenging difficulty settings and rewarding visceral melee combat system with a lot of variety. Although the most difficult setting in the game is playing solo on ANY difficulty. The bot AI and pathing in this game is the worst I've ever seen, in any game I've ever played. If you don't have three other buddies to play with, or mind grouping with random players, I would not recommend the game unless you, like me, are a hardcore Warhammer fan and enjoy losing to the dice gods (loot) or are just a masochist in general. In any case, great game, if you liked L4D2, you will love this.

Vermintide would be easy to write off as a Left 4 Dead clone but after a couple of hours you quickly realise it’s anything but. Sure the combat and core mechanics are definitely inspired by the grand daddy of this genre but the extra elements that Vermintide has makes it on its own. The character classes and loot system help keep the game fresh, even after you’ve played the same map a dozen times over. The combat retains that same high tension feeling that we all grew to love in Left 4 Dead whilst distinguishing itself with a bunch of Warhammer inspired mechanics. The crafting system and few rough edges are the few let downs of vermintide but it says a lot that those are the only negative things I have to say about it. For those who were let down by Evolve Vermintide could very well be the game that resells you on the genre.

An excellent co-op fantasy game which offers a blend of melee and ranged combat from a first-person perspective. The objectives of each scnario are varied, but readily-understood, and I haven't yet found myself lost or confused. Exploration is rewarded in the form of boosted loot rewards for the whole team, buff and healing items, and ammunition. However, your team mustn't dally, as enemies will continue to spawn if you linger in an area.
During certain events, the characters (whether controlled by a player or AI) will interact verbally, offering congratulations, warnings, and banter, but never chattering so much as to obstruct conversation or become too repetitive. Playing with a full party of humans is ideal since each team member can communicate and coordinate, but the NPC AI is perfectly adequate for playing with just two or three players.

"Planet Explorers takes place in the year 2287, one of the first colony ships sent out by Earth arrives at the planet Maria, an unknown planet in the Epsilon Indi Star System. During its landing sequence, something goes wrong, the massive ship loses control and crashes into the planet. What originally was a first colony mission has now turned into a mission for mere survival on an unforgiving planet filled with creatures ready to outlast the visitors from Earth. In order to survive in this new world the survivors will have to explore, gather, build, create, fight or befriend the planet inhabitants, and ultimately, establish a lasting new home."
+ Unlimited power...I mean creativity (Want to fly a X-Wing? Milenium Falcon? Heck you can even build your own Death Star)
+ Large open world to explore
+ Enchanting atmosphere, real alien planet feeling, vivid colors, everything is alive
+ Day-night cycle
+ The terrain deformation is absolutely great (voxel based game which means the terrain deforms a lot more natural than a block game would)
+ You can ride animals
+ Mineral mining
+ The music is fantastic
+ Able to build colony
+ Character creation tool
+ Storyline is solid
+ Decent co-op mode
+ You can cancel quests
+ Never lags even on full detail at full view distance
+ Very few game crushing bugs have ever popped up
- Infinite NPC shop storage and basically-infinite inventory (it lacks the urgency a survival-oriented game might have)
- Unpolished elements in game (Character walking into large trees when chopping them, Creatures walking on vertical surfaces)
- Not optimized good enough (not my issue but many people have issue with this)
- Mainly fetch quests
- Ground vehicles need physics adjustments
- AI pathfinding
If you like survival, exploration, crafting and building this is totally the game for you! Needs some polishing but it's definitely worth the price.

I'm on the fence about recommending this game. Reading the other reviews pretty much echoes most of my thoughts: "great game, fun, BUT..."
It's this BUT that has me worried about recommending the game. Yes, I've played over 70 hours. However, the tail end of those 70 hours were more grind and doing ridiculous things to make the game fun again. The world generator is still quite broken as many of the worlds it produces has ridiculous geography that makes no natural sense.
The beginning, I was hooked on this game. It was my digital crack. I absolutely LOVE survival+crafting games and this was my latest digital heroin. However, about halfway through it just stopped being as fun, and, as I mentioned above, the last 10-20 hours were just me randomly tapping at keys in the world generator trying to get something fun.
Don't get me wrong, the crafting system was actually pretty neat, especially the built-in mini-CAD. However, as a whole, the game just doesn't have that spark for me anymore.
The story was very meh, but still it produced moments of interest for me. The replay value, however, still needs quite a bit of work. And from the looks of things, I don't think we'll be getting anything anytime soon. Last update was in May.
Anyways, for first time players, I'd recommend this game, but caveat emptor: it's still not polished as well as it should be, be prepared for random bugs.
Is it worth the $20 or whatever I paid for? 70 hours says yes. Is it worth playing more than that? Probably not. I really wish steam had a "meh", "maybe" or sideways thumb...

Airstrike HD is a modern clone of "Bomber" from 1983 released on ZX Spectrum. The game objective is the same as in original - descending plane must destroy the buildings below before it crashes hitting them. In this version of game you can pick one of five available planes, each with set of upgrades. Game features light music, simplistic cartoon graphics and non-challenging ganeplay. There are steam achievements to unlock and trading cards, also cheats incorporated in options menu. This is definetely not a title that will be a new indie mega-hit and bestseller but it can take some of your time if you get into it. Considering price to gameplay time, it is worth its price, but dont get your expectations too high. Game doesnt offer much more besides what you see in intro.  From me it gets thumbs up for bringing back old game for modern platform, but i recommend it only for those, who like nostalgic returns to really old games. Best regards.

Far Cry 3 is a great open world FPS. Its set on a couple of tropical islands where the main character, Jason, finds himself and his friends captured by pirates. The game sees you fighting the pirates to free your friends and the locals of the islands. You can fight using stealthier methods or go in loud and you get plenty of weapons that lets you do either. For the most part its an enjoyable game even if it suffers a bit from the "Ubisoft formula", and is my favourite Far Cry game.
Good points:
- The islands the game is set on are great with some beautiful tropical scenery. You can capture outposts from the pirates or hunt the local wildlife as well as having a variety of vehicles to help get around.
- Vaas is one of my favourite video game villains and he really stands out as a great character.
- The realistic way fire spreads in this game is really cool and it can sometimes be an ally or enemy depending on luck. It does lead to some hilarious situations when a fire spreads out of control.
Bad points:
- The game relies on a ridiculous amount of collectables to pad out the gameplay.
-The way enemies detect you is a bit inconsistent at times. Sometimes they'd spot me hiding in bushes or from a distance while other times I could sneak right up to them unseen.
Game itself is amazing, but the ♥♥♥♥ing uplay stuff just makes it unnecessary "complicated".

I’ve been playing Ylands for around six hours now and the first thing I want to say is - buy it. The game is worth the £13 (think it’s discounted at the moment to £10). This is probably one of the best early access games I have played for some time with very few bugs.
The game itself is beautiful. From the trees, flowers, greenery and water to the character, building materials, random huts, houses and buildings they are all amazingly detailed.
With these types of games the devil is in the detail and it definitely is in Ylands. When it snows the surrounding areas get covered and you can see your footprints as you walk through it, then see the snow melt as it warms up. The bad weather stops you sleeping because who would sleep outside in the rain with no covers - very logical.
The controls are super easy and you’ll find the small codex (F1) quite helpful to get you started but then there is a level of guessing what you need to make certain items. For example some items you want to make require nails but if you haven’t found nails then you need to make numerous other things until nails are available. It takes time but you get used to it and away you go.
There are a few bugs but the developers are on top of it and in the last day I think three updates have been released to rectify the issues - and they have. They are listening to the community and that’s the most important aspect.
It really is a very fun game to play and as I said previously - it’s worth every penny you spend.

Vermintide would be easy to write off as a Left 4 Dead clone but after a couple of hours you quickly realise it’s anything but. Sure the combat and core mechanics are definitely inspired by the grand daddy of this genre but the extra elements that Vermintide has makes it on its own. The character classes and loot system help keep the game fresh, even after you’ve played the same map a dozen times over. The combat retains that same high tension feeling that we all grew to love in Left 4 Dead whilst distinguishing itself with a bunch of Warhammer inspired mechanics. The crafting system and few rough edges are the few let downs of vermintide but it says a lot that those are the only negative things I have to say about it. For those who were let down by Evolve Vermintide could very well be the game that resells you on the genre.

An excellent co-op fantasy game which offers a blend of melee and ranged combat from a first-person perspective. The objectives of each scnario are varied, but readily-understood, and I haven't yet found myself lost or confused. Exploration is rewarded in the form of boosted loot rewards for the whole team, buff and healing items, and ammunition. However, your team mustn't dally, as enemies will continue to spawn if you linger in an area.
During certain events, the characters (whether controlled by a player or AI) will interact verbally, offering congratulations, warnings, and banter, but never chattering so much as to obstruct conversation or become too repetitive. Playing with a full party of humans is ideal since each team member can communicate and coordinate, but the NPC AI is perfectly adequate for playing with just two or three players.

This is probably a long overdue review. This game has taken the most hours from my life outside of any non-steam games. This game is playable again and again. You can pick and choose your character, how you look, your stats, your beginning equipment and stats, the difficulty is completely changeable.
For difficulty you can decrease the dmg the ai do to you as well as switch out the number of combatants per side per battle- perfect for new players to get the hang of things. For my first 100 hours of this game I was mainly getting the combat and mechanics of the game down as well as figuring out the multiplayer. Singleplayer and multiplayer are great crossovers as you learn things from both sides of this game that affect the other sides. Now with well over 200 hours I am up for more of a challenge, with 60 combatants in a battle instead of the basic 30 (the basic is great for when one is just starting and especially when one is new to the game.)
I believe the replayability is most of what keeps me coming back time and time again to this awesome game. I only play the vanilla (in general) but I also play fire and sword and Napoleon. Of them all, warband is my favorite for single player. Napoleon is my favorite for multiplayer. However fire and sword has taught me more than a few lessons that carry into warband just as well as vice versa.
As you may have guessed I am not really a mod person. That said, there are some really awesome mods for this game (youtube has pretty good videos if your on the fence about the M&B series- I do not recommend getting the original M&B as warband is better, unless you get all the M&B in a bundle).
I first was drawn to this from my TW gaming. At the time I had played over 200+ hours of RTW, and I was eager to get into an actual unit, to fight the way the men i commanded fight. M&B Warband provided that experience for me.
I have played as every faction in the game and led my side to victory. Currently I am leading the Swadians to victory- but i have a plan to consolidate my position in the north of the map and then crush the Swadians through a rebellion, effectively making myself the ruler of all Calradia.
My point is this. This game allows you to fight using authentic weaponry, develop your own skills and preferences, develop your own way of fighting, use amazing (in both look and function) equipment, AND choose how YOU want to end the game (Glorified Vassal or Emperor). This game has amazing replayability. If your on the fence after reading all these reviews, look up some campaigns on youtube. That's what helped me decide.
